WHY THIS IS NOT A ONE-FILE CHANGE, which is the main thing a future session needs to know before starting: `src/codegen/mono.rs` emits its OWN monomorphized probe loops against the same three constants (its comment at the `BUCKET_*` consts says they 'must match the runtime's'), and `src/codegen/control_flow_for.rs` iterates occupied slots the same way. The status encoding is a codegen/runtime ABI with a pinned offsets test (`karac_map_field_offsets_match_codegen`). Changing it means changing lookup, find_insert_slot, insert, remove, resize and the iteration in BOTH places consistently; if they disagree the failure mode is a silent wrong answer (a lookup that misses a present key), not a crash. Suggested encoding, which keeps the sentinels distinguishable: EMPTY = 0, TOMBSTONE = 1, OCCUPIED = 0x80 | (hash7 & 0x7f) so any occupied byte is >= 0x80 and can never alias a sentinel.
investigation:
TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE ORIGINAL REPORT, both established by experiment rather than reasoning. Recording them in full because each one would otherwise be re-guessed by the next person.

CORRECTION 1 -- THE INDIRECT CALLS ARE NOT THE COST. The original entry named the erased runtime's per-probe indirect hash_fn/eq_fn calls as the prime suspect, by analogy with the ~2.3x qsort callback handicap #274 measured. That analogy is FALSE here. Control: KaracMap's exact probe re-implemented in Rust twice over the same 3,125-key data, once reaching hash/eq through stored fn pointers and once calling them directly, everything else identical -- 3.6ms +/- 0.3 vs 3.7ms +/- 0.2, a wash. An indirect call whose target is identical on every iteration predicts perfectly; qsort's callback is expensive because it blocks inlining of a comparison that would otherwise be two instructions, which is not the situation for a String hash. The FFI boundary still cost something -- removing it is worth the measured 1.13x in fix 2 -- but that is the opaque call and the out-param protocol, not the indirection.

CORRECTION 2 -- THE MAP IS NOT WHERE THE KATA DEFICIT LIVES. The original entry asserted that the 2.45x map microbenchmark ratio 'accounts for the whole #127 deficit'. That was an INFERENCE from a microbenchmark, never a measurement, and intervention refutes it: with BOTH fixes landed, #127 measures 265.3ms +/- 14.2 against the equal-hash Rust lane's 145.7 +/- 5.3 = 1.82x, against 287.5 vs 177.3 = 1.62x before (absolute times on this container are not stable across sessions -- an unmodified rust binary has measured 164.1ms and later 123.7ms on the same program -- so only the ratios travel). Improving the map twice moved the kata ratio not at all. Per-A/B on the kata itself: fix 1 gave 267.9 vs 269.8 (wash), fix 2 gave 260.1 vs 256.6 (wash). The reason is visible once looked for: ~20 of every 25 candidate lookups in #127 MISS, and a miss terminates at the first EMPTY bucket -- one status byte load, no eq call -- so the probe was never the hot part of that kata.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED AND SHOULD NOT BE RE-DERIVED:
* The mono approach is sound and its ceiling is parity. Map[i64,i64] lookup, which already takes the scalar mono path, measures 2.2ms +/- 0.2 against Rust's 2.1ms +/- 0.2 on the same shape -- 1.05x. That is the proof the probe design is not the limit.
* Map[String,i64] lookup after fix 2 is 3.5ms net vs Rust's 1.8ms -- still ~1.94x, so roughly 9ns per lookup is unaccounted for and is NOT in the probe loop. Prime remaining suspect is the CALL SITE rather than the map: each lookup materializes the key's {ptr,len,cap} aggregate into an alloca and hands over its address, then wraps the result in an Option through PHIs, where the Rust comparison passes an existing &String.
* Insert splits as: steady-state update 1.9x, growth 3.2x (before fix 1). Allocation counts are IDENTICAL between the two languages (191,288 vs 191,292 mallocs on the insert benchmark), so no extra key clone is happening -- it is pure per-operation compute.

NEXT STEP, and the methodological point: re-attribute the kata deficit BY INTERVENTION, not by microbenchmark. The remaining #127/#126 gap is spread across the per-candidate String lifecycle (build a 5-byte String, probe, free it) at roughly 4.25M candidates per run; the isolated String build already measures at parity with Rust (5.5ms vs 5.4ms over 104k builds), so the cost is in the surrounding lifecycle, not in push. Land one change at a time and measure the kata, because this entry is now a two-for-two record of isolated microbenchmarks predicting the wrong thing.

SESSION 2026-07-27 — NOT ADVANCED; RECORDING ONE NEGATIVE RESULT AND A HARD BLOCKER, so neither is re-derived.
BLOCKER (why the prescribed next step was not attempted): this entry's own methodological rule is 're-attribute the kata deficit BY INTERVENTION, not by microbenchmark ... land one change at a time and measure the kata'. That requires the kara-katas repo (the #127 bench plus its equal-hash Rust lanes) and hyperfine. NEITHER is present in the cloud container this session ran in (`../kara-katas` absent; `which hyperfine` empty). Doing microbenchmark-driven work here would repeat exactly the error this entry is already two-for-two on, so no speculative change was landed. Whoever picks this up needs a developer environment with the kata repo checked out.
NEGATIVE RESULT (cheap, and it retires the named suspect for these shapes): the entry's 'prime remaining suspect is the CALL SITE ... each lookup materializes the key's {ptr,len,cap} aggregate into an alloca and hands over its address, then wraps the result in an Option through PHIs'. The PRE-OPTIMIZATION IR does show exactly that — a `%map.get.key` alloca receiving a load-then-store copy out of the key's own slot, plus four `opt.*` PHIs feeding an `insertvalue` chain (`examples/dump_ir` on `fn probe(m: ref Map[String,i64], k: String) -> i64 { match m.get(k) { Some(v) => v, None => 0 } }`). But it does NOT survive the real pipeline: in the `karac build` binary the redundant copy is gone (SROA collapses the two allocas to one stack slot, whose address is `lea`'d straight into the call), the Option aggregate never materializes, and — because the runtime archive is built with `lto = "fat"` — the monomorphized probe from fix 2 (54aac61) is INLINED at link time: the emitted binary contains no `karac_map_str_i64_get` call symbol at all, only `map_new` / `map_insert_old` / `map_free_*`. So for this shape the call-site materialization, the Option PHIs, AND the residual FFI boundary are all already optimized away, and the ~9ns/lookup must be elsewhere. CAVEAT, stated because it matters: this was observed where the caller inlines the probe; a call site that does not inline was not measured, and none of this was measured on the kata itself — per the blocker above.
INCIDENTAL, worth knowing when benchmarking this: a naive 'N rounds x M lookups' Kara probe is NOT a valid harness — auto-par claims the lookup loop (the emitted binary calls `karac_par_reduce`), so any such timing must be taken with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` or it measures the scheduler.

SESSION 2026-07-27 (part 2) — kata repo obtained; ATTRIBUTION DONE ON THE KATA, as this entry demanded. No fix landed yet; what follows is measurement, and it REFRAMES the search a third time.
METHOD: `hyperfine` is still unavailable, so wall-clock is 5 interleaved reps per lane (medians) and the real attribution comes from valgrind callgrind/cachegrind, which are DETERMINISTIC and immune to this container's timing drift. Both lanes verified to print the same answer (755481159). Lanes: `word_ladder.kara` built by `karac build` vs `word_ladder_fasthash.rs` at `rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on` (equal hash, equal safety).
SAME-SESSION BASELINE: kara 313.7ms vs rust 149.2ms = 2.10x (min-based 2.12x). Recorded as the baseline for future interventions; do not compare it to the 1.82x in the section above — different session, and this entry already notes only ratios travel.
FINDING 1 — ALLOCATION IS NOT THE COST, NOW PROVEN ON THE KATA (previously only shown on the insert microbenchmark). Allocation COUNTS are essentially identical: 3,959,415 allocs / 3,959,415 frees (kara) vs 3,959,119 / 3,959,118 (rust) — 0.007% apart. Allocator INSTRUCTIONS are a dead wash too: summing every malloc.c/arena.c entry gives kara 567.1M Ir vs rust 574.6M Ir. So the per-candidate String lifecycle does not differ in allocator traffic; the 'build/probe/free 4.25M times' framing above is right that the lifecycle is the arena, but the free half is not where the time goes.
FINDING 2 — THE GAP IS ENTIRELY NON-ALLOCATION WORK. Total Ir: kara 2,360.7M vs rust 1,588.7M (1.49x). Net of the allocator: 1,793.6M vs 1,014.1M = 1.77x. That 1.77x is the whole deficit and it lives in emitted user/runtime code.
FINDING 3 — A NEW AXIS THIS ENTRY HAD NOT IDENTIFIED: instruction count does NOT explain the wall-clock. The 5.4x LL-ref figure is the standout — kara pushes 5x more traffic past L1. CONSEQUENCE FOR PLANNING: closing the instruction-count gap alone cannot reach parity; there is a data-locality component, and any candidate fix must be judged on D1/LL misses as well as Ir.
WHERE THE INSTRUCTIONS SIT: the emitted binary's hot code is one inlined blob — fat LTO folds the monomorphized map probe into the caller (no `karac_map_str_i64_get` call symbol survives, consistent with part 1's negative result), so callgrind attributes 50.6% to a single unnamed region and the rest to `main`. Function-level attribution therefore needs a build with symbols preserved / inlining restrained — that is the first concrete step for the next session, before any code change.
SUGGESTED NEXT STEP (unchanged in spirit, sharpened by the above): build the kata lane with debug symbols and reduced inlining to get per-function Ir, then attack whichever of {extra conditional branches (1.65x — bounds checks / Option tag tests / overflow checks), extra D refs (1.38x), poor locality (2.14x D1)} dominates. Measure each intervention on the kata with callgrind Ir + cachegrind D1, not wall-clock, so the result is not lost in container noise.

SESSION 2026-07-27 (part 3) — STEP 1 (per-function attribution) ATTEMPTED AND BLOCKED. Recording the negative result and the four things tried, so the next person does not repeat them.
GOAL: split the 1.77x non-alloc Ir gap across the kata's three per-candidate phases — `nth_letter` (an O(26) `.chars()` walk), `replace_char` (a `.chars()`+push String build) and `word_set.get(cand)` (the probe).
FAIRNESS CHECK FIRST (worth knowing): the Rust lane is a FAITHFUL mirror — its `nth_letter` does the same O(26) `alphabet.chars()` walk and its `replace_char` the same char-push loop. So the 2.10x is not a kata-authoring artifact; both languages do the same algorithmic work.
WHY ABLATION DOES NOT WORK HERE: the BFS is self-referential — the probe result decides whether a candidate is enqueued — so removing or stubbing any phase changes the traversal and therefore the amount of work measured. Ablation cannot isolate a phase on this kata.
WHAT WAS TRIED FOR SYMBOLS, ALL FOUR FAILED: (1) thin-LTO + debuginfo runtime archive (`CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=thin CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG=line-tables-only`, linked via `KARAC_RUNTIME=`) — does not help, because the probe is NOT a runtime symbol at all: `karac_map_str_i64_get` does not exist in the runtime archive (its exported map surface is `karac_map_get`/`_insert`/`_lookup_slot`/...). Fix 2's monomorphized probe is emitted by CODEGEN into the user module, so runtime LTO settings are irrelevant to it. (2) `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1` on `karac build` — the linked binary has ZERO `.debug_*` sections. (3) the same env var on the `compile_to_ir` path (examples/dump_ir) — the emitted IR contains no `llvm.dbg.cu` / `DICompileUnit` / `DISubprogram` either, so codegen is not emitting DWARF on these paths regardless of the gate (the gate additionally requires a `source_filename` to be threaded in — see `di_init`). CONCLUSION: there is currently NO end-to-end way to get per-function or per-line attribution out of an AOT kara binary. That is a compiler TOOLING gap, filed separately as B-2026-07-27-4, and it blocks this entry and any successor perf investigation. Closing it is the real Step 1: either make `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO` produce DWARF that survives to the linked binary, or add a profiling mode that gives emitted user functions external linkage + noinline. Until then the only usable signals on this bug are the WHOLE-PROGRAM aggregates recorded in part 2 (Ir, D refs, D1/LL misses, branches), which do narrow the search but cannot name a function.

BASELINE HERE IS 1.34x, NOT 2.10x: kara 141.6ms +/- 2.2 vs the equal-hash Rust lane 105.4ms +/- 3.2. Part 2 measured 2.10x on x86. Same sources, same equal-hash Rust twin, both built -O2/-O with overflow checks on. So a LARGE PART OF THIS DEFICIT IS ARCHITECTURE- OR TOOLCHAIN-DEPENDENT, and any future number must say which machine produced it. Sigma here is ~1.5% of the mean, so a 3% effect is detectable — this box is a usable measurement environment despite having no valgrind.
ATTRIBUTION BY INTERVENTION ON THE KATA — what this entry has demanded since part 2, and what no earlier session could do. Two cumulative variants, each still printing 755481159:

  A = nth_letter without its .chars() walk     128.1ms   1.21x   (-13.5ms, 9.5% of runtime)
  B = A + replace_char built over .bytes()     122.9ms   1.17x   (-5.2ms,  3.7% of runtime)

So THE TWO `.chars()` LOOPS ARE 18.7ms OF THE 36.2ms GAP — 52% of the deficit — and the residual after removing both is 1.17x. This finally puts a number on part 4's callgrind read (`neighbors` at 50.6%) and confirms it: the cost is candidate generation, not the map. Note the variants are DIAGNOSTIC instruments, not proposed kata edits — they are kept out of the kata repo deliberately, since the Rust lane does the same O(26) walk and changing only one side would break the comparison.
THE ASCII CONST-CHARS FAST PATH IS FIRING, so B-2026-07-27-7 works and is NOT the remaining problem: `nth_letter`'s emitted IR contains ZERO `karac_string_decode_char` calls. Its residual 9.5% is therefore the ITERATION COUNT, not per-char decoding — 26 iterations x 4.25M calls of a branch-free byte loop. Removing it needs the linear search over a CONSTANT string to collapse to a single indexed load, which LLVM does not do even given the stride-1 shape that module was written to expose.
WELL-POSED NEXT STEP, with its ceiling already measured: the remaining `.chars()` cost that a compiler change can actually reach is `replace_char`'s — a loop over a RUNTIME string (a `ref String` param), which cannot qualify for the const-literal proof. The shape to try is an ASCII FAST INNER LOOP WITH DYNAMIC BAILOUT: a stride-1 loop that runs while the current byte is < 0x80 and exits to the existing decoder on the first byte that is not. It needs NO compile-time proof (unlike ascii_const_chars) so it applies to every `.chars()` loop over a runtime string. Ceiling on THIS kata: 3.7%. Deliberately NOT attempted in this session — the failure mode of getting it wrong is a silent miscompile (binding each byte as a char, so `é` yields two bogus chars), the same class ascii_const_chars documents at length, and it wants a full verification budget rather than the tail of a long session.
TWO METHOD NOTES worth keeping. (1) f569aac's symbol retention WORKS ON macOS TOO, not just Linux: `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1 karac build` yields a binary whose symbol table contains `_neighbors` etc. (451 text symbols vs none by default), so per-function profiling is available here via `sample`. (2) RECONFIRMING THIS ENTRY'S OWN WARNING the hard way: a small driver written to call `nth_letter` in a loop compiled to a binary whose `main` calls `karac_par_reduce` — auto-par claimed the loop and the disassembly showed no `nth_letter` at all. Any probe harness here needs `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, or it measures the scheduler.

SESSION 2026-07-28 — RE-MEASURED ON x86 AFTER B-2026-07-27-7 / -8, AND RETITLED. Part 5 measured the intervention on arm64; this is the same kata on the x86 container every earlier part used, so the two architectures can finally be compared on the same code.
#127, callgrind Ir (deterministic; wall-clock on this container is not): kara 1,962.3M vs the equal-hash Rust lane 1,588.7M = 1.235x, against the part-2 baseline of 2,360.7M vs 1,588.7M = 1.45x. `neighbors` itself went 1,194.5M -> 796.9M Ir (-33%), and its share of the program 50.60% -> 40.61%. Both lanes still print 755481159.
#126 (Word Ladder II), same method: kara 2,268.6M vs rust 1,899.4M = 1.194x. Both lanes print 125559906.
ARCHITECTURE SPLIT, SHARPENED — and it CORRECTS a part-5 statement. Part 5 concluded that `nth_letter`'s residual 9.5% is iteration count because 'the linear search over a CONSTANT string [does not] collapse to a single indexed load, which LLVM does not do even given the stride-1 shape that module was written to expose'. That is true on arm64 but NOT on x86: an isolated equal-source `nth_letter` probe (4.25M calls) goes 699,426,390 -> 42,802,319 Ir with B-2026-07-27-7, which is EXACTLY the figure the already-branch-free `.bytes()` spelling of the same program produces, and the disassembly shows the walk gone — `movzbl (%r14,%rcx,1)`, a direct indexed load, with the outer loop unrolled 4x. So on x86 LLVM does collapse it once the offset PHI is removed; the arm64 backend apparently does not. Anyone chasing the 9.5% should measure their own architecture first rather than assume part 5's number.
DISPOSITION. Not closed, because the residual is real and unattributed. But the original claim this entry was opened on — that `Map[String, _]` is where the kata deficit lives — is now refuted by three independent measurements (CORRECTION 2's intervention A/B, part 4's callgrind attribution putting the probe primitives at ~13.7%, part 5's intervention), so the title now says what the entry is actually about. The ONE remaining fix that a compiler change can reach — the dynamic-bailout ASCII `.chars()` loop for RUNTIME strings, ceiling 3.7% on this kata — is split out as B-2026-07-28-2 so it can be picked up as a bounded piece of work instead of being buried at the end of a five-part investigation log. What stays here is the residual with no named cause: after both `.chars()` loops are removed the kata is still 1.17x (arm64), and part 2's cachegrind figures (D1 misses 2.14x, LL refs 5.40x) say part of that is data locality rather than instruction count.

title: Calling a closure bound as a `for`-loop element returns 0 under `karac build`/JIT (interp correct). `for op in ops { v = op(v); }` where `ops: Array/Vec[Fn(i64)->i64]` — the loop-var closure call yields 0; `let op = ops[0]; op(5)` and `ops[0](5)` both work.
detail: The codegen `for`-loop ELEMENT BINDING mishandles a closure-typed element: the loop variable `op` bound by `for op in ops` does not receive the correct closure value (`{fn_ptr, env}`), so a subsequent `op(v)` call returns 0 instead of invoking the closure. Silent — no crash, no diagnostic; `karac run --interp` is correct. The for-loop codegen (src/codegen/control_flow_for.rs, a large file with many element-type-specialized paths) almost certainly routes the Fn-typed element through a scalar/other path that loads the wrong width/pointer, or a fallback that leaves the loop var's closure fn_ptr null. NOT the closure representation itself: `let op = ops[0]` (index-element binding) + call works, and direct `ops[0](5)` / `ops[1](5)` work — only the for-loop element binding is wrong.
investigation: Probe round 13 batch 11 (HOF). Minimal: `fn main() { let ops = [|x| x + 1, |x| x * 10]; let mut v = 5; for op in ops { v = op(v); } println(f"{v}"); }` -> JIT prints 0, interp prints 60 (5->6->60). Localization: h4 `let op = ops[0]; op(5)` = 6 on both (OK); h2 `ops[0](5)`/`ops[1](5)` = 6/50 on both (OK); h5 same over `Vec[Fn]` = 0 (JIT)/60 (interp) — so NOT array-specific; h6 over an array of CAPTURING closures = 0 (JIT)/10100 (interp) — so NOT capture-specific; h3 single-element array in a for-loop = 0 (JIT)/105 (interp). Consistently: the `for`-loop element binding of a closure is the broken construct. Note batch 4's closure-in-Vec test passed because it applied the closures via an index/`.iter().map()` chain, not a bare `for op in ops` element binding.
resolution: ROOT CAUSE CORRECTION: the entry's hypothesis (a bad for-loop element binding) was WRONG. The emitted IR bound the loop var correctly — `%for.v.elem = load { ptr, ptr }` then `store { ptr, ptr } %for.v.elem, ptr %op` is the right closure fat pointer. The defect was in the CALL: `compile_call` routes an indirect closure call on `closure_fn_types.contains_key(name)`, and the for-loop element binding never registered the loop var there, so `op(v)` missed that dispatch and fell through to the unknown-callee path, which emits a constant `i64 0` (the body was literally `store i64 0, ptr %v`). `let op = ops[i]; op(v)` always worked because the `let` path has its own registration via `let_binding_fn_value_type` — which is precisely why the bug presented as for-loop-specific and looked like a binding bug. FIX (efc5d46, src/codegen/types_lowering.rs): register a `Fn(..) -> R` binding's env-first closure `FunctionType` in `register_var_from_type_expr`, the shared registrar every binding form routes through — one arm covers for-loop elements (incl. the `(k, v)` map-value pattern), function params, and synthesized temporaries. Dispatch metadata only: no slot/cleanup state changes and closure env ownership stays on `heap_env_closure_vars`. VERIFIED: 4-backend agreement (interp/JIT/AOT-O2/AOT-O0) on the array-literal repro (60), a `Vec[Fn]` built by push (57), a single-element array (105), CAPTURING closures (10100), and a String-returning closure applied through the loop binding (x-a-b); valgrind 0 errors on each. Suites green: codegen 2581 (2 new regression tests — an E2E over all five shapes and an IR guard asserting the body emits a real `closure_call` rather than a folded constant), par_codegen 200, memory_sanitizer 853, interpreter 1307, typechecker 2091, lib 990, selfhost_codegen oracle; clippy (both feature sets) + fmt clean.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara, Phase-12 port): a FIELD-receiver Vec method call — `self.<vec>.push(x)` / `self.<vec>.pop()` — was a NO-OP. push and pop resolved only an `Ident` receiver (`v.push`), so a struct-field receiver fell through with no slot and emitted nothing. A hard self-hosting blocker: the port builds EVERY table via `self.<field>.push` (152 sites) and manages its loop-label stacks via `self.loop_cont.push`/`self.loop_break.pop` (13 pop sites), so the emitter could not build its own state.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found by real-shape differential probing (impl-method / self-field sweep) vs the seed `karac run` oracle, after noticing my own Slice-57 pop handled only Ident/SelfVal receivers while the port's actual pops are `self.loop_cont.pop()` (a Field receiver). Quantified: 152 self-field push + 13 self-field pop across codegen.kara (locals/locals_kind/en_names/en_var_pl/loop_cont/…). FIX (Slice 59, b686bdb): both push and pop now resolve the receiver to a {ptr,len,cap} STORAGE POINTER for two shapes — an Ident local yields the %vN alloca; a Field (`self.f` / `local.f`, inner object Ident or SelfVal) GEPs the field via the Slice-27 `self.x = v` field-address pattern (getelementptr struct_ty, ptr self, i32 0, i32 fidx) and reads the field's declared kind. The existing kind-3/4/struct push and kind-3/4 pop bodies then run on (sp, vk) unchanged. NOTE: a sibling SEED double-free (returning a Vec[String] FIELD element by value, `fn top(ref self,i)->String { return self.stk[i] }`) surfaced during probing but is orthogonal — the port's push/pop path is valgrind-clean; corpus uses index-print, not element-return, to stay seed-comparable.
resolution: Fixed in Slice 59 (b686bdb): field-aware receiver resolution (Ident to alloca, Field to GEP) shared by push and pop. Selfhost oracle + valgrind green.

title: SEED codegen double-free: `return <struct>.<vecfield>[i];` — returning a heap (String) element of a STRUCT-FIELD Vec directly as a `return` STATEMENT expression — hands back the vec's OWN element buffer without materializing a copy, so the caller frees the returned String AND the vec's element drop frees the same block. Valgrind: Invalid free() of the same malloc'd block. The identical read as a TAIL EXPRESSION (no `return` keyword), or via a local binding, is CLEAN.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found by real-shape differential probing of the Phase-12 selfhost port (impl-method / self-field sweep) against the seed `karac run` oracle, while landing Slice 59 (field-receiver push/pop, B-2026-07-23-29). The PORT emits this shape correctly; the SEED crashes — so it is a seed bug, orthogonal to the port work, and is filed separately here rather than folded into -29. TRIGGER — all four required: (1) the Vec is a STRUCT FIELD (`s.xs`), not a plain local/param Vec; (2) its element type is HEAP (String) — Vec[i64] is clean; (3) the element read is the ENTIRE expression of an explicit `return` STATEMENT; (4) codegen (BOTH JIT `karac run` and AOT `karac build` abort with SIGABRT) — `--interp` is clean, so this is a run-vs-build divergence in the codegen ownership path. NOT `self`-specific: a free fn `fn get(s: ref S, i: i64) -> String { return s.xs[i]; }` crashes identically, so the discriminator is struct-FIELD-vec + direct return, not the receiver form. CLEAN CONTRASTS (each isolates one requirement): a TAIL expression `{ self.xs[i] }` with no `return` keyword; `let t = self.xs[i]; return t;`; `return self.xs[i] + "!";` (a consuming/concat context copies); `println(self.xs[i]);` inline; a Vec[i64] field element; and a non-field `fn get(v: ref Vec[String], i) -> String { return v[i]; }`. MECHANISM (hypothesis): the indexed read of a Vec[String] yields a BORROW of the element's {ptr,len} (the vec keeps ownership), and the return paths that ARE clean each force a materialize (deep copy) — the tail-expression path, the let-binding path, and the concat path all do. The `return`-statement path over a struct-field vec misses that materialize, so the borrowed {ptr,len} is returned as if owned: the caller's temp cleanup frees the buffer and the struct's Vec[String] element drop frees it again at scope exit. The tail-vs-return asymmetry on the SAME expression is the sharpest clue for the fix — the return-statement lowering should route a borrowed heap element through the same materialize the tail path uses.
resolution: The entry's own MECHANISM hypothesis was correct and its tail-vs-return asymmetry note was the key: the indexed read of a Vec[String] yields a BORROW of the element's {ptr,len,cap} and the clean shapes each force a materialize. Concretely, the TAIL path routes through `compile_tail_final_expr`, whose field-rooted index arm deep-clones (added for B-2026-07-11-35's return leg); the explicit-`return` arm (`ExprKind::Return` in src/codegen/exprs.rs) only reached that helper when the fn returned `Option[shared]` and otherwise fell straight to `compile_expr`, skipping the clone. FIX (42d8e96): extracted the gate as `compile_field_rooted_index_return` (src/codegen/stmts.rs) and called it from BOTH return spellings — the tail path keeps identical behaviour (same gate, now via the shared fn) and the explicit-return arm gains it. Sharing one gate is what prevents the two spellings diverging again. Stays narrow: FieldAccess-object element index only, range slices excluded (already fresh), and `clone_owned_vec_index_element` self-gates on a non-trivially-copyable element and on the read value's LLVM type, so a `Vec[i64]` field or a mis-typed monomorph read is a no-op. No double-clone risk: `maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg`'s gate requires an Identifier object, so it never fires on a field-rooted read. VERIFIED: 4-backend agreement (interp/JIT/AOT-O2/AOT-O0) on the method form, the free-fn `ref S` form (confirming it is not self-specific), and a `Vec[Vec[String]]` field; every clean contrast from this entry (tail, let-binding, concat, `Vec[i64]` field) stays clean; valgrind 0 errors on all shapes — no double-free AND no leak from an over-eager second clone. Tests: an E2E + an IR guard in tests/codegen.rs (the IR guard also pins that a Copy `Vec[i64]` field emits NO clone) and a looped ASAN/LSan regression in tests/memory_sanitizer.rs covering all four trigger conditions plus the contrasts. Suites green: codegen 2583, memory_sanitizer 854, par_codegen 200, interpreter 1307, typechecker 2091, lib 990, selfhost_codegen oracle; clippy (both feature sets) + fmt clean. UNRELATED OBSERVATION (not filed, pre-existing and LOUD): a nested field-rooted read `s.g[0][0]` still bails with the actionable v1 diagnostic 'nested indexed read requires the outer container to be a named variable' — a documented codegen limitation, not a silent miscompile, and disjoint from this fix.

title: Struct-FIELD `Map[_, Vec[String]]` leaks the inner Vec's element buffers at drop. A struct whose field is a Map with a HEAP VALUE (`Map[i64, Vec[String]]` / `Map[String, Vec[String]]`) frees the map and the value Vec headers at scope exit but never the per-element String buffers inside those Vecs. Valgrind: 'definitely lost'. A LOCAL map of the same type is CLEAN, and a struct-field map with a SCALAR value is CLEAN — the leak needs the field + heap-value combination.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while verifying B-2026-07-25-4 (lazy keys()/values()/entries() routing) — valgrind on a heap-map shape sweep showed a residual 'definitely lost', and a stash-and-rebuild baseline proved it BYTE-IDENTICAL without that change, i.e. pre-existing and orthogonal. Filed rather than routed around. TRIGGER (isolated by three-way contrast, all built with `karac build`): LEAKS — `struct H { m: Map[i64, Vec[String]] }` with one entry whose Vec holds one String; CLEAN — the same `Map[String, Vec[String]]` as a LOCAL binding (no struct field); CLEAN — `struct H { m: Map[String, i64] }` (struct field, SCALAR value). So neither the field alone nor the heap value alone is sufficient: the drop path for a struct FIELD map recurses one level too few, freeing the map and the value Vec's `{ptr,len,cap}` but not walking that Vec's elements. The key half is irrelevant (a String key leaks the same 1 byte, no more). Magnitude scales with the number of elements across all value Vecs, so a real workload (an adjacency map, a multimap index) leaks proportionally, not by a constant.
resolution: The FIX DIRECTION recorded on this entry was right, and the mechanism is now pinned exactly. The LOCAL-binding path routes through `emit_free_one_map_handle`, which prefers `karac_map_free_with_val_drop_fn` whenever `map_val_drop_fn_for_type_expr` yields a per-VALUE drop fn (a value owning heap BELOW its header). The struct-drop `MapOrSet` arm (src/codegen/synth_drop.rs) hand-rolled its own shared-half rc_dec walks plus a flag-only `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec` call and never reached that branch — which is precisely why a LOCAL map of the same type was clean and only the struct FIELD leaked, and why a SCALAR value was clean (the flag free is exact there). FIX (44b606e): that arm now takes the field value's per-VALUE drop fn and, when present, calls `karac_map_free_with_val_drop_fn` (key side still on the flag contract). Kept surgical rather than swapping the arm for `emit_free_one_map_handle` wholesale: `map_val_drop_fn_for_type_expr` returns None for a shared value (the pre-existing rc_dec walk owns that side) and for an exact one-level overlay, so the new route fires ONLY where the flag free was already incomplete — it can remove a leak but cannot introduce a double free. SCOPE IS WIDER THAN THIS ENTRY'S TITLE: the same arm also under-freed any other heap-below-header value, so `Map[_, Map[_, String]]`, `Map[K, <struct with heap fields>]` and `Map[_, Option[String]]` struct fields were affected too and are fixed by the same change. VERIFIED by emitted-call inspection that the split lands where intended: `Map[_, Vec[String]]` / `Map[String, Vec[String]]` / `Map[_, Map[_, String]]` now emit `karac_map_free_with_val_drop_fn`, while `Map[String, String]`, `Set[String]`, `Map[_, Vec[i64]]` and `Map[i64, i64]` still emit `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec` — unchanged. Valgrind 0 errors on an 8-shape struct-field matrix at O2 AND O0 with 3-backend output agreement, and 0 errors on the newly-activated `Map[i64, Holder]` / `Map[_, Option[String]]` shapes (the double-free direction). The new ASAN/LSan regression (`asan_struct_field_map_heap_value_drop_no_leak`, covering both the leaking pair and every must-stay-on-the-flag-path contrast) was confirmed to FAIL with the source fix reverted and pass with it. Suites: memory_sanitizer 855, codegen 2586, par_codegen 200, interpreter 1307, typechecker 2091, cli 532, lib 990, selfhost_codegen oracle; clippy (both feature sets) + fmt clean. NOT DONE (arm64): x86 only in this container — the CI `memory-sanitizer-arm64` job is the standing gate for that leg.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara, Phase-12 port): a BOOL-valued `if` or `match` in VALUE position emitted INVALID IR. Both route branch/arm tails through an i64 result slot, but a bool branch yields an i1, so the emitter wrote `store i64 false` (an i1 constant into an i64 store) and the module failed LLVM verification. 8 such sites in the real lexer.kara alone.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by feeding REAL self-host modules through the port end-to-end (the natural next step after Slice 59 closed the last structural gap) rather than by synthetic probing — the port emitted 43/43 functions for lexer.kara but the IR would not verify. Numbered -3 (concurrent sessions hold -1, my own seed double-free, and -2, a Map field leak). REPRESENTATIVE SITE: `fn match_char(mut ref self, expected: u8) -> bool { if self.current >= self.bytes.len() { false } else if ... { false } else { ...; true } }` — the value-if allocates an i64 result slot and stores the i1 `false` into it. FIX (Slice 60, 6740872): rather than restructure emission order (the result-slot alloca is emitted BEFORE the branches, so it cannot see their kind), reuse the established Vec[bool] i64-LANE convention from B-2026-07-23-24: `to_i64_lane` zext's an i1 branch/arm value on store, and at the join the lane is trunc'd back to i1 (returning kind 1) whenever any branch/arm was bool — so the value re-enters bool contexts (`if` / `and` / `not` / a `-> bool` return) correctly. Both branches/arms of a well-typed value-if/match share a type, so the then-branch kind (value-if) or an any-arm-was-bool flag (match) decides the result. Applied to THREE sites: the value-if path and BOTH match paths (enum-variant and int-literal). MILESTONE: with this, lexer.kara (1611 lines, 43 fns) emits FULLY VALID IR through the Kara-written emitter — the first complete self-host module to do so. STILL OPEN (pre-existing, verified against the pre-change baseline so they are NOT regressions of this fix): (a) a STRING/aggregate-valued value-match still stores a {ptr,i64} into the i64 result slot — the same slot-typing limitation one level up, needing a real typed/aggregate result slot; (b) `match <String-scrutinee> { _ => ... }` yields the wrong arm value even for an i64 result; (c) ast.kara emits all 3 fns but its IR fails with 'expected integer' on an extractvalue over a large nested aggregate.

LEDGER CORRECTION (2026-07-29): the `fix` field read `6740872`, which is not a commit on main — a pre-rebase SHA recorded before the branch was replayed onto main, a hazard of this repo's concurrent-session workflow. The actual fix is 14a65d4, whose commit message names this bug. Corrected so the pointer resolves.
resolution: Fixed in Slice 60 (6740872): i64-lane widen on store + trunc-to-i1 at the join, applied to the value-if path and both match paths. Selfhost oracle + valgrind green; lexer.kara now emits valid IR.

title: No working per-function / per-line PROFILING attribution for an AOT kara binary. Emitted user functions carry internal linkage and never reach the symbol table (at any `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL`), and `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1` produces no DWARF in either the emitted IR or the linked binary — so callgrind/perf can only report whole-program aggregates or one unnamed blob. This blocks every codegen perf investigation that needs to know WHICH construct costs.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: hit head-on while doing B-2026-07-26-2's prescribed Step 1 (attribute the #127 Word Ladder deficit per function). EVIDENCE, four independent attempts: (1) `nm -a --defined-only` on a `karac build` binary lists no user function — all 228 text symbols are Rust runtime internals; the kata's `neighbors`/`replace_char`/`nth_letter` are absent. (2) Same at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=1`, so this is internal linkage / symtab omission, not just inlining. (3) `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1 karac build` yields a binary with ZERO `.debug_*` sections (`readelf -S | grep -c debug_` = 0). (4) `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1` on the `compile_to_ir` path emits no `llvm.dbg.cu` / `DICompileUnit` / `DISubprogram` in the IR at all — note `di_init` also requires a `source_filename` to be threaded in, which not every path does. CONSEQUENCE: callgrind attributes ~50% of the #127 binary to a single unnamed region and the rest to `main`; cachegrind gives only whole-program totals. Whole-program aggregates still work and are genuinely useful (they proved allocation is not the cost and surfaced a 5.4x LL-ref gap), but no measurement can currently say WHICH emitted construct is responsible, so no perf fix can be targeted or verified at function granularity. NOT a correctness bug — filed as tooling because it gates the whole perf-investigation class.
investigation:
# all four reproduce on a plain `karac build` of any program:
nm -a --defined-only <binary> | awk '$2=="t"||$2=="T"'      # no user fns
KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=1 karac build prog.kara && nm -a ...          # still none
KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1 karac build prog.kara && readelf -S <bin> | grep -c debug_   # 0
KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1 cargo run --features llvm --example dump_ir -- prog.kara | grep -c llvm.dbg.cu  # 0
// FIX DIRECTIONS (either suffices): (a) make the existing `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO` / `force_debug_info` DWARF path actually thread a source filename and survive the link, giving per-LINE attribution of the .kara source — the most useful outcome; or (b) add a profiling build mode that emits user functions with external linkage + `noinline`, giving per-FUNCTION attribution. (a) is strictly better for perf work and reuses machinery that already exists in src/codegen/debug_info.rs.
resolution: ROOT CAUSE was NOT the debug-info machinery — that works and has a passing IR test. `link_executable_impl` (src/codegen/driver.rs) runs `strip -x` on every linked executable as a binary-size measure, and `strip -x` discards ALL non-global symbols. Codegen gives user functions INTERNAL linkage, so the strip erased exactly those — and the `.debug_*` sections with them. That single cause explains all four failed approaches recorded above (thin-LTO runtime archive, the env gate, the compile_to_ir path, -O1). FIX (f569aac): skip the strip when `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO` is set, reusing the shape of the pre-existing SANITIZER carve-out sitting immediately above it — which exists for the identical reason (sanitizers walk local symbol tables to symbolicate). A build that asked for symbolic information keeps its symbol table. Chose the strip-skip over threading a flag through the link signature so the check sits next to the strip it guards. DEFAULT PATH UNTOUCHED and verified: gate-off still gives 0 local symbols, 0 debug sections and the same binary size; gate-on gives 7 `.debug_*` sections plus a live symbol table — the binary-size floor the strip protects is intact for ordinary builds. PAYOFF (measured on the #127 kata that motivated this): callgrind now reports `./word_ladder.kara:neighbors` 50.60%, `karac_hash_String` 8.99%, `karac_eq_String` 4.68%, `karac_free_buf` 2.57%, `./word_ladder.kara:main` 2.11% — named functions resolved against the .kara source, where the same run previously produced one unnamed region. The DWARF line table is present and correct (`objdump --dwarf=decodedline` shows word_ladder.kara:47/49/52 mapped to addresses). TEST: `tests/cli.rs::test_build_debug_info_keeps_symbols_and_dwarf` asserts BOTH directions (default stays stripped; gate-on keeps symbols + DWARF), confirmed RED with the fix reverted. Suites green: cli 533, codegen 2586, memory_sanitizer 855, par_codegen 200, interpreter 1307, typechecker 2091, lib 990; clippy (both feature sets) + fmt clean. KNOWN REMAINING GAP (does not block per-FUNCTION attribution, which was the point): callgrind's per-LINE auto-annotation warns 'information recorded about lines past the end of word_ladder.kara' — spliced stdlib / synthetic code is stamped with line numbers in the USER's DIFile instead of its own file or line 0, so ~8% of Ir lands on unidentified lines. Per-line accuracy is a separate follow-up slice; per-function is correct today.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara, Phase-12 port): value-position `if` and `match` used a HARDCODED `alloca i64` result slot, so a STRING / struct / enum-valued if-or-match stored a `{ ptr, i64 }` (or wider) aggregate into an i64 slot — invalid IR — and the join returned `kind: 0`, LOSING the result type so any downstream field access resolved against the wrong layout.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by feeding real self-host modules through the port (the ast.kara capstone) plus targeted probing; a struct-valued `match e { A(n) => clone_p(n), ... }` reproduced it minimally. IN-SURFACE and heavily used: 66 `= match` sites across the port, 54 in parser.kara alone, and `ast.kara`'s `expr_span` returns a `Span` STRUCT from a 30-arm match. Numbered -5 (concurrent sessions hold -1..-4). FIX (Slice 61, 999cd9c): the result-slot alloca is emitted BEFORE the branches and therefore cannot see their kind, so it is now DEFERRED — the branch/arm IR is buffered into a fresh `self.body` and the correctly typed `alloca` (plus a zero-init for match) is spliced in front once a branch/arm kind is known. Cheap because `self.body` is reset per FUNCTION, bounding the clone to one function's IR. The join then loads at that type and propagates BOTH the kind and the ownership (heap) flag — so a match with two `.to_string()` arms yields a properly OWNED String rather than a borrowed one, keeping frees balanced. A BOOL result deliberately keeps the i64 lane and narrows at the join (the Slice-60 / Vec[bool] convention). Applied to three sites: the value-if path and both match paths (enum-variant and int-literal). Verified no regression: lexer.kara still emits fully valid IR.

LEDGER CORRECTION (2026-07-29): the `fix` field read `999cd9c`, which is not a commit on main — a pre-rebase SHA recorded before the branch was replayed onto main, a hazard of this repo's concurrent-session workflow. The actual fix is 304e86c, whose commit message names this bug. Corrected so the pointer resolves.
resolution: Fixed in Slice 61 (999cd9c): deferred, correctly typed result slot spliced in front of the buffered branch IR; kind and heap flag propagated at the join. Selfhost oracle + valgrind green.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara, Phase-12 port): a heap-bearing payload inside a `shared enum` could not always be released. Closed across slices 63/65/67 and 2026-07-28; the last blocker was NOT the shape this entry named but a LAYOUT CAP — a by-value enum carried exactly two aggregate payload slots, and ast.kara's `Stmt` needs three, its `Item` ten.
detail: ROOT CAUSE CORRECTED 2026-07-27 (supersedes this entry's original diagnosis — see CORRECTION below). The emitter treats EVERY enum as by-value and packs aggregate payloads into exactly two slots (`en_extra` = slot 3, `en_extra2` = slot 4). A third distinct aggregate payload type has nowhere to live. VERIFIED: the port's PARSER does record shared-ness (`parse_shared_or_par` threads `is_shared` into `parse_enum_def`/`parse_struct_def`), but codegen.kara never reads it — grepping `shared|retain|release|rc_` in codegen.kara yields only unrelated comments, and the enum-registration loop that fills en_extra/en_extra2 inspects payload KINDS only. So shared-ness is parsed and then dropped on the floor. CORRECTION — the original entry prescribed 'a union-style payload area (max-size aggregate region + per-variant offsets)' to replace the two slots. That is the WRONG DIRECTION and would be substantial wasted work: `Expr` is declared `pub shared enum`, i.e. an RC REFERENCE type, so its correct representation is a POINTER-width handle with each variant's node heap-allocated — not a flat inline aggregate of any width. ast.kara's own header comment states the intent explicitly: 'shared enum Expr IS the recursive node ... every child edge is a field of type Expr, an RC handle = a POINTER, so node structs embed only scalars / String / Expr pointers / Span'. Under a pointer representation the '~30 distinct payload types' problem DISAPPEARS — each variant's node is allocated separately and the handle is one word — so the two-slot capacity limit is a SYMPTOM of the missing `shared` support, not the defect to fix. SCOPE of the real fix (a dedicated architectural slice): give `shared enum`/`shared struct` a pointer kind; construction allocates a per-variant node (tag + that variant's payload) and yields the handle; match loads the tag through the pointer and projects the payload; field access, drops/RC (retain/release or at minimum a correct free), and materialize/copy paths all follow the handle. PARTIAL FIX ALREADY LANDED (ae2b9d8): the SENTINEL LEAK half is closed — `en_agg_slot` now REFUSES with an actionable panic naming this limitation instead of returning -1 for its two callers to interpolate into `extractvalue`/`insertvalue` (which produced literal `extractvalue <ty> %x, -1` and a bare LLVM 'expected integer'). Safe by construction: the -1 path could never produce runnable IR. Verified ast.kara now stops with the clear message while lexer.kara (43 fns), span and token still emit fully valid IR. NOTE on that message: it is a string LITERAL because the seed's `panic` only propagates literals (a computed message degrades to 'explicit panic'). PROGRESS 2026-07-27 (Slice 63, 3e173b6): the REPRESENTATION half is done — a `shared enum` is now an RC pointer handle to a per-variant heap node `{ i64 rc, i64 tag, <payload> }`, with construction, tag-load-through-handle matching, payload binding, and a recursive per-enum `@sh_release_<ei>` RC drop. `ty_text` of a shared kind stops at `ptr`, so a self-referential payload is one word and RECURSION now works (verified: a 3-deep chain, leak-clean under valgrind). The old `en_agg_slot` two-slot sentinel no longer fires for shared enums, because a shared enum allocates no by-value aggregate slots at all — confirming the sentinel was a SYMPTOM, as this entry was corrected to say in 6803acc. STILL OPEN: STRUCT payloads, which is `ast.Expr`'s actual shape (every variant wraps a node struct such as IntLit/BinaryExpr). Slice 63 refuses those LOUDLY with an actionable message rather than mis-emitting. That is the remaining work to unblock ast.kara, and with it typechecker/resolver/ast_render. PROGRESS 2026-07-27 (Slice 65, 5341bc64): STRUCT payloads now work. The blocker turned out NOT to be layout but REGISTRATION: `collect_sigs` resolved struct field types and enum payload types to kinds in ONE pass, and `kind_of_ty` returns 0 (i64!) for a name it cannot find. A shared enum and its payload structs are MUTUALLY recursive, so whichever came second in the source resolved and the first did not -- structs-then-enum silently typed every `Expr` field as i64, enum-then-structs silently typed every payload as i64, and NO declaration order worked. A new Pass A0 collects struct/enum NAMES (and `en_shared`, which `ty_text` needs to render a handle as `ptr`) before any kind is resolved, making the i64 fallback unreachable by a forward reference; both orders are pinned in the corpus. With that, `sh_payload_ok` admits a struct whose fields are all releasable (`sh_struct_ok`), and `sh_struct_release_text` emits the release -- construction and match-projection needed no new code, both were already generic in `ty_text(payload_kind)`. FOUR OWNERSHIP DEFECTS fixed on the way, three predating this slice: (a) `emit_materialize_enum` read the by-value layout for a shared enum, emitting `extractvalue ptr %h, 0` -- invalid IR; owning a second reference is a RETAIN, so `sh_emit_retain` was added; (b) `en_has_heap` called a shared enum heap-free when no variant carried a String, so a struct field of that type was judged POD and its handle never released (subtree leak) -- a shared enum ALWAYS owns its node; (c) `emit_free_struct_val` dropped a shared field through `emit_free_enum_val`, reading the handle POINTER as a by-value aggregate; (d) construction stored a BORROWED handle without retaining, so the node and the source local each believed they owned the single reference and both released it. NOTE on (d), because it governs how this area must be tested: the identical IR aborted with SIGTRAP on some runs and exited 0 on others, so a single green run is NOT evidence -- the fix was confirmed with 25 consecutive runs per RC-heavy program. VERIFICATION METHOD, reusable: the port's oracle cannot execute on macOS because the emitter hardcodes an x86-64 Linux triple and the glibc `@stdout` (the JIT fails `Symbols not found: [ _stdout ]`); rewriting ONLY the module header -- drop datalayout/triple, map `@stdout` to Apple's `__stdoutp`, leave every function body as emitted -- restores it. All 183 corpus programs (179 pre-existing + 4 new) match the seed over 3 full runs; the same 179 also pass on the parent commit, so the slice is additive. STILL OPEN: a Vec field inside a struct payload (elements may be handles needing per-element release) and a heap-bearing by-value enum field -- both REFUSED loudly by name. `ast.Expr` needs the Vec case (`CallExpr.args`), so that is the next slice. PROGRESS 2026-07-28 (Slice 67, 117a847): VEC PAYLOADS DONE — the shape this entry named as the next slice (`ast.Expr`'s `CallExpr.args: Vec[Expr]`). Implementing it surfaced TWO defects one level further out, both emitting SILENTLY, which is the class this port keeps finding: (1) a `Vec[<shared enum>]` LOCAL freed each element through the BY-VALUE enum free, emitting `extractvalue ptr %el, 0` — IR LLVM rejects outright ('extractvalue operand must be aggregate type'); an element is an RC HANDLE, so dropping the vec RELEASES each one. Exactly Slice 65's defect (c), one level out. (2) the element STRIDE: `en_has_heap` is true for every shared enum, so the 16/32 ladder sized a handle at 32 while `ty_text` renders it `ptr` (8) and element access GEPs at 8 — `emit_materialize_vec` would `malloc`/`memcpy` `len*32` out of a `len*8` buffer (a heap OVER-READ) and scatter the copies at stride-8 offsets in the oversized destination. Three sites open-coded that ladder; they now share a single `en_stride`, which additionally fixes `st_stride` silently UNDER-counting an aggregate-slot enum field at 32 when `ty_text` renders 32 + the slot strides (an under-count makes elements overlap, the worse direction). The named slice itself: `sh_struct_release_text` never set `deep` for ANY Vec kind, so a Vec field inside a shared node was skipped entirely and its buffer plus every element handle leaked with no diagnostic. `sh_vec_ok` / `sh_vec_release_text` now admit and release Vec[i64] / Vec[String] / Vec[<struct>] / Vec[<shared enum>]. REFUSAL HOLE CLOSED, and it is worth stating on its own because it made the leak invisible: the `sh_payload_ok` check lived ONLY at the CONSTRUCTION site, but a release arm is emitted for every DECLARED variant. A variant declared and never constructed therefore slipped past the refusal and emitted a release that silently skipped whatever it could not handle. `sh_emit_release_fn` now refuses there too — the emitter's last chance to notice. That shape is pinned in the corpus. VERIFIED: the 183-program corpus still matches the seed, plus 4 new programs pinning these shapes; each is valgrind-clean at 0 bytes in use at exit, and each survives 25 consecutive runs with no divergence — the bar B-2026-07-27-15 set when identical IR exited 0 on some runs and aborted on others. STILL OPEN, and ast.kara is NOT yet unblocked: it now stops on the NEXT limitation — a heap-bearing BY-VALUE enum field in a payload struct. ast.kara has 36 such fields. Two sub-cases, confirmed by isolated probe: `Option[String]` (kind 1001) is REFUSED loudly, correct behaviour pending implementation; `Option[<shared enum>]` is NOT refused because `kind_of_ty` only special-cases an `Option` whose generic is String and otherwise collapses to `Option[i64]` (kind 1000) — the handle is stored as a raw i64 payload, judged POD, and never released. That one emits INVALID IR (`insertvalue { i64, { i64, i64 } } %t5, { i64, i64 } 0, 1` — 'integer constant must have integer type'), so it fails at LLVM parse rather than miscompiling silently. It is split out as B-2026-07-28-5 because it is a REPRESENTATION change (an `Option[shared]` kind), not more release plumbing. Both must land before ast.kara emits, and with it typechecker/resolver/ast_render. PROGRESS 2026-07-28 (84253a7): `Option[String]` payload fields DONE — the shape this entry named as its remaining sub-case, and 17 of ast.kara's Option fields. TITLE CORRECTED IN THIS EDIT, because it had gone stale enough to mislead: it read '`shared enum` / `shared struct` are NOT IMPLEMENTED — the emitter has no concept of `shared`', which was true when filed but has been contradicted by this entry's own detail for several slices (Slices 63/65/67 built `en_is_shared`, `sh_node_ty`, `@sh_release_<ei>`, the Vec payload machinery). Anyone reading only the title would have estimated a rewrite; the actual remaining work is one release shape. MECHANISM of this slice: a heap-bearing BY-VALUE enum field is an AGGREGATE `{ tag, i64, { ptr, i64 } }` whose String buffer is live exactly when the tag says so — structurally different from the `Option[<shared enum>]` field closed as B-2026-07-28-5, which is a one-word HANDLE. `@sh_release_<ei>` would be both the wrong function and the wrong argument type for it, so the old refusal was correct rather than conservative. `sh_byval_enum_release_text` emits one compare-and-branch per String-payload variant. Worth noting WHY it is expressible now: the entry previously recorded that 'the text-returning release path cannot currently emit a tag-conditional free', and that stopped being true in Slice 67 when `sh_vec_release_text` became `mut ref self` and started minting labels off the shared `nlbl` counter. WHAT REMAINS, now NAMED rather than guessed: ast.kara's Option fields are `Option[String]` x17 (this slice), `Option[Expr]` / `Option[Pattern]` / `Option[TypeExpr]` / `Option[Block]` x19 (shared enums — B-2026-07-28-5), and `Option[GenericParamsNode]` x7 — a plain STRUCT payload, i.e. an AGGREGATE-slot enum (`en_extra >= 0`), which `sh_byval_enum_ok` still refuses because those slots hold structs and Vecs needing the recursive walk inside the tag branch. One shape, and it is the last Option shape ast.kara uses. VERIFIED: the 187-program differential corpus matches the seed; the new corpus program exercises BOTH arms (a `Some` that frees and a `None` that must not — the latter is the one worth pinning, since getting it wrong frees an uninitialised slot rather than leaking), is valgrind-clean at 0 bytes in use at exit, and survives 25 consecutive runs.
resolution:
FIXED 2026-07-28 (dd14643). THE ENTRY NAMED THE WRONG LAST SHAPE, and correcting that is most of the value here. It recorded `Option[GenericParamsNode]` x7 as the one thing left, described as 'an AGGREGATE-slot enum (en_extra >= 0) which sh_byval_enum_ok still refuses'. Feeding ast.kara to the port disagrees on both counts: the emitter stopped on `Block.stmts: Vec[Stmt]`, and `Option[<plain struct>]` is not an aggregate-slot enum at all — `kind_of_ty` collapses it to `Option$i`, the two-word POD layout, so it is never seen by `sh_byval_enum_ok` and instead fails at LLVM parse on CONSTRUCTION. That shape is split out as B-2026-07-28-14, matching how B-2026-07-28-5 was split for the same reason (a representation change, not release plumbing).

WHAT ACTUALLY BLOCKED IT was a layout CAP the entry treated as already-diagnosed: `en_extra`/`en_extra2` gave a by-value enum exactly TWO aggregate payload slots and refused a third. ast.kara's `Stmt` has three distinct struct payloads and its `Item` has ten. The cap and the Vec refusal are COUPLED — a release arm is emitted for every declared variant, so admitting `Vec[Stmt]` without lifting the cap would have emitted a release that silently skipped the unslotted variant, which is the exact failure mode Slice 67 closed at `sh_emit_release_fn`.

THE FIX, four parts: (1) the two fields become a flat per-enum run (`en_agg` + off/cnt) so the j-th DISTINCT aggregate payload type takes slot 3+j with no cap; `en_agg_slot`'s user-facing refusal becomes an internal-consistency panic, and every consumer (`ty_text`, `en_stride`, `en_has_heap`, the materialize and free paths) loops over the run. Enums that already fit two slots lay out byte-identically, which is why the pre-existing corpus was unaffected. (2) `sh_byval_enum_ok` admits an aggregate-slot enum whose payloads are themselves releasable. (3) `sh_byval_enum_release_text` grows an aggregate leg beside its String leg, recursing through `sh_struct_release_text` / `sh_vec_release_text`. (4) `sh_vec_ok` / `sh_vec_release_text` admit `Vec[<heap-bearing by-value enum>]`. Also removed `emit_enum_extratag_test`, dead since it was written.

A SECOND DEFECT surfaced on the way and it was SILENT, which is the class this port keeps producing. A String reaches slot 2 from EITHER position of a two-payload variant (Slice 35 routes by KIND, not by index), but the release keyed off `en_var_pl` alone. So `V(i64, String)` inside a shared node emitted valid IR, printed the right answer, exited 0, and leaked the buffer — measured at 5 bytes definitely lost under valgrind on the new corpus entry, 0 after. Both the admission gate and the release now consult both payload positions.

VERIFIED: the 190-program differential corpus matches the seed. Three new entries pin three aggregate slots, `Vec[<by-value enum>]` with a variant DECLARED-but-never-constructed, and the two-payload leak; each emits IR `llvm-as` accepts, matches the seed's stdout, is valgrind-clean at 0 errors and 0 bytes lost, and survives 25 consecutive runs (the B-2026-07-27-15 bar). Two of the three panicked on the parent commit and the third leaked there, so all three are real regression tests. NOTE the ASAN leg of scripts/selfhost-memcheck.sh could not run in this container (no libclang_rt.asan); valgrind memcheck covers the same use-after-free / double-free ground and is the stronger leak tool, so the verdicts above are valgrind's.

SCOPE OF 'UNBLOCKED', stated precisely because the entry's own wording invites over-reading. ast.kara now emits IR that `llvm-as` accepts, and so do the other five modules (parser, typechecker, resolver, ast_render, codegen) — none of them reach a refusal any more. But five of the six emit INVALID IR, and the cause is not this bug: the emitter has no IMPORT resolution, so every type a module imports hits `kind_of_ty`'s i64 fallback SILENTLY. `@u_clone_span` in the emitted ast.kara is `(i64) -> i64` though `Span` is a four-field struct. That is filed as B-2026-07-28-15 and is now the real gate on module-level self-hosting. A cost note on this fix: a slot per distinct payload type is space, not a union, so an `Item` value is wide; correct and uncapped, with a union-with-offsets layout as the follow-up if the width ever bites.

title: `for ch in <str>.chars()` over a COMPILE-TIME-CONSTANT string runs ~21.7x the instructions of the identical Rust source, because the ASCII/multibyte branch leaves a phi on the byte offset that stops LLVM reducing the walk to an indexed read. Measured on the #127 kata's `nth_letter` shape: kara 699.4M Ir vs rust 32.3M Ir for 4.25M calls, byte-identical output. This is the dominant remaining component of B-2026-07-26-2.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found by per-function profiling of the #127 Word Ladder kata, newly possible after B-2026-07-27-4 unblocked symbols/DWARF. That profile put `./word_ladder.kara:neighbors` at 50.60% of program Ir, and `nth_letter` — an O(26) `alphabet.chars()` walk called once per candidate, ~4.25M times per run — is inlined into it. ISOLATED MEASUREMENT (equal source, equal safety: `rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on`): 4.25M `nth_letter` calls, kara 699,424,636 Ir vs rust 32,250,118 Ir = 21.7x, both printing 465374916. Per call that is ~165 Ir (kara, actually walking ~13 chars at ~12 Ir each) vs ~7.6 Ir (rust, walk eliminated). NOT the causes already ruled out: the emitted string literal IS `internal constant` (LLVM may fold loads from it), and the opaque `karac_string_decode_char` call is ALREADY gone from the optimized binary — the ASCII fast path plus LLVM's DCE removes it, so the previously-suspected opaque-call blocker is disproven. MECHANISM (best current reading): kara's loop advances the byte offset by a PHI — 1 on the ASCII arm, the decoder's return on the multibyte arm — so even after the multibyte arm dies, LLVM does not recover the fact that `offset == iteration index` with stride 1, and cannot reduce the walk to `data[target]` the way it does for Rust's fully-inlined `.chars()`. The per-iteration cost (~12 Ir) is itself reasonable; the whole gap is that Rust ELIMINATES the loop and kara executes it. NOT the String build: this entry's sibling measurement already found `replace_char` (a `.chars()`+push build) at parity with Rust (5.5ms vs 5.4ms over 104k builds), and the push lowering has an ASCII fast path with amortized doubling — so `push` needs no work; the walk is the target.
resolution: FIXED by emitting a BRANCH-FREE STRIDE-1 chars loop when the iterated string is a proven compile-time all-ASCII constant. New `src/codegen/ascii_const_chars.rs` decides the NAMES that qualify per block: bound exactly once by `let NAME[: String] = "<all-ascii literal>"`, never an assignment-target root, never a mutating-method receiver, never the root of a `mut`-marked call argument (the three complete mutation channels — Kara has no free-standing borrow expression, so a callee can only write through `mut ref`, which requires the call-site `mut` marker). `compile_block` registers each qualifying name against THE ALLOCA ITS `let` CREATED, and `compile_for_string_chars` takes the fast path only when the receiver resolves to that same alloca — so a shadowing binding, a same-named parameter, or a stale cross-function entry all MISS and keep the general decode loop. Direct string-literal receivers (`for c in "abc".chars()`, `for c in "abc"`) are self-proving and need no analysis. New loop driver `compile_for_string_chars_ascii_inner` (control_flow_for.rs) is the `.bytes()` shape with the byte zero-extended to i32 and the binding tagged `char`. MEASURED: isolated `nth_letter` probe (4.25M calls, 26-char literal) 699,426,390 -> 42,802,319 Ir, byte-identical output 465374916 — 16.3x, and exactly the figure the already-branch-free `.bytes()` spelling of the same program produces, against 32,250,118 for equal-safety Rust (21.7x -> 1.33x). On the #127 kata bench harness `neighbors` 1,194.5M -> 796.9M Ir (-33%, 50.60% -> 40.61% of program) and whole program 1,962,274,658 Ir vs the equal-hash Rust lane's 1,588,749,056 = 1.235x I-refs, down from 1.45x. CORRECTION to this entry's original text: the claim that `karac_string_decode_char` was ALREADY GONE from the optimized binary was WRONG — disassembly of the baseline shows a live `call karac_string_decode_char` inside the loop at main+0x7e. The offset-PHI mechanism the entry identified was right; the ruled-out-suspect note was not. VERIFIED: 12-shape gauntlet at 4-backend parity (interp / JIT / AOT-O2 / AOT-O0) covering let-bound ASCII const, let-bound MULTIBYTE const, bare ASCII and multibyte literal receivers, the no-`.chars()` spelling, a binding mutated by `push` after its `let`, a reassigned binding, break/continue, the empty string, glyph rendering, and a SHADOWING inner binding holding runtime multibyte text; valgrind memcheck clean (0 errors, no definite leaks); 3 regression tests in tests/codegen.rs — one IR guard on the fast path's shape, one FAIL-CLOSED IR guard asserting the param / multibyte / mutated cases keep `@karac_string_decode_char`, and one 12-case E2E oracle.

title: `continue` inside `for ch in <s>.chars()` is an INFINITE LOOP in compiled code on every backend (JIT and AOT, -O0 and -O2), because the general chars loop advances the byte offset at BODY-TAIL and `continue` branches straight past that store to a no-op incr block — so the loop re-reads the same character forever. The interpreter is correct. With a `break` also present the program terminates but silently returns a WRONG answer instead of hanging.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while building the 4-backend parity gauntlet for B-2026-07-27-7; proven pre-existing by reproducing it on unmodified main. It is NOT a JIT-vs-AOT divergence — plain `karac build` hangs too, at both KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and the default -O2, with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0. MECHANISM (from the code, `compile_for_string_chars_inner` in src/codegen/control_flow_for.rs): the decoded post-char offset `new_off` is stored into the `for.s.offset` alloca at the END OF THE BODY (`build_store(byte_offset, new_off)` on the fall-through path), and the incr block is documented as a deliberate no-op ("body already wrote the new offset"). `continue` branches directly to that incr block, skipping the store, so the offset never advances. The body-tail placement exists so a mid-body `break` cannot corrupt the offset — but `break` exits via exit_bb, not incr_bb, so moving the store INTO the incr block preserves that property and fixes `continue`. `new_off` is defined in the merge block that dominates the whole body, so it dominates incr_bb. NOT affected: the `.bytes()` loop and range loops both advance in their incr block and handle `continue` correctly — this is specific to the chars loop. The branch-free ASCII chars loop added by B-2026-07-27-7 also advances in its incr block, so a proven-ASCII-constant receiver is already correct; the bug is confined to the general decode loop (any String parameter, any multibyte or mutated binding), which is the common case.
resolution: FIXED by moving the decoded byte-offset store out of the body tail and into the INCR BLOCK of `compile_for_string_chars_inner` (src/codegen/control_flow_for.rs). `continue` branches to incr_bb, so a body-tail store is simply skipped on that path; storing in incr_bb puts the advance on every path that loops back. The property the body-tail placement was originally chosen for still holds — a mid-body `break` must not advance the offset — because `break` exits via exit_bb and never reaches incr_bb. `new_off` is defined in the ASCII/multibyte merge block, which dominates the whole body and therefore incr_bb, so no PHI or re-load is needed. VERIFIED: 5-shape gauntlet at 4-backend parity (interp / JIT / AOT-O2 / AOT-O0), every shape deliberately routed through the GENERAL decode loop (the branch-free ASCII loop from B-2026-07-27-7 already advanced in its incr block and was never affected, so an ASCII-only test would have missed this entirely): (1) the multibyte hang repro `continue` with no `break` -> 2; (2) `continue` + `break` over an ASCII binding mutated by `push` -> 296, the value the interpreter and the ASCII fast path both give and which the stuck-offset build got wrong; (3) `continue` over a String PARAMETER -> 3; (4) LABELED `continue outer` from a nested loop -> 452; (5) `continue` as the last body statement so every iteration skips -> 2. All four backends agree on all five. Valgrind memcheck clean. Regression test `test_e2e_continue_in_chars_loop_advances_the_byte_offset` in tests/codegen.rs pins all five shapes.

title: A non-`mut` `let` binding can be REASSIGNED and MUTATED IN PLACE with no diagnostic — `let s: String = "abc"; s = "xyz";` and `let s: String = "abc"; s.push('z');` both pass `karac check` and really take effect, so `mut` is not enforced on bindings at all (it IS enforced at call sites, where a `mut ref` parameter correctly demands a `mut` argument marker).
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while establishing the safety premise for B-2026-07-27-7's constant-string proof. The fix there was designed to lean on `is_mut == false` as an immutability guarantee; probing showed the guarantee does not exist, so the analysis was rewritten to prove non-mutation directly (no assignment-target root, no mutating-method receiver, no `mut`-marked argument). That rewrite is sound regardless of this bug, but any FUTURE analysis tempted to trust `is_mut` must read this entry first. SCOPE: the parser records `is_mut` on `StmtKind::Let` and the formatter round-trips it, but no phase rejects a write to a non-`mut` binding. Both write kinds are affected — direct reassignment (`StmtKind::Assign` whose target root is a non-`mut` `let`) and in-place mutation through a mutating built-in method (`ast::is_mutating_collection_method`). The interpreter and codegen agree with each other and perform the write, so this is a MISSING CHECK, not a backend divergence. Contrast with the call-site path, which is correctly enforced: passing a binding to a `mut ref String` parameter without the `mut` marker is rejected with a focused diagnostic ("parameter expects `mut ref String`; call with fresh binding requires a `mut` marker at this argument"). EXPECTED: a diagnostic at the write site naming the binding and pointing at its `let`, with a machine-applicable `karac fix` suggestion inserting `mut`.
resolution:
FIXED in 6a855bdc. The missing check now lives in the ownership checker, next to the `let x: T;` first-assignment machinery that already emitted the same diagnostic. A new per-function `immutable_lets` map (name -> the `let` statement's span) is populated for every non-`mut` `let` and consulted at four write sites: direct reassignment, compound assignment, a write through a field/element place, and a `mut ref self` method call. Receiver modes come from the existing `method_self_borrow_kind`, so user `impl` methods and the stdlib table (Vec.push / Map.insert / String.push / ...) are covered by one rule -- design.md's own worked example `let seen = Map.new(); seen.insert(k, v)` is now the error that section says it is.

DIAGNOSTIC, as this entry's EXPECTED asked: the message points at the WRITE site and names the declaration's line; the machine-applicable edit targets the DECLARATION instead (a `TextEdit` carries its own offset independent of the diagnostic span), inserting a zero-length " mut" right after the `let` keyword -- which renders `let mut x` regardless of intervening whitespace. `karac fix` turns this entry's own repro into a passing program in one pass, verified end-to-end. New kind `MutateImmutableBinding` (E0510) for the method-call case so it reads as in-place mutation rather than a rebind; the three assignment forms reuse `ReassignToImmutable` (E0506).

FOUR FALSE-POSITIVE CLASSES, all found by running the rule against the corpus and the test suites and all fixed in the checker rather than worked around. Recording them because each is a trap for any future binding-scoped analysis: (1) CROSS-FUNCTION LEAK -- the map is keyed by bare name like the sibling `states` map, so it must be cleared per function or an immutable `let cmd` in one function freezes `cmd` in every later one. (2) PATTERN SHADOWING -- a match-arm / if-let / while-let / for binding is a NEW binding; cleared in `define_pattern_states`, the single choke point every binding form flows through, so no form can be missed. Both fired on examples/tangle/src/undo_redo.kara. (3) REFERENCE HANDLES -- a binding whose own type is Shared/Rc/Arc/Ref/MutRef/Weak/Pointer names storage it does not own, so `*p = v`, the deref-elided `r += 1` from `entry().or_insert()`, and a field write through a `shared struct` handle all mutate the REFERENT and leave the binding pointing exactly where it did. A write whose place merely passes THROUGH a shared hop (`cmd.cell.value = v`) is exempt too. Note `Type::Ref`/`MutRef` must NOT recurse into the referent here, or a `mut ref i64` binding gets judged by `i64` and loses the exemption. Fired on runtime/stdlib/autograd.kara (`let tp = self.tape; tp.values.push(v)`) and two codegen tests. (4) INTERIOR-MUTABILITY PRIMITIVES -- Atomic/Mutex/RwLock/Arc, the same set `effectchecker::modbind_synth::type_is_concurrency_primitive` already exempts and for the same stated reason: design.md names them as THE supported paths for mutable shared state, so `let m = Mutex.new(0); lock m { m = m + 1; }` is the sanctioned idiom and requiring `let mut m` would contradict the section recommending it.

Under-reporting is the deliberate safe direction throughout: a binding introduced in an inner block stays visible to the outer scope after it ends, exactly as it already does for `states`.

THE RULE FOUND REAL BUGS. runtime/stdlib/embeddings.kara's `cosine_similarity_matrix` built its result tensor with a non-`mut` `let out` and index-wrote every cell; 14 inline test programs across tests/codegen.rs and tests/memory_sanitizer.rs did the same with Vec/String/Tensor. All fixed by adding `mut`.

CORPUS IMPACT, measured before and after: 0 of 194 repo .kara files (examples, selfhost, runtime/stdlib) and 0 of 663 kara-katas files report the new diagnostic. 659 of those 663 katas check fully clean, which is what confirms the ownership phase actually ran on them rather than the scan passing vacuously -- the remaining 4 fail on pre-existing move-checker / concurrency diagnostics unrelated to `mut`.

Gates: fmt clean; clippy --all --all-targets clean and again with --features llvm; non-llvm suite green; codegen 2590/0; memory_sanitizer 855/0; par_codegen 200/0; ownership 377 including 11 new tests covering all four write forms, the fix edit, and one regression test per false-positive class.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara, Phase-12 port): a DESTRUCTURING `let S { a, b } = s;` bound NOTHING — the Let handler matched only a plain BindingPat, so a struct pattern fell through its `_ => {}`. Every later reference to a destructured field then hit the emitter's `0` fallback: SCALARS SILENTLY READ AS 0 (a silent miscompile, not an error) and a String field emitted `{ ptr, i64 } 0`, which LLVM rejects.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found by mapping the capstone frontier across every self-host module — three modules (typechecker, resolver, ast_render) failed with the SAME 'integer constant must have integer type' error, which reduced to `call ... ({ ptr, i64 } 0)`: a String argument emitted as the integer fallback. Minimal repro isolated it to the destructuring `let`. PERVASIVE: codegen.kara's own dominant idiom is `let Val { op, kind, heap } = v;`, and the AST walkers destructure in nearly every function. The SILENT half is the dangerous one — `let S { a, b } = s; a + b` evaluated to 0 instead of 12 with no diagnostic, so any scalar destructure was quietly wrong. FIX (Slice 62, 7bd2de1): a StructPat arm projects each named field out of the struct aggregate with `extractvalue` at its DECLARED index and binds a fresh local carrying that field's kind; both the `{ a }` shorthand and the `{ a: x }` renaming form are supported. Bindings are BORROWS (heap=false), matching the existing field-READ convention — the source binding keeps ownership and its scope-exit drop frees heap fields exactly once, so destructuring a named local or an owned param neither double-frees nor leaks (the oracle's valgrind leg confirms). SCOPE NOTE: this does NOT by itself unblock typechecker/resolver/ast_render. Their remaining failures trace to the missing `shared enum` support (B-2026-07-27-6) — the structs they destructure carry `Expr` fields, and `Expr` is a `pub shared enum` the emitter cannot yet represent. So the module blockers converge on the `shared` gap rather than being independent bugs.
resolution: Fixed in Slice 62 (7bd2de1): StructPat arm in the Let handler — per-field extractvalue at the declared index, bound as borrows. Selfhost oracle + valgrind green.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara, Phase-12 port): `.clone()` is UNIMPLEMENTED and silently lowers to the i64 default `0` — `let b = a.clone()` on a String prints `0`/empty instead of the string, with no diagnostic
detail: SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while probing Slice 63 (`shared enum`). A probe of `match t { Leaf(s) => s.clone(), ... }` diffed against the seed; narrowing showed the BY-VALUE enum control failed identically, so this is NOT a shared-enum bug but a pre-existing, independent gap. Narrowed further to `let a = "deep".to_string(); let b = a.clone(); println(b);` — nothing to do with match or enums at all. The method name `clone` appears NOWHERE in codegen.kara's method dispatch (grep '"clone"' -> 0 hits), so the call falls through to the emitter's scalar fallback and yields the constant 0: a String receiver prints empty, an i64 receiver prints 0. SILENT — the emitted IR is well-formed, so neither the verifier nor a build failure catches it; only output parity does. IMPACT: `.clone()` is used 706 times in codegen.kara itself and 4 times in parser.kara, so the self-host FIXPOINT (the port compiling its own source) cannot be correct until this lands. NOTE for the frontier map: lexer.kara uses `.clone()` ZERO times, so the 'lexer.kara emits valid IR' milestone is NOT retroactively invalidated by this bug — but 'emits valid IR' was never a correctness claim for modules that do use it.
resolution: Fixed in Slice 64: a `clone` arm in the emitter's method dispatch, placed AFTER user-method dispatch so a type with its own `clone` impl still wins. A clone is exactly the per-kind DEEP COPY the emitter already performs when materializing a borrow into an owned slot, so it reuses those helpers — emit_materialize (String), emit_materialize_vec, emit_materialize_struct, emit_materialize_enum — rather than growing a second copy path; scalars (i64/bool/f64) copy by value. A `shared enum` receiver RETAINS (bumps the refcount) instead of deep-copying, which is Slice 63's RC contract. SCOPE NOTE discovered while building the corpus entry: the SEED rejects `.clone()` on a user struct and on a user `shared enum` ('no method clone on type S'), so those two arms are unreachable for any seed-accepted program; they are written out anyway so the representation stays coherent — the alternative, letting a shared handle fall through to the by-value enum materializer, would deep-copy a POINTER as if it were an aggregate. The corpus entry deliberately exercises only what the seed itself admits: String locals, a struct-field String, i64/f64/bool, Vec[i64], Vec[String], and a match-bound String payload.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara, Phase-12 port): a `to_string()` result produced INSIDE a match arm and returned from a fn leaks — the caller never frees the returned buffer
detail: SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while building the Slice 63 (`shared enum`) corpus entry — valgrind flagged 24-byte definite losses inside the emitted `u_show`. Confirmed PRE-EXISTING and unrelated to shared enums: the BY-VALUE enum control leaks identically, and the same fn with only STRING-LITERAL arms (`Num(n) => "num".to_string()`) is leak-clean.
