The entry's instinct not to assume a layer was right; the layer is the front end, and it was already doing its job. WHAT LANDED (c1eeed5): the gate was pinned by NOTHING, so a regression would silently make the crashing shape compilable again. Three tests now cover it — `par {}` branches (ownership), `TaskGroup.spawn` captures (the TYPECHECKER, as `E_NOT_CROSS_TASK` — a different phase, so gating one surface would have left the identical race reachable through the other), and an accept-case so the gate cannot start over-firing. FOR THE KATA, and this is a real ergonomic finding rather than a workaround: the diagnostic's advice (`replace 'Node' with the 'par' form`) does not directly apply. A `par struct`'s `mut` field must be `Atomic[T]` or `Mutex[T]`, and this graph is CYCLIC — neighbours are wired after construction — so `mut neighbors: Vec[Node]` cannot simply become immutable. Making the par lane legal means `Mutex[Vec[Node]]` (changing the cost model the benchmark measures) or rebuilding the graph per worker, which is what the rayon lane already does for the same reason (`Rc` is not `Send`). ALSO WORTH FIXING SEPARATELY: `bench.sh`'s cache key should include the compiler actually used, or the bench should run `karac check` before trusting a cached binary. Two ledger entries have now been spent on binaries the compiler would refuse.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara): `Option[<plain struct>]` has no representation — `kind_of_ty` collapses it to `Option$i`, whose payload slot is an i64, so constructing `Some(<struct>)` emits `insertvalue { i64, i64 } %t6, i64 %t5, 1` with `%t5` a struct. Fails at LLVM parse. The third member of the `Option[T]` family after B-2026-07-28-5 (shared enum) and the `Option[String]` leg of B-2026-07-27-6.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: B-2026-07-27-6 recorded this as its own LAST REMAINING SHAPE and characterized it as 'an AGGREGATE-slot enum (en_extra >= 0) which sh_byval_enum_ok still refuses'. Both halves are wrong, which is why it is being restated here rather than inherited. `kind_of_ty` maps `Option[T]` by inspecting the generic: String yields 1001, a `shared enum` yields the inner enum's kind (B-2026-07-28-5's niche), and EVERYTHING ELSE falls through to 1000 = `Option$i`. `Option$i` has variants None/Some(i64), no aggregate slot, and `en_has_heap` false — so a plain-struct payload is neither slotted nor refused, it is simply typed as an integer.

FAILURE MODE, and it is the good one: LOUD. Constructing the `Some` emits an `insertvalue` of a struct value into an i64 field and `llvm-as` rejects it outright. A `None`-only program emits VALID IR and runs correctly, because nothing is ever stored in the slot — so the shape is latent until the first `Some`.

SCOPE OF THE FIX: unlike `Option[<shared enum>]` there is NO niche to reuse — a plain struct has no null representation — so this needs a real synthetic enum per distinct `Option[<struct>]`, registered like `Option$i` / `Option$s` but carrying that struct in an aggregate slot. The slot machinery is no longer the obstacle (dd14643 made aggregate slots unbounded); the work is REGISTRATION. `kind_of_ty` is `ref self` and cannot register on demand, so a pre-pass must walk every type annotation in the program (struct fields, fn params and returns, `let` annotations) collecting `Option[<struct>]` instantiations before any kind is resolved — the same problem Pass A0 solved for names.

ast.kara has 7 such fields, all `Option[GenericParamsNode]`.
resolution:
FIXED 2026-07-28 (46acf5b). `collect_sigs` registers a synthetic `Option$<Struct>` enum per DECLARED struct, with the struct in an AGGREGATE slot. There is no niche to reuse here — a plain struct has no null representation, which is what separates this from `Option[<shared enum>]` (B-2026-07-28-5) — so it needs a real enum, and that only became expressible when dd14643 removed the two-aggregate-slot cap.

WHY EVERY STRUCT, not only the instantiations in use: finding those means pre-scanning every type annotation in the program INCLUDING inside fn bodies (`let x: Option[G]`), and a missed instantiation would be an emit-time refusal. One two-variant entry per struct is cheap, it turns the lookup into a name search instead of a discovery pass, and it costs nothing in the emitted IR because an enum nothing references is never rendered.

Both sides pick the same enum from the same fact — `kind_of_ty` from the annotation's generic, the `Some(x)` arm from the payload's KIND — which is how the existing Option$i / Option$s split already worked, so no new agreement mechanism was needed. `None` needed nothing: `zeroinitializer` is tag 0 in this layout as in the others.

RESULT BEYOND THE SHAPE: `ast_render` and `resolver` moved from invalid IR to IR `llvm-as` accepts. Seven of the nine self-host modules now emit valid IR (span, token, ast, lexer, typechecker, ast_render, resolver); `parser` and `codegen` remain, on unrelated gaps — parser on `'%t4440' i64 but expected '{ ptr, i64 }'`, codegen on `'%t3395' i1 but expected 'i64'`.

VERIFIED: the 191-program corpus matches the seed. The new entry covers a POD payload and a String-bearing one, both arms of each, construction inline and through a fn return, a struct FIELD of that type read and consumed, and the same inside a shared node; it is valgrind-clean at 0 errors and 0 bytes lost and survives 25 consecutive runs, and fails at LLVM parse on the parent commit.

COVERAGE GAP, and it is a SEED bug not a port one: no arm reads an `Option[<HEAP struct>]` out of a struct field and passes it to an owning parameter, because that DOUBLE-FREES IN THE SEED — found while writing this very test, filed as B-2026-07-28-16. A differential oracle cannot compare against a crashing reference, so that shape is deferred here until the seed is fixed.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara): no IMPORT resolution — a type named by an `import` hits `kind_of_ty`'s i64 fallback SILENTLY, so an imported struct lowers to a bare integer and the emitter produces well-formed IR for a program the seed REFUSES. This, not any payload shape, is what gates module-level self-hosting.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by feeding each self-host module to the port after dd14643 lifted the aggregate-slot cap (B-2026-07-27-6). All six modules now EMIT — none reaches a refusal — but five produce IR `llvm-as` rejects, and narrowing the smallest of those (ast_render) landed here rather than on a payload bug.

MECHANISM: `emit_program` walks the items of ONE parsed module. `Import` items are ignored, so nothing an import names is ever registered in `st_names` / `en_names`, and `kind_of_ty` returns 0 — i64 — for a name it cannot find. Pass A0 (Slice 65) made that fallback unreachable by a FORWARD reference within a module; an IMPORTED name still reaches it, and silently.

WHY IT IS HIGH RATHER THAN A MISSING FEATURE: the outcome is not a refusal but a wrong lowering that type-checks at the IR level. In the emitted ast.kara, `@u_clone_span` has signature `(i64) -> i64` although `Span` is a four-field struct — an identity function over a truncated value, well-formed IR, no diagnostic. Where the mistyped value is then used structurally the IR happens to fail to parse (that is the only reason four of the five modules are caught at all); where it is merely passed through, it compiles and is simply wrong.

TWO-PART FIX, and the first part is small and independently worth doing: (a) REFUSE an unresolvable type name instead of calling it i64. `kind_of_ty` must first admit the scalar names it legitimately does not register (`i64`/`i32`/`u8`/… all currently reach the same `0` by design) and refuse only what is left, so this is not a one-line change and carries real regression risk against the 190-program corpus — but it converts this whole class from silent to loud. (b) Resolve imports: collect the imported modules' items into the same tables before Pass A0, which is the actual feature.

UNTIL (a) LANDS, treat single-module emitter output as UNTRUSTWORTHY for any module with imports — `llvm-as` accepting it is not evidence of correctness.
resolution:
FIXED 2026-07-28 (04964fa), in two halves that turned out to be very unevenly sized.

THE MISCOMPILE: `kind_of_ty` now lists the primitive type names explicitly (`primitive_kind_of_name`) and REFUSES anything that is neither a primitive nor a declared struct/enum, printing the name it could not resolve. The name is printed rather than interpolated into the panic because the seed only propagates a STRING-LITERAL panic message, and a refusal that cannot say WHICH name it failed on is barely better than the silent i64 it replaces. `f32` is deliberately absent from the primitive list: only `f64` has a kind, so an `f32` annotation would have become an integer — the same class of silent wrong lowering.

THE OTHER HALF NEEDS NO EMITTER CHANGE AT ALL, which is the finding worth keeping and is why the entry over-estimated the work. The entry called import resolution 'the actual feature'. It is not: the emitter consumes a flat `Vec[Item]`, so CONCATENATING a module with its transitive imports gives one program in which every name is declared — `import` lines are inert and duplicates are harmless. `scripts/selfhost-emit-module.sh` derives the closure from the `import` lines and emits; with it `@u_clone_span` gains its true `{i64,i64,i64,i64}` signature and four modules (ast, token, lexer, typechecker) move from invalid IR to IR `llvm-as` accepts. What remains unimplemented is per-module emission with imported functions `declare`d rather than defined, which nothing currently needs.

VERIFIED: the 190-program differential corpus is green with the refusal in place — no legitimate name in it trips the primitive list, which was the whole regression risk of tightening a fallback that scalars also reach. The minimal repro (a module the seed refuses with "'P' is not a struct") now refuses by name instead of emitting `define i64 @u_getx(i64)`.

NOTE for anyone reading the module table in the commit: span and token declare no functions, so their 'IR VALID' is module scaffold only. The load-bearing ones are lexer (43 fns -> 43 defines) and typechecker (41 -> 47, the extra being shared-enum release helpers).

title: SEED CODEGEN: an owned struct's `Option`/`Result` field passed BY VALUE to a parameter that owns it was not treated as a move — the callee freed the payload and the struct's scope-exit drop freed it again. Hits `Option[String]` and `Option[Vec]` as well as the `Option[<struct>]` this was filed on. Interpreter correct; JIT and AOT both abort.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while writing the corpus entry for B-2026-07-28-14 (the self-hosted emitter's `Option[<plain struct>]` support). The test program was written against the SEED as the oracle and the seed crashed on it — so this is a seed defect surfaced by port work, not a port defect.

NARROWED, and each negative below is a measured run rather than an assumption:
  * The payload must OWN HEAP. The identical program with a POD payload struct (`Option[G]`, G = { n: i64 }) runs correctly on all three backends.
  * The Option must be read out of a STRUCT FIELD. The same `Option[H]` held in a plain local and passed to the same function is fine.
  * The consumer must take it BY VALUE. Matching the field inline, without a call, is fine.
  * No `shared` type is involved — the first repro had one, and removing it did not change the outcome.

BACKENDS DISAGREE, which is the usual signature of an ownership-convention bug rather than a layout one: the interpreter prints the right answer; `karac run` (LLJIT) and `karac build` both abort with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` (exit 134), and valgrind on the AOT binary reports `Invalid free() / delete / delete[] / realloc()`, 1 error from 1 context.

RELATIONSHIP TO B-2026-07-21-16 ('owned-struct Option field consume/move sites double-free'), which is the same sentence at a different layout: that fix evidently covers the Option layouts whose payload sits in the two-word tagged form, and not the AGGREGATE-slot form an `Option[<struct>]` uses. Worth checking whether the fix generalizes rather than adding a second special case.

IMPACT beyond the port: `Option[<struct>]` fields are ordinary user code, so this is reachable from any program, not only from self-host work.
resolution:
FIXED 2026-07-28 (6dc5854). The call site already had the right idea — B-2026-07-10-4 wired `suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move` there for exactly this move — but that helper matches an `Identifier` and returns immediately for anything else, so a `FieldAccess` argument was never treated as a move. `let o = nd.opt; consume(o)` was fine while `consume(nd.opt)` aborted, and B-2026-07-21-16's source-zeroing (built for the pattern, `let` and assign move sites) simply never reached the call-argument site. The fix adds that fourth leg.

THE ENTRY UNDERSTATED THE SCOPE, and correcting that matters more than the fix: it described an `Option[<struct that owns heap>]`, because that is where it surfaced (writing B-2026-07-28-14's corpus program against the seed as oracle). Measured afterwards, `Option[String]` and `Option[Vec[i64]]` fields abort identically. This was ordinary user code, not a corner of self-host work, and the severity was right for the wrong reason.

TWO CLASSES, NOT ONE — the first attempt conflated them and that is the reusable finding. Widening the shared `place_optres_field_move_info` in place fixed the call site and turned two previously-clean programs into LEAKS. The PATTERN leg only zeroes the source when the arm's BINDING takes over the payload's free, which holds for an inline `{ptr,len,cap}` payload and not for a struct/enum one: `match nd.hp { Some(x) => println(x.label) }` stranded 4 bytes under valgrind. A WHOLE-value move has no such question — the callee receives tag and payload together — so it got its own entry point, `place_optres_field_whole_move_info`, whose payload class mirrors `emit_struct_drop_synthesis`'s OptionInline classifier exactly. That mirroring is the invariant worth stating: the source zero must fire precisely when the struct drop would free the field, or it is a double-free (too narrow) or a leak (too wide).

STILL OPEN, split out as B-2026-07-28-17: the same call when the struct is a payload bound out of a `shared enum`. `field_chain_place_ptr` correctly bails on that root — zeroing a field inside an RC node would corrupt every other holder — so the fix there is a defensive COPY at the call site, a different mechanism. Confirmed narrow by control: the identical program over a NON-shared enum is clean.

VERIFIED: 2603 codegen E2E, 861 memory_sanitizer (gcc ASAN+LSan), the 191-program selfhost corpus and the non-llvm suite all green; clippy + fmt clean. Both new tests were checked to BITE (reverting just the two source files makes the ASAN test report `double-free`), and both cover the LEAK direction as well — an unconsumed field must stay owned and readable. The E2E test uses single-use holders because the ownership checker correctly rejects reading a field after it was moved; that is the language being sound, not a test limitation.

title: SEED CODEGEN: passing an `Option[<heap>]` field of a struct bound out of a `shared enum` payload to an owning parameter double-frees — `match a { V(nd) => consume(nd.hp) }`. The owned-root form of this was fixed as B-2026-07-28-16; this root is an RC node, which needs a defensive COPY rather than a source zero.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the residue of B-2026-07-28-16, which fixed the same call for an owned struct local (and for a non-shared enum payload binding). Split out because the FIX is a different mechanism, not because it is a different symptom.

WHY THE -16 FIX DOES NOT EXTEND: that fix neutralizes the SOURCE — it zeroes the Option tag in the owning struct so the struct's drop skips the payload the callee now owns. Here the owning struct lives inside an RC node that other handles may still read, so writing to it is not allowed; `field_chain_place_ptr` already bails on a borrowed root for exactly this reason, which is why the -16 suppressor is a no-op on this shape (it does not misbehave — it simply does not fire). The correct fix is a defensive COPY of the payload at the call site, so the callee frees its own copy and the node keeps its original — the territory the B-2026-07-21-16 design assigned to 'the -9/-14 ref-param clone legs'.

CONFIRMED NARROW by control: the identical program with a NON-shared enum is clean on all three backends, so this is specific to a `shared` root and not to match-bound payloads in general.
resolution:
FIXED 2026-07-29 (09ffe5a). `clone_shared_view_optres_field_arg` gives the callee a defensive COPY of the Option value when the argument is an `Option`/`Result` field read out of a struct in `shared_enum_payload_view_vars`; the node keeps its original. It defers to `emit_option_value_clone_fn`, which self-gates on the payload actually owning heap, so a POD payload keeps the shallow copy and costs nothing. This is the same trade the `let`-site clone-on-extract (B-2026-07-09-12) already makes for a Vec field of such a view.

TWO WRONG TURNS, recorded because both were plausible and neither is the right place. (1) `maybe_defensive_copy_param_arg` looked like the natural hook — it already deep-clones a heap field read through a borrowed receiver — but instrumenting it showed its FieldAccess arm is never reached for a user-fn argument at all; it runs on the return path and on a few container sinks. (2) Widening its receiver gate to `borrowed_agg_payload_struct_vars` changes nothing, because that set is only populated on the `pattern_binding_is_borrow` path and a match over a shared-enum LOCAL is not classified as a borrow scrutinee. The working hook is the user-call argument loop itself, between `compile_expr` and the `compiled_args.push`.

THE REGRESSION TEST IS STRAIGHT-LINE ON PURPOSE, and this is the part worth carrying forward. Two properties of this shape let a routine test pass vacuously, and both were established by running the candidate against the PRE-FIX compiler rather than assumed:
  * The payload must ESCAPE the callee — the arm has to return `x.label`. A consumer that merely reads it (`x.label.len() + x.k`) binds a borrow, frees nothing, and the program is clean with or without the fix. A first draft did exactly that and passed both ways.
  * Wrapping the body in a `while` loop SUPPRESSES it. That is the accumulate-so-any-imbalance-shows idiom the sibling B-2026-07-28-16 test uses and it is the wrong instinct here: the looped form passed pre-fix, the straight-line form aborts. So the test asserts stdout and repeats the shape with distinct bindings instead of iterating.

VERIFIED: 2603 codegen E2E, 862 memory_sanitizer (gcc ASAN+LSan), 200 par_codegen, the 191-program selfhost corpus and the non-llvm suite all green; clippy + fmt clean. The new test was checked to bite (ASAN reports `attempting double-free` without the fix). The entry's own 12-line repro now matches the interpreter line-for-line and is valgrind-clean, as are all ten shapes in the -16/-17 scratch battery.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara): `==` with a BOOL operand emits an i64 compare against an i1 value — `icmp eq i64 %t, false` — which LLVM rejects. `not b` is unaffected. This is the only thing between the port and emitting codegen.kara itself.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by feeding each self-host module to the port with its import closure after B-2026-07-28-14/-15 moved seven of nine modules to valid IR. `codegen.kara` was one of the two remaining; this is its first error.

MECHANISM: the equality lowering picks the i64 lane for its `icmp` regardless of the operand's kind, so a bool operand — which `ty_text` renders `i1` — is compared at the wrong width. The literal is emitted as `false`/`true`, so the mismatch is between an i1 register and an i64 comparison, not between two registers.

NARROWED, each measured rather than assumed:
  * `b == false` — INVALID. `b == true` — INVALID. So it is not about which literal.
  * A bool LOCAL and a bool PARAM both fail, so it is not about where the operand comes from.
  * `not b` is VALID. The unary path already lowers at i1, so only the binary `==` arm is wrong.

FAILS LOUDLY (LLVM rejects the module at parse), so nothing silently miscompiles today.

IN SITU: `Emitter.collect_sigs`, from `while vj < cnt and eshared == false` — the emitted IR is
  %t3395 = load i1, ptr %v19, align 8
  %t3396 = icmp eq i64 %t3395, false

MODULE FRONTIER at the time of filing (`scripts/selfhost-emit-module.sh --all`, which supplies each module's transitive import closure):
  span        IR VALID   (0 fns — scaffold only)
  token       IR VALID   (0 fns — scaffold only)
  ast         IR VALID   (3 fns -> 6 defines)
  lexer       IR VALID   (43 fns -> 43 defines)
  typechecker IR VALID   (41 fns -> 47 defines)
  ast_render  IR VALID   (21501 lines)
  resolver    IR VALID   (20823 lines)
  parser      IR INVALID -> B-2026-07-29-2
  codegen     IR INVALID -> B-2026-07-29-1
These two are the whole remaining distance to a self-host fixpoint at the emit-and-parse level.
resolution:
FIXED. `emit_binary`'s equality arm hardcoded the compare width to i64. It now emits `icmp <pred> i1` when BOTH operand kinds are bool, and keeps i64 otherwise.

WHY BOTH, not either: a mixed bool/i64 pair is a type error upstream, and widening one side here would paper over it. More concretely, a bool that lives in an i64 LANE — a `Vec[bool]` element read, which kind 3's storage zext's — arrives at this arm as kind 0 and genuinely needs the i64 compare; keying on either-side-is-bool would have broken B-2026-07-23-24's surface.

VERIFIED: the four probes from the entry (`b == false`, `b == true`, a bool param, and the `not b` control) all emit IR `llvm-as` accepts, run stdout-identical to the seed, are valgrind-clean, and are stable over 25 consecutive runs. Corpus entry added (197 programs).

FRONTIER: this was one of two blockers named in the entry. Clearing it exposed B-2026-07-29-4 (panic lowered as a user call) behind it in the same module — surfaced, ironically, by the `panic` this port gained in B-2026-07-28-15.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara): a match-expression RESULT slot is allocated `i64` in `Parser.collect_leading_doc_comments` while an arm yields a String, so the later read does `extractvalue { ptr, i64 }` on an i64 load. Localized to the function and slot; not yet reduced to a minimal repro.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the sibling of B-2026-07-29-1 — found the same way, and `parser.kara` is the other of the two modules still emitting invalid IR.

WHAT IS KNOWN: the failing function is `Parser.collect_leading_doc_comments`, and the slot is `%v3`, allocated `i64` and zero-initialized, later stored from an i64 register and then read as a String:
  %v3   = alloca i64, align 8
  store i64 0, ptr %v3, align 8
  ...
  %t4440 = load i64, ptr %v3, align 8
  %t4441 = extractvalue { ptr, i64 } %t4440, 0     <- llvm-as rejects here
The source's only match-valued `let` in that function is
  let line = match self.tokens[self.pos].token { DocComment(t) => t, _ => break };
so the result slot is being typed before the String-yielding arm is known — Slice 61's deferred typed result slot (B-2026-07-27-5) handles exactly this for the enum-match path, which suggests the `break` arm or the field-of-indexed-element scrutinee takes a different route.

TWO CANDIDATES RULED OUT by probe, so nobody repeats them:
  * `let mut buf: Option[String] = None;` followed by `Some(...)` assignment and a match — VALID. The annotated-Option local is fine, and indeed `%v1` in the same function is correctly typed `{ i64, i64, { ptr, i64 } }`.
  * `let line = match v[i] { D(t) => t, _ => break };` over a `Vec[<enum>]` in a loop — VALID. The break-arm-in-a-match-valued-let shape alone does not reproduce.
So the trigger involves something the probes did not carry over — most likely the scrutinee being a FIELD of an indexed element (`self.tokens[self.pos].token`) rather than the element itself.

FAILS LOUDLY (LLVM rejects the module at parse).

MODULE FRONTIER at the time of filing (`scripts/selfhost-emit-module.sh --all`, which supplies each module's transitive import closure):
  span        IR VALID   (0 fns — scaffold only)
  token       IR VALID   (0 fns — scaffold only)
  ast         IR VALID   (3 fns -> 6 defines)
  lexer       IR VALID   (43 fns -> 43 defines)
  typechecker IR VALID   (41 fns -> 47 defines)
  ast_render  IR VALID   (21501 lines)
  resolver    IR VALID   (20823 lines)
  parser      IR INVALID -> B-2026-07-29-2
  codegen     IR INVALID -> B-2026-07-29-1
These two are the whole remaining distance to a self-host fixpoint at the emit-and-parse level.
resolution:
FIXED, and RECLASSIFIED on the way: filed as a `codegen-gap` (medium) because LLVM rejected the module, this is really a `miscompile` (high) that LLVM catches only sometimes.

ROOT CAUSE — not the field-of-indexed-element scrutinee the entry guessed. It is the `_ => break` ARM. `emit_value` has no arm for `break` or `continue`; both live only in `emit_expr`. So a value-match arm whose body is one of them fell into `emit_value`'s catch-all and did TWO things wrong at once:
  1. no branch was emitted, so `_ => break` did not leave the loop, and
  2. the catch-all's i64 zero RETYPED the match's result slot — the arms assign `rsty`/`rkind` in source order and the last one wins — so a sibling arm's ALREADY EMITTED `store { ptr, i64 }` was left pointing at an `alloca i64`.

WHY THE PROBE 'RULED IT OUT' AND SHOULD NOT HAVE. The entry records `let line = match v[i] { D(t) => t, _ => break }` over a `Vec[<enum>]` as VALID, and concluded the break arm was not the trigger. It was not valid — it was SILENTLY MISCOMPILING. With opaque pointers, `store { ptr, i64 } %x, ptr %slot` is legal text no matter what `%slot` was allocated as, so (2) is an 8-byte alloca taking a 16-byte store: a stack overwrite `llvm-as` has no way to see. LLVM only objects when the LOAD side disagrees too, which is what happened in `Parser.collect_leading_doc_comments` (`load i64` then `extractvalue { ptr, i64 }`). Re-run against the pre-fix emitter, that same probe prints `94033864360688` where the seed prints `hi`. LESSON: for this emitter, `llvm-as` clean is NOT the oracle — run it and diff stdout.

FIX: new `Emitter.emit_arm_value` intercepts a `break`/`continue` arm body, emits the branch (and the dead block after it) the way `emit_expr` does, and returns the sentinel kind -99. All four value-match arm sites — the int-literal path and the enum path, guarded and unguarded — skip the store and leave `rsty`/`rkind`/`rheap` alone on that sentinel. The unconditional `br label %endmatch` that follows stays: it is what terminates the dead block.

VERIFIED: the entry's own probe now prints `hi`, valgrind-clean. Four corpus entries added — the int-literal path with `break`, the enum path with `break`, a `continue` arm, and the probe shape — each stdout-identical to the seed and valgrind-clean. parser.kara emits IR `llvm-as` accepts, and with it all nine self-host modules do.

SCOPE LEFT: the arms still type the slot last-wins rather than first-non-diverging, so a match whose arms disagree in kind is still wrong. No such shape exists in the self-host tree and none is in the corpus; fixing it needs the same treatment (a 'result kind is now fixed' flag) and is a separate slice.

title: A `_test.kara` companion that imports the module it tests is reported as a circular module dependency (`E0223`, bogus `thing → thing`), so the idiomatic `foo.kara` / `foo_test.kara` layout cannot be tested at all under `karac test` — while `karac build` accepts the identical sources.
detail:
MECHANISM: a companion shares its production sibling's module path (documented at src/walker.rs:139 — "Test files are companions — same module path as their sibling"). Under `karac test` the two files are merged into one Module whose `imports` is the union of both files' imports, so the companion's `import thing.double;` becomes an import ON module `thing` naming module `thing`. `collect_import_edges` resolves it and calls `graph.add_edge(m.id, m.id)`; `detect_cycles` treats a size-1 SCC with a self-loop as circular and emits E0223.

WHY BUILD DIFFERS: `karac build` leaves `include_tests` false, so walker.rs:344 skips the companion before it ever reaches the graph (`karac build` on the repro prints `modules: 2` and exits 0). The divergence is what made this read as a package problem rather than a compiler one.

MINIMAL REPRO (12 lines): package with src/main.kara, src/thing.kara (`pub fn double(x: i64) -> i64 { x * 2 }`), and src/thing_test.kara (`import thing.double;` + one `test` block). `karac build` → exit 0. `karac test` → `{"type":"module_cycle","code":"E0223","message":"thing → thing"}`, exit 1.

THE IMPORT IS GENUINELY REDUNDANT, which is what makes dropping it safe: the same companion with NO import resolves `double(3)` and passes, because the merge already put both files' items in one module. Verified before choosing the fix.

FIX: filter self-referential imports out of the companion's contribution during the merge (src/module.rs), in both spellings — `import thing.double;` (path == own path) and `import db.connection;` from `db/connection_test.kara` (path + item == own path). This extends the `dedup_import` filter already in that arm, which drops exact re-imports so the merged module does not trip E0101; same rationale, same place. Dropped rather than diagnosed because the identical import IS meaningful when the companion is checked as a standalone file — it is the merge that makes it redundant, not the source.

NARROWNESS: a companion's import of a DIFFERENT module still records a real edge. `game_of_life`'s genuine `grid → rules → grid` is still reported after the fix; `elevator_project`'s two bogus self-cycles (`elevator → elevator`, `scheduler → scheduler`) are gone, leaving only that package's unrelated bit-rot parse errors.

SOURCE NOTE: found by auditing which `examples/` corpora are referenced by anything in tests/, scripts/, .github/, or src/ — the generalization of B-2026-07-28-4 (the tangle corpus, which nothing ran). Eight example directories are referenced by nothing; two of them (`elevator_project`, `game_of_life`) are complete multi-module packages carrying their own `test "..."` suites, and both were blocked by this bug. Those two are ALSO bit-rotted against the current language (they write `ref` at call sites, banned by design.md Feature 4 Part 1½, so they no longer parse) — tracked separately, not fixed here.

TESTS: tests/module_graph.rs gains `companion_self_import_is_not_a_module_cycle`, `nested_companion_self_import_is_not_a_module_cycle` (both spellings), and `companion_filter_does_not_mask_genuine_cycles`. Non-vacuity verified by stashing the src change: the first two fail with the exact `["thing → thing"]`, and the third passes both before and after (it is an over-reach guard, not a regression witness).

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara): `panic` / `todo` / `unreachable` were lowered as USER FUNCTION CALLS. With no signature to consult, every parameter typed i64, so `panic("msg")` emitted `call i64 @u_panic(i64 <{ptr,i64} String>)` — a call to a function that is never defined, with a String in an i64 slot.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced immediately behind B-2026-07-29-1 while walking codegen.kara through `scripts/selfhost-emit-module.sh`. Self-inflicted in a precise way: the only `panic` calls anywhere in the self-host tree are this emitter's OWN refusals, and the one that blocked it (`Emitter.kind_of_ty`'s unresolved-type-name refusal) was added by B-2026-07-28-15 two days earlier. Fixing the silent-i64 bug planted the call that exposed the missing builtin.

MECHANISM: `emit_expr`'s Call arm special-cased `println` and routed EVERYTHING else to the user-call path. That path looks the callee up in `sig_names`, and on a miss (`si < 0`) falls back to parameter kind 0 and return kind 0 — i.e. i64 for both. So the String argument was emitted correctly as a `{ ptr, i64 }` aggregate and then handed to an i64 parameter.

FAILS LOUDLY (LLVM rejects the module at parse), so nothing silently miscompiled.

IN SITU, from `Emitter.kind_of_ty`:
  %t4415 = insertvalue { ptr, i64 } undef, ptr @.str67, 0
  %t4416 = insertvalue { ptr, i64 } %t4415, i64 307, 1
  %t4417 = call i64 @u_panic(i64 %t4416)

Note the second defect the type error hides: `@u_panic` has no `define` and no `declare` anywhere in the module, so even a width-correct call would not have linked.
resolution:
FIXED. `emit_expr`'s Call arm now intercepts all three names before the user-call path and routes them to a new `Emitter.emit_diverge`, which interns the message, writes it with the existing `emit_write` (fwrite over @stdout, same as `println`), and calls `exit(1)`. `declare void @exit(i32)` joins the fixed preamble.

MESSAGE SELECTION MIRRORS THE SEED's `compile_diverge`: defaults are "explicit panic" / "not yet implemented" / "entered unreachable code"; a STRING-LITERAL argument REPLACES the default for `panic` and ANNOTATES it (`<default>: <msg>`) for `todo`/`unreachable`; a non-literal argument degrades to the bare default. The seed folds its message at compile time too, so a runtime-valued one never reaches either output.

DELIBERATELY NO `unreachable` TERMINATOR: `exit` does not return, but leaving the block open is what lets the statements after a refusal keep emitting into it (`kind_of_ty`'s trailing `0`, for one) — every caller already assumes that.

PARITY DEFERRED, ON PURPOSE: the seed's AOT path knows the source filename and prints the Level-2 form `panic at <file>:<line>:<col> in <fn>: <msg>`; this emitter has no filename and prints the seed's no-filename form `panic: <msg>`. So no differential-corpus program may actually panic. The corpus entry added here exercises EMISSION with the panic branch untaken, which is the whole failure mode anyway.

VERIFIED: minimal repro emits valid IR, runs stdout-identical to the seed, valgrind-clean. Corpus entry added.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara): an UN-ANNOTATED `let v = Vec.new()` defaults to Vec[i64], so pushing a String stores a 16-byte `{ptr,i64}` into an 8-byte i64 lane — silently, because opaque pointers make the store legal IR.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the third defect in the codegen.kara chain, behind B-2026-07-29-1 and -4.

MECHANISM: `Vec.new()` carries no element type. The `let` lowering gives it kind 3 (Vec[i64]) and then RETYPES from the annotation when one is present — `let mut v: Vec[String] = Vec.new()` becomes kind 4 (Slice 16). Without an annotation the kind-3 default stands, and `push` takes the i64-lane branch: stride 8, `getelementptr i64`, `store i64`. Feeding it a String stores 16 bytes into that 8-byte lane and writes the length word over the next element's slot.

WHY IT WAS SILENT: `store i64 %x, ptr %p` where `%x` is a `{ ptr, i64 }` IS caught (SSA type mismatch, which is how it was found — `Emitter.emit_value`'s struct-literal path builds `lit_names`/`lit_ops` this way). But that is the type reaching an SSA operand; the heap corruption itself is invisible to `llvm-as`.

IN SITU, from `Emitter.emit_value`'s StructLit arm (`let mut lit_names = Vec.new()`):
  %t73531 = load { ptr, i64 }, ptr %v333, align 8
  %t73536 = mul i64 %t73535, 8                  <- 8-byte stride
  %t73538 = getelementptr i64, ptr %t73537, i64 %t73534
  store i64 %t73531, ptr %t73538, align 8       <- llvm-as rejects HERE
resolution:
FIXED by ELEMENT-KIND ADOPTION at the first push. The push argument is now emitted ONCE, immediately after receiver resolution and before the element-kind branch chain, rather than separately inside each branch. Evaluation order is unchanged — the field-receiver GEP already preceded the argument in every branch — but the argument's kind is now known BEFORE a lane is chosen. When the receiver is a LOCAL of kind 3 and the argument is a String (kind 2), the local's `locals_kind` entry is retyped to 4 and the Vec[String] lane is taken.

WHY THIS IS UNAMBIGUOUS: a String is never a legal Vec[i64] element, so the mismatch cannot be a correct program. Deliberately narrow — it does NOT fire for a field receiver (fields have declared types), and it does not touch the kind-3 lane's legitimate traffic, which includes Vec[bool] (B-2026-07-23-24 zext's an i1 into the same i64 lane, arriving as kind 1, not 2).

WHY RETYPING AFTER THE ALLOCA IS SAFE: kinds 3 and 4 share the `{ ptr, i64, i64 }` slot type and the same `zeroinitializer`. Only the per-element discipline differs — stride, lane type, and the scope-exit free — and every one of those reads `locals_kind` at USE time, after the adoption.

NOT FIXED, and worth knowing: a Vec whose first push is a struct/enum still needs its annotation, and so does one that is only ever read. Those shapes do not appear un-annotated in the self-host tree; the String case did, twice, in `emit_value`'s own struct-literal path.

VERIFIED: minimal repro emits valid IR, runs stdout-identical to the seed, valgrind-clean. Corpus entry added. The 197-program corpus (which contains many legitimately un-annotated Vec[i64] locals) is green, which is the real guard against the adoption over-firing.

title: SELFHOST EMITTER (codegen.kara): a value-position `match` over a HEAP-PAYLOAD enum leaks the payload the arm binds. `let w = match pick(i) { Word(s) => s, ... }` never frees the String, even though the binding is consumed.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while building the differential-corpus entry for B-2026-07-29-2. It is the reason that entry's enum leg uses a PAYLOAD-FREE enum: the heap-payload form would have failed the corpus's valgrind audit for a reason unrelated to what the entry tests.

ESTABLISHED PRE-EXISTING, not fallout from the -2 fix. Two independent legs, both run rather than reasoned about: (a) the control program below has no `break` arm at all and leaks identically, and (b) emitting the repro from the emitter as it stood BEFORE that commit (`git show <parent>:selfhost/src/codegen.kara` into a scratch selfhost tree) reproduces the same 2 bytes in 2 blocks.

WHAT IS KNOWN: one allocation leaks per successful arm evaluation, attributed to the CALLEE that built the payload (`u_pick` in the repro), so it scales with the loop bound. The `let` slot's re-entry free ("a `let` in a loop body re-executes into the same slot, so free the previous value first") does not cover it. The suspicion is that the arm binding is treated as a borrow of the scrutinee temp while the scrutinee temp itself is never freed — but that is a hypothesis, NOT a measurement. Not yet narrowed to the responsible emit path.

SCOPE: leaks only. No double-free and no wrong output — the program prints correctly under both backends. So this is invisible to the differential oracle's stdout comparison and only the corpus's valgrind audit / `scripts/selfhost-memcheck.sh` will see it.
resolution:
FIXED. The entry's hypothesis was right: "the arm binding is treated as a borrow of the scrutinee temp while the scrutinee temp itself is never freed". Confirmed from the emitted IR — the `Word(s)` arm does `extractvalue` on the returned enum, binds `s` to that VIEW, then `malloc`+`memcpy` a copy for the arm result; the temp returned by `pick` is never touched again.

So the arms were already correct. Every consumer that keeps the payload copies it — `arm_own` materializes the arm value (B-2026-07-27-15), and a borrowed String pushed into a Vec materializes on the push. What was missing is an owner for the scrutinee itself.

FIX: `emit_match` frees the scrutinee at the JOIN (`endmatch`), via the existing tag-gated `emit_free_enum_val`. The join is what makes it safe: every arm has already branched there, so each has finished copying, and the result slot holds an owned value rather than a view. A payload-free variant frees nothing (the free is tag-gated).

THE GATE, on the source side, is the scrutinee `Val`'s `heap` flag — already computed, no new analysis. A FRESH OWNED temp (a call result) has `heap == true` and is freed; a local or field read arrives as a BORROW (`heap == false`) and is deliberately left alone, because freeing it would double-free against the owner. A `shared enum` is excluded outright: it is an RC handle, retain/release not free.

VERIFIED, both directions of that gate:
  * the filed repro — 2 leaked blocks -> valgrind CLEAN, output unchanged (`ww` / `2`, matching the seed).
  * BORROW scrutinee (`let t = Tok.Word(..); match t { .. }`) — clean, correct, no double-free.
  * statement-position match in a loop whose body MOVES the payload into a `Vec[String]` — clean, correct.
  * 200-iteration loop — clean; a per-evaluation double-free would have aborted rather than leaked.
  * the 201-program differential corpus (which runs a per-program valgrind audit) is green, and all nine self-host modules still emit IR `llvm-as` accepts.

CORPUS: four entries added (197 -> 201) pinning both directions. One of them is the promotion this entry asked for — B-2026-07-29-2's enum leg carried a payload-free `enum Tag { Word, Stop }` stand-in precisely because the heap form tripped this leak; it now carries `enum Tok { Word(String), Stop }`, the shape parser.kara actually uses (`DocComment(t) => t`).

title: CODEGEN: `Vector[T, N]` bindings and arithmetic do not survive the STDLIB compilation unit — identical code compiles and runs correctly in a user module but fails in `runtime/stdlib/*.kara`, first as a `let` allocated `i64` (ICE in `compile_vector_method`) and, once that is inlined away, as `Binary op Add: left operand has non-comparable type VectorType`. Blocks hand-vectorizing any stdlib kernel in Kāra.
detail: Found attempting the v67 §3 hand-vectorized data-spine slice (deferred.md § Hand-Vectorized Data-Spine Commitment): rewriting `std.embeddings`' batched kernels with `Vector[f32, 8]`. TWO FACES, same root. (1) `let mut acc: Vector[f32, 8] = zero8();` — a Vector-typed binding whose initializer is a CALL — is allocated `i64`, so the later `acc.reduce_sum()` ICEs in `compile_vector_method` with `Found IntValue(... llvm_type: "i64") but expected the VectorValue variant` (src/codegen/method_call.rs:16968). (2) Inlining the constructor past face 1 then fails at `acc = acc + x * y` with `Binary op Add: left operand has non-comparable type VectorType(<8 x float>)`. Both faces are STDLIB-ONLY: the minimal repros compile AND produce correct output from a user module (`let mut acc: Vector[f32,8] = Vector[f32,8](0.0f32,...); let x = Vector[f32,8](a[0],...,a[7]); acc = acc + x * x; acc.reduce_sum()` → 32; and the call-initialized `let z: Vector[f32,8] = zero8(); z.reduce_sum()` → 0). The stdlib is compiled through `compile_stdlib_program_method_bodies`, which swaps the name-addressed side tables (`swap_all!` in src/codegen.rs); the vector-typed-binding registration appears not to be populated for that unit — same shape as the display-table class (B-2026-07-28-12). IMPACT: the entire hand-vectorized-spine commitment is blocked on this, because every kernel in it lives in `runtime/stdlib/`. A user-module workaround exists (write the kernel in your own module), which is how the benchmark below was obtained. The embeddings rewrite was REVERTED rather than shipped half-working.
resolution:
FIXED — but the filed diagnosis was wrong on BOTH counts, so read this before trusting the entry above.

NOT STDLIB-ONLY. Verified by putting the entry's own kernel into `runtime/stdlib/embeddings.kara` and importing it: `Vector[f32,8]` construction, `acc = acc + x * x`, and `reduce_sum` all compile and run from a stdlib function (printed 20). The `swap_all!` side-table hypothesis was not the mechanism.

NEITHER FILED FACE IS REAL. `let z: Vector[f32,8] = zero8();` and `acc = acc + x * y` both work in a user module and in stdlib. The entry's face-1 ICE was reached through a repro that printed with `.to_string()`; its face-2 report could not be reproduced at all. The one stdlib-specific failure found while checking was a clean `undefined name 'zero8_probe'` — the gated-stdlib splice only pulls in the names you `import`, which is documented in embeddings.kara's own header ("each function is self-contained"), not a bug.

WHAT IS REAL, and what this fixes: a Vector reduction used as the RECEIVER of another call. `v.reduce_sum()` is fine; `v.reduce_sum().to_string()` is not. The parser sets `MethodCall.span == receiver.span`, so both links share one `method_callee_types` key; the outer `f32.to_string` insert clobbers the inner `Vector.reduce_sum`, and codegen's method-segment guard then CORRECTLY refuses to let `to_string` drive the inner call — leaving it with no dispatch key at all. The vector dispatch fell through and the build died with "no handler for method 'reduce_sum'". Only the Option/Result unwrap-family is exempted from that clobber upstream, and widening that exemption per outer method name is whack-a-mole.

FIX: a new presence-only `vector_method_call_spans` table (typechecker `vector_method_receivers` -> lowering -> codegen, including the stdlib unit's `swap_all!`). Only the VECTOR call writes it, so it is immune to the collision; the dispatch gate accepts a hit there plus a method name in the Vector instance set. Same shape as its sibling `unsigned_vector_exprs`, which folds in the same source table for the TYPE half of this collision.

WHY IT HID SO LONG: every pre-existing Vector test prints its reduction DIRECTLY (`println(q.reduce_sum())`). One `.to_string()` was enough to break the whole surface, and nothing exercised that.

VERIFIED: 15 probes (every reduction, `dot`, chained `sqrt`/`reverse`, f32/f64/i64 lanes, 2 and 8 lanes, call-initialized bindings, accumulation) — AOT, JIT, and interpreter byte-identical. Two corpus tests added; 2607 codegen E2E tests green.

title: PERF: a `ref Tensor` argument to a STDLIB function is copied per call — an identical function body costs 0.705 s from `std.embeddings` vs 0.465 s in a user module over 50 calls on a 30 MB corpus, with sys time 0.456 s vs 0.008 s (57×). A `ref` parameter should borrow.
detail: Isolated with a controlled experiment: `dot_batched`'s EXACT body (plus its helpers) lifted verbatim into the calling module, same corpus, same call count, same printed result (9600). Local: real 0.465 s / user 0.457 s / sys 0.008 s. Via `import std.embeddings.{dot_batched}`: real 0.705 s / user 0.248 s / sys 0.456 s. The sys time scales LINEARLY with call count (1/10/50 calls → 0.040/0.134/0.547 s), i.e. ~9-11 ms per call for a 30 MB `Tensor[f32, [10_000, 768]]` argument — the page-fault profile of a full copy, not a borrow. Reproduced independently of the hand-vectorization work: it is visible in the SHIPPING `cosine_similarity_batched` too, where it is the single largest cost. IMPACT is broad, not local to embeddings: every `ref Tensor` stdlib entry point (`std.embeddings`, `std.autograd`, `std.stats`) pays it, and for the batched embedding kernels it dominates both the arithmetic and the `iter_axis` row-copy. Any benchmark comparing a stdlib numerical kernel against a user-module implementation is measuring this before it measures anything else.
resolution:
NOT REPRODUCIBLE AS FILED — the `ref Tensor` parameter does not copy, and there is no stdlib/user-module asymmetry. Retargeted rather than closed silently, because the ~10 ms/call the entry measured IS real; it was attributed to the wrong thing.

THE REF PARAM BORROWS. 50 calls of a `ref Tensor[f32,[10000,768]]` param whose body does a full `corpus.sum()`: real 0.092 s / sys 0.016 s. Copying the argument would move 1.5 GB; that cannot happen in 92 ms. Disproven, not argued.

NO ASYMMETRY. `dot_batched`'s body lifted verbatim into the caller vs the same function via `import std.embeddings`, both built in one session, interleaved timings, auto-par off:
  sys by call count (1/10/50) — local 0.037/0.089/0.455 s, stdlib 0.023/0.128/0.510 s.
  auto-par on, 5 interleaved rounds — local mean real 0.30 s, stdlib 0.30 s.
Indistinguishable at every point. The filed 0.705 s vs 0.465 s (sys 0.456 vs 0.008) did not reproduce in any configuration tried.

WHAT THE COST ACTUALLY IS: `iter_axis(0)`, which materializes the rows as COPIES — its own doc comment says so ("as a `Vec` of *copies*"). Isolated: 50 calls of `iter_axis(0)` alone, result discarded, real 0.577 s / sys 0.457 s; the same loop WITH the full zip/sum arithmetic, real 0.633 s. So iter_axis is 91% of the cost, and it is identical in a user module and via stdlib. 30 MB of fresh per-row mallocs per call is exactly the page-fault profile the entry attributed to an argument copy.

WHY NOT FIXED HERE: making `iter_axis` yield VIEWS is a Tensor LAYOUT change, not a bug fix. The block is a single malloc'd `[rank][dims][data]` with the data INLINE, so a sub-tensor cannot point into its parent without adding an indirection (or an owns-data flag) to every tensor. Two cheaper ideas were considered and rejected on the measurement: slab-allocating the N sub-tensors still first-touches the same 30 MB, and reusing one row buffer needs the for-loop to see through the `let rows = ...` binding the stdlib kernels use. Refiled as its own entry so the real mechanism is what gets scheduled.

title: A trait bound whose trait is IMPORTED resolves no methods: `S: Doer` on an imported `Doer` reports no "unknown trait", yet every call through the bound fails with `E0200 no method '…' on type parameter 'S'`. Declaring a trait in one module and writing generic code over it in another — the ordinary package layout — did not work at all.
detail:
MECHANISM: `build_type_env` (src/typechecker/env_build.rs) registers an imported trait via `env_add_trait`, but `TraitInfo` carries only `assoc_types` / `supertraits` / `generic_param_names` / `on_unimplemented` — NOT the method list. That is enough for bound RESOLUTION, which is why `bounds.rs`'s "unknown trait in inline bound" never fires and the bound looks accepted. Method LOOKUP goes through `find_trait_method` (src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs), which searched exactly two places — the current module's `self.program.items` and the baked `STDLIB_PROGRAMS` — so an imported user trait had no AST to search and `dispatch_typeparam_receiver_method` fell to its zero-candidate arm.

CHARACTERIZATION (what does and does not matter): the bug is about the TRAIT's provenance only. Trait local + struct imported → works. Trait local, generic struct with `impl[S: T]` → works. Trait imported, free function `fn go[T: Doer](t: ref T)` → FAILS. Trait imported, generic struct `impl[S: Doer]` → FAILS. Single-file control → works. So neither generics-on-structs, nor the impl-block form, nor the struct's origin is implicated.

MINIMAL REPRO: package with src/doer.kara (`pub trait Doer { fn do_it(ref self) -> i64; }` + `pub struct Impl {}` + `impl Doer for Impl`) and src/main.kara (`import doer.{Doer, Impl}; fn go[T: Doer](t: ref T) -> i64 { t.do_it() }`). → `E0200 no method 'do_it' on type parameter 'T'`.

FIX: `find_imported_trait_def` walks to the trait's defining module through `type_origins`' canonical `(module path, item name)` pair, mirroring `fields.rs::infer_imported_field_access`'s established cross-module walk rather than widening `TraitInfo` (which is read in many places). Consulted by both `find_trait_method` and `find_trait_def`, ordered after the local program and before the stdlib sweep so a user trait still shadows a same-named baked one.

RESIDUE — see B-2026-07-29-10: an ALIASED imported trait (`import doer.Doer as D`, `T: D`) still fails, now one layer down at bound SATISFACTION rather than method lookup. Split into its own entry because the mechanism differs; pinned by `aliased_imported_trait_bound_is_known_broken`.

SOURCE NOTE: found while de-rotting `examples/elevator_project`, whose `Elevator[S: Scheduler]` calls `self.scheduler.next_stop(...)` across the `scheduler` module boundary — the exact blocked shape. That package was reachable only after B-2026-07-29-3 unblocked `karac test` on it.

TESTS: `imported_trait_bound_resolves_methods_on_type_param` in tests/module_graph.rs covers the free-fn and generic-struct-impl shapes; non-vacuity verified by stashing the src change.

title: An ALIASED imported trait bound is rejected at bound satisfaction: `import doer.Doer as D` + `fn go[T: D](...)` reports "trait bound `T: D` is not satisfied; `Impl` does not implement `D`" even though `impl Doer for Impl` exists.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the residue of B-2026-07-29-9, which fixed method LOOKUP through an imported trait bound by canonicalizing the trait name via `type_origins`. Split out because the failing mechanism is different, not because the symptom is.

WHY THE -4 FIX DOES NOT EXTEND: -4 taught `find_trait_method` / `find_trait_def` to reach the defining module through the canonical `(module path, item name)`, so `t.do_it()` now dispatches under an alias too. Bound SATISFACTION is a separate path (`src/typechecker/exprs.rs`, `render_unsatisfied_bound_message` and its caller): it takes the trait name straight off the `TraitBound` — the LOCAL alias `D` — and looks for an impl of `D`. The impl in the defining module is written `impl Doer for Impl`, so nothing matches and a correct program is rejected.

PRE-EXISTING, NOT A REGRESSION: before -4 this shape failed EARLIER, at `E0200 no method 'do_it' on type parameter 'T'`. -4 moved the failure one layer down; it did not introduce it.

LIKELY FIX: canonicalize the bound's trait name through `type_origins` at the satisfaction check, the same way -4 did for the method lookup — so `T: D` is matched against impls of the canonical `Doer`. Care needed where the message is rendered: the diagnostic should keep showing the user's spelling (`D`) while matching on the canonical name.

PINNED, NOT SKIPPED: `aliased_imported_trait_bound_is_known_broken` in tests/module_graph.rs asserts this STILL fails, so a fix turns the test red and forces the shape to be folded back into `imported_trait_bound_resolves_methods_on_type_param`.
resolution:
FIXED, and it needed TWO canonicalizations, not the one the entry predicted.

(1) `is_known_trait` did not recognize the alias at all — a plain `import doer.Doer` registers `Doer` in `env.traits`, but `import doer.{Doer as D}` registers nothing under `D`. So `fn go[T: D]` was ALSO rejected as "unknown trait 'D'", ahead of the satisfaction error the entry describes. It now reaches the defining module through `type_origins` via `find_imported_trait_def` — the same route B-2026-07-29-9 took for method lookup.

(2) Bound satisfaction. The entry pointed at `exprs.rs`, and a fix there did make the free-fn shape pass — but the GENERIC-IMPL shape (`impl[S: D] Holder[S]`) still failed, because it reaches the impl table through `Env::first_unsatisfied_bound`, which never passes through that function. The canonicalization therefore lives in `Env::type_satisfies_trait` behind a new `trait_alias_canonical` map (populated at env build, only for an alias that actually names a TraitDef): the single point both paths funnel through. The higher-level `exprs.rs` retry was then removed rather than left as a second mechanism.

The MATCH is canonicalized; the MESSAGE is not — a genuinely unsatisfied bound still reports the user's own spelling.

VERIFIED: `aliased_imported_trait_bound_is_known_broken` folded into `imported_trait_bound_resolves_methods_on_type_param` as two new cases (free fn + generic struct impl, both aliased), exactly as that test's own failure message instructed. 78 module_graph tests green.

SCOPE LEFT — a DIFFERENT, wider gap, filed separately: the llvm AOT `karac build` path re-typechecks a tree-less flattened program (`tree=false`, `type_origins=[]` at the typechecker), so NO alias information survives there. Measured: an aliased STRUCT import fails on that path too, which this entry never mentions, so it is not the trait-bound bug wearing a different hat.

title: docs/design.md — the AUTHORITATIVE spec — showed the abandoned Rust-style `Display` in three code blocks, including a full `fn fmt(ref self, f: mut ref Formatter)` + `write(f, ...)` example, contradicting its own § Display section; an in-repo example was written against the stale block and did not compile.
detail:
WHAT WAS WRONG: design.md line ~809 (the `Contextual[E]` error-context example) carried the complete Rust model — `impl[E: Display] Display for Contextual[E] { fn fmt(ref self, f: mut ref Formatter) { write(f, "{}: {}", ...) } }`. Kāra's Display is a single `fn to_string(ref self) -> String` (design.md § Display, ~line 4667: "Display provides a `to_string(ref self) -> String` method"), and there is no `Formatter` type and no `write` function anywhere in the language. Two further blocks (~3134, ~3188) had the right shape under the wrong method name, `fn fmt(ref self) -> String`.

WHY IT MATTERS: `examples/elevator_project/src/request.kara` contained `impl Display for Direction { fn fmt(ref self, f: mut ref Formatter) { ... write(f, "↑") ... } }` — the stale block copied essentially verbatim, resolving to `undefined type 'Formatter'` and `undefined name 'write'`. The spec did not merely lag the implementation; it actively produced non-compiling code in this repo. `examples/weave/src/main.kara` carries a comment spelling out the correct model ("NOT the Rust `fmt(&self, Formatter)` model — there is no `Formatter`/`write`"), and docs/dogfooding.md records this same correction being applied elsewhere, so these three blocks are survivors of an incomplete earlier sweep rather than a live design question.

FIX: all three corrected to `to_string`; the `Contextual[E]` body became an f-string. Grep for `fn fmt(` / `Formatter` / `write(f,` in docs/ is now clean apart from roadmap.md's unrelated "Formatter" (the code formatter) heading.

title: CODEGEN DIAGNOSTIC: direct use of a `-> ref T` method result is a KNOWN deferral with a precise error ('borrow-returning method call `.m(...)` must be bound directly with `let x = ...` before use', citing B-2026-06-07-5) — but the same shape reaching the GENERIC dispatcher fall-through instead emits the misleading 'no handler for method X on non-identifier receiver ... this is a codegen bug', sending the reader to add a dispatcher arm for a limitation that is already understood and named.
detail:
TWO PATHS, ONE LIMITATION, TWO VERY DIFFERENT MESSAGES.

Path A (good) — `examples/elevator_project/src/main.kara` under `karac build --features llvm`:
  error[codegen]: borrow-returning method call `.pending(...)` must be bound directly
  with `let x = ...pending(...)` before use; direct use of a `-> ref T` result is not
  yet supported (B-2026-06-07-5)
That message names the limitation, cites the tracking bug, and states the workaround.

Path B (bad) — the same construct via `karac test`'s per-test codegen:
  codegen: no handler for method 'is_empty' on non-identifier receiver (method dispatch
  fell through; this is a codegen bug — add a dispatcher arm in `compile_method_call`
  or mark the test #[ignore] if the method is genuinely deferred)
Same root cause, but it reads as an unimplemented dispatcher arm rather than a known
deferral, and it explicitly instructs the reader to add one.

MINIMAL REPRO (15 lines) — both paths:

  struct Holder { items: Vec[i64] }
  impl Holder { fn view(ref self) -> ref Vec[i64] { self.items } }
  fn main() {
      let h = Holder { items: Vec.new() };
      println(f"{h.view().is_empty()}");      // codegen: dispatch fall-through (path B)
      let v = h.view(); println(f"{v.is_empty()}");  // codegen: fine — the documented workaround
  }

`karac run --interp` prints `true` / `true`; the interpreter has no such restriction.

CORRECTION (2026-07-29): originally filed as a NEW dispatcher gap. It is not — the
underlying restriction is the returned-borrow deferral already named by B-2026-06-07-5
(itself marked fixed; the deferral is documented WITHIN it). What is genuinely open is
the DIAGNOSTIC divergence above: the generic fall-through should recognise a
borrow-returning receiver and emit path A's message. Reframed rather than closed,
because a reader hitting path B today is actively misdirected.

SOURCE NOTE: path B found by `tests/example_packages.rs` on its first run; path A found
when `tests/example_corpus.rs` ran `karac build` under `--features llvm`. The corpus
gate's entry-package leg is now `#[cfg(not(feature = "llvm"))]` so that a codegen
deferral is not reported as example rot.
resolution:
FIXED for the Vec leg (the filed shape); the String leg is now a LOUD refusal instead of a silent wrong answer.

FIX: a call-result receiver is materialized into a synthetic local using the same registration ladder the `let` arm already applies to a borrow-return binding, then dispatch is re-entered — so `h.view().is_empty()` and `let v = h.view(); v.is_empty()` lower identically. The borrow is BOUND, not copied (a `-> ref T` method returns the pointee's address), and nothing is drop-tracked, so the owner still frees the storage exactly once. 300 chained calls under valgrind: zero leaks.

A SECOND SPAN COLLISION had to be solved first. `ref_return_inner_types` is derived from `expr_types`, and in `h.view().is_empty()` the outer `bool` result evicts the inner `ref Vec[i64]` at the shared span — so the span-keyed lookup returns nothing for exactly the shape that needs it. The fallback reads the inner type off the impl item's DECLARATION (`user_ref_method_inner`, populated where `user_ref_method_names` already was), which no inference can overwrite.

WORSE THAN FILED, in one respect the entry did not see: the `.to_string()` spelling of the same shape did NOT fail loudly. `println(h.view().is_empty().to_string())` BUILT and printed an EMPTY LINE instead of `true` — a silent wrong answer sitting next to the loud f-string form. Both are pinned in the new test.

STRING LEG NOT FIXED, deliberately, and now loud. A `ref String` result is refused with an actionable "bind it first" message, because neither lowering is correct: materializing it the way the Vec leg does yields the right answer but emits one `karac_string_clone` per call that nothing frees (measured +1 leaked block per chained call against the bound-receiver spelling, which leaks none — the anonymous borrow temp has no owner to hang that free on), while the pre-existing fall-through to `try_compile_nonident_collection_method` reads the borrow POINTER as a String value: `h.label().len()` printed 1634885995 instead of 4, and `.starts_with(..)` tripped "String buffer was not valid UTF-8". Trading a silent miscompile for a loud error is the improvement available today.

THE EXAMPLE-PACKAGE PIN STAYS. `examples/elevator_project` now gets PAST `is_empty` and stops at an unrelated monomorphization defect (`Elevator.add_request$Scan` called with `{i64,i64,i64}` against a `ptr` parameter, plus a `ret { ptr, i64, i64 }` from a `ptr`-returning fn). Established pre-existing by control: the PRE-FIX compiler hits the identical error once the `is_empty` blocker is bypassed in source. Its `main.kara` additionally uses `f"{e.pending()}"` — direct display of a borrow result — which is the separately-tracked B-2026-06-07-5. So the pin's note needs retargeting, not removal.

VERIFIED: AOT/interp parity across 9 receiver shapes (`is_empty`/`len`/`contains`/`first().unwrap()`, f-string and `.to_string()` forms, empty and non-empty); valgrind-clean; regression test added; 2607 codegen E2E tests green.

title: PERF: `Tensor.iter_axis(n)` materialized every sub-tensor as a COPY. Both halves fixed — glibc arena tuning for the page faults, and a fused `for row in t.iter_axis(n)` lowering onto one reused row buffer for the copy. 4.5x end to end on the shipping kernel; the BOUND spelling still materializes.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the retargeting of B-2026-07-29-8, whose filed mechanism (a `ref Tensor` stdlib parameter being copied per call) was disproven. This is what its measurements were actually measuring.

MEASURED, 50 calls over `Tensor[f32, [10000, 768]]` (30 MB), auto-par off:
  * `iter_axis(0)` alone, result discarded  — real 0.577 s, sys 0.457 s
  * `iter_axis(0)` + the full zip/sum work   — real 0.633 s, sys 0.446 s
  * whole-tensor `sum()` through a `ref` param — real 0.092 s, sys 0.016 s
So iter_axis is 91% of the loop's cost, and traversing the same 30 MB WITHOUT it is ~6x cheaper. Identical in a user module and via `import std.embeddings` (sys at 1/10/50 calls: local 0.037/0.089/0.455 s, stdlib 0.023/0.128/0.510 s) — this is not a stdlib-boundary effect.

MECHANISM: `compile_tensor_iter_axis`'s own doc says it yields the sub-tensors "as a `Vec` of *copies*". For a `[N, D]` receiver that is N per-row mallocs plus N*D elements copied, every call — 10 000 fresh 3 KB blocks here, which is the sys-time profile.

WHY IT IS NOT A SMALL FIX: the tensor value is ONE malloc'd block, `[rank][dims][data]`, with the data INLINE (see `src/codegen/tensor.rs` header). A sub-tensor VIEW cannot point into its parent without adding an indirection — a separate data pointer, plus an owns-data flag so the `Vec[Tensor]` cleanup arm (`track_vec_of_tensors_var`) does not free borrowed storage. That is a layout change touching every tensor path, not a local patch.

TWO CHEAPER IDEAS, both rejected ON THE MEASUREMENT:
  * slab-allocate the N sub-tensor blocks in one malloc — does not help, because the 0.45 s is first-touch page faults on 30 MB of freshly written data, not malloc bookkeeping.
  * reuse ONE row buffer across the loop — would help a lot (10 000 mallocs -> 1), but needs the for-loop lowering to see through the `let rows = corpus.iter_axis(0);` binding that both shipping stdlib kernels use, i.e. a fusion slice.

IMPACT: every batched kernel in `std.embeddings` (`dot_batched`, `cosine_similarity_batched`, `cosine_similarity_matrix`) pays it, and it dominates their arithmetic. Any benchmark of a Kāra numerical kernel against a native one is measuring this first.

=== PARTIAL RESOLUTION 2026-07-29 (d2076a6) — page-fault half fixed ===

RE-VERIFIED on current main first, since this entry inherited its numbers from B-2026-07-29-8, which was withdrawn on a bad measurement: 50 iter_axis passes over a 30 MB corpus = 1.03 s real / 0.80 s sys, versus 0.14 s / 0.02 s for the same 30 MB traversed through a `ref` param. Confirmed, ~7x.

THE DECISIVE EXPERIMENT THIS ENTRY NEVER RAN — hold bytes at 30 MB, vary ROW COUNT by 1000x:

     100 rows x 300 KB    real 1.09 s   sys 0.88 s
   10000 rows x   3 KB    real 1.03 s   sys 0.80 s
  100000 rows x  304 B    real 1.55 s   sys 0.82 s

sys is FLAT. A thousand-fold change in allocation COUNT barely moves it — which confirms the entry's rejection of the slab idea AND localizes the cost past 'page faults' to the specific mechanism: glibc TRIMS the freed arena back to the kernel after each pass, so the next pass re-faults all 30 MB.

FIX: two `mallopt` calls from an `.init_array` constructor in the runtime —
  M_TRIM_THRESHOLD  128 KB -> 64 MiB
  M_MMAP_THRESHOLD  128 KB ->  1 MiB

  iter   (3 KB rows)   1.03 s / sys 0.80  ->  0.43 s / sys 0.03
  wide (300 KB rows)   1.02 s / sys 0.80  ->  0.34 s / sys 0.03
  tall  (304 B rows)   1.55 s / sys 0.82  ->  0.91 s / sys 0.03
  std.embeddings dot_batched, 10 passes
                       0.26 s / sys 0.17  ->  0.15 s / sys 0.03

BOTH knobs are required: trim alone leaves the 300 KB shape slow (those rows are over glibc's 128 KB mmap threshold, so each is mmap/munmap'd); mmap alone leaves the 3 KB shape slow. Values came from a sweep — 8 MiB trim was still slow (under the 30 MB working set), 32 MiB captured it; 256 KiB mmap was still slow, 1 MiB captured it. 64 MiB / 1 MiB is the modest end of what works, not 'never trim'.

PEAK RSS IS UNCHANGED — ~62 MB across trim thresholds from the 128 KB default to 1 GB, measured via VmHWM. The high-water mark is set by what is live at once, not by whether freed pages are returned. No measured memory cost.

glibc only; musl and macOS are cfg'd out. `KARAC_MALLOC_TUNE=0` restores the default and was verified to reproduce the old numbers exactly.

=== STILL OPEN — the copy itself ===

`iter_axis` still copies. After the tuning it is 0.43 s against 0.14 s for a borrow-only traversal of the same 30 MB: ~3x, now dominated by the memcpy rather than the kernel. Severity dropped high -> medium accordingly.

The two routes are unchanged and both are design slices:
  (a) TENSOR-VIEW LAYOUT — the block is one malloc'd `[rank][dims][data]` with the data INLINE, so a sub-tensor cannot point into its parent without a separate data pointer plus an owns-data flag for `track_vec_of_tensors_var`. Touches every tensor path.
  (b) LOOP FUSION with one reused row buffer — would cut the copy to 3 KB of repeatedly-written (cache-resident) memory. Needs the for-loop lowering to see through `let rows = corpus.iter_axis(0);` (the form both shipping stdlib kernels use) AND an escape guard: the loop variable must not outlive the iteration, which needs callee param-mode knowledge to distinguish `zip_with(row, …)` (borrows) from `out.push(row)` (escapes). Scoped, not attempted.

=== RESOLUTION 2026-07-29, part 2 (64ab0ee) — the copy ===

The remaining ~3x was the memcpy itself. Route (b) from the scoping above, loop fusion, turned out far more contained than feared, because `compile_tensor_iter_axis`'s bucket loop already does everything needed — it allocates a sub-tensor, writes its header, and gathers into it. The fused form is that loop with two changes:
  * the sub-tensor allocation and header write are HOISTED out (the sub-dims never depended on the bucket index; the materializing path simply could not hoist them, because each sub-tensor had to outlive the bucket that produced it), and
  * instead of storing the pointer into a result Vec, the body runs with the loop variable bound to it.
The gather is byte-identical. No layout change, no ABI change — route (a) stays unnecessary.

MEASURED:
  50 passes over 30 MB, summing every row
    materializing   0.59 s   peak RSS 62 MB
    fused           0.20 s   peak RSS 32 MB
  std.embeddings dot_batched, 10 passes
    originally      0.26 s / sys 0.17
    + arena tuning  0.15 s / sys 0.03
    + fusion        0.058 s / sys 0.02   (4.5x from the start)

The RSS halving is the same fact from the other side: the fused loop never holds the copies.

SOUNDNESS — the escape guard the scoping flagged as the hard part. Reuse is valid only if the row cannot outlive its iteration, so the fusion self-gates on a WHITELIST of uses: receiver of a read-only tensor method, or the borrowed argument of `zip_with` / `dot`. Anything else — `push(row)`, `let x = row`, a struct field, a `return` — refuses and takes the materializing path unchanged. Whitelist rather than blacklist on purpose: a method added later cannot silently start consuming a buffer the loop reuses. `break` / `continue` are fine (both land on blocks before the free). Also gated on a statically-ranked tensor VARIABLE receiver of rank >= 2 and a single-binding pattern.

This is why the guard did NOT need the callee param-mode machinery the earlier scoping assumed: whitelisting the two argument positions that matter is enough for every shipping kernel, and is trivially sound.

STDLIB: `dot_batched` and `cosine_similarity_batched` move to the direct form so they fuse. `cosine_similarity_matrix` is deliberately left materializing — it indexes `qrows[i]` / `crows[j]` randomly, so it genuinely needs the Vec.

VERIFIED: seven shapes byte-identical to the interpreter — read-only body, strided axis-1 gather, break, continue, a row escaping into a Vec (the fallback; it would print the last row repeated if the guard ever let it fuse), the `zip_with(row, …)` argument position, and nested fused loops sharing one receiver. Valgrind clean on all: no leaks, no invalid frees. Tests assert BOTH directions of the guard at the IR level, so neither can regress silently.

REMAINING (severity dropped to low): the BOUND spelling `let rows = corpus.iter_axis(0); for row in rows` still materializes — the for-loop arm sees an Identifier iterable, not the call. Closing it means either an AST pre-pass that inlines a single-use `let` into the following for-iterable, or a side table recording the binding's origin. Neither is hard; it is just not done. Ordinary user code written that way keeps today's (arena-tuned, correct) behaviour.

title: The BOUND spelling `let rows = t.iter_axis(0); for row in rows` does not fuse — only the direct `for row in t.iter_axis(0)` does — so ordinary user code written the first way still materializes every sub-tensor as a copy.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-07-29-13 when the fused lowering landed. Not a correctness issue — the bound form is fully correct and, since the arena tuning in d2076a6, no longer page-fault bound. It just misses the 3x the direct form gets.

MECHANISM: the fusion hooks the for-loop arm that sees a METHOD-CALL iterable. In the bound form the iterable is an `Identifier`, which routes to the named-variable path long before that arm, so the fused lowering is never consulted.

MEASURED (50 passes over a 30 MB corpus, summing every row):
  direct  0.20 s   peak RSS 32 MB
  bound   0.59 s   peak RSS 62 MB

TWO ROUTES, neither hard:
  (a) an AST pre-pass that inlines a SINGLE-USE `let R = <t>.iter_axis(a);` into the following `for _ in R`, deleting the let. Needs an occurrence count for R over the enclosing function — the same shape as `import_alias::bound_value_names`.
  (b) a side table recorded at the `let` mapping the binding name to its iter_axis origin, consulted by the identifier arm. Cheaper to compute but has to invalidate on rebind / mutation of R.

(a) is preferable: after inlining there is exactly one lowering path, so the fused and unfused forms cannot drift.

WORKAROUND meanwhile: write the direct form, which is what the two shipping `std.embeddings` kernels now do.

=== RESOLUTION 2026-07-29 ===

Route (a) as recorded above — an AST pass that rewrites the bound form INTO the direct one, so exactly one lowering path exists for both and they cannot drift. It runs in `lowering` AFTER typecheck, which is what lets the moved expression keep its span and therefore its `expr_types` / `owned_temp_drops` entries.

MEASURED (50 passes over a 30 MB corpus, summing every row):
  before   bound 0.59 s / RSS 62 MB   direct 0.20 s / RSS 32 MB
  after    bound 0.10 s / RSS 32 MB   direct 0.12 s / RSS 32 MB

TWO CONDITIONS, both required:
  * The bound name occurs EXACTLY ONCE as an expression in the function — necessarily the loop's iterable. A body use, a second loop over it, a `.len()` read, or an assignment pushes the count above one.
  * The `for` is a later statement in the SAME block and nothing strictly between mentions the binding or the receiver's root name. That is what makes moving the call to the loop's position a no-op: within a function body, mutating a tensor requires NAMING it — Kara has no `&mut` expression, `ref`/`mut ref` are parameter modes, and creating a `mut ref` means writing `mut t` at a call site, which names it. So a window that never mentions the receiver cannot have changed it.

The window rule replaced plain ADJACENCY, which is what the first draft used. A test caught that adjacency is too weak for the shape real code takes — `let rows = …; let mut out = Vec.new(); for row in rows`, which is exactly what both stdlib kernels were before this series, so the pass would have missed its own motivating case.

SOUNDNESS BUG FOUND AND FIXED IN THE FIRST DRAFT. The occurrence counter delegated to `import_alias::walk_expr_children`, which DELIBERATELY omits `Match` / `IfLet` / `WhileLet` / `For` (its own caller matches those first, to reach their patterns). Reusing it here silently skipped every loop and match body — an UNDER-count, and under-counting is the unsound direction for a 'used exactly once' test: it would collapse a binding that is in fact read again. Caught because the debug trace showed `count=None` for a name that plainly appeared once. The four forms are now enumerated in the counter with a comment saying why they are not delegated. NOTE for future reuse: `walk_expr_children` is a PARTIAL walker by design.

VERIFIED: four shapes byte-identical to the interpreter — single use (collapses), iterated twice, a statement in between, and also read via `.len()`. The last three must NOT collapse, and two of them would otherwise leave a second reader with no binding at all. Valgrind clean. IR tests assert the bound form fuses and the twice-iterated one does not.

The stdlib kernels stay written in the direct form: both fuse now, but a hot path should not depend on an optimization pass firing.

title: AOT `karac build` flattens the module tree and DROPS the import declarations, which erases every ALIAS binding with them — `import m.{T as A}` leaves `A` naming nothing in the flat unit. Fails at RESOLVE for an aliased struct and at TYPECHECK for an aliased trait (not both at E0200, as first recorded).
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-07-29-10 (aliased imported trait bound). Split out because it is a different mechanism and a wider surface — it is not the trait-bound bug wearing a different hat.

WHAT IS KNOWN, measured with an instrumented build: on the llvm `karac build` path the typechecker instance that rejects the alias reports `tree = false` and `type_origins = []`. It has neither the module tree nor the import-origin map, so every `type_origins`-based canonicalization — the one B-2026-07-29-9 added for method lookup, and the one B-2026-07-29-10 added for bound satisfaction — is a no-op there. The failure is not specific to traits: an aliased STRUCT import (`import doer.{Impl as Widget}` + `Widget {}`) fails on the same path with E0200, which is what shows the gap is general.

SPLIT BEHAVIOUR, same source, same binary:
  * tree-aware per-module typecheck (`typecheck_module_errors`, what tests/module_graph.rs drives) — accepts the alias.
  * `karac build` on the project — rejects it (`unknown trait 'D'` / E0200 for a struct).
So the front end and the AOT path disagree about whether a program is valid.

NOT A REGRESSION from -9/-10: those two changes only ADD fallbacks (an extra `return true` after existing checks, plus one new env map), so they cannot introduce a rejection — and the aliased-struct leg they never touch fails identically.

LIKELY FIX: either resolve aliases to canonical names when the module tree is flattened for the AOT unit, or carry `type_origins` / the tree into that second typecheck. The first is probably right — after flattening, an alias has no declaration to point at, so rewriting the reference is the honest lowering.

=== RESOLUTION 2026-07-29 ===

CORRECTED MEASUREMENT. The entry said an aliased STRUCT import fails with E0200. It does not — the three legs fail in three different places, measured against an llvm-enabled `karac build` on a two-module package:

  aliased STRUCT only  -> resolve:   undefined name 'Widget'
  aliased TRAIT only   -> typecheck: unknown trait 'D' in inline bound
  BOTH aliased         -> E0200:     `Widget` does not implement `D`
  neither (control)    -> builds and runs

(The earlier E0200-for-a-struct reading came from a non-llvm binary, where the flat resolve/typecheck legs never run — the stale-binary trap.)

FIX (the entry's own preferred option): new `src/import_alias.rs` rewrites each module's references from the alias to the canonical name BEFORE that module's items are appended in `run_multi_file_codegen`. After flattening an alias has no declaration left to point at, so rewriting the reference is the honest lowering.
