The walk reuses `desugar`'s substitution helpers (written for trait type-param substitution, exhaustive over ExprKind / StmtKind / TypeKind, promoted to `pub(crate)`) and adds the three slots an alias needs that a type param does not: trait-bound NAMES, `impl Trait for` names, and pattern paths.

BLAST RADIUS is exactly 'programs using `import … as …`'. A module with no aliased import produces an empty substitution and `rewrite_item` returns immediately, so every other program is copied byte-identically — and every program in scope was rejected outright before. An alias colliding with a local declaration is SKIPPED rather than redirected; the resolver reports that collision on its own terms.

SECOND, SMALLER HALF: `Env::type_alias_canonical`, the type-side twin of the `trait_alias_canonical` retry B-2026-07-29-10 added. The impl table is keyed by the type's own name, so a bound checked against an aliased type matched nothing. -10 shipped with only the trait half because only the both-aliased shape exercises the type half.

TEST: `tests/cli.rs::test_build_project_accepts_aliased_type_and_trait_imports` builds a real two-module package through `karac build`.

NOT FIXED, split out (see B-2026-07-29-22 / -23):
  * BOTH aliased at once still fails E0200. Instrumenting `type_satisfies_trait` shows BOTH retries firing correctly — (Widget, D) -> (Widget, Doer) -> (Impl, Doer) — and `has_impl("Doer", "Impl")` returning FALSE because the importing module's env holds NO (Doer, Impl) entry at all, only stdlib impls. A per-module impl-table gap, upstream of and independent from the flattening bug.
  * An aliased FUNCTION import (`import m.{mk as build}`) still fails resolve. The rewrite deliberately covers TYPE positions only: a bare `Identifier` in value position is left alone because a local binding can legitimately shadow the name, and rewriting it would silently redirect a variable reference.

title: An importing module's per-module env carries NO impl entries from the module it imports from, so a trait bound on an imported type is rejected whenever the impl-table lookup is actually reached (`import m.{Impl as W, Doer as D}` + `run[T: D](w: W)` -> E0200).
An aliased FUNCTION import (`import m.{mk as build}`) still fails the flattened AOT build with `resolve: undefined name`. The B-2026-07-29-14 alias rewrite covers TYPE positions only.

A method on a borrow-returning call result (`h.label().len()` where `label() -> ref String`) had no leak-free lowering, because the materialize-the-borrow helper emitted the accessor TWICE and the extra call's result was leaked. Hoisting the helper ahead of every receiver-compiling arm fixes it; the String refusal, which rested on that mismeasurement, is removed.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the String leg of B-2026-07-29-12, split out when the Vec leg landed. The receiver-materialization fix there was gated to non-String inners on leak evidence that turned out to be an artifact.

ROOT CAUSE (found later than the original diagnosis). `compile_method_call` runs a long ladder of arms, several of which COMPILE THE RECEIVER and then fall through on a miss. `try_compile_ref_return_receiver_method` was added near the END of that ladder, so by the time it ran the receiver had already been emitted, and the helper's own `compile_expr(object)` produced a SECOND call whose result was dropped on the floor:

    %usermethod  = call ptr @H.view(ptr %h)   ; discarded
    %usermethod1 = call ptr @H.view(ptr %h)
    store ptr %usermethod1, ptr %__refrecv_tmp_0

Pure for `view`/`label`, so the Vec leg SHIPPED with this defect and nothing caught it — output assertions cannot see a discarded duplicate call. It is wrong for any accessor with an effect, and for an allocating one the discarded result is leaked outright. That is exactly what the String leg's "+1 leaked block per chained call" measurement was seeing.

THE ORIGINAL ENTRY'S SECOND CLAIM WAS WRONG. It said the bound spelling `let b = h.label(); b.len()` "leaks none". Re-measured under valgrind with the helper hoisted:

    program      h.label() calls   definitely-lost blocks
    lbl1_bound          1                   1
    lbl3_bound          3                   3
    lbl3_chain          3                   3

Leaks scale with accessor INVOCATIONS and are identical in both spellings. The refusal therefore bought nothing — the form it pointed users at leaks the same. The residual per-call `karac_string_clone` is a separate pre-existing leak in `-> ref String` accessors, filed as B-2026-07-29-21.

The OTHER half of the original entry stands and is what the fix preserves: falling through to `try_compile_nonident_collection_method` reads the returned borrow POINTER as if it were the `{ptr,len,cap}` String value — `h.label().len()` printed 1634885995 instead of 4, and `.starts_with("ka")` tripped "String buffer was not valid UTF-8". A silent miscompile.

FIX: move the helper to immediately after the borrow-return direct-use guard, ahead of every arm that compiles the receiver, and delete the String gate. The helper self-gates to a borrow-returning user call, so running it first changes nothing else.

TESTS: `ref_returning_accessor_receiver_is_called_exactly_once` counts `@H.view` / `@H.label` calls in main's emitted IR — the property no output assertion can see, and the one the shipped Vec fix silently violated. Plus `test_e2e_string_method_on_ref_returning_call_receiver` for `.len()`, `.starts_with`, `.to_uppercase`, f-string interpolation and the empty case.

title: OWNERSHIP FALSE POSITIVE in the single-file `karac check` path: a `mut` binding initialized from a FREE FUNCTION and then passed to an IMPORTED `ref` parameter is reported as moved, though the parameter only borrows. The package-level path accepts the identical program and it RUNS correctly.
resolution:
FIXED. The entry's framing was exactly right — `karac check` was the component in the wrong — and the mechanism is one layer below where the two ingredients pointed.

ROOT CAUSE: single-file `karac check <file>` parses ONE file, so an IMPORTED free function has no entry in `callee_param_modes`. Confirmed independently: a deliberately WRONG-ARITY call to the same imported function (`peek(a, 1, 2)`) raises no arity error either — that path simply does not have the signature. With no modes, the args fell to the consume default, which manufactures a move.

WHY THAT DEFAULT IS WRONG HERE: consume-by-default is a safe over-approximation for the RC-promotion side of the ownership pass. It is NOT safe for the use-after-move DIAGNOSTIC, which is a claim about the program — and this one cannot be substantiated, which is why `karac build` (full module tree, real modes) accepts the identical program and it runs correctly.

FIX: args of a callee whose name is IMPORTED and absent from `callee_param_modes` are classified as reads, in BOTH the predicate pipeline (`use_classifier`) and the legacy states machine (`ownership/borrow.rs::arg_is_borrow_position`) — the two must agree or closure classification diverges, a coupling the existing relational-operator gate already exists to preserve.

THE GATE TOOK TWO TRIES, worth recording. Keying on 'nameable callee, no table entry' is too loose: a CLOSURE binding is also a nameable identifier with no entry, and calling one genuinely does consume its owned args. That version regressed closure param-mode inference from `Own` to `Ref` and was caught by `nested_closures_each_get_their_own_mode_entry`. Gating on the name being IMPORTED is precise — only an imported name can be both a real function call AND legitimately absent, and only because its definition lives in another module.

DIRECTIONALITY: this can only ever REMOVE a diagnostic, never add one, and only for a callee whose signature genuinely is not in this unit. A locally-declared or baked-stdlib function always has an entry, so a real move through a known callee is still reported. The package path remains the authority.

VERIFIED: the minimal two-module repro and `examples/game_of_life/src/main.kara` (the motivating case — 14/14 of its own tests pass while `check` called it a move error) both come back clean; a move through a LOCAL owned-param fn and through an owned-self method still report; the package still builds and its 10 tests still pass. Full suites green, 2607 codegen E2E green.

TESTS: two entries pin both directions. Both needed a String field to be NON-VACUOUS — an all-scalar struct is Copy, so no move is possible and the first drafts asserted nothing. The second use also has to be a real consume: `println` args are borrows, so a read-after-move there is not a use-after-move witness. Both traps are noted in the test bodies.

NOTE for the corpus gate: `tests/example_corpus.rs` was shaped by this bug (entry packages verified only with a package-level `karac build`, never per-member `karac check`). That constraint can now be revisited.

title: RESOLVER HOLE: `effect resource R: SomeTrait;` accepts a trait name that is not defined ANYWHERE — no error, all checks pass. The undefined-name check that covers ordinary type positions does not reach an effect resource's trait bound.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO (5 lines, checks CLEAN):

  effect resource Thing: NoSuchTraitAnywhere;

  fn main() {
      println("checked");
  }

`karac check` reports "All checks passed." `NoSuchTraitAnywhere` is not
defined in the file, in any import, or in the baked stdlib. Compare an
ordinary type position, where the resolver is strict and even offers a
suggestion: `undefined type 'Error', did you mean 'Err'?`.

WHY IT MATTERS: the trait in an `effect resource` declaration is what binds a
provider at a `with_provider` site, so a typo'd or renamed trait name silently
produces a resource that nothing can ever satisfy — and the failure surfaces
later and further away (or, for a program that never calls through the
resource, not at all).

SOURCE NOTE: found in `examples/phase0/dashboard.kara`, which declares three
resources against `DatabaseProvider` — a trait that file never defines and
never imports. The file now checks clean after the unrelated `Error`->`DbError`
fix, with the undefined trait still present and still unreported.

FIXED 2026-07-29 (9ddb52e): `resolve_items` had no `Item::EffectResource` arm at all — every other item kind had one. Added `resolve_effect_resource_def`, mirroring the existing `resolve_effect_group_def`. Deliberately an EXISTENCE check, not a kind check: an imported trait resolves to `SymbolKind::Import` and an aliased one to the alias, so demanding `SymbolKind::Trait` would reject the cross-module spelling db_pipeline and cartographer rely on; narrowing to 'resolves to something trait-like' needs the typechecker's import-following and is left as a separate change. `EffectResourceDecl` gained `provider_trait_span` so the error points at the trait, not the whole declaration.

COROLLARY worth recording: a provider trait IS consulted for call typing once it exists. Defining `DatabaseProvider` in examples/phase0/dashboard.kara (with an associated `type Row`) made the three fetches type-check AGAINST it and fail with `expected Result<Vec<Notification>, DbError>, found Result<Vec<Row>, DbError>` — the associated type cannot resolve without a concrete impl per resource. So the hole was not merely cosmetic: it let a declaration that would not have type-checked sit unexamined. That example now uses the bare `effect resource R;` form, which declares no provider contract.

title: `env.args()` reported the HOSTING PROCESS's argv rather than the program's, differently on each executor: `karac run --interp prog.kara` gave [karac, run, --interp, prog.kara]; the JIT (the DEFAULT backend) gave [karac_jit_runner, /tmp/karac_run_<pid>_jit.ll]; only an AOT binary was right. design.md's own CLI skeleton reads the first user argument as `args[1]`, which was the literal string "run".
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO:

  fn main() {
      let args = env.args();
      println(f"len={args.len()}");
      let mut i: i64 = 0;
      while i < args.len() { println(f"  [{i}] = {args[i]}"); i = i + 1; }
  }

  $ karac run --interp args.kara
  len=4
    [0] = target/debug/karac
    [1] = run
    [2] = --interp
    [3] = /.../args.kara

EXPECTED: `args[0]` is the program and `args[1..]` are the arguments passed to
IT. design.md § I/O surface documents `fn env.args() -> Vec[String] with
reads(Env)`, and the spec's canonical CLI skeleton reads the first user
argument as `args[1]` (`fs.read_to_string(args[1])` on a `args.len() < 2`
guard). Under `karac run` that index lands on the literal string "run".

RUN-VS-BUILD: an AOT binary gets its own argv and is unaffected, so this is a
divergence between the two executors rather than a wrong answer everywhere —
any argv-reading program behaves differently under `karac run` than as a built
binary, which is precisely the pairing `karac run` exists to preview.

SOURCE NOTE: found running `examples/phase0/dashboard.kara` after the de-rot;
it reads `args.get(1)` as a user id and therefore parses the string "run". The
example now defaults instead of erroring, so the demo is not held hostage to
this bug, but the underlying divergence is untouched.

SCOPE CORRECTION: as first filed this said the JIT was unaffected because 'an AOT binary gets its own argv'. That is true of a BUILT binary but not of `karac run`'s default backend — the JIT executes through a `karac_jit_runner` subprocess, so the program saw the runner's path plus the temp `.ll` file. Three executors, three different answers.

FIXED 2026-07-29: `karac run` now computes the program's argv once — the script path, plus anything after a literal `--` — and hands it to whichever executor runs.
  - interpreter: new `Interpreter::program_args` + `set_program_args`; `Env.args` prefers it and falls back to `std::env::args()` for embedders that never set it (REPL, comptime, playground).
  - JIT: the runner is spawned with `KARAC_PROGRAM_ARGS` (unit-separator packed, because an env value is a NUL-terminated C string and so cannot contain NUL); `karac_runtime_env_args_into` prefers it. Chosen over a new extern setter deliberately — a new `karac_*` symbol needs a `__preserve_no_mangle_symbols` keep-list entry, the B-2026-07-12-22 footgun.
  - AOT: untouched. No variable is set, so it keeps the process-argv path, which is correct there because the process IS the program.

`--` forwarding is new surface: `karac run prog.kara -- a b c`. Documented in `karac run --help`. Without it a program's argv is just the script path.

TESTS: tests/cli.rs asserts the interpreter's argv, the no-forwarding case, and — llvm-gated — that JIT and interpreter output is byte-identical, plus explicit assertions that neither karac's flags nor the runner internals appear. Fixture: tests/snapshots/env_args_echo.kara.

title: docs/design.md — the AUTHORITATIVE spec — writes `ref` AT CALL SITES in 9 code blocks, a form the parser rejects outright ('`ref` is not written at call sites'). Same rot class as B-2026-07-29-11 (the abandoned Rust-style Display), in the same document.
detail:
The parser is unambiguous:

  error[parse]: `ref` is not written at call sites. The parameter's mode is
  declared on the callee's signature. Remove the `ref` keyword.

yet design.md still shows the banned form at these lines:

  1397  self.tokens.get_or_init(|| tokenize(ref self.source))
  4512  let s = first_word(ref line);
  4776  let content = fs.read_to_string(ref args[1])?;     // the CLI skeleton
  5120  log(ref headers)
  6840  let it = count_logged(xs, ref logger);
  8611  send(ref conn, data);
  9563  let a = sum_first_half(ref data);
  9564  let b = sum_second_half(ref data);
  9601  observe(ref counter);

NOT purely cosmetic, for the same reason B-2026-07-29-11 was not: examples get
written against these blocks and then do not compile. `examples/db_pipeline`
is currently pinned KNOWN_BROKEN in `tests/example_corpus.rs` for exactly this
form at `src/executor.kara:38`.

NOT fixed in one sweep because the sites need individual judgment rather than
a blanket delete: line 8611's block is DEMONSTRATING a type error
(`// ERROR: expected Connection[Connected]`), so the `ref` is incidental to a
point about state machines, and lines 9563-9601 sit in effect/borrow-conflict
examples where the mode is the subject of the prose around them. Each needs

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing `examples/word_count.kara`'s sibling error;
the spec's own CLI skeleton (4776) was the block being consulted.

title: REPL cross-cell value snapshot was taken at each binding's INITIALIZER, so EVERY in-cell mutation was lost crossing to the next cell — on both lanes and for every type, not just the container tier: `let mut n: i64 = 0; n = 5;` read back 0. The JIT lane's `is_mut` container exclusion, added to work around that capture point, was itself what turned the loss into a silent empty read.
detail:
SURFACE NOTE: the REPL is the user-facing surface; the defect sits in the codegen snapshot capture/replay (`src/codegen/stmts.rs`, `SnapshotPrimKind`) and, for the Map/Set rows, in the interpreter lane too.

SOURCE NOTE: found by sweeping the `--features llvm` test files that CI does NOT run. CI's `codegen-e2e` job runs only `--lib --test codegen --test interpreter --test typechecker --test selfhost_lexer --test lljit_prototype` (plus abi_repr_c_struct and memory_sanitizer in their own jobs), leaving ~25 llvm-gated files ungated. `tests/repl_jit.rs` is one of them, and 6 of its 27 tests were red.

TWO INDEPENDENT DEFECTS, stacked so neither was visible:

(1) TEST-FIXTURE BUG (fixed in this commit). Six tests embedded invalid Kara in their fixture source -- `let v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(1);` with no `mut`. The ownership checker correctly refuses `push` on a non-`mut` binding, so every one of the six failed at `assert!(r.errors.is_empty())` BEFORE reaching its real assertion. The tests therefore never exercised the behaviour they were written for. Adding `mut` to the nine fixture sites turns 4 of the 6 green and lets the other 2 reach their assertion -- which is where defect (2) surfaces.

(2) THE REAL BUG. The REPL cross-cell value snapshot does not carry an IN-CELL MUTATION for the container tier. `docs/implementation_checklist/phase-7-codegen.md:720` marks B.5.3a (Vec) / B.5.3b (Map) / B.5.3c (Set) as `[x]` shipped 2026-05-30, and the code is present (`src/repl/util.rs:983/997/1018`, `src/codegen.rs:188/204` SnapshotPrimKind). It does not work today.

MEASURED MATRIX (real `karac repl` binary over piped stdin; cell 1 binds + mutates, cell 2 reads):
  tier                 JIT (default)   --interp
  B.5.1 i64            42  OK          42  OK
  B.5.2 String         hi  OK          hi  OK
  B.5.3a Vec + push    0   WRONG       1   OK
  B.5.3b Map + insert  0   WRONG       0   WRONG
  B.5.3c Set + insert  0   WRONG       0   WRONG
(want 1 in every container row.)

So the scalar tiers (B.5.1/B.5.2) are healthy on both lanes; the whole container tier is broken on the JIT lane, and Map/Set are broken on BOTH lanes.

SHAPE DISCRIMINATION -- the defect is specific to a mutation applied by a top-level statement in the binding cell:
  * `let xs: Vec[i64] = mk();` where `mk()` returns a populated container -- CORRECT on both lanes, both Vec and Map. The snapshot captures the initializer's value.
  * `let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(7);` -- the push is LOST crossing to cell 2.
  * Mutate and read in the SAME cell -- correct (prints 1). Only the cell boundary loses it.
This is consistent with the snapshot capturing the binding at its `let` initializer rather than at end-of-cell state.

WHY IT MATTERS: silent wrong answers, not a refusal or a crash -- the REPL reports an empty container with no diagnostic. `let mut v = Vec.new()` followed by pushes is the single most ordinary interactive-notebook shape there is. It is also a lane divergence: JIT and `--interp` disagree for Vec, so `--interp` is a workaround for that row only.

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: `tests/repl_jit.rs` is not in any CI job, and its own fixtures failed before reaching the assertion. The two tests that DO target this shape (`repl_jit_map_let_rhs_is_not_re_evaluated`, `repl_jit_set_let_rhs_is_not_re_evaluated`) are pinned `#[ignore]` against this id in this commit; un-ignoring them is the single trigger that flips them back to regression tests. The two Vec tests that now pass do NOT cover the broken path -- one binds from a fn return, the other mutates and reads within one cell.

NOT YET INVESTIGATED: whether this ever worked and regressed, or never worked past the fixture bug. The clone here is shallow (50 commits), so no blame history was available. Also unverified: the `#[ignore]`d Vec JIT row has no test at all -- worth adding one alongside the fix.

REPRO (no test harness needed):
  printf 'let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(7);\nprintln(v.len() as i64);\n:quit\n' | karac repl
    -> 0   (want 1;  `karac repl --interp` prints 1)
  printf 'let mut m: Map[i64, i64] = Map.new(); m.insert(1, 100);\nprintln(m.len() as i64);\n:quit\n' | karac repl
    -> 0   (want 1;  `--interp` also prints 0)

=== RESOLUTION 2026-07-29 ===

SCOPE WAS WIDER THAN FILED. The entry described the container tier; the defect is every type on both lanes. Re-measured matrix (cell 1 binds + mutates, cell 2 reads):

  row                        JIT      --interp   want
  let mut n: i64 = 0; n=5      0         0         5
  let mut f: f64 = 0.0; f=2.5  0         0         2.5
  let mut b: bool; b=true    false     false      true
  String + push_str            a         a         ab
  Vec + push                   0         1         1
  Map + insert                 0         0         1
  Set + insert                 0         0         1

ROOT CAUSE (one, shared by both lanes): the snapshot was taken as each binding was made — codegen from the `StmtKind::Let` arm, interpreter from `eval_stmt`'s `Let` arm. Anything the cell did afterwards was invisible to it.

WHY VEC LOOKED HEALTHY ON `--interp`: accident, not design. `Value::Array` is an `Arc<RwLock<Vec<Value>>>`, so the clone taken at the `let` ALIASES the same storage and observes later pushes. `Map(Vec<(Value, Value)>)` and `Set(Vec<Value>)` are by-value and froze. That representation split is why two container rows disagreed with each other on one lane.

SECOND LAYER ON THE JIT LANE: `compute_snapshot_sets_for_cell` EXCLUDED `let mut` String/Vec/Map/Set from capture (the slice B.5.2 / B.5.3 "mut filter"), reasoning that capture's cap-zero ownership transfer would break a same-cell mutation running after it. True — but only because capture fired at the `let`. Its actual effect was to leave those bindings with NO snapshot, so cell N+1 re-evaluated the RHS and read an empty container. The mitigation was the bug.

FIX: capture at END OF CELL on both lanes.
  * codegen — `emit_pending_snapshot_captures`, called from `compile_function`'s `main` tail immediately before scope cleanup: after every statement, before anything is freed. The `is_mut` exclusion is removed; the cap-zero transfer has no live use left to invalidate.
  * interpreter — `capture_watched_bindings`, at every `eval_block_inner` scope exit. Uniform across all three value representations. It runs for EVERY block, not just `main`'s, because `Env::scopes` is a plain stack: inner scopes pop first, so `main`'s body block (holding the cell's top-level bindings) writes last and wins. Only names in the popping scope are read, so a callee frame cannot overwrite a caller's binding of the same name.

VERIFIED: all 13 probed rows agree across `karac repl` and `karac repl --interp`, including a three-cell chained mutation (`q.push` in cell 1, two more in cell 2, len 3).

TESTS: the two `tests/repl_jit.rs` tests pinned `#[ignore]` against this id are un-ignored and pass. The four `*_mut_let_falls_through_to_passthrough` tests documented the removed design and only ever asserted SAME-CELL behaviour — rewritten as `*_carries_in_cell_mutation_across_cells`, asserting both halves. New `tests/repl.rs::in_cell_mutation_survives_the_cell_boundary_on_the_interpreter_lane` covers the interpreter lane across all eight shapes. `docs/implementation_checklist/phase-7-codegen.md`'s B.5.x entry — which marked the container tier shipped — is corrected in place.

STILL OPEN (not this bug): `tests/repl_jit.rs` remains outside every CI job, which is why 6 of its 27 tests sat red. The CI-coverage gap is the meta-issue the SOURCE NOTE above describes.

title: Every call to a `-> ref String` accessor leaks one `karac_string_clone` block under AOT. Unbounded: a 1000-iteration loop over `let a = h.label()` leaks 1000 blocks. The `ref Vec[T]` sibling leaks nothing.

An IMPORTED type alias is not expanded to its underlying type: `import types.Row;` where `pub type Row = Map[String, i64]` leaves `Row` nominal, so `let mut r: Row = Map.new();` fails with `expected 'Row', found 'Map<?T0, ?T1>'`. An alias declared in the SAME file works.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO (two-module package, with a same-file control that PASSES):

  // src/types.kara
  pub type Row  = Map[String, i64];
  pub type Nums = Vec[i64];

  // src/main.kara
  import types.{Row, Nums};
  type LocalRow = Map[String, i64];      // control, declared HERE
  fn main() {
      let mut local: LocalRow = Map.new();   // OK
      let mut r: Row  = Map.new();           // E0200 expected 'Row', found 'Map<?T0, ?T1>'
      let mut v: Nums = Vec.new();           // E0200 expected 'Nums', found 'Vec<?T2>'
  }

The control is the whole point: alias transparency works, so this is not about
aliases-to-generic-stdlib-types. It is specifically that the alias's DEFINITION
does not reach the importing module. `env_build.rs` populates
`env.type_aliases` from a walk that sees the local program (and the baked
stdlib); an imported alias never gets an entry, so `Row` stays an opaque
nominal and unifies with nothing.

SAME FAMILY as B-2026-07-29-9 (an imported trait's methods did not resolve
because `TraitInfo` carried no method list and the search never left the
current module) and B-2026-07-29-16 (an imported `ref` parameter's mode did not
reach call-arg classification). Three phases, one shape: cross-module item
detail is not plumbed to the consumer. The -9 fix walked to the defining module
through `type_origins`' canonical (module path, item name); the same route
should serve here.

IMPACT: this is what blocks `examples/db_pipeline` (pinned KNOWN_BROKEN in
`tests/example_corpus.rs`). 8 of its 12 remaining errors are this bug —
`Row` is declared in query.kara and consumed in executor.kara, main.kara and
planner.kara, where it variously reports `expected 'Row', found 'Map<?T10,
?T11>'`, `expected 'Row', found 'HashMap<String, Value>'`, and `tuple pattern
used but type is 'Row'` (iterating a Map through the alias). A `Row` alias
shared across modules is the ordinary way to name a record type, so this makes
multi-module data code impractical.

SOURCE NOTE: found de-rotting db_pipeline after B-2026-07-29-19 removed the
call-site `ref` parse error that had been masking every downstream phase.

FIXED 2026-07-29 (0a23cf8). Two parts, and the second is the interesting one.

1. REGISTER IT. `collect_import_origins`' candidate match listed StructDef / EnumDef / TraitDef / TraitAlias / MarkerTrait and not `Item::TypeAlias`, so the alias never entered `imported_items`. Added that arm plus an `env_add_type_alias` registration arm, and a `type_alias_referenced_names` helper so the alias BODY's types are registered from its DEFINING module — the same treatment an imported struct's field types already get, without which `Row = Map[String, Value]` lowers `Value` in the consumer's namespace.

2. REGISTER IT EARLY — this is what the bug really turns on. `collect_import_origins` runs at the END of `build_type_env`. Harmless for every other imported kind, because those stay NOMINAL: lowering a signature before the import is registered and an expression after it both yield the same `Type::Named`, and they unify. An alias must EXPAND, so late registration yields TWO different lowerings of one source name. Shipping part 1 alone made db_pipeline strictly WORSE — 12 errors to 28 — with a trait signature's nominal `Row` refusing to unify against an impl body's expanded `Map<String, Value>` (`expected 'Map<String, Value>', found 'Row'`). A narrow `register_imported_type_aliases` pre-pass runs before every local item walk; the rest of `collect_import_origins` has no ordering requirement and was left in place rather than hoisted.

`local_type_names` also gained `Item::TypeAlias` so a local alias shadows an imported one — inert while imported aliases were never registered, load-bearing now.

RESULT on examples/db_pipeline: the whole `Row` class is gone, 12 errors down to 6 unrelated (the `Map.get` owned-key requirement, a missing `#[derive(Eq)]` on `Value`, and B-2026-07-29-27's absent `.clone()`). Still KNOWN_BROKEN, now for those alone.

TEST HONESTY: `imported_type_alias_unifies_between_signature_and_body` passes both WITH this fix and with NO fix — with nothing registered, both sides are nominal and unify vacuously. It fails only in the intermediate state, so it guards against a partial fix rather than demonstrating expansion. `imported_type_alias_is_expanded` is the one that fails without the fix; it covers the annotated-let, signature-parameter, and aliased-import spellings.

FOLLOW-ON (6de8b3b): an alias can also arrive WITHOUT being imported by name — through an imported aggregate's field or variant payload. db_pipeline's planner.kara imports `Query` and never `Row`, meeting it only via `Query.Insert { row: Row }`. `register_transitive_type_deps` chased StructDef and EnumDef dependencies but had no TypeAlias arm, so the alias arrived opaque there and iterating it reported `tuple pattern used but type is 'Row'`. Both halves needed the arm, for the same ordering reason: the late walk registers it (plus its own referenced names, so an alias whose body names another alias resolves), and the early pre-pass gained an alias-only transitive sweep from an imported aggregate's referenced names — bounded by a `seen` set so a cyclic aggregate cannot spin. Covered by `transitively_reached_type_alias_is_expanded`.

title: A GENERIC REFINEMENT alias is opaque to its base's operations: `type NonEmpty[T] = Vec[T] where self.len() > 0;` then `for r in rows` binds `r` to `NonEmpty`, so `r.price` fails with `no field 'price' on type 'NonEmpty'`. The same alias WITHOUT the `where` clause iterates correctly.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO (one file, with the control that PASSES):

  struct Item { price: f64 }
  type NonEmpty[T] = Vec[T] where self.len() > 0;   // refinement
  type Plain[T]    = Vec[T];                        // control, no `where`

  fn sum_refined(rows: NonEmpty[Item]) -> f64 {
      let mut t = 0.0;
      for r in rows { t = t + r.price; }   // no field 'price' on type 'NonEmpty'
      t
  }
  fn sum_plain(rows: Plain[Item]) -> f64 {
      let mut t = 0.0;
      for r in rows { t = t + r.price; }   // OK
      t
  }

Both the refinement and the generic argument are lost: the element binding
takes the alias's own name rather than `Item`, so the for-loop is not seeing
through to `Vec[T]` at all.

NOT simply 'refinements should be transparent'. `env_build.rs` deliberately
stores a refinement alias as `Type::Refinement { name, base }` — a NOMINAL
identity — where a plain alias stores the transparent base; that is by design,
since a refinement type's whole purpose is to be distinct from its base at
construction sites (design.md § Refinement Types). The defect is that nothing
sees THROUGH the nominal wrapper for read operations: iteration and field
access should project to `base`, the way construction is gated against it. So
the fix is a projection rule on `Type::Refinement`, not deleting the nominal
identity.

IMPACT: blocks `examples/weave` (pinned KNOWN_BROKEN in
`tests/example_corpus.rs`), whose `aggregate(rows: NonEmpty[EnrichedRow])` is
the example's headline demonstration of a refinement type carrying a
'at least one row' precondition in the signature.

SOURCE NOTE: separated from B-2026-07-29-25 by control. Both surfaced as
'alias not expanded', but -25 is cross-module and shape-independent while this
one is same-file and specific to the `where` clause.

FIXED (5445e85). Root cause confirmed as filed: the nominal wrapper is
correct and stays; what was missing is a base-PROJECTION rule for read
operations. Four sites, each the same shape as the method base-deref that
already existed (`expr_method_call.rs` § "Refinement base-deref"):

  1. `substitute_type_params` (inference.rs) had no `Type::Refinement` arm,
     so a GENERIC alias fell to `_ => ty.clone()` and dropped the use-site
     argument — `NonEmpty[Item]` kept an unsubstituted `Vec<T>` base. This is
     the half the report saw as 'the generic argument is lost'. The nominal
     `name` is identity-only; only `base` is walked.
  2. `element_type_of` (lowering.rs) had no `Refinement` arm, so iteration
     fell to the `_ => ty.clone()` tail and bound the element to the whole
     wrapper — the 'r takes the alias's own name' half.
  3. `infer_field_access` (fields.rs) had no `Refinement` arm, so field
     access fell to `field_access_on_fieldless_type`. Projection is
     UNCONDITIONAL here, unlike the per-method-name decision for methods: a
     refinement cannot declare a field, so there is no refined identity for
     one to win with. It peels inside a borrow, so `ref Adult` resolves like
     `ref Person`; an absent field still errors, now naming the base struct.
  4. `check_cast_pair` (typechecker.rs) judged a refined SOURCE opaquely.
     Found only after 1-3 landed — clearing the field error let `examples/
     weave` reach line 263's `r.qty as f64` and report "cannot cast
     'PositiveQty' to 'f64'". The source now widens to its base first: the
     cast twin of the arithmetic-returns-base rule (anything writable as
     `q + 1` is writable as `q as f64`). Deliberately applied AFTER the
     refinement-TARGET arm so `p as Positive` stays a no-op assertion and
     `E_REFINEMENT_CAST_SOURCE_MISMATCH` still fires for `Wide as Narrow`.

DIVERGENCE NOTE (why this survived a 2600-test codegen suite): codegen was
already CORRECT on all four. It resolves refinement aliases through its own
`refinement_base` / `refinement_generic_params` maps rather than the
typechecker's `Type`, and `tests/codegen.rs::e2e_refinement_alias_collection
_method_and_iteration` pins the exact `for r in rows { n = n + r.v; }` shape
— green the whole time. The E2E harness calls `karac::typecheck` and hands
the result to codegen WITHOUT gating on typecheck errors, so a
check-rejects / codegen-accepts divergence is invisible to it. The two new
codegen tests pin the lanes together; the real end-to-end gate is the
`examples/weave` corpus promotion, which goes through `karac build`.

IMPACT CLEARED: `examples/weave` type-checks, builds, and runs (interpreter
and AOT agree byte-for-byte), and its `KNOWN_BROKEN_PACKAGES` pin is removed.

FOUND WHILE FIXING (separate, pre-existing, still open): B-2026-07-30-7 —
a PLAIN type alias over a non-`i64`-shaped base in a parameter/return
position is a codegen layout gap. The `where`-free control from this bug's
own repro (`type Plain[T] = Vec[T]`) passes `karac check` and then fails
LLVM module verification under `karac build`. Untouched by this fix — no
`Type::Refinement` is involved.

title: `#[derive(Clone)]` synthesizes NO callable `.clone()` method: `s.clone()` on a derived struct or enum fails with `no method 'clone' on type 'S'`, while the very same derive DOES satisfy a `T: Clone` bound. Silently accepted, so the attribute reads as working.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO — the asymmetry in one pair:

  #[derive(Clone)]
  struct S { n: i64 }

  fn takes_clone[T: Clone](x: T) -> T { x }

  fn main() {
      let s = S { n: 1 };
      let a = takes_clone(s);   // OK — the bound IS satisfied
      let b = s.clone();        // no method 'clone' on type 'S'
  }

Running the bound half alone reports 'All checks passed'. Adding the method
call is what fails. Same for `enum`, and same for a `shared enum` (RC), so it
is not struct-vs-enum and not the ownership tier.

WHY IT LOOKS LIKE IT WORKS: `derives.rs`'s `type_supports_clone` consults
`info.derived_traits.contains("Clone")` for structs, enums, distinct types and
`Type::Shared`, so the derive IS recorded and IS honored wherever a `Clone`
BOUND is discharged. What is missing is method synthesis — nothing adds a
`clone` entry to the type's method table, so dispatch falls through. The
attribute is accepted without a warning, which makes the gap silent: the
program says `#[derive(Clone)]` and the reader has every reason to expect
`.clone()`.

CORROBORATION from inside the compiler: `ownership.rs`'s use-after-move
auto-fix already encodes this. It inserts `.clone()` ONLY for types that
'DEFINITELY have .clone()' — the built-in heap collections and RC types —
because 'a plain move-only struct has NO .clone(), so a blind insertion there
produces no method clone'. That comment describes exactly this hole; the
auto-fix routes around it rather than the derive filling it.

IMPACT: `.clone()` is the documented remedy in the use-after-move diagnostic's
own suggestion text ('clone the value at the move site'), so for a user struct
the suggested fix cannot be followed. Also blocks one of
`examples/db_pipeline`'s remaining errors (`values[i].clone()` on a `Value`
enum, executor.kara:118) — adding the derive there does not help.

SOURCE NOTE: found while de-rotting db_pipeline; the derive was added to `Value`
as the apparent fix and changed nothing.
resolution:
FIXED on all three surfaces, which -31's work list required to land together.

TYPECHECK. `.clone()` method resolution now routes through the env-aware `clone_receiver_self_type` (typechecker/derives.rs) instead of the pure free fn `clone_self_type_for` (typechecker/types.rs) — the split that WAS the bug. The free fn is still consulted first, so the stdlib-collection surface is byte-for-byte unchanged; what is added is `Option[T]`, user struct / enum / distinct types carrying `#[derive(Clone)]` or a `Clone` impl, `Rc` / `Arc` / `shared` handles, and a `T: Clone`-bounded generic param. The bound is discharged against `enclosing_bounds` — the same table `gat_rhs_satisfies_bound` proves TypeParam bounds against, supertrait closure included — so an UNBOUNDED `[T]` still reports `no method 'clone'`. A user-written `fn clone` WINS: when `env.find_method` resolves one on the receiver's nominal type the built-in arm declines and ordinary impl dispatch runs the user's body.

INTERPRETER. The `clone` arm in method_call_seq.rs gained `Value::Struct` / `Value::EnumVariant` / `Value::SharedStruct`, routed through `deep_clone_value` rather than the derived Rust `Clone`: the latter bumps the `Arc<RwLock<..>>` behind an `Array` FIELD, so `let b = a.clone(); b.items.push(x)` would be visible through `a`. It declines when a user `<Type>.clone` exists, mirroring the typechecker.

CODEGEN. `try_compile_clone` (entry_chains.rs) gained an aggregate arm. Nothing had to be invented, exactly as -31's investigation predicted: `emit_struct_clone_fn`, `emit_enum_clone_fn`, `emit_option_value_clone_fn` and `emit_owning_clone_fn_for_type_expr` (the RETAINING variant, which is what a `shared` handle's clone means) already shipped. The emitter is resolved EXPLICITLY per shape rather than by handing the TypeExpr to `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`, whose fallback arm is the shallow `emit_primitive_clone_fn`: for a heap-owning aggregate that would alias the source's buffer and both drops would free it (the B-2026-06-14-12 double-free shape). Where a deep clone is missing the arm falls THROUGH to the loud `no handler for method 'clone'` instead of mis-building. A scalar-identity arm was also needed: a MONOMORPHIZED `T: Clone` param carries the erased `T` in its dispatch key, so the existing primitive check never saw it and the generic body would not lower.

DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED — `Result[T, E]`, the one item left of the MEASURED SURFACE list. It has `Option`'s inline-payload overlay but no in-place deep-copy helper (recorded in `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`'s `Option` arm), so admitting it would take exactly the shallow path above. `Result.clone()` stays rejected at typecheck rather than ship a double free; filed as B-2026-07-30-10.

GATES: `derive_clone_makes_clone_callable` + `clone_still_rejected_without_derive_or_bound` (tests/typechecker.rs), `test_derived_clone_is_deep_on_struct_enum_and_option` + `test_user_clone_impl_wins_over_derive_synthesis` (tests/interpreter.rs), `e2e_derived_clone_is_callable_and_deep` + `e2e_option_clone_deep_copies_payload` (tests/codegen.rs — the deep-copy assertions mutate the copy and read the source back, so a shallow bitcopy fails on output, not only under a sanitizer), and `asan_derived_clone_deep_copies_no_leak_no_double_free` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs, 200 iterations under Linux LSan).

title: A call's PARAMETER MODES change with syntactic position: a bare (owning) param is CONSUMED in statement position but only BORROWED inside an f-string interpolation. `fn consume(t: Tracked)` (no `ref`, so it owns `t`) called as `let n = consume(t);` runs Tracked's `impl Drop` INSIDE the callee before it returns; written as `let a = f"{consume(t)}";` it does not consume `t` at all — two such calls on one value are accepted by `karac check` and the destructor runs ONCE, at `t`'s last use in the CALLER. So the ownership pass does not enforce the callee's declared mode in that position, and a value the callee declared ownership of outlives it. NOT memory unsafety: exactly one drop, no double-free, nothing poisoned reading the payload under MallocScribble=1 MallocPreScribble=1, and --interp / JIT / `karac build` all agree — the checker and codegen are self-consistent, both treating it as a borrow. The USER-VISIBLE defect is release TIMING: for a value whose purpose is release-on-consume (a lock guard, a file handle, a `Secret`), writing the consuming call inside an f-string silently defers the release from inside the callee to the caller's last-use point, and `karac check` accepts reuse the declared signature forbids. RULED OUT BY PROBE, each of which looked likely first: (1) NOT the print-borrow rule of B-2026-07-02-21 — that gave the print family `ref` argument modes for println's OWN argument and does not reach a nested call's params; the control `println(consume(t)); println(consume(t));` (no f-string) is correctly REJECTED with `value 't' moved here, used again here`, so the interpolation is the entire difference. (2) NOT `Slice` semantics — bare `Slice[T]`/`Vec[T]` params consuming their argument is deliberate design settled in B-2026-07-01-10 (which chose `ref Slice[f64]` on stats.kara over giving `Slice[T]` borrow mode by default); the repro uses a plain user struct, no `Slice` involved. (3) NOT run-vs-build — all three surfaces agree. CALL-FORM MATRIX: of `stmt` (`let _ = f(o);`), `bare` (`f(o);`), `arith` (`f(o) + f(o)`) and `fstring` (`f"{f(o)}"`), only `fstring` is accepted; the callee's return type is irrelevant, and `Array[i64, N]` escapes only because it is `Copy`. ROOT-CAUSE HYPOTHESIS: design.md L4667 (§ String Interpolation) specifies `{expr}` desugars to `expr.to_string()` with `Display.to_string(ref self)` BORROWING the receiver, so 'the same value can appear in multiple {} slots without being consumed' — correct and intended for the interpolated VALUE (`f"{t}"` must not consume `t`). The behaviour here looks like that borrow applied one level too deep: the ownership pass appears to treat the whole interpolated expression as a borrow context rather than borrowing only its result, so it never descends into a nested call's arguments to classify them against the callee's declared modes. FIXED c8bce5d3: root cause was NARROWER than the hypothesis above — not the interpolation's documented borrow applied one level too deep, but `ExprKind::InterpolatedStringLit` grouped with the LEAF literals in TWO walkers, so the pass never looked inside the hole at all: use_classifier.rs (classifies uses; arm body `{}`) and cfg.rs (lowers to CFG nodes; returned `cur` unchanged, leaving `direct_uam_candidates` no node to find a witness at). BOTH had to be fixed — either alone is an observable no-op, which is why the first attempt looked like it did nothing. Holes now walk in `Mode::Reading`, preserving design.md L4667 (a value may still appear in multiple `{}` slots unconsumed); the Call/MethodCall arms derive argument modes from the callee's signature independently of the enclosing mode, which is what restores the nested move. VERIFIED: cargo test --all 8739 passed / 0 failed; llvm --lib/interpreter/typechecker/lljit green; selfhost_lexer green; codegen 2304 passed / 309 failed BYTE-IDENTICAL to the pre-change baseline on the same machine (those 309 fail at baseline too, environmental) — zero regressions. Six codegen tests newly failed as TRUE POSITIVES (by-value fn called repeatedly on one value) and their PROGRAMS were repaired, not the signatures under test, with every expected output unchanged. Corpus A/B over all 687 .kara files in kara-katas: katas #87 and #93 newly rejected, both genuine latent use-after-moves, fixed there by declaring the read-only params `ref` (fixed in kara-katas ba154c1, all four surfaces re-verified). SIDE EFFECT, now MEASURED and NIL: making these uses visible also exposes them to rc-promotion, so kata #93 now draws a conservative `perf[rc-fallback]` for `path` whose consume and use are on DISJOINT branches (the `part == 4` arm returns) — `rc_values` fires for dominance-INCOMPARABLE consume/use by design, so the Rc is unnecessary but safe; a precision limit of that policy, not a new defect. MEASURED 2026-07-29: the emitted code is BYTE-IDENTICAL pre- and post-fix — `restore_ip.kara` builds to the same sha256 under both compilers (4e1668d6f54151f7c104), as does a scaled 40k-punch harness around the same backtrack/path shape, under BOTH `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` and the default auto-par build (45233e37d55840f47d39). So no Rc reaches the binary and the performance impact is zero by construction, not merely below the noise floor. Timing was attempted first and is worthless here: a hyperfine A/B of the two identical binaries reported '1.13 +- 0.24x', and a self-vs-self control on one binary reported '1.05 +- 0.21x' at load 6.22 — same spread, so nothing under ~1.15x on that machine at that load means anything. DIAGNOSTIC DEFECT EXPOSED BY THIS: the note's wording asserts an insertion that does not occur — it reads `RC fallback inserted for 'path'` while codegen emits no Rc at all. The note is analysis-level only for this shape. Unfiled; the wording should either say what it means (a candidate/what-if) or the analysis should stop reporting where codegen does not act. The bench at bench/restore_ip.kara could not have answered this either way: it measures `restore_fold`, a different formulation with no `path` threading, and draws no rc note. Two incidental gaps found while repairing the tests are filed as B-2026-07-29-31 and B-2026-07-29-32.
detail: REPRO (kara-katas oracle/fstring-arg-borrow-divergence/, three programs + a 20-file ablations/ matrix): `moves.kara` shows the sanctioned semantics (DROP inside the callee); `borrows.kara` is the divergence (two `consume(t)` calls inside f-strings accepted, one DROP at the caller's last use); `rejected.kara` is the print-borrow control (rejected). SOURCE NOTE: surfaced writing kata #243 Shortest Word Distance, whose first draft declared `words: Slice[String]` and called a `report` helper repeatedly on one array. That first diagnostic was CORRECT (bare Slice param consumes, per B-2026-07-01-10) and its hint — 'declare the callee parameter `ref` if it only reads' — was the fix; the kata ships `ref Slice[String]` and is unaffected by this entry. The f-string exemption was noticed while narrowing that diagnostic and is a separate finding. CORRECTION RECORDED: an intermediate reading of the drop ORDER in a `let s = f"..."` variant looked like an early consume followed by a use-after-destructor (i.e. a high-severity UAF). That was wrong — it was drop-at-last-use (cf. B-2026-07-21-1 on Drop timing). Re-probed with the payload printed on both the callee and destructor sides, plus MallocScribble, before filing; hence class=soundness (the ownership pass's declared-mode guarantee does not hold in this position) rather than use-after-free. INVESTIGATION NOT DONE: no bisect, and no check of whether the interpreter and codegen reach the borrow by the same path or independently. Also unprobed: method calls in interpolation position (`f"{obj.consume(x)}"`), and whether the same one-level-too-deep borrow reaches other borrow-context desugarings.

title: `karac query concurrency` reports statement-level parallel groups but NOT loop-reduction fan-out, so the Tier-2 decision the entire kata parallel lane rests on is invisible in the query surface: four programs that differ in whether they get loop fan-out return indistinguishable JSON.
detail:
THE GAP. `karac query concurrency` emits `parallel_groups` / `serialization_points` / `reorder_opportunities` — all statement-level. It emits nothing about LOOP-REDUCTION fan-out (design.md § 8876's "compute fan-out ... the path for parallel `let`-groups and associative reductions"), which is the mechanism behind the kata parallel lane (31 programs, median 1.13x hand-tuned rayon). A user asking the compiler "did you parallelize my loop?" gets no answer, and the flagship claim is that every compiler decision is queryable as JSON.

PROBE (4 programs, identical workload, only the accumulation shape differs; `work()` is a 400-iteration integer mix, n = 200000):

  A  sum = sum + work(src[k]);        // scalar commutative reduction
  B  out[k] = work(src[k]);           // indexed map into a pre-filled Vec
  C  out.push(work(src[k]));          // while-loop collect/push
  D  for k in 0..n { out.push(...) }  // for-range collect/push

`karac query concurrency` on all four returns effectively the same `parallel_groups` — and what it does report is the trivial setup statements ("pure computations" / "no data or effect dependencies"), never the loop. Ground truth from binary hashes under KARAC_AUTO_PAR=1 (default) vs KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0:

  A  0686f43c... vs bfe800a6...   DIFFERS  -> fan-out emitted
  B  identical                             -> no fan-out
  C  identical                             -> no fan-out
  D  identical                             -> no fan-out

So the query cannot distinguish a program that gets loop fan-out from three that do not.

THE DATA ALREADY EXISTS. `src/concurrency.rs` builds `LoopReduction { accumulator, op, stmt_index, loop_line, collect_tabulate, seq }` records (see the `out.push(LoopReduction {...})` site and `collect_is_tabulate_shape`). Nothing needs to be computed; it is not plumbed to the query emitter.

SUGGESTED SHAPE. A `loop_reductions` array on the concurrency query, one record per recognized loop reduction: accumulator name, `op` (Sum/Max/Collect/...), loop line, `collect_tabulate`, and — the part that matters most — whether the COST GATE accepted it. Recognition and emission are different questions: the analysis may recognize a reduction that codegen then declines as unprofitable, and today NEITHER is visible. A query that reported recognition alone would be actively misleading, since it would say "reduction found" for programs B/C/D-style shapes that never fan out.

SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while checking whether auto-par fires under the `wasm-threads` target (it does — `set_wasm_threaded_pass` lifts the wasm disable; sequential leg byte-identical under the env flag, threaded leg differs). Establishing that took four build-and-hash experiments precisely because the query could not answer it. Related but distinct: why `ReductionOp::Collect` did not fire for shapes C/D despite being a recognized op is a separate open question, not filed here.
resolution:
FIXED for the reported shape: the query now distinguishes every outcome. The data already existed on `FunctionConcurrency::loop_reductions` and the TEXT renderer already consumed it — only the JSON twin was missing.

LANDED. `effect_graph::loop_reductions_json`, wired into BOTH the single-function emitter (`cli::query_concurrency`) and the whole-program emitter (`build_concurrency_graph_json`) — the second is easy to miss and would have left Cartographer's whole-program view blind.

FIELD NAMING IS THE FIX, not just the presence of a field. `lowering` is `parallel_fanout` or `sequential_tabulate`, keyed on `LoopReduction::seq`; `cost_gate` is `deferred_to_codegen` on a parallel entry and `n/a` on a sequential one. That was the entry's own warning: recognition reported AS emission would be actively misleading, so the field states which question was answered rather than implying the binary outcome.

VERIFIED against the binary A/B ground truth that exposed the gap — all five probes now match:
  sum = sum + work(k)        -> parallel_fanout      (binary DIFFERS)
  #[par_unordered] + push    -> parallel_fanout      (binary DIFFERS)
  out.push(work(k))          -> sequential_tabulate  (binary identical)
  for k in 0..n { push }     -> sequential_tabulate  (binary identical)
  out[k] = work(k)           -> []  not recognized   (binary identical)

ALSO FIXED — the same conflation in the human channel. `--concurrency-report` printed both lowerings as a bare `reduction` next to `parallel_group` blocks, so a sequential tabulate read as parallelized. Now `parallel_reduction` vs `sequential_tabulate`; snapshot `tests/snapshots/concurrency_report_parallax_lite.txt` updated. `dogfooding.md § Parallax` locks the `parallel_group` shape only, not this line, so no doc lock was broken.

TEST: `test_query_concurrency_reports_loop_reduction_lowering` (tests/cli.rs) pins all three outcomes distinguishable AND that a recognized-but-sequential loop is never labelled parallel.

RESIDUAL, filed as B-2026-07-29-33: the query reports the ANALYSIS decision, not codegen's final verdict. See that entry for why the extraction is viable but wants its own slice.

UNBLOCKS the P1 entry `deferred.md § Auto-Parallel Loops over Provably-Disjoint Indexed Writes`, which names this bug as a hard prerequisite — with one caveat: that entry's acceptance surface wants a definitive `fanned_out`, which needs -33 too.

tracker: src/ast/types.rs (Attribute::is_par_order_free, accepts the deprecated par_unordered spelling); src/parser/exprs.rs (loop attribute gate + diagnostics); src/concurrency.rs (recognition + ReductionOp::Collect docs)
title: `#[par_unordered]` asserts a behaviour that does not occur: it is the required opt-in for Collect loop fan-out, but BOTH Collect paths preserve iteration order exactly today, so the attribute name and its justifying comment describe a reordering hazard that no shipped code path exhibits — discouraging the fastest data-parallel idiom.
detail:
THE GATE IS CORRECT; THE NAME AND COMMENT ARE NOT. `src/concurrency.rs` places Collect-style recognition inside `if par_unordered { ... }`, so `#[par_unordered]` is the required opt-in for parallel collect fan-out. Requiring an opt-in is right: it keeps "auto-par never changes what your program prints" an unconditional invariant, and it preserves the freedom to ship work-stealing later (`runtime/src/scheduler.rs`: "No work-stealing per-worker queues", deques "land iff a real workload measures" it) without silently reordering existing programs. This entry is NOT a request to remove the gate.

WHAT IS WRONG. The attribute states a fact about behaviour that is false today. Its comment:
  "The combine model is per-worker partial Vecs concat'd in worker-order, so the output ordering differs from iteration-order — the attribute is the user's explicit opt-in to that property."
Measured with a position-sensitive digest (digest = digest*131 + out[i], folded over all 200000 elements) under KARAC_AUTO_PAR=1 vs =0, n=200000, 400-iteration per-element work:

  bare `out.push(work(k))`            tabulate / direct-slot path   digest 23969007  IDENTICAL
  `if k%3!=2 { out.push(work(k)); }`  partials-concat path          digest 566860803 IDENTICAL

Both Collect paths preserve iteration order. Structurally, not by luck: with no work-stealing, chunks are statically assigned and contiguous, so concatenating partials in worker order IS iteration order; and the tabulate specialization writes each element directly into its final slot (phase-10-targets.md, 2026-07-16).

WHY IT COSTS SOMETHING. The tabulate collect is the FASTEST form measured (LBM 123.6 -> 57.0 ms, ties C-OpenMP, 1.7x rayon). The attribute that unlocks it tells the developer their output will be scrambled, so a careful reader declines to use it on anything order-sensitive — which is most data-parallel maps. The fastest idiom sits behind a warning label for a hazard no shipped path exhibits.

SUGGESTED FIX. (1) Rename to express the user's PROMISE rather than a description of behaviour — e.g. `#[par_order_free]`; note the runtime already uses this vocabulary at the other end of the pipe (`KARAC_PAR_ORDER_FREE_FLAG`, bit 63 of the descriptor cost field), so aligning the surface attribute makes both ends one concept. (2) Rewrite the comment to state the real contract: order is preserved by today's lowering; the attribute reserves the right to reorder (e.g. if work-stealing lands), so programs must not depend on it. Deliberately NOT "the ordering differs".

SEQUENCING — CHEAP NOW, EXPENSIVE LATER. 22 occurrences total across the tree: one kata (kara-katas leetcode/201-300/204-count-primes, incl. its bench + README), compiler tests (tests/concurrency.rs, tests/par_codegen.rs, tests/parser.rs), and bench infra (BENCH.md, scripts/bench-lib.sh). Pre-1.0 this is an afternoon; post-1.0 an attribute rename is a breaking change needing a deprecation cycle.

SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while chasing why `ReductionOp::Collect` never fired on un-attributed push loops during the B-2026-07-29-29 probe. A second, unrelated path explains the confusion and is working as intended: `classify_seq_collect_tabulate` emits `LoopReduction { seq: true }` when there is no reduction AND no par opt-in — a SEQUENTIAL push-to-in-place-store optimization, not parallelization. Related: B-2026-07-29-29 (the query surface cannot report which Collect path a loop got, and the two differ in ordering guarantees on paper).

FIXED 2026-07-30, as suggested: renamed to `#[par_order_free]`, comments rewritten to state
the real contract. The gate is unchanged -- this entry was explicit that it is correct and
that removing it was not the request.

RE-MEASURED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING, rather than taking this entry's numbers on trust. Same
position-sensitive digest, n=200000, 400-iteration per-element work, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=1 vs =0:
  bare `out.push(work(k))`            tabulate / direct-slot path   digest 23969007  IDENTICAL
  `if k%3!=2 { out.push(work(k)); }`  partials-concat path          digest 566860803 IDENTICAL
Both digests reproduce the values recorded above exactly. Both Collect paths preserve
iteration order.

WHAT CHANGED. `Attribute::is_par_order_free()` (src/ast/types.rs) is now the single predicate
every consumer asks. It accepts BOTH spellings: `par_unordered` stays valid, unchanged in
meaning, so out-of-tree sources survive the rename -- specifically the kara-katas #204
count-primes lane and its bench harness (BENCH.md, scripts/bench-lib.sh), which live in a
separate repository this session cannot edit. Deliberate deviation from the entry's
delete-the-old-name plan: breaking a kata that cannot be fixed in the same change is not worth
the tidiness, and the alias costs one `||`. A name-specific `is_bare("par_order_free")`
anywhere downstream would silently drop the alias, so
`tests/parser.rs::test_par_unordered_deprecated_alias_still_parses` pins both spellings
against the predicate.

Renamed in-tree: the parser gate + its two diagnostics (src/parser/exprs.rs), analyzer
recognition + the `ReductionOp::Collect` doc comment (src/concurrency.rs), codegen comments
(src/codegen/reduce.rs, src/codegen/stmts.rs), the AST field doc, and the
tests/{parser,concurrency,par_codegen}.rs suites. The two comments this entry quotes as false
-- "the output ordering differs from iteration-order" and "the worker-combine order is not
input-order-preserving" -- are rewritten to say what is actually true: order IS preserved by
today's lowering, and the attribute reserves the right to reorder (e.g. if work-stealing
lands), so programs must not depend on it.

Historical prose in docs/implementation_checklist/phase-7-codegen.md and phase-10-targets.md
is left naming `#[par_unordered]`, since it accurately records what the attribute was called
when those slices landed; a new phase-7-codegen.md entry records the rename, and the one
FORWARD-looking sentence (phase-10-targets.md "Idiom guidance: prefer ...") is updated with a
parenthetical pointing here.

title: `.clone()` is callable ONLY on the built-in heap/RC types. It is missing on `Option`/`Result` and on EVERY user type — including ones carrying `#[derive(Clone)]` — rejected at TYPECHECK with `no method 'clone' on type '<T>'`. The sharp half: `#[derive(Clone)]` still DISCHARGES a `T: Clone` BOUND (typechecker/derives.rs consults `info.derived_traits.contains("Clone")` for both structs and enums), so a `T: Clone` bound can be REQUIRED and satisfied but never INVOKED — `fn dup[T: Clone](x: T) -> T { x }` type-checks with a `#[derive(Clone)]` struct argument, while changing the body to `x.clone()` is rejected `no method 'clone' on type 'T'`. The bound is decorative. MEASURED SURFACE (all via `karac check`, same verdict under --interp and build): WORKS — String, Vec, Map, Set, VecDeque, SortedMap, SortedSet, Rc/Arc/shared (the `type_supports_clone` allowlist in typechecker/exprs.rs, mirrored by `moved_type_supports_clone` in ownership.rs). REJECTED — `Option[String]`, `Option[i64]` (so not payload-heap-specific), `Result[String, i64]`, a user `struct` with `#[derive(Clone)]`, a user `enum` with `#[derive(Clone)]`, a user `enum` without it, and a `T: Clone`-bounded generic parameter inside the generic body. CONSEQUENCE — the ownership checker's own advice recommends this. A use-after-move diagnostic prints `suggestion: clone '<x>' at the move site (`<x>.clone()`), declare the callee parameter `ref` if it only reads, or restructure` REGARDLESS of whether the type has `clone`; following it on an `Option`/`Result` or a user type yields code that does not typecheck. The MACHINE-APPLICABLE half is safe — `moved_type_supports_clone` gates the `TextEdit` to the built-ins, so `karac fix` will not insert a broken `.clone()` — but the human/LLM-facing sentence is unconditional, which is exactly how this was hit (see detail). DESIGN QUESTION ANSWERED 2026-07-30 (investigated, NOT yet implemented — the direction was this entry's open question, and the evidence now settles it). The answer is SYNTHESIZE/EXPOSE the method, not tighten the bound discharge, because codegen ALREADY HAS every clone emitter needed: `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr` (src/codegen/clone_drop.rs) dispatches Vec/VecDeque, Map, Set, String, tuples, `Option` via `emit_option_value_clone_fn`, user STRUCTS via the struct arm, and user ENUMS via `emit_enum_clone_fn` — the last two described in that file as 'the `#[derive(Clone)]` analog of the synthesized drop'. Nothing needs inventing; the capability is already shipped and used for element clones. Tightening the bound instead would break code that compiles today for no gain. THE ONE GATE: `clone_self_type_for` (src/typechecker/types.rs:958) is a PURE FREE FUNCTION with an allowlist of `Str`, `Array`, `Vector`, and Named `Vec|Set|SortedSet|VecDeque|Map|SortedMap|TreeMap`. It takes no `env`, which is exactly WHY user types are excluded — it cannot consult `info.derived_traits.contains("Clone")`, while `type_supports_clone` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs), which CAN and does, is only wired to bound discharge. That split is the whole bug. WORK LIST, three surfaces (each small, but they must land together — this session twice shipped half of a two-sided binding and got a different bug each time, cf. -32): (1) TYPECHECK — route `.clone()` method resolution through an env-aware predicate rather than the free fn; `Option`/`Result` are `Type::Named { name, args }` so they need only an allowlist entry plus a payload-cloneability rule, and note scalar payloads are typed by a SEPARATE path (expr_method_call.rs handles Copy primitives), so `Option[i64]` must not be rejected for its payload not being in the allowlist. (2) INTERPRETER — the clone arm in method_call_seq.rs:1508 covers Sender/Array/Slice/String/Map/Set/SortedSet/SortedMap and needs Option/enum/struct value arms; method_call.rs:2316 already handles Copy scalars. (3) CODEGEN — wire a `clone` method-call dispatch arm to the existing emitters. Then verify on all four surfaces per the corpus rule. NOT DONE and deliberately not rushed: the implementation. Filed this way because it is a cross-surface language feature rather than a bug fix, and half-landing it is a known failure mode on this exact machinery. B-2026-07-29-36 (fixed) already removed the sharp edge — the ownership diagnostic no longer advises `.clone()` on a type that has none — so nothing is actively misleading users while this waits.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while repairing the six codegen tests that B-2026-07-29-28's fix correctly turned red. Two of those repairs reached for `.clone()` on the advice of the diagnostic's own suggestion text — `Option[String].clone()` in `e2e_generic_enum_heap_eq_through_params` and `Vec.clone()` into a `Slice[T]` param in `e2e_generic_slice_elem_nonint_return` — and both failed. The first is this entry; the second is B-2026-07-29-32. Both repairs were changed to fresh `let` bindings instead, so the tests and the -28 fix do not depend on either gap being closed. AN EARLIER MISREADING, recorded so it is not repeated: the test harness reports this as `codegen: no handler for method 'clone' on variable 'a' (method dispatch fell through; this is a codegen bug — add a dispatcher arm in compile_method_call)`, which reads as a missing codegen arm. It is not — the harness bypasses `karac check`, and the user-facing failure is a clean TYPECHECK rejection on every surface. Filed as typecheck/missing-feature accordingly. REPRO: kara-katas has no oracle for this one; the nine one-file probes are trivial to re-derive from the MEASURED SURFACE list above (`let b = a.clone();` for each type, plus the two `dup[T: Clone]` variants). INVESTIGATION NOT DONE: no decision on what the fix should be — whether `#[derive(Clone)]` should synthesize a real method (and where: derives.rs synthesis vs a codegen intercept like the built-ins use), or whether `Option`/`Result`/user types should get `clone` some other way, or whether the bound discharge should instead be tightened to reject `T: Clone` until the method exists. Not bisected; no check of whether the bound-discharge path ever mattered to a real program before now.
resolution:
FIXED on all three surfaces, which -31's work list required to land together.

TYPECHECK. `.clone()` method resolution now routes through the env-aware `clone_receiver_self_type` (typechecker/derives.rs) instead of the pure free fn `clone_self_type_for` (typechecker/types.rs) — the split that WAS the bug. The free fn is still consulted first, so the stdlib-collection surface is byte-for-byte unchanged; what is added is `Option[T]`, user struct / enum / distinct types carrying `#[derive(Clone)]` or a `Clone` impl, `Rc` / `Arc` / `shared` handles, and a `T: Clone`-bounded generic param. The bound is discharged against `enclosing_bounds` — the same table `gat_rhs_satisfies_bound` proves TypeParam bounds against, supertrait closure included — so an UNBOUNDED `[T]` still reports `no method 'clone'`. A user-written `fn clone` WINS: when `env.find_method` resolves one on the receiver's nominal type the built-in arm declines and ordinary impl dispatch runs the user's body.

INTERPRETER. The `clone` arm in method_call_seq.rs gained `Value::Struct` / `Value::EnumVariant` / `Value::SharedStruct`, routed through `deep_clone_value` rather than the derived Rust `Clone`: the latter bumps the `Arc<RwLock<..>>` behind an `Array` FIELD, so `let b = a.clone(); b.items.push(x)` would be visible through `a`. It declines when a user `<Type>.clone` exists, mirroring the typechecker.

CODEGEN. `try_compile_clone` (entry_chains.rs) gained an aggregate arm. Nothing had to be invented, exactly as -31's investigation predicted: `emit_struct_clone_fn`, `emit_enum_clone_fn`, `emit_option_value_clone_fn` and `emit_owning_clone_fn_for_type_expr` (the RETAINING variant, which is what a `shared` handle's clone means) already shipped. The emitter is resolved EXPLICITLY per shape rather than by handing the TypeExpr to `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`, whose fallback arm is the shallow `emit_primitive_clone_fn`: for a heap-owning aggregate that would alias the source's buffer and both drops would free it (the B-2026-06-14-12 double-free shape). Where a deep clone is missing the arm falls THROUGH to the loud `no handler for method 'clone'` instead of mis-building. A scalar-identity arm was also needed: a MONOMORPHIZED `T: Clone` param carries the erased `T` in its dispatch key, so the existing primitive check never saw it and the generic body would not lower.

DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED — `Result[T, E]`, the one item left of the MEASURED SURFACE list. It has `Option`'s inline-payload overlay but no in-place deep-copy helper (recorded in `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`'s `Option` arm), so admitting it would take exactly the shallow path above. `Result.clone()` stays rejected at typecheck rather than ship a double free; filed as B-2026-07-30-10.

GATES: `derive_clone_makes_clone_callable` + `clone_still_rejected_without_derive_or_bound` (tests/typechecker.rs), `test_derived_clone_is_deep_on_struct_enum_and_option` + `test_user_clone_impl_wins_over_derive_synthesis` (tests/interpreter.rs), `e2e_derived_clone_is_callable_and_deep` + `e2e_option_clone_deep_copies_payload` (tests/codegen.rs — the deep-copy assertions mutate the copy and read the source back, so a shallow bitcopy fails on output, not only under a sanitizer), and `asan_derived_clone_deep_copies_no_leak_no_double_free` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs, 200 iterations under Linux LSan).

title: A FRESH-TEMP (non-`let`-bound) `Vec` argument passed to a `Slice[T]` parameter fails LLVM MODULE VERIFICATION under `karac build`, while the tree-walk interpreter runs it correctly — a run-vs-build divergence. `fn first[T](s: Slice[T]) -> T { s[0] }` called as `first(vs.clone())` or `first(make())` aborts with `Module verification failed: "Call parameter type does not match function signature!\n %clone.val = load { ptr, i64, i64 }, ptr %clone.dst, align 8\n { ptr, i64 } %call = call i64 @first({ ptr, i64, i64 } %clone.val)"` — the Vec's 3-word header {ptr, len, cap} is handed to a parameter whose lowered type is the 2-word Slice header {ptr, len}, i.e. the Vec->Slice COERCION that is applied to a place expression is NOT applied to a fresh rvalue. NARROWED (each a separate one-file probe; `karac check` passes on all of them, so this is loud only at build time): FAILS — `first(vs.clone())`, and `first(make())` where `fn make() -> Vec[String]`. PASSES — `let tmp = vs.clone(); first(tmp)` (binding the temp is the workaround), and plain `first(vs)`. IRRELEVANT AXES — element type (`Vec[i64]` fails identically, so not heap-element-specific) and genericity (a concrete `fn first(s: Slice[String]) -> String` fails identically, so it is not monomorphization). The trigger is purely that the argument is a fresh temp rather than a place. RELATED: B-2026-07-06-1 (fixed) was the same fresh-temp-Vec-argument class at a different callee — `Column.from_vec(<temporary Vec[String]>)` unsupported under `karac build`, where the fix was specific to that constructor. This looks like the same hole surviving at the generic Slice-coercion site; worth checking whether -06-1's fix generalizes before writing a new one. CORRECTION 2026-07-29 — THE WORKAROUND ABOVE IS NOT SAFE FOR EVERY SHAPE. `let`-binding the temp does dodge THIS bug, but for a GENERIC `fn f[T](s: Slice[T]) -> T` over a HEAP element it lands on B-2026-07-29-35, which returns an EMPTY/garbage value under `karac build` with no diagnostic while the interpreter is correct. So the advice is sound only for a CONCRETE `Slice[<T>]` parameter or a scalar element; for the generic heap case there is currently no safe spelling. FIX PROTOTYPED AND WITHHELD: a `fresh_vec_rvalue_slice_parts` arm in `coerce_to_slice` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs), modelled on the existing `collection_literal_slice_parts` literal path and reusing `materialize_owned_temp` for the caller-scope free, closes this cleanly for a concrete param (`f(vs.clone())` -> correct) and for scalar elements (`Vec[i64]` -> correct). It was NOT landed: for the generic heap shape it turns this bug's LOUD module-verification abort into B-2026-07-29-35's SILENT wrong answer, and `coerce_to_slice` cannot see the outer callee's return type, so there is no clean place to bail for just that shape. Landing it would trade a failure nobody can ship for one nobody can see. FIX -35 FIRST, then this arm should go in as-is. The gate must stay enumerated (`Call` to a declared-`Vec`-returning named fn, and `<vec>.clone()`) rather than 'any rvalue that compiles to a Vec struct': the slice only borrows, so the path queues a free, and queueing it for a value we do not own (a field read, an index, a `ref`-returning accessor) would be a double-free. UNBLOCKED 2026-07-29: B-2026-07-29-35 is fixed (5f2cb6ad), so the reason this entry's prototyped coercion was withheld — that it converted this bug's loud abort into -35's silent wrong answer for the generic heap shape — no longer applies to a `Vec` argument. The withheld arm can be revisited. NOT yet re-tested against the fixed compiler, so 'unblocked' is an inference from -35's fix, not a measurement; re-run the b1/b2/b5/b6 probes before landing it. Note B-2026-07-29-37 (an `Array` arg to a generic `Slice[T]` param) is still open, so an Array-argument coercion would still land on a silent miscompile — keep the enumerated gate. FIXED 0c3fea05. Needed THREE coordinated parts, which is why it outlived -35 rather than falling out of it. (1) The withheld coercion landed as designed: `fresh_vec_rvalue_slice_parts` in src/codegen/expr_ops.rs, modelled on the existing bare-literal path and reusing `materialize_owned_temp` for the caller-scope free, with the accepted shapes ENUMERATED (a named `Vec`-returning fn, and `<vec>.clone()`) exactly as this entry required. (2) That alone was NOT sufficient: once those arguments compiled they arrived with `T` unbound, because BOTH mono substitution sources gated on the argument being a plain identifier — so the very shape -35 had just fixed for named locals came straight back for fresh rvalues. Lifted that gate in `augment_subst_from_arg_elem_types` (its four name-keyed arms — Vec/VecDeque, Set, Map key, Map value — now demand an identifier individually; only the Slice arm may see a fresh rvalue) and taught -35's `resolve_container_param_elem_substs` the same two shapes. (3) The NAME and the LLVM TYPE must move together, now guaranteed by the paired helpers `arg_container_elem_type_expr` and `fresh_container_arg_elem_llvm`. Binding one without the other is not a partial fix but a DIFFERENT bug, and both were hit on the way: name-only yields `Function return type does not match operand type of return inst` (the mono returns i64 while its body clones a String); type-only reproduces -35's `karac_clone_T`. Anyone touching either helper should change both. DELIBERATELY NOT WIDENED: the shared `infer_elem_from_source`, which has three other callers whose behaviour should not shift for a fix that needs only the mono call site — the fresh-rvalue fallback sits beside it instead. Same restraint that kept -37 out of -35. THE 'UNBLOCKED' NOTE ABOVE WAS RIGHT BUT FOR AN INCOMPLETE REASON: re-measuring before landing (as that note instructed) confirmed -35 had fixed the `let`-bound form, so the silent-miscompile trade was gone — but it also showed the fresh-rvalue form still produced a raw pointer, i.e. -35's fix did not reach this argument shape at all. Landing the coercion on the strength of the inference alone would have shipped the silent wrong answer this entry was withheld to avoid. VERIFIED: all six probes named in this entry now match the interpreter. cargo test --all 8741/0; llvm --lib 1116/0, interpreter 1322/0, typechecker 19/0, lljit 2092/0. Codegen A/B in one tree with the revert asserted before measuring: 2606 passed / 9 failed with the fix vs 2605 / 10 at baseline — zero regressions, one repair, and that repair is the new regression test, confirmed FAILING at baseline. The 9 residual failures are 6 regex + 3 Arrow IPC on both arms, a runtime-archive provisioning gap on this machine, not codegen. No kata uses this shape, so kara-katas is unaffected.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while repairing the six codegen tests that B-2026-07-29-28's fix correctly turned red — `e2e_generic_slice_elem_nonint_return` was repaired with `gsum(vs.clone())`, which hit this. The repair was changed to a fresh `let vs2` binding, so neither that test nor the -28 fix depends on this being closed. Sibling of B-2026-07-29-31, found the same way. One probe in the original batch was INVALID and is excluded from the narrowing above: `first(["a", "b"])` failed at PARSE, but only because the probe was written through a shell heredoc that escaped the inner quotes — `{f(\"x\")}` inside an f-string interpolation is a real parse error with its own good diagnostic, unrelated to this bug. Whether a BARE collection literal argument coerces to a `Slice[T]` param is therefore still unmeasured. INVESTIGATION NOT DONE: not bisected; no check of whether the same fresh-temp/place asymmetry affects other coercion sites (`Array[T, N]` -> `Slice[T]`, `String` -> `StringSlice`); and no check of whether the interpreter is right by accident (it materializes Slice from Vec, per the note at src/ownership.rs:2842) rather than by applying the coercion.
tracker: src/codegen (Vec->Slice argument coercion for fresh rvalues)

title: `query concurrency`'s `loop_reductions` reports the ANALYSIS decision, not codegen's final verdict: a recognized `parallel_fanout` loop can still be declined by codegen's memory-bound and cost-model gates, so the query cannot answer "did this loop actually fan out".
detail:
B-2026-07-29-29 made the loop-fanout decision queryable and named the honest limit in the output itself (`"cost_gate":"deferred_to_codegen"`). This entry is that limit.

WHY IT MATTERS. `deferred.md § Auto-Parallel Loops over Provably-Disjoint Indexed Writes` (P1) names -29 as a hard prerequisite and specifies its acceptance surface as a definitive `fanned_out: true`. Today the query can say "the analysis chose fan-out" but not "the binary fans out", so that acceptance surface is not yet fully satisfied.

THE GATES NOT VISIBLE (all in llvm-gated `src/codegen/reduce.rs`):
  1. `body_is_memory_bound` — declines a memory-streaming body whose compute-unit estimate looks parallelizable (kata-153: 3.5ms -> 11.8ms User-CPU, no wall win).
  2. Const-K cost gate — `const_eval_iter_count * per_iter_cost < REDUCE_DISPATCH_THRESHOLD_UNITS`.
  3. Variable-K floor — `per_iter_cost < VARIABLE_K_PER_ITER_FLOOR_UNITS` AND the bound references a function parameter (B-2026-07-23-25).
