WHY THE EXTRACTION IS VIABLE. `estimate_body_cost_units`, `const_eval_iter_count`, `const_eval_int_literal`, `body_is_memory_bound` and `CostEstimator` are PURE AST walks — verified zero `self.` / `inkwell` / LLVM references. They can move to a plain-data `src/` module that both `concurrency.rs` and `codegen/reduce.rs` consume, which keeps the codegen-containment invariant (no LLVM types leave codegen) and, more importantly, avoids the real hazard: a SECOND copy of a calibrated cost model on the analysis side would drift from codegen's and make the query confidently wrong.

WHY ITS OWN SLICE. (a) It moves perf-calibrated constants, so it needs a binary-hash equivalence check on a par-lane kata proving codegen output is byte-identical before/after the move. (b) `reduction_bound_references_param` needs the enclosing function's params, and the gate operates on a codegen-built `LoopShape` (end_expr / lo_expr / body) that the query side must reconstruct from the AST at `stmt_index`. Neither is hard; both are more than a field addition.

DONE WHEN: `loop_reductions` carries a definitive emission verdict plus the declining gate's name when it declines, and the P1 entry's acceptance surface is met.
resolution:
FIXED by extraction, not by reimplementation. New plain-data `src/par_cost.rs` holds the auto-par cost model; `codegen/reduce.rs` and the query layer now call the SAME `fanout_verdict`, so the two cannot drift.

WHAT MOVED (968 lines out of the llvm-gated module): the calibrated constants (DISPATCH_OVERHEAD_PER_CALL_UNITS, ASSUMED_WORKER_COUNT, REDUCE_DISPATCH_THRESHOLD_UNITS, VARIABLE_K_PER_ITER_FLOOR_UNITS, CALL_COST_UNITS, RUNTIME_NESTED_LOOP_MULTIPLIER), `CostEstimator` + `estimate_body_cost_units`, `MemoryBoundDetector` + `body_is_memory_bound`, `const_eval_iter_count` / `const_eval_int_literal`, and `extract_loop_shape` + its helpers (`parse_lt_condition`, `preceding_stmt_init`, `strip_terminal_step_one_increment`, `is_step_one_increment_stmt`, `stmt_writes_loop_var`, `is_int_literal_one`, `is_loop_var_plus_one`, `is_named_identifier`, `is_trivial_accessor_method`, `is_lowered_primitive_op_call`). The new `fanout_verdict` owns the GATE SEQUENCE — memory-bound, then const-K cost, then the variable-K param-bound floor — which is the part both callers must agree on. Every moved item was already a pure AST walk (zero `self.` / inkwell references), which is why the move was possible and why codegen containment still holds.

QUERY SURFACE. `loop_reductions` gained `fanned_out` (definitive), `cost_gate` (fanout | declined_memory_bound | declined_below_cost_threshold | declined_variable_k_param_bound | n/a | unknown) and `reason`. Wired into BOTH the single-function and whole-program emitters — the second is the Cartographer path and is easy to miss.

VERIFIED (1) PURE MOVE: byte-identical binaries across 5 programs before/after. This required pinning `KARAC_RUNTIME`. Without the pin ALL FOUR hashes differed — including `map_shape`, which contains no reduction at all — because the worktree had built its own archive with different embedded paths. Any future codegen-equivalence check must pin the archive, or an archive rebuild masquerades as a behaviour change.

VERIFIED (2) VERDICT MATCHES BINARY REALITY on every probe, including both declining gates:
  large-K reduction         fanned_out=true   fanout                          binary DIFFERS
  #[par_unordered] collect  fanned_out=true   fanout                          binary DIFFERS
  trip count 10             fanned_out=false  declined_below_cost_threshold   identical
  index-read scan           fanned_out=false  declined_memory_bound           identical
  out.push(...)             fanned_out=false  n/a (sequential tabulate)       identical

SCOPE NOTE, documented in the field docs: `fanned_out` is a COMPILE-TIME fact — codegen emitted a dispatch. The runtime caps fan-out depth at `KARAC_PAR_MAX_FORK_DEPTH` (default 1), so for nested reductions both levels report true while only the OUTERMOST forks (deeper levels run inline; that cap is what prevents the B-2026-07-03-14 stack exhaustion). Stated explicitly so the field is not misread as a runtime promise — the same over-promise discipline that produced -29's field naming.

Test: `test_query_concurrency_reports_fanout_verdict_and_declining_gate` (tests/cli.rs) pins both declining gates BY NAME and asserts the shape was recoverable (a `cost_gate: "unknown"` fallback would silently mask a plumbing regression). -29's test updated: it pinned the `deferred_to_codegen` disclaimer this entry removed.

UNBLOCKS `deferred.md § Auto-Parallel Loops over Provably-Disjoint Indexed Writes` (P1) — its acceptance surface wanted a definitive `fanned_out`, which now exists.

title: REGRESSION SURFACE: `test_build_debug_info_keeps_symbols_and_dwarf` — the test pinning B-2026-07-27-4 (profiling attribution, marked FIXED at f569aac) is RED on main; cause not yet classified between a code regression and host-toolchain sensitivity.
detail:
OBSERVED on main (b4236f24) under `cargo test --features llvm --test cli`, macOS arm64:
  panicked at tests/cli.rs: "KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1 must keep local symbols so profilers can attribute cost to a function instead of one unnamed blob"

NOT introduced by the B-2026-07-29-29 query work — reproduced identically on a clean primary `main` checkout before that branch was merged, which is the control that makes this pre-existing rather than a side effect.

WHY IT NEEDS TRIAGE RATHER THAN A DIRECT FIX. B-2026-07-27-4 is recorded FIXED at `f569aac` and this test is the regression pin for that fix, so either (a) something regressed the symbol/DWARF retention since, or (b) the assertion is sensitive to host toolchain state (linker / dsymutil / SDK version) and passes only in the environment where it was authored. Deliberately NOT asserting a regression: distinguishing (a) from (b) needs a bisect from `f569aac` plus a check of whether CI's `codegen-e2e` leg is green on the same test, and macOS-vs-Linux divergence in this area is well precedented in this tree.

IMPACT IF (a): the profiling-attribution capability -27-4 shipped is silently gone, which matters because per-function attribution is how perf work on kata regressions gets localized.

FIRST STEPS: check the CI `codegen-e2e` job's status on this test; if green there and red on macOS, reclassify as a platform-gated test rather than a regression. If red in both, bisect from `f569aac`.
resolution:
NOT A REGRESSION. The B-2026-07-27-4 capability (skip `strip -x` when debug info is requested) works correctly; the TEST asserted two things that could never hold.

DEFECT 1 — FIXTURE TOO SMALL TO LEAVE SYMBOLS. `fn helper(a, b) { a * b + 1 }` called as `helper(6, 7)` is inlined and constant-folded at every `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL >= 1`, so the program collapses to a `println` of a literal and there is NO local symbol left for the carve-out to preserve. Measured on the old fixture: 53 local `t` symbols at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, 0 at 1/2/3 — i.e. it could only ever have passed at O0. Replaced with a Collatz-search program that survives the optimizer: 497 local `t` symbols at the DEFAULT opt level, which is the level anyone profiling actually uses.

DEFECT 2 — DWARF CHECK WAS ELF-SHAPED. The predicate scanned the linked executable for `__debug_info`. On Mach-O that is wrong by construction: `ld` leaves DWARF in the `.o` files and writes an `N_OSO` DEBUG MAP into the executable (which is how lldb and dsymutil locate it); `__debug_info` sections appear only after `dsymutil` bundles a `.dSYM`, and `karac build` never runs dsymutil. Verified: `nm -pa` shows 2 `OSO` entries with `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO=1` and 0 without, while the byte scan finds nothing in either case. Predicate is now per-object-format (OSO on macOS, `.debug_*` scan on ELF).

Both changes make the test STRONGER than filed: it now pins the property at the default optimization level and on both object formats, where before it could only have passed at O0 on ELF.

TRIAGE PATH the entry asked for, resolved: the entry left open whether this was a code regression or host-toolchain sensitivity. Answer: NEITHER — it is a test-fixture and test-predicate defect. No bisect from f569aac was needed once the O0-vs-O1 symbol counts and the OSO/dSYM mechanism were measured.

title: SILENT WRONG OUTPUT (run-vs-build): a GENERIC `fn f[T](s: Slice[T]) -> T` returning a HEAP element yields an EMPTY/garbage value under `karac build` while the tree-walk interpreter is correct — no diagnostic, no crash, just the wrong answer. `fn first[T](s: Slice[T]) -> T { s[0] }` with `let vs: Vec[String] = ["one", "two"]; let tmp: Vec[String] = vs.clone(); println(f"[{first(tmp)}]")` prints `[one]` under --interp and `[]` under build. NARROWED — the axis is the RETURN TYPE being a generic parameter bound to a heap element, combined with how the Vec reached the call: CONCRETE param is always correct (`fn first(s: Slice[String]) -> String` prints `one` for a plain local, a `let`-bound `.clone()`, and an annotated `let`); GENERIC param with a SCALAR element is correct (`Vec[i64]` -> `10`); GENERIC param with a heap element is correct when the argument is the ORIGINAL local (`first(vs)` -> `one`) but WRONG when the argument is a `let` bound to a `.clone()` (`first(tmp)` -> empty), with or without a type annotation on that `let`. NOT the clone: `Vec[String].clone()` and a `Vec[String]`-returning fn are both correct on their own (len and elements read back fine) — the corruption appears only on the way into the `Slice[T]` parameter. RELATED: B-2026-07-03-22 (fixed) was 'a generic `-> T` return whose T is bound from a Slice/container ELEMENT is not resolved to its concrete type'. This looks like a surviving residual of that, for heap elements, on the non-original-local argument path. BLOCKS B-2026-07-29-32: see that entry — a fresh-temp Vec->Slice coercion was prototyped, works for concrete params and scalar elements, and was WITHHELD because for this shape it converts -32's loud build failure into silently wrong output. -32 should not be closed before this is. FIXED 5f2cb6ad. ROOT CAUSE (from the IR, which the entry above flagged as not yet inspected): the monomorph's signature and return type were already correct — `augment_subst_from_arg_elem_types` binds `T`'s LLVM TYPE for exactly this shape, which is what B-2026-07-03-22 fixed. Nothing bound `T` by NAME, so the callee body's element clone emitted `call void @karac_clone_T(...)` — a clone helper for a type that does not exist — where the concrete twin emits `@karac_clone_String`. The element was therefore never deep-cloned and the returned `s[0]` shallow-aliased the container's buffer. So this IS adjacent to B-2026-07-03-22 as guessed, but not a residual of it: -03-22 closed the LLVM-type half, this closes the name half. Two resolvers already filled the name maps (a param that IS a bare `T`; a param nested in a user generic struct); neither covered the plainest shape, a CONTAINER param whose element is the type param. `resolve_container_param_elem_substs` now does, binding `subst_names` + `subst_type_exprs` from the argument's registered element TypeExpr, `or_insert` so no earlier binding is overwritten. THE NARROWING IN THIS ENTRY WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED: `.clone()` is a RED HERRING. The trigger is that the elements are heap-OWNED and the result is used INLINE. `let mut vs: Vec[String] = Vec.new(); vs.push("on" + "e"); println(f"[{first(vs)}]")` reproduces it with no clone anywhere. The 'correct for the original local' cell in the matrix above was correct only BY ACCIDENT: a `Vec` of string LITERALS holds static globals with `cap 0`, so the container's drop frees nothing and the shallow alias stays readable. That is also why `e2e_generic_slice_elem_nonint_return` passed throughout — it uses literals. Binding the result to a `let` first was correct pre-fix, which is the other half of the condition. REPAIRED, each verified against the interpreter: bare `Slice[T]`, `ref Slice[T]`, and generic-to-generic forwarding go from empty to correct. `ref`/bare `Vec[T]` and scalar elements were already correct and stay so. NOT REPAIRED, filed as B-2026-07-29-37: an `Array[T, N]` argument to a generic `Slice[T]` param. VERIFIED: cargo test --all 8740/0; llvm --lib 1116/0, interpreter 1322/0, typechecker 19/0, lljit 2092/0. Corpus: no kata uses a generic container param at all, so nothing published was ever affected, and `check` verdicts across all 688 .kara files are unchanged. NOTE ON A DISCARDED TEST RUN: an early full-codegen run against this change reported 2074 passed / 540 failed and was GARBAGE — SELF-INFLICTED feature thrash, not a regression and not another session. Two of MY OWN cargo invocations were live in the same worktree at once with DIFFERENT feature sets (`cargo test --all`, no llvm, and `cargo test --features llvm --test codegen`), so each kept rebuilding the shared `target/` artifacts the other needed. The tell was the breadth: the failures included `test_assert_eq_int_pass`, `raw_pointer_is_null_method`, tracing, arenas and atomics — none of which a mono type-name binding can reach. A concurrent session WAS running cargo at the time but in its own worktree (`.claude/worktrees/autopar-cost-gate-and-debuginfo`) with its own target dir, so it was never involved; an earlier version of this note wrongly blamed it. Re-run cleanly under an isolated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. Two rules fall out: never run two differently-featured cargo commands against one target dir, and treat any mass-failure sweep whose failures span unrelated subsystems as an environment fault until proven otherwise.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while attempting the B-2026-07-29-32 fix. The probe set that isolated it (d1/d2/d3 and b1-b6 in that session) varied four axes independently — param concrete vs generic, element scalar vs heap, argument original-local vs let-bound-clone vs fresh rvalue, and `let` annotated vs inferred. The interpreter is the oracle throughout and is correct in every cell. WHY THIS IS THE MORE SERIOUS OF THE PAIR: -32 fails LOUDLY (LLVM module verification aborts the build), so nobody ships a wrong binary from it. This one produces a wrong binary with no signal at all, and it is reachable today WITHOUT any of -32's shapes — a plain `let`-bound clone is enough, which is exactly the workaround -32's entry recommended. That recommendation has been corrected in -32. INVESTIGATION NOT DONE: not bisected. No IR inspected — the diagnosis is entirely black-box from the probe matrix, so 'residual of B-2026-07-03-22' is a hypothesis from the symptom shape, not a confirmed root cause. Unknown whether `Array[T, N]` -> `Slice[T]`, `Map`/`Set` element returns, or a generic returning a heap STRUCT (rather than String) behave the same way. Unknown whether the empty output is a zeroed String struct or a freed buffer; LSan/ASan not run on it.
tracker: src/codegen (generic Slice[T] -> T return, heap element)

title: The use-after-move suggestion advised `.clone()` for EVERY type: 'clone 'x' at the move site (`x.clone()`), declare the callee parameter `ref` if it only reads, or restructure'. `moved_type_supports_clone` already gated the machine-applicable TextEdit, so `karac fix` never inserted an invalid `.clone()` — but the human-readable sentence was unconditional, and `.clone()` resolves only on `String`, the built-in heap collections and RC types (B-2026-07-29-31). On an `Option`/`Result` or any user type the advice produced code that does not typecheck. FIXED 697e6de8: the sentence reuses the same predicate. Cloneable types are unchanged; everything else gets "declare the callee parameter `ref` if it only reads, or restructure to avoid reuse ('x' has no `.clone()` — that exists only on `String`, the built-in heap collections and RC types)". WHY THIS IS NOT A COSMETIC WORDING NIT: the Mend loop is an LLM reading these diagnostics and acting on them, so a confident wrong steer costs more than an absent suggestion. Both gaps filed off B-2026-07-29-28's session (-31 and -32) were walked into by following this exact sentence.
detail: Verified: cargo test --all 8740 passed / 0 failed; llvm codegen suite 2613 passed / 0 failed. INCIDENTAL AND WORTH KNOWING: the 309 codegen failures reported in this machine's earlier runs (including in B-2026-07-29-28's verification note) were entirely the missing KARAC_RUNTIME staticlib — `cargo rustc -p karac-runtime --release --crate-type staticlib`, NOT plain `cargo build`. With it built the suite is fully green, so 'byte-identical to baseline at 2304/309' in -28 was a comparison between two equally under-provisioned runs; the conclusion (zero regressions) is unaffected, but the absolute numbers there are an artifact. Both directions checked by hand through `karac check --output=json`: an `Option[String]` gets the no-clone hint and no `replacement`; a `String` keeps the clone hint and the `replacement`.

title: SILENT WRONG OUTPUT (run-vs-build), residual of B-2026-07-29-35: an `Array[T, N]` argument to a GENERIC `Slice[T]` param still yields an empty/garbage element under `karac build` while the interpreter is correct. `fn f[T](s: ref Slice[T]) -> T { s[0] }` with `let arr: Array[String, 2] = ["lit-x", "lit-y"]; println(f"[{f(arr)}]")` prints `[lit-x]` under --interp and `[]` under build. A `Vec` argument to the same signature is CORRECT after -35; only the `Array` argument form is left. ROOT CAUSE, already localised: -35's `resolve_container_param_elem_substs` reads the argument's element TypeExpr from `var_elem_type_exprs`, which `register_var_container_types` (src/codegen/types_lowering.rs) populates for `Vec`, `Slice` and `Map` locals but NOT for `Array[T, N]` — there is no `Array` arm and no `array_inner_type_expr` helper to build one from. So `T` stays unbound by name for an Array arg and the element clone falls back to `karac_clone_T`, exactly as -35 described. WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED WITH -35: the obvious fix — give `register_var_container_types` an `Array` arm — writes into a side table with 167 readers across codegen, so it is a materially broader change than -35 and needs its own blast-radius review rather than riding along. The narrow alternative (teach only `resolve_container_param_elem_substs` to synthesise the element TypeExpr from an Array local's declared type) was not attempted. SEVERITY vs -35: same class, smaller reach — an `Array` local passed to a GENERIC container param is a rarer shape than a `Vec`, and no kata in kara-katas uses a generic container param at all. RETRACTED AND SUPERSEDED 2026-07-30 — THIS ENTRY IS WRONG ON THREE COUNTS, all traceable to one broken measurement. (1) WRONG SYMPTOM: the shape does not 'print an empty element', it CRASHES — SIGTRAP (133) for literal elements, SIGSEGV (139) for owned elements and for SCALARS. (2) WRONG SHAPE: a bare `Slice[T]` param with an `Array` argument is CORRECT on main, for literal AND owned elements, at index 0 and 1. The crashing shape is a `ref Slice[T]` param. (3) WRONG ROOT CAUSE: the missing `Array` arm in `register_var_from_type_expr` is not it. That fix was built (a dedicated `array_elem_type_exprs` map, one writer and one reader, avoiding the 167-reader table this entry worried about) and changed NOTHING observable in any probe, so it was reverted rather than landed as dead code. ROOT CAUSE OF THE MISDIAGNOSIS, worth more than the entry: every probe harness in this session's -35/-37 work captured the program's exit status as `o=$(./prog 2>&1 | head -1); e=$?`, which reads the exit status of `head`, NOT of the program. A crashing binary therefore presented as 'empty output, exit 0' — indistinguishable from a silent wrong value. That is precisely how a crash became 'prints empty' here, and it also invalidates this entry's claim that 'decomposing it one shape per program showed NOTHING crashes in isolation': re-measured with the exit code captured correctly, `ref Slice[T]` + Array crashes in isolation, on plain main, with no fix of mine involved. Redirect to a file and check `$?` before believing any 'empty output' result. The real bug is filed as B-2026-07-30-3, which supersedes this entry. Closing -37 as invalid rather than fixed. PARTIAL VINDICATION 2026-07-30 (B-2026-07-30-3, f0395667): this entry's DIRECTION was right even though its diagnosis was not. There really is no registered `Array` element TypeExpr, and that really does cause a silent miscompile — but the `karac_clone_T` one, visible only with TWO instantiations of the same generic, not the crash this entry measured. It stays invalid: the symptom, the shape, and the causal chain as written are all wrong. The reverted `array_elem_type_exprs` map was ultimately the right fix; it 'changed nothing observable' at the time because a second, unrelated defect (the missing header synthesis on the mono path) masked it end-to-end.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-07-29-35's fix against shapes beyond the original probe matrix (`ref Slice[T]`, `ref Vec[T]`, generic-to-generic forwarding, Array arg). Five of the six new shapes were either already correct or repaired by -35; this is the sixth. A CRASH WORTH KNOWING ABOUT, and why it is not filed separately: a program combining this broken shape with several working ones aborted — SIGTRAP (133) pre-35, SIGSEGV (139) post-35. Decomposing it one shape per program showed NOTHING crashes in isolation, so the abort is this bug's memory corruption surfacing through whatever runs next, and the differing signal is luck rather than a -35 regression. If this is fixed, that crash should go with it; if a crash survives, it is a NEW bug and wants its own entry. INVESTIGATION NOT DONE: no IR captured for the Array form specifically (the diagnosis is by analogy to -35's confirmed IR plus the absence of an Array arm in the side-table registration). Not bisected. Unknown whether an `Array` argument to a generic `Vec[T]`/`Set[T]` param, or a Map value position, has the same hole.

title: PREMATURE DROP on move-out: a binding moved into an aggregate literal is dropped AT THE MOVE POINT, because the shared NLL last-use analysis is a purely syntactic free-identifier walk that cannot tell a move from a read. For `TcpListener` this closes the fd before `accept`, hanging the process.
resolution:
FIXED in BOTH backends. The move-suppression machinery already existed and was merely under-applied: `suppress_user_drop_for_var` (codegen/runtime.rs) and `suppress_let_rebind_user_drop` (interpreter/eval_stmt.rs) matched a move source only from a bare `Identifier` / `SelfValue` RHS — the `let g = f;` rebind. Both sites now also collect bare-identifier field initializers from a `StructLiteral` RHS and suppress each. ~15 lines per side, reusing the existing helpers rather than reimplementing the move classification (a second copy would drift from `ownership_oracle`'s `Role::Move`, the hazard that motivated B-2026-07-29-33).

`spread` (`..base`) is deliberately NOT treated as a move source: it copies remaining fields from a base that stays live and keeps its own drop.

VERIFIED with the pure-language oracle from the entry, both backends agreeing byte-for-byte:
  before: 10 20 99 30 1 40   (drop fires AT THE MOVE)
  after:  10 20 30 1 40
Control — a plain binding's NLL drop timing is unchanged (`5 99 1` before and after), so the fix suppresses only the moved-out case.

`tests/coro_e2e.rs` is now 34/34; `coroutine_method_handler_services_connection` passes because the listener's fd stays open through `accept`. Regression test: `test_user_drop_no_premature_fire_when_moved_into_struct_literal` (tests/interpreter.rs).

RESIDUAL, tracked as B-2026-07-29-39: with only this entry fixed, the premature close becomes an fd LEAK until process exit — strictly safer than a use-after-close, but still wrong. -39 is the other half.

title: An aggregate NEVER runs its fields' user `impl Drop` when it dies: a struct holding a Drop-implementing value drops nothing at scope exit, so any resource stored in a struct field leaks (fd, handle, buffer) for the program's lifetime.
detail:
BOTH BACKENDS AGREE. Discovered while triaging B-2026-07-29-38; the two are distinct defects that happen to cancel into 'one drop at the wrong time' for a trivial payload.

MINIMAL REPRO — no source binding, so B-38's premature-move drop cannot be involved:
  struct Res { id: i64 }
  impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(99); } }
  struct Holder { r: Res }
  fn main() {
      let h = Holder { r: Res { id: 7 } };   // temporary straight into the field
      println(h.r.id);
      println(1);
  }
  actual   (interp AND compiled): 7 1        <- no drop at all
  expected:                       7 1 99     <- h dies, so its Res field drops

So user-`impl Drop` is dispatched for a DIRECT binding of a Drop type but never recursively for a Drop-implementing FIELD of an aggregate. The scope-exit drain drops the aggregate binding itself; nothing walks its fields looking for user drop glue.

CONSEQUENCE. Every resource type with a synthesized drop — `TcpListener`, `TcpStream`, `WebSocket`, `TlsStream`, `TlsListener` (`src/codegen/synth_drop.rs::emit_hardcoded_stdlib_drop_bodies`) — leaks its fd whenever it is held in a struct field rather than a bare local. That is the normal way to write a server (`struct Server { listener: TcpListener }`), so the leak shape is the idiomatic one. A long-running accept loop that stores its listener in a struct never closes it; process exit is currently what reclaims the fd.

FIX SHAPE. Drop glue for an aggregate must recurse into fields whose type has a registered `drop_method_keys` entry, in reverse declaration order, at the point the aggregate is dropped — and must NOT fire for a field that was itself moved out. Interacts with B-2026-07-29-38: correct behaviour needs both (source drop suppressed on move-in, field drop added on aggregate death), and shipping only this one would DOUBLE-drop the B-38 shape (source dropped early AND field dropped at exit). Sequence them together, or gate this one behind B-38.

Same blast radius and validation bar as B-38: pinned drop-timing tests plus the `drop_differential` fuzzer corpus; verify under ASAN/LSan on Linux (macOS asan has no leak detection — see CLAUDE.md).

── UPDATE 2026-07-29, after fixing B-2026-07-29-38 ──

INTERPRETER HALF IS IMPLEMENTED, VERIFIED, AND THEN DELIBERATELY REVERTED. A ~40-line recursive field walk (`drop_user_drop_fields_of_binding` + a value-level worker, hung off `invoke_user_drop_if_applicable` after the parent's own body and OUTSIDE the `if !has_user_drop { return; }` early-out that was skipping the field entirely) produced the correct result: `7 1` -> `7 99 1`. Reverted because CODEGEN CANNOT MATCH IT YET, and shipping it interpreter-only is a run-vs-build divergence.

WHY CODEGEN NEEDS NEW MACHINERY, not a mirror edit: a type like `Holder` has NO `impl Drop` of its own, so no `karac_drop_Holder` wrapper exists to hang field drops on. One must be SYNTHESIZED for any aggregate that merely CONTAINS a Drop-implementing field, and bindings of such types registered in the cleanup frame even though the type declares no Drop. That is this entry's real scope.

PREREQUISITE FOUND: `drop_differential` PASSED (13/13) while the interp/codegen divergence was live. Its cases do not cover the aggregate-holding-a-Drop-field shape, which is exactly why this class stayed invisible. Add that shape to the differential corpus FIRST — otherwise the fix ships with no gate able to catch a regression in it.

SEQUENCING now concrete: -38 is fixed, so the source's slot is suppressed and this entry can no longer double-drop the move shape. Field-drop synthesis is therefore safe to add on its own, provided it also declines to fire for a field that was itself moved out.

SHARED-STRUCT CAVEAT for the implementer: do NOT recurse into `shared struct` fields. Their drop is refcount-driven, so firing on the holder's death would drop a value other holders still reference — the reason the existing interpreter path gates on `count == 1`.

── UPDATE 2026-07-29 (second pass): GATE LANDED, and the earlier gate identification was WRONG ──

CORRECTION. This entry previously said to add the aggregate-field shape to the `drop_differential` corpus. That is not the right gate. `drop_differential` compares codegen's emitted drops against the ownership ORACLE's schedule, and the oracle models HEAP ownership (String/Vec/Map buffers) — neither `ownership_oracle.rs` nor `drop_differential.rs` references `drop_method_keys`, so a user `impl Drop` body is invisible to it. A case added there would not have constrained this class, which also explains cleanly why it passed 13/13 while the interp/codegen divergence was live.

GATE THAT ACTUALLY WORKS, now landed (b42f466f): `test_user_drop_on_aggregate_field_run_build_parity` in tests/cli.rs — a `karac run --interp` vs `karac build` OUTPUT parity test, since program output is the observable signal for a user drop. It asserts parity and correctness SEPARATELY so a one-sided fix and a missing drop are distinguishable failures. Landed `#[ignore]`d with this bug id because it is genuinely red today (`got 0 in "7\n1\n"`); UN-IGNORE IT AS PART OF THIS SLICE.

CODEGEN SCOPE, now read in detail — this is why the slice did not land with the gate:
  1. `emit_user_drop_wrapper` bails at `module.get_function("{Type}.drop")?`, and `emit_user_drop_wrappers` only iterates `drop_method_keys` keys. A type like `Holder` that merely CONTAINS a Drop field is never considered, so no wrapper exists to extend.
  2. The wrapper body is (a) user body, then (b) `emit_struct_drop_synthesis` for heap-owning fields. A third step is needed: GEP each Drop-bearing field and call its `karac_drop_<FieldType>`.
  3. The tracking gate in `stmts.rs` is `has_user_drop = drop_method_keys.contains_key(&struct_name)`; it must become a TRANSITIVE predicate, and re-routing a binding from the `track_struct_var_inst` branch to `track_user_drop_var` must not lose the per-monomorph instantiation threading.

THE HAZARD TO RESPECT (the reason this is not a mirror of the interpreter edit): `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl` is per-MONOMORPH. B-2026-07-11-35 and B-2026-07-15-24 record that a generic struct needs one drop fn per instantiation AND per-monomorph GEP layout, because binding a generic param to a wider heap type shifts every subsequent field offset. A field-drop call added without honouring the active subst and the mono layout is a wrong-offset write, i.e. heap corruption, not a leak. A field whose declared type is a bare generic param is additionally instantiation-dependent for 'does it have a Drop at all' — the interpreter sees the runtime value and would drop it while codegen cannot, so the parity gate above will catch any scoping mismatch between the two backends. Decide that scoping deliberately.

VALIDATION BAR: the gate above, plus `drop_differential`, plus the ASAN suite, plus Linux LSan — macOS `-fsanitize=address` has no leak detection, so use `scripts/lsan-local.sh` (colima) or the CI `memory-sanitizer` job. An under-suppressed field drop double-frees; an over-suppressed one leaks.
resolution:
FIXED in BOTH backends, with run/build parity.

THE SHAPE AS LANDED DIFFERS FROM THIS ENTRY'S `FIX SHAPE` NOTE IN ONE LOAD-BEARING WAY, and the difference is what makes it safe: the field glue runs the user drop BODIES ONLY and never frees memory. The tempting design — have the parent's drop call each Drop-bearing field's `karac_drop_<F>` (or its `__karac_drop_struct_<F>`) — DOUBLE-FREES, because `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl` already reaches that field through its `NestedStruct` classification. Restricting the new pass to `<F>.drop` calls makes it purely additive: not one existing free moves, and no path releases memory twice. It also defuses the per-monomorph hazard this entry flagged — GEPs are still computed against the mono layout (`mono_struct_type_from_subst` + `nested_struct_field_subst`), but nothing is FREED at a computed offset, so a wrong offset could at worst call a body, not corrupt the heap.

CODEGEN. `emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn` (synth_drop.rs) emits `__karac_dropbodies_<T>[$mono]`: each Drop-bearing field's `<F>.drop` in REVERSE declaration order, recursing into nested aggregates. `type_runs_user_drop` is the transitive predicate and declines `shared` types at every level — their drop is refcount-driven, this entry's SHARED-STRUCT CAVEAT. `karac_drop_<T>` calls it right after the user body, which covers every existing wrapper call site (bindings, fresh temps, owned-aggregate returns) in one edit. A type that merely CONTAINS a Drop field has no wrapper to extend, so `stmts.rs` registers the bodies fn on the `CleanupAction::UserDrop` channel — the only one `fire_due_user_drops` fires at the binding's NLL live-range end, which is where the interpreter places it — alongside the unchanged `StructDrop` for memory. Two actions, disjoint work, and the memory stays valid until scope exit so a body reading `self.<field>` at its NLL point is safe.

INTERPRETER. `drop_user_drop_fields_of_value` (eval_stmt.rs) walks a `Value::Struct`'s fields in reverse DECLARATION order — read off the `StructDef`, because the interpreter stores fields in a `HashMap` whose iteration order is neither source order nor stable — running each field's body then recursing. `run_user_drop_body_on_value` composes body-then-walk so every discarded-temp hook matches codegen's wrapper; the binding drain composes them separately so the walk goes through the name-keyed entry point that consults the moved-out set.

MOVED-OUT FIELDS, which this entry required. `let x = h.a;` hands the field's `Drop` to `x`, so the source is disarmed or the body runs twice (a double close for a resource type). Codegen re-points the source's registered action to `karac_dropnf_<T>` — literally the pre-fix wrapper, body + heap cleanup, no field bodies — when the parent has a `Drop` of its own, and removes the bodies action outright when it does not; the interpreter records the source in `moved_out_drop_field_bindings`. Coarse on purpose: it disarms the parent's WHOLE field walk, not just the moved field. Exact for the single-Drop-field aggregate; for a multi-field one it UNDER-drops, which is the correct side of this entry's own bar ('an under-suppressed field drop double-frees; an over-suppressed one leaks').

GATE. `test_user_drop_on_aggregate_field_run_build_parity` (tests/cli.rs, landed `#[ignore]`d with b42f466f) is un-ignored and green. Added alongside it: `e2e_aggregate_runs_field_user_drop` (tests/codegen.rs) and `test_aggregate_runs_field_user_drop` (tests/interpreter.rs) — the SAME program on both backends, pinning reverse-declaration order and the moved-out single drop — and `asan_aggregate_field_user_drop_fires_once` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs), which loops the shape 200x under Linux LSan so an under-drop surfaces as a definite leak report and an over-drop as a double-free abort. `drop_differential` and the full ASAN suite stay green.

RESIDUALS, each checked to be pre-existing or backend-symmetric:
  * a struct holding ONLY a `shared` Drop field still diverges (codegen rc-drops it at scope exit, the interpreter does not). Reproduced WITH AND WITHOUT this change on a program containing no other Drop field, so it is untouched by this fix — it is the interpreter's field-held-shared-ref gap already noted in `invoke_user_drop_if_applicable` and tracked under the L940 drop-reconciliation item.
  * enum PAYLOADS are not walked, and a by-value aggregate param whose type declares no `Drop` of its own runs no field bodies. Both backends agree on both, so parity holds; filed as B-2026-07-30-11.

tracker: src/iter_local.rs (new module: provenance fixpoint + freshness predicate); src/concurrency.rs (loop_body_types_cross_task_safe: whitelist consult + KARAC_PAR_ITER_LOCAL_SHARED opt-out)
title: Auto-par's cross-task-safety gate is TYPE-based, so it declines a reduction whose body allocates an iteration-LOCAL shared value (kata #23, #86 par lanes get zero speedup)
detail:
CORRECTION to this entry's first revision, which guessed the mechanism wrong. The blocker is
NOT the `allocates` effect and NOT the effect-conflict check (`allocates + allocates` is
explicitly NOT a conflict, concurrency.rs:3099). It is the B-2026-07-16-6 soundness gate
`loop_body_types_cross_task_safe` (concurrency.rs:2195), called from
`recognize_reductions_in_block`.

MECHANISM. That gate walks EVERY expression type whose span falls inside the loop body and
declines the reduction if any fails `cross_task_safe::is_cross_task_safe`. A plain `shared`
(non-`par`) handle carries a NON-ATOMIC refcount header, so racing rc-inc/rc-dec across
workers is a lost update -> use-after-free. Declining is CORRECT for a handle that actually
crosses workers.

THE IMPRECISION: the gate is purely TYPE-based -- there is no escape analysis. A `shared`
value allocated and fully consumed inside ONE iteration never has a handle reach a second
worker, so its non-atomic refcount is only ever touched by the thread that made it. The gate
cannot express that, so it declines on the type alone.

THREE-WAY PROBE isolating it (scratchpad pa1/pa2/pa3.kara, identical `sum = sum + f(k)`
reduction over k in 0..170000, differing only in what the body allocates):
  pa1  pure compute, no allocation          -> 162 karac_par_* calls   FIRES
  pa3  Vec[i64] heap alloc per iteration    -> 162 karac_par_* calls   FIRES
  pa2  `shared struct Node` list per iter   ->   0 karac_par_* calls   DECLINES
pa3 is the load-bearing one: heap allocation per iteration parallelizes fine, so allocation
is not the discriminator -- `shared`-ness is.

MEASURED IMPACT (x86 container, karac 9dd8aa325021). Two katas' par lanes have been silently
publishing a second copy of their sequential number:
  #23 merge-k-sorted-lists  kara seq 3399.5 -> par 3411.9 ms  (1.00x)  cpu 100.0%
  #86 partition-list        kara seq  884.9 -> par  866.4 ms  (1.02x)  cpu 100.0%
Peers on the same workloads reach 335-392% CPU: rust seq->par 2.85x / 2.55x, C 2.06x / 1.99x.
Both kata sources assert in a comment that the default build parallelizes the loop.

WHY IT IS WORTH PRECISION WORK RATHER THAN A DOC FIX: Kara WINS both sequential lanes on
equal safety (#23 0.82x, #86 0.93x vs rust_ovf) and converts none of it. The par rows read as
a 2.33x / 2.36x deficit that is entirely unrealized upside. Per-iteration-local `shared`
allocation is a COMMON shape -- any kata that builds a linked list / tree per iteration and
folds it hits this.

LIKELY FIX: an escape check to sit alongside the type check -- if every `shared`-typed value
in the body is created inside the iteration and neither stored into an outer-scope binding nor
returned, the non-atomic refcount cannot be touched by two workers, so the reduction is safe.
Strictly a precision improvement; the existing gate stays as the fallback. Do NOT weaken the
type gate itself -- B-2026-07-16-6 documents the UAF it prevents.

Not defer/errdefer related (B-2026-07-16-10). Found only after the par lane got an
equal-safety rayon twin (kara-katas 0a93109); before that the lane could only be read against
a wrapping `rustc -O` baseline, which hid whether the gap was the overflow tax.

FIXED 2026-07-30. Root cause confirmed exactly as this entry's corrected revision described:
`loop_body_types_cross_task_safe` (concurrency.rs) declines on the TYPE of any expression in
the body, with no escape analysis to distinguish a handle that crosses workers from one that
never leaves the iteration that made it.

THE FIX is a new module, `src/iter_local.rs`, consulted by that gate. It answers one question
-- which expressions in this loop body provably cannot evaluate to a handle on an object that
existed before the iteration began, or that outlives it? -- and the gate then declines only
for unsafe-typed spans OUTSIDE that set. The type gate is untouched and remains the fallback,
per this entry's own instruction not to weaken it (B-2026-07-16-6).

SHAPE OF THE ARGUMENT. Two flows have to be closed.
  INFLOW  -- a pre-iteration object entering. Every such object must be NAMED to be reached
             (a param, `self`, an outer local, or a projection of one), so freshness is rooted
             at name provenance: an identifier is iteration-local only if it is bound inside
             the body AND every value that can flow into it is itself iteration-local.
             Provenance is a GREATEST fixpoint, so it is order-insensitive and admits
             loop-carried bindings (`cur = n.next` in a walk loop) without a phase-order bug.
  OUTFLOW -- a handle surviving the iteration. A write into a local's field (`node.next = X`)
             is recorded as a write to the local itself, so a non-local X demotes `node`.
             `return`, `break value`, closures, and nested par/seq/lock/provider regions
             decline the whole body. Writes to an OUTER name need no separate check: the only
             one that survives `classify_loop_body` is the reduction accumulator, which is an
             outer name and therefore swept -- an unsafe-typed accumulator declines on its own
             reads, and a safe-typed one cannot hold an unsafe value, by typing.

FAIL-CLOSED, which is what preserves the original gate's stated design property (its doc
comment records that a span sweep was chosen over an AST walk precisely because a walk with a
missed `ExprKind` silently reopens the hole). The polarity is inverted here: the walk never
CLEARS a span the sweep flagged, it only ADDS spans on positive evidence of freshness. An
`ExprKind` the module does not model -- today's or tomorrow's -- is simply absent from the
whitelist and the decline stands. A missed variant costs a sequential loop, never a
miscompile. `visit_children` is additionally exhaustive over `ExprKind` with no catch-all, so
a new variant is a compile error rather than a silently unvisited subtree.

ONE NON-OBVIOUS PIECE, worth recording because the first implementation was wrong without it:
`is_local` short-circuits on the expression's TYPE before any structural rule. A loop body is
full of plain scalars that are outer-scope reads -- `k + j` where `k` is the loop counter --
and an `i64` cannot possibly alias a `shared` object, but a purely provenance-based predicate
calls it non-local and poisons every expression built from it. With the type short-circuit the
probe fires; without it, it still declines. Symmetrically, unit enum variants (`None`, whose
type IS `Option[shared Node]` while holding no handle at all) are whitelisted by name, else
every `Option[shared T]` list shape declines at its first `let head = None`.

MEASURED (this container, x86, 4 cores). Probe: 400000 iterations, each building a 12-node
`shared` list head-first and folding it back down.
  precision pass ON  (KARAC_PAR_ITER_LOCAL_SHARED unset): 0.04-0.05 s wall, 0.15 s user  ~330% CPU
  precision pass OFF (KARAC_PAR_ITER_LOCAL_SHARED=0):     0.10-0.11 s wall, 0.11 s user   100% CPU
  ~2.3x, and the three builds (par / precision-off / KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) all print 960024000000.

MEMORY SAFETY -- the load-bearing verification, since this puts a NON-ATOMIC refcount inside a
parallel region for the first time. New E2E under ASAN+LeakSanitizer:
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_auto_par_reduction_iteration_local_shared_list_no_leak_no_uaf`
(60000 iterations x 12-node chain, trip count chosen to clear
REDUCE_DISPATCH_THRESHOLD_UNITS so the lowering actually fires rather than passing vacuously).
Clean. If the escape analysis were wrong, the failure mode is exactly what LSan/ASAN catch: a
lost rc-dec is a leak, a lost rc-inc is a use-after-free.

NOT VERIFIED -- stated plainly. The kata #23 / #86 numbers in this entry could NOT be
re-measured: kara-katas is a separate repository and is not in this session's scope. What is
verified is the MECHANISM (the three-way probe reproduces, and the fix flips it) and a
synthetic workload of the same shape. Whether those two katas' par lanes actually convert
depends on their exact body shape -- in particular, a `break` anywhere in the body, including
one that targets a NESTED loop and cannot exit the reduction body at all, is still declined by
`block_has_early_exit` in codegen/reduce.rs. That is a separate imprecision, found while
building the probe for this entry and filed as B-2026-07-30-8. Re-run the two kata par lanes
against a kara-katas checkout before claiming the 2.33x / 2.36x deficit is closed.

OPT-OUT: KARAC_PAR_ITER_LOCAL_SHARED=0 restores the pure type gate (precedent:
KARAC_RC_ELIDE_REF_PARAMS=0). TESTS: 4 analyzer tests in tests/concurrency.rs -- one accept
(the bug's shape) and three declines, one per way a handle reaches outside one iteration
(built outside the loop / escaping to an outer binding / arriving as a parameter). The accept
test alone would pass just as well against a gate that had been deleted outright, which is
what the three decline tests exist to catch.

VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY (2026-07-30, karac 7d6915298a43, x86 container) by the reporter,
against the numbers this entry was filed with. Fix CONFIRMED, fully:
  probe pa2.kara (shared-allocating reduction body): par calls 0 -> 162; output unchanged
    (1631993952).
  kata #86 partition-list, same sink (84997457408934):
    kara par  866.4 ms @ cpu 100.0%   ->  391.2 ms @ cpu ~383%
    seq->par speedup  1.02x           ->  2.18x
    vs rust_ovf       2.36x           ->  ~1.07x
Auto-par now fires on the shape and the par-lane deficit is essentially gone.

title: Vec.sort_by calls the comparator through a function pointer, so sort-bound katas track C's qsort instead of Rust's monomorphized sort (~2x)
detail:
`karac_vec_sort_by` (runtime/src/lib.rs:7925) takes the comparator as
`cmp: extern "C" fn(*mut u8, *const u8, *const u8) -> i64` -- a FUNCTION POINTER. Element
moves are already well optimized (`sort_fixed_width::<W>` monomorphizes the 8- and 16-byte
widths so every move is an inlined register copy), but the COMPARISON itself is an indirect
call per probe that cannot be inlined into the merge.

That is structurally what C's `qsort` does, and the measurements line up exactly. #1665
minimum-initial-energy, quiet x86 host, 200 runs, karac 9dd8aa325021:
  kara      17.9 +- 2.2 ms      ordered.sort_by(|a,b| (b.1-b.0).cmp(a.1-a.0))
  c_v3      18.4 +- 3.3 ms      qsort(tasks, n, sizeof(Task), task_cmp)   <- function ptr too
  rust_ovf   9.1 +- 2.7 ms      ordered.sort_by(...)  <- closure monomorphized into the sort
  rust       9.2 +- 1.8 ms

So Kara is at PARITY WITH C (0.97x) and both are ~2x behind Rust. This is not a Kara-is-slow
result against C; it is that Rust's `sort_by` monomorphizes the comparator and Kara's and C's
do not. kara/rust_ovf = 1.97x, which reproduces the 1.99x the corpus recorded, and #1665 is
one of only two katas left above 2x once every comparison is put on equal safety footing.

This is the standing explanation for BENCHMARKS.md's 'the low-cardinality sort in #1665'
residual-gap note, which until now described the symptom without the mechanism.

POSSIBLE FIXES, cheapest first:
  1. Codegen a monomorphized sort per call site when the comparator is a literal closure --
     the comparator body is known statically at every sort_by site in the corpus.
  2. Specialized runtime entrypoints for the common comparator shapes (ascending/descending
     on a scalar field or key expression), chosen by codegen from the closure body. Narrower
     than (1) but no per-site code growth.
  3. Leave as-is and document -- acceptable, since the gap only shows on sort-dominated
     workloads, but note it costs ~2x on every one of them.

Related, same corpus pass: #30 concat_words is the other kata still at ~2x vs safety-matched
Rust (350.5 vs 174.4 ms, quiet host, 40 runs). Its cause is NOT this one and is NOT yet
root-caused -- Kara allocates only once per distinct word there (16 words) so it is not
allocation, and Kara's FxHash should beat Rust's SipHash, so the obvious hypotheses are both
wrong. Its 9.6x vs c_v3 is a benchmark-parity artifact, not a Kara result: that C mirror does
not implement the same algorithm (it packs 4-char words into a u32 and linear-scans <=64
entries instead of hashing strings into a map), which its own header comment describes as the
'moral equivalent' of the map the other mirrors use. Tracked for the mirror-parity sweep.

FIXED 0139427 — monomorphized stable merge sort, gate removed.

FIX (option 1 from the list above, which was also the cheapest). The mono
infrastructure already existed: `emit_sort_by_mono` (codegen/vec_method.rs) has
inlined the comparator body at the compare since Slice 6.1. What it emitted was an
INSERTION SORT, so it could only be used below a runtime `len > 64` check and
everything larger fell to `karac_vec_sort_by`. The entry describes the function
pointer as the defect; the operative cause was one level up — the mono path's
O(N^2) algorithm is what forced the length gate that routed large sorts to the
pointer in the first place.

Replaced it with a stable bottom-up merge sort, an IR mirror of the runtime's
`sort_fixed_width` so the two backends order equal elements identically:
insertion-sort 32-element runs (same RUN as the runtime), then merge adjacent runs
of doubling width, ping-ponging between the data buffer and one scratch malloc,
copying back only when an odd number of passes leaves the live data in scratch.
The merge takes the LEFT run on a tie (`cmp <= 0`) — the stability guarantee.
Stability was not optional: design.md requires an in-place stable sort, which the
runtime's own comment cites as the reason heapsort/introsort are excluded, so the
much shorter in-place O(N log N) options were off the table.

The `len > 64` dispatch is deleted. An inline non-capturing comparator now
monomorphizes at EVERY N and emits no runtime sort call. `karac_vec_sort_by`
remains the path for the shapes the mono gate declines (capturing closure, named
fn, closure-typed local, non-eligible element type), so it is not dead code.

MEASURED (this container, 200 sorts of 50,000 `(i64, i64)` pairs). The A/B is
within one program shape: a capturing comparator still routes to the runtime path,
so it reproduces the old behaviour exactly.
  mono merge sort (new)        0.09 s   (0.09/0.09/0.09)
  runtime fn-pointer (old)     0.18-0.23 s
  construction-only baseline   ~0.005 s
Construction is negligible, so this is ~2.3x on the sort itself — consistent with
the 1.97x kara/rust_ovf this entry recorded for #1665. NOT re-benchmarked against
the kata corpus (not available in this container), so the #1665 figure remains a
projection; re-bench before quoting a new corpus number.

VERIFIED: sortedness AND stability at n = 0, 1, 2, 31, 32, 33, 64, 65, 1000, 2000,
50000 — the boundaries that matter are the insertion base run (32) and the removed
threshold (64), plus the degenerate lengths that skip the scratch allocation.
Stability checked by sorting `(key, original_index)` on key only and asserting the
indices stay ascending within every equal-key group. interp/AOT parity on the same
program. valgrind clean for the new scratch malloc/free (the only leak reported is
11 bytes from the probe's own `Env.args()`, present in a no-sort baseline too).
Suites: codegen 2621, memory_sanitizer 863 (Linux, so LSan), fmt, clippy
--all-targets. Three regression tests added in tests/codegen.rs, one of them an IR
assertion that no `karac_vec_sort_by` call survives for an inline comparator at
N=5000 — the direct gate on this entry.

NOT DONE: no arm64 leg. No kata-corpus re-bench. The `#30 concat_words` note at the
end of this entry is a separate, still-unroot-caused gap and is untouched.

VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY (2026-07-30, karac 7d6915298a43, x86 container, 200 runs, same
sink 12625000). Fix delivers a real win but does NOT fully close the gap -- worth stating
plainly, since 'fixed' could otherwise be read as 'now at parity with Rust':
  kara      17.9 -> 13.9 ms   (22% faster)
  rust_ovf   9.1 ->  7.9 ms
  c_v3      18.4 -> 18.3 ms
  kara/rust_ovf  1.97x -> 1.76x
  kara/c_v3      0.97x -> 0.76x   (Kara now clearly ahead of matched-ISA C)
So monomorphizing the comparator recovered about a fifth of the runtime and moved Kara
from parity-with-C to comfortably ahead of it, but Rust remains 1.76x faster. The
comparator indirect call is therefore NOT the whole story; the residual is most likely
the sort ALGORITHM (Rust's driftsort/pdqsort vs the merge sort in karac_vec_sort_by),
which is a separate and larger piece of work. Re-open or file a follow-up if that
remaining 1.76x is judged worth chasing.

title: CRASH (run-vs-build): an `Array[T, N]` argument passed to a GENERIC `ref Slice[T]` parameter builds and then aborts — SIGTRAP (133) with literal elements, SIGSEGV (139) with owned elements AND with scalar elements — while the interpreter is correct. `fn f[T](s: ref Slice[T]) -> T { s[0] }` with `let a: Array[String, 2] = ["lit-x", "lit-y"]; println(f"[{f(a)}]")` prints `[lit-x]` under --interp and traps under `karac build`. Element type is IRRELEVANT (an `Array[i64, 2]` segfaults too), which rules out the clone/heap-element class entirely. NOT the generic-ness alone and NOT `ref` alone: a CONCRETE `ref Slice[String]` param with the same Array argument is correct, and a BARE generic `Slice[T]` param with the same argument is correct. It takes generic + `ref` + Array together. THIS IS B-2026-06-19-1 SURVIVING ON THE MONOMORPHIZED PATH. That entry (fixed) was the same crash for the non-generic case: an Array binding's storage is its raw elements with no `{ptr,len}` header, so the `get_data_ptr` identifier fast-path handed `&array[0]` to a param expecting a header pointer and the callee read `ptr = elem0, len = elem1` — a bogus slice. Its fix synthesizes the header for Array sources at src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs:1300, but that synthesis is GATED on `slice_elems.get(i)` being `Some(Some(elem_ty))`, read from `fn_param_slice_elem`. For a generic param that table is filled by `declare_mono_function` via `extract_slice_elem_type(Slice[T])`, which resolves `T` through `type_subst_names` — the NAME map. With an Array argument that name binding is absent, the entry is `None`, the synthesis is skipped, and the bogus fast-path runs. The pre-fix symptom described in B-2026-06-19-1 (ptr = elem0, len = elem1) matches what is observed, including why scalars crash. FIXED f0395667 — AND THIS ENTRY'S ROOT CAUSE WAS WRONG, in a way worth recording. The synthesis is NOT skipped because `fn_param_slice_elem` holds `None` for a generic param: `extract_slice_elem_type` recurses through `Ref` and ends in `llvm_type_for_type_expr`, which returns a type rather than an Option, so `slice_elems[i]` is `Some(..)` here and the gate FIRES the moment the code exists. The actual cause is simpler and dumber: THE ARRAY->HEADER SYNTHESIS DID NOT EXIST ON THE MONOMORPHIZED PATH AT ALL. B-2026-06-19-1's fix lives in the non-generic `compile_call` (call_dispatch.rs); the generic mono direct-call path's ref-arg arm (mono.rs, `compile_generic_call`) went straight to `get_data_ptr` with no Array interception. That also explains this entry's own recorded negative result exactly: the `is_ref` arm never READS `slice_elems`, so supplying the missing name binding could not possibly have helped, and its 'either declare_mono_function reads its substitution state too early, or extract_slice_elem_type is not the gate' — the second disjunct was right. THREE DISTINCT DEFECTS had to be fixed; each was individually verified to still reproduce after the previous one landed. (1) The missing header synthesis above — ported into the mono ref-arg arm. (2) A SECOND, INDEPENDENT DEFECT the header fix then exposed: two instantiations of ONE generic fed Arrays shared a single `karac_clone_T`. An Array argument bound `T`'s LLVM TYPE (the `Slice` arm of `augment_subst_from_arg_elem_types` reads the array slot through `infer_elem_from_source`) but not `T`'s NAME, because an Array local had no registered element `TypeExpr` anywhere — precisely the name/type split -32 established must never happen, since the NAME is what specializes the clone helper. Order-dependent and nastier than the crash: `i64` then `String` ran the String through an 8-byte i64 clone leaving len/cap as uninitialized alloca garbage (SIGSEGV), while `String` then `i64` copied 24 bytes out of an 8-byte alloca — corrupting the stack while PRINTING THE CORRECT ANSWER. Fixed with a dedicated `array_elem_type_exprs` (one writer at the Array let site + the shared registrar, one reader in `arg_container_elem_type_expr`), deliberately NOT by widening `var_elem_type_exprs`, whose ~170 readers treat a present entry as 'this binding is a Vec/Slice/Map'. The mono's mangled name now carries the binding (`first$struct$T_ct_String`) and each mono calls its own `karac_clone_String`. (3) An Array REF PARAM forwarded to a `Slice[T]` param, which reproduces WITHOUT generics and is therefore filed separately as B-2026-07-30-6.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while attempting B-2026-07-29-37, which turned out to be a misdiagnosis of this bug (see that entry's retraction for the harness fault behind it). NEGATIVE RESULT WORTH KEEPING: supplying the missing name binding for an Array argument — the obvious consequence of the chain above — did NOT fix it. A dedicated `array_elem_type_exprs` map wired into `arg_container_elem_type_expr` (so `subst_names[T]` gets the Array's element) left every probe byte-identical. So either `declare_mono_function` reads its substitution state before that resolver runs, or `extract_slice_elem_type` is not the gate that matters here. That is the next thing to check, and it is why this is filed rather than fixed. INVESTIGATION NOT DONE: no IR captured for the crashing form (the diagnosis is by symptom-match to B-2026-06-19-1 plus reading the gate at call_dispatch.rs:1300). Not bisected. Unknown whether `mut ref Slice[T]`, a generic `ref Slice[T]` fed a `Vec` (rather than an Array), or a `ref Array[T, N]` param behave the same way. No ASan/valgrind run. CLOSED f0395667. WHAT -37 GOT RIGHT AFTER ALL: its direction — that no `Array` element TypeExpr is registered anywhere — was a REAL defect (number 2 above), even though it was NOT the cause of the crash -37 was measuring, and -37 stays invalid on that basis. The sequencing is the lesson: the`array_elem_type_exprs` attempt was abandoned earlier for 'changing nothing observable', which was true and misleading — the header defect masked it completely, so the second fix only became measurable once the first had landed. Two defects on one shape, where fixing either alone leaves the program still crashing, will read as 'my fix did nothing' every time. EVIDENCE UPGRADED over the original filing, which recorded no IR and inferred the mechanism by symptom-match: `s.len()` over `Array[i64,4] = [100,7,3,4]` returned 7 under build and the JIT versus 4 under the interpreter — literally elem1, a direct observation of `ptr = elem0, len = elem1` and a SILENT WRONG ANSWER rather than a crash. IR was captured and confirms both defects (a single `define internal void @karac_clone_T` loading i64, called by both monos). A NEW SURFACE FACT the original filing missed: the JIT lane (`karac run`) also failed on every affected shape — exit 1 with NO diagnostic on stdout or stderr, which is why it read as 'interpreter correct, build broken' when in fact only `--interp` was correct. The JIT is fixed too, and all four surfaces (`--interp` / `run` / `build` / `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build`) now agree byte-for-byte on 13 probe programs. RESOLVED UNKNOWNS from the original filing: a generic `ref Slice[T]` fed a `Vec` was always correct (its storage starts with a `{ptr,len}` header superset), and `mut ref Slice[T]` + Array never reaches codegen — the typechecker rejects it even with a call-site `mut` marker. STILL NOT DONE: no ASan/valgrind run; the STATE-MACHINE arg path in mono.rs (`compile_generic_call`'s per-mono state-struct store, for a network-yielding generic) has the IDENTICAL missing-Array-interception shape and was left alone because constructing a yielding generic with a `ref Slice[T]` param needs the async harness — untested either way, so it is called out here rather than silently 'covered'. VERIFICATION NOTE, since it produced a false result mid-fix: `run_program` in tests/codegen.rs returns `None` when libkarac_runtime.a is absent and the accept-on-None convention then makes the test VACUOUSLY PASS. An early 'passes with the fix' claim here was exactly that — both arms had skipped. The real A/B sets KARAC_RUNTIME and shows `left: ""` (crash, empty stdout) at baseline for all three regression tests, each individually confirmed to fail before its fix.
tracker: src/codegen/mono.rs (compile_generic_call ref-arg arm: Array->header synthesis + array_elem_type_exprs reader); src/codegen/stmts.rs (Array let element registration); src/codegen/expr_ops.rs (arg_is_array_source)

title: #3629 bfs_sieve trails C on the sequential lane — the buffer cache's park withholds a large chunk and glibc's SUBSEQUENT SMALL allocations degrade 2.15x. NOT kara-specific: a pure-C mirror retaining the same array reproduces it at 1.82x. Fixed by a churn-gated malloc_trim on park: sieve 1.75x -> 1.14x vs C, bigbuf cache win 6.79x -> 7.22x
detail:
Quiet x86 host, 6 runs, karac 9dd8aa325021, seq lane:
  kara_seq  24.88 s +- 1.96
  rust_ovf   8.60 s +- 0.30     -> kara/rust_ovf = 2.89x
  rust      10.14 s +- 1.02
  c_v3      10.15 s +- 0.61     -> kara/c_v3    = 2.45x

This is the ONLY kata left in the corpus above 2x once every comparison is put on equal
safety footing, and the only one where Kara trails C as well -- so unlike #228 (overflow tax)
and #1665 (B-2026-07-30-2, comparator indirect call, where Kara is AT PARITY with C), this
one is not explained by a semantics difference or by C/Rust doing less work.

MEASUREMENT NOTE: three readings exist -- 1.93x, 2.61x, 2.89x. Kara's own absolute time is
stable across the last two (24.7 s, 24.9 s); the low 1.93x came from a low Kara reading AND a
high rust_ovf reading in the same noisy batch. Treat ~2.5-2.9x as the figure.

THREE HYPOTHESES TESTED AND REFUTED (recorded so nobody re-tests them):
  1. The sieve. The kata header says the O(cap log log cap) sieve 'dominates wall-clock'.
     It does not, for Kara. Isolated probe (scratchpad nv.kara/nv.c, cap=50000, the same
     `factors[j].push(i)` over a Vec[Vec[i64]]): kara 16.5 ms vs clang -O3 -march=v3 18.5 ms
     -- Kara is FASTER. At 50 calls that is ~0.8 s of a 24.9 s run.
  2. Nested-Vec element mutation (`outer[i].push(x)`). Same probe as (1). Not it.
  3. The Map-of-Vec bucket build, `bucket.entry(p).or_insert(Vec.new()).push(j)` -- the
     worry being that or_insert does not hand back a true in-place reference, making each
     push O(len). Probe (scratchpad me.kara): 400,000 entry/or_insert/push over 200 keys
     (avg 2000 elems per inner Vec) in 10.2 ms = ~25 ns/op. Flat, not O(len). Not it.

REMAINING CANDIDATES, none tested: the BFS deque itself (`queue.push_back((i, d+1))` -- a
deque of TUPLES, so check for per-push boxing/copying), `for p in factors[v].iter()` and
`for j in indices.into_iter()` iterator lowering, and the `visited: Vec[bool]` accesses.
The deque-of-tuples is the most suspicious of these because it is the one construct in the
hot path that none of the three probes above touched.

No profiler on the measurement container (no perf), which is why this is bisected by probe
rather than profiled. A perf/samply run on a host that has one should localize it quickly.

── ATTRIBUTION TO B-2026-07-30-5 NOW QUANTIFIED (2026-07-30). It was an assertion; here is
   the arithmetic, and the one measurement still needed to settle it. ──

-5 claims to be this entry's root cause, but its own supporting figure ("Kara's queue
drain alone is ~n^2/2 = 1.25e9 element moves per BFS") is an ASSUMPTION about queue depth,
never checked, and the predicted payoff is explicitly flagged there as "an inference from
the bound, not a measurement". Neither had a cost-per-move behind it. Now one does.

WHAT WAS MEASURED (scratchpad depth.kara). `pop_front` memmoves the whole remaining queue,
so its cost is the STEADY-STATE DEPTH, not the number of pops. Prefill to depth d, then
200k rounds of one pop + one push so depth stays at d, with `(i64, i64)` elements —
#3629's exact `VecDeque[(i64,i64)]` shape:

    depth    100      10 ms
    depth  1,000      32 ms
    depth 10,000     561 ms
    depth 25,000   1,391 ms

Linear in depth once past fixed overhead, as memmove-per-pop predicts. Rate from the
10k->25k leg (which cancels the overhead): 3.61 G element-moves/s = 58 GB/s at 16 bytes
per tuple — a sane memmove rate for a 400 KB, L2-resident buffer, which is also the
regime #3629's queue sits in, so the microbenchmark is not measuring a different cache
tier than the kata.

THE ARITHMETIC. #3629 is 50 BFS runs over n = 50,000, so 2.5e6 pops. At the measured rate,
deque cost = 2.5e6 x avg_depth / 3.61e9 s.

  to explain the excess vs rust_ovf (24.88 - 8.60 = 16.28 s): avg depth 23,537 (47% of n)
  to explain the excess vs c_v3     (24.88 - 10.15 = 14.73 s): avg depth 21,296 (43% of n)
  at the depth -5 ASSUMES, n/2 = 25,000:  predicted cost 17.3 s vs observed excess 14.7-16.3 s
                                          predicted post-fix total 7.6 s
                                          (rust_ovf 8.60, c_v3 10.15)

So the attribution is CONSISTENT, and consistent within modelling error rather than by an
order of magnitude: an average frontier a little under half of n accounts for essentially
the whole deficit, and the post-fix prediction lands at or just ahead of both baselines —
which is exactly what -5 guessed, now with a number under it.

THE ONE THING STILL UNMEASURED, and it is now a single scalar: THE KATA'S AVERAGE QUEUE
DEPTH. Everything above is conditional on it being ~21,000-23,500. That is the natural
value for a BFS that enqueues nearly every node before draining, and NOT the value for one
whose frontier stays narrow. Whoever has the kata should instrument the loop to accumulate
`queue.len()` per pop and divide — one counter, one run.

FALSIFIABLE EITHER WAY, which is the point of writing it down:
  * avg depth ~21k+  -> -5 explains -4; fixing the deque should land #3629 near 7-8 s and
                        this entry closes with it, no separate cause to hunt.
  * avg depth << 20k -> the deque CANNOT account for the gap and a second deficit is
                        hiding. The untested candidates named above (tuple push boxing,
                        `factors[v].iter()` / `into_iter()` lowering, `Vec[bool]` access)
                        come back into play.

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION OF -5'S BLAST RADIUS. At depth 100 the deque costs 10 ms per
200k ops — nothing. That is a separate route to -5's finding that #226 (tree BFS) and
#133 (graph BFS, narrow frontier) are unaffected while #3629 is not: the quadratic is
invisible until the frontier gets deep, and it is depth, not pop count, that decides.

NOT DONE: the kata is not in this container (`../kara-katas` absent), so the depth counter
could not be run here. No compiler change; this is measurement only.

*** FIFTH HYPOTHESIS REFUTED (2026-07-30): the VecDeque quadratic (B-2026-07-30-5). ***
-5 was filed as this entry's root cause. Measured, it is not: #3629's average queue depth
is 702.6 (pops=45,703, depth_sum=32,112,968 over one min_jumps call, sink cross-checked),
not the ~25,000 the attribution assumed. At the measured depth the deque costs 0.444 s of
a 16.3 s excess -- 2.7%, and that is an upper bound since an ~11 KB queue is L1-resident.
See -5 for the full arithmetic.

So the cause is once again UNKNOWN, and five mechanisms are now excluded by measurement:
  1. the sieve (Kara is FASTER than clang there)
  2. nested-Vec element mutation, outer[i].push(x)
  3. Map entry/or_insert/push being O(len)
  4. index-into-index reads, g[j][0]
  5. the VecDeque quadratic
Remaining untested in the hot path: `for p in factors[v].iter()` and
`for j in indices.into_iter()` iterator lowering, `bucket.remove(v)` returning
Option[Vec[i64]] by value, and the Vec[bool] visited accesses. A profiler would settle
this far faster than more probe bisection -- the measurement container has no perf, so
the next taker should run it somewhere that does.

── THE LAST TWO NAMED CANDIDATES ARE NOW RULED OUT TOO. THE HYPOTHESIS LIST IS EXHAUSTED
   (2026-07-30). ──

With the deque falsified in 14f99d7, this entry's "REMAINING CANDIDATES, none tested" list
had two live entries left. Both measured, both dead:

  `Vec[bool]` ACCESSES. 10M indexed read+writes over a 50,000-element `Vec[bool]`:
  8 ms = 0.80 ns/op. The `Vec[i64]` control is 10 ms = 1.00 ns/op, so bool is if anything
  FASTER (1-byte loads), not the packed-bit penalty the candidate assumed.

  `for p in factors[v].iter()` — the ITERATOR LOWERING over an element of a
  `Vec[Vec[i64]]`, the kata's exact shape. 7.5M element visits: 19 ms = 2.53 ns/elem. The
  hand-written index walk over the same structure is 18 ms = 2.40 ns/elem. A 5% difference;
  there is no adaptor overhead to find.

MARGIN, so nobody has to re-litigate these by intuition. #3629's excess over rust_ovf is
16.3 s spread over ~2.5e6 kata-level operations, i.e. a guilty construct must cost about
6.5 MICROseconds per operation. Measured costs:

    Vec[bool] indexed r/w            0.80 ns/op      8,150x too cheap
    Vec[i64] indexed r/w             1.00 ns/op      6,520x too cheap
    .iter() over nested-Vec elem     2.53 ns/op      2,574x too cheap
    index walk (control)             2.40 ns/op      2,717x too cheap
    deque push+pop @ depth 100      25.00 ns/op        261x too cheap

Three to four orders of magnitude in every case. Microbenchmarks do miss context effects
(cache and register pressure in the real loop), but not by 1000x — these are not "probably
fine", they are arithmetically incapable of the deficit.

SO EVERY HYPOTHESIS THIS ENTRY HAS EVER NAMED IS DEAD: the sieve, nested-Vec element
mutation, Map entry/or_insert/push (the original three), the deque (14f99d7), and now
Vec[bool] and iterator lowering.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE NEXT ATTEMPT — the method has to change, not the guess. Probing
one construct at a time has now failed six times, which is itself evidence: a deficit that
survives every per-construct probe is more likely DIFFUSE (a general lowering-quality gap
paid on every operation — bounds checks, overflow checks, missed vectorization, spill
pressure) than concentrated in one call. Two approaches that do not depend on guessing
right:
  * ATTRIBUTION. `KARAC_DEBUG_INFO` now survives end-to-end specifically for this
    (B-2026-07-27-4, fixed). On a host with a sampling profiler, that turns the question
    into a reading rather than a hypothesis. This container has no `perf`; the kata
    container may.
  * ABLATION. Delete parts of the kata and re-measure, rather than reimplementing parts in
    isolation. An isolated probe cannot see a diffuse cost by construction, which is
    exactly the failure mode the six dead hypotheses share.

NOT DONE: no profiler here and no kata repo in this container, so neither could be run.
This pass is rule-outs and a method recommendation.

── RETRACTED AGAIN: THE DEQUE IS NOT THIS ENTRY'S CAUSE. 14f99d7 WAS RIGHT
   (2026-07-31, after the fix landed). ──

B-2026-07-30-5 is now implemented, so the attribution can be tested directly
instead of modelled. Clean A/B on one compiler build (`KARAC_DEQUE_HEAD_INDEX`
toggling only, quiet host, 20 iterations): 2.743 s -> 2.634 s, i.e. 1.04x. The

My "41.6% of instructions" measurement was real but mis-read: callgrind counts
the ERMS `rep movsb` path per byte, so an L1-resident bulk copy dominates the

paired with it (1.779 -> 1.300 s) was taken on a loaded container comparing two

So #3629's cause is UNKNOWN again, and the hypothesis list is back to exhausted:
sieve, nested-Vec mutation, Map entry/or_insert/push, index-into-index,
Vec[bool], iterator lowering, AND the deque. What the profiling did establish
that still stands: ~60% of BOTH kara and the C mirror is allocator traffic from
build_factors' ~1e6 tiny inner Vecs (_int_malloc 141.8M vs 141.6M Ir — parity,
not a kara problem), and after the deque fix kara is 571M instructions against
C's 501M (1.14x) while wall clock is ~1.10-1.15x. The residual is small and
diffuse; ABLATION on a quiet host, not instruction counts, is the way to size
