No test pinned the old strings (checked before editing — the only test-side matches were comments, not assertions). Pure string change, no behavior delta. fmt + clippy (--all-targets AND the CI form) clean; full `--features llvm` suite green. REVERT INCIDENT (recorded for bisect): the first attempt, 9d70e52, was rebuilt onto a newer origin/main by saving `git diff origin/main HEAD -- src/` while HEAD still sat on the OLDER upstream. That diff carries the REVERSE of every upstream commit in between, so applying it silently reverted ef85e85 (container-bodies drop disarm) and 5e7c2e9 (http method-check arms) — 18 files, 583 deletions, where 15 string lines were intended. tests/codegen.rs::e2e_container_bodies_whole_value_move_single_fire, the direct oracle for ef85e85, caught it with double-fired drop bodies. a6f5df7 restores src/ to upstream byte-for-byte and re-applies only the strings (15 insertions / 15 deletions, every changed line containing the phrase). LESSON: `git diff <new-base> <old-tip>` is only 'my changes' when both share a base; use the merge-base, or cherry-pick/rebase --onto, which are commit-relative by construction.

tracker: src/codegen/runtime.rs (transfer_map_handle_on_rebind), src/codegen/stmts.rs (Let move-suppression site), src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs (suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex Map/Set arm)
title: A whole-map rebind (`let m5 = m4;`) leaks the ENTIRE map — handle, bucket arrays, and every stored value's heap — on every execution of the shape.
detail:
Found by the B-2026-07-30-11 Map-values leg's LSan case; confirmed PRE-EXISTING by valgrind on a src-stashed baseline — identical loss either way (50-iteration loop: 3,600 B / 50 blocks definitely lost + 47,200 B / 150 indirectly, i.e. one whole karac_map_new allocation set per iteration, values included).

The fresh-handle tracking arm in stmts.rs says a rebind 'bypasses this since it's an Identifier RHS, so the source's existing track stays the unique cleanup owner' — but the measurement says otherwise: neither the source's FreeMapHandle fires (something on the let-rebind path suppresses it) nor does the destination register one. Isolate which suppressor fires on the `let m5 = m4;` path first (the Assign-arm `m = m2` shape has explicit suppression at stmts.rs ~6706; the LET path's equivalent is what needs the audit), then either stop suppressing the source or register the destination — the Vec-rebind pattern (source cap-zeroed + destination tracked) is the model.

LSan CAVEAT for the re-prober: the leak hides from LSan in some binary layouts — the dead stack slot still holds the handle pointer and the conservative scan calls it reachable. Use valgrind (definitely-lost) or vary the program; a clean LSan run on this shape proves nothing.

Interp is unaffected (Value::Map is GC'd), so output parity holds and this is a pure leak — but it is the everyday move shape, so a long-lived process that rebinds maps grows without bound.
resolution: Root-caused via IR dump (KARAC_JIT_RUNNER hijack): `let m5 = m4;` emits `store ptr null, ptr %m4.slot` from the Map/Set arm of `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` (call_dispatch.rs ~4933) — the Let path's struct-centric move-suppression (stmts.rs ~5618) reaches it because its gate is only 'destination has a var_type_names entry', which "Map"/"Set" satisfies. The null store is a branch-safe move sentinel and is LOAD-BEARING (without it, rebind-then-`return m5` would have the source's drain free the returned handle — a UAF), so the fix is the ledger's prescribed model, destination tracking: new `transfer_map_handle_on_rebind` (runtime.rs) copies the source's queued FreeMapHandle config (key/val vec-ness, shared-heap types, val_drop_fn) onto the destination's slot in the current frame, called from the Let move-suppression site right after the suppressor. Self-gating on 'source actually carries a queued FreeMapHandle', so a caller-retains alias (`let mm = s.m;`) and `ref Map` params are untouched (container stays sole freer), and a dest already tracked is not double-registered. The source's retained null-safe drain still frees on branch paths that never executed the move. Verified: valgrind 'All heap blocks were freed' on Map + Set rebinds, rebind-then-return, branch-buried rebind (both paths), Map[i64,String] heap values, chain rebind with mutation, Drop-bearing values (bodies fire once, three-way parity), and the place-source alias chain. Non-vacuity: the extended asan_map_value_user_drop_bodies_fire_once rebind block (loop shape makes the leak LSan-visible — dead iterations' maps are unreachable once allocas are overwritten) FAILS with the fix stash-reverted, passes with it. Behavior twins e2e/test_map_whole_rebind_transfers_ownership pin the rebind-then-return + chain-rebind + Set shapes. The stale 'source stays the unique cleanup owner' comment at the fresh-handle gate is corrected.

title: RC-fallback analysis is not path-sensitive across a branch JOIN: a value consumed exactly once on each of two MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE `if`/`else` (or `match`) arms is reported as a re-use and gets a real RC inserted, even though only one arm can run. The same mutual exclusion expressed with an early `return` is analyzed correctly.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found writing examples/sha256.kara (SHA-256 + HMAC-SHA256 against the NIST / RFC 4231 vectors) for the AWS SigV4 prerequisite. Three rc-fallback notes fired on ordinary code; two reduced to this shape.

MINIMAL REPRO:
  fn takes(s: String) -> i64 { s.len() }
  fn f(l: String, b: bool) -> i64 { if b { takes(l) } else { takes(l) } }
->  perf[rc-fallback]: RC fallback inserted for 'l' (direct re-use after consume);
    consume at line 2:39, other use at line 2:59
Only one arm ever executes, so `l` is consumed exactly once on every path and no RC is needed.

MEASURED MATRIX (`karac check`, main @834d493):
  if/else, both arms consume          -> RC FALLBACK   (false positive)
  match, both arms consume            -> RC FALLBACK   (false positive)
  only one arm consumes               -> clean         (correct)
  early-return then consume           -> clean         (correct)
  sequential double consume           -> error[ownership] 'moved here, used
                                         again here'    (correct)

THE EARLY-RETURN ROW IS THE KEY COMPARISON. `if b { return takes(l); } takes(l)` is semantically the same mutual exclusion as the `if`/`else` form and IS analyzed correctly, so this is not general flow-insensitivity — it is specifically that the branch JOIN does not carry "consumed on this path only" per-predecessor. The last row confirms the genuine double-consume is still caught, so tightening this must not regress it.

IMPACT is perf + diagnostics, not correctness: an unnecessary retain/release pair on a path that cannot need one, plus a perf lint instructing the author to restructure code that is already single-consume. Restructuring does NOT clear it — in the dogfood, collapsing to the single-expression form `let normalized = if key.len() > 64 { sha256(key) } else { key };` still reports, so `#[allow(rc_fallback)]` is the only escape.

SECOND, UNEXPLAINED INSTANCE in the same file, recorded honestly as observed-in-context rather than diagnosed: `inner` in `hmac_sha256` reports "consume at the `sha256(inner)` line, other use at the earlier `inner.push(b)` line" — the flagged re-use PRECEDES the consume in source order. It did not reduce: a vec built across two loops and then consumed, a vec built in a while loop and then consumed, and two vecs built in one loop and both consumed are all clean on their own. Whether it is the same join defect or a separate loop/back-edge issue is unresolved.

REPRO FILE: examples/sha256.kara carries `#[allow(rc_fallback)]` on `hmac_sha256` and `check` with comments pointing here; removing those attributes reproduces all three reports.

title: `karac build` and `karac run` DO NOT GATE on ownership errors: a use-after-move that `karac check` reports as `error[ownership]` (exit 1) still compiles to a binary and runs (exit 0). Type errors gate correctly on both, so the two lanes disagree about whether the same program is valid.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while characterizing B-2026-07-31-28 — a probe intended as the "genuine double-consume is still caught" control turned out to be caught by `check` and ignored by `build`.

MEASURED on main @834d493:
  fn consume(v: Vec[i64]) -> i64 { v.len() }
  fn main() {
      let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new();
      v.push(7); v.push(8);
      let a = consume(v);
      let b = consume(v);          // use after move
      println((a + b).to_string());
  }
  karac check uam.kara -> error[ownership]: value 'v' moved here, used again
                          here (moved at line 5:21)
                          1 error(s) found.        exit 1
  karac build uam.kara -> Built: uam                exit 0
  ./uam                -> 4                         (runs, correct answer)
  karac run --interp   -> 4                         exit 0

CONTROL — TYPE ERRORS GATE CORRECTLY:
  let x: i64 = "str";  karac check -> exit 1
                       karac build -> exit 1
So the asymmetry is specific to the ownership phase, not a general "build skips checks".

NOT (OBSERVABLY) A MEMORY-SAFETY HOLE. The built binary produces the right answer and does not crash — the RC fallback keeps the moved value alive, which is presumably why the violation is survivable. So the practical damage is not corruption but AUTHORITY: `karac check` is the Mend loop's gate and the AI-first surface's contract, and it is declaring an error that the compiler itself does not honor. Any workflow gating on `karac build` ships code `check` rejects, and any workflow gating on `check` blocks code that builds and runs fine.

TWO READINGS, NOT RESOLVED HERE — deliberately not asserting a root cause after B-2026-07-30-16 was filed with the wrong one:
  (a) BUG: `build`/`run` should propagate ownership errors and exit nonzero.
  (b) DESIGN: ownership violations are intended to DEGRADE to the RC fallback
      rather than be fatal, in which case the defect is that the diagnostic is
      emitted as `error[ownership]` and counted in "1 error(s) found" (making
      `check` exit 1) when it should be a warning or a perf note like the
      rc-fallback lint it is adjacent to.
Which reading is right determines the fix: (a) is a gating change in the driver, (b) is a severity/classification change in `ownership.rs`. Both leave `check` and `build` agreeing, which is the actual requirement.

RESOLVED — BOTH READINGS WERE PARTLY RIGHT, PER KIND. The entry deliberately left the root cause open between (a) a driver gating bug and (b) a diagnostic severity misclassification. Measuring each ownership kind separately showed the surface splits, and the two halves need OPPOSITE fixes:

  kind                        check  build   verdict
  use-after-move                1      0     advisory BY DESIGN -> reading (b)
  reassign-to-immutable         1      0     spec says compile error -> reading (a)
  mutate-immutable-binding      1      0     spec says compile error -> reading (a)
  use-of-uninitialized          1      1     already agreed

READING (a) — THE IMMUTABILITY CASES WERE ACTIVELY WRONG, not merely inconsistent. design.md:2322 states: "`let` declares an immutable binding. Reassigning the binding or calling a method with `mut ref self` on it is a compile error." It was not one. `let x = 1; x = 2;` built cleanly and the binary PRINTED 2; the `mut ref self` form built and printed the mutated value too. So immutability was unenforced in compiled code and `let` vs `let mut` carried no meaning past `check`. Corroborating evidence that this is a gap rather than a design choice: the MODULE-level form of the identical rule is a *typechecker* error (`ReassignToImmutableModuleBinding`, E0252) and was therefore already fatal — only the local form leaked.

READING (b) — USE-AFTER-MOVE IS GENUINELY ADVISORY, confirmed from the source rather than inferred from behavior. `ownership.rs` at the UAM emission site says the reuse "is exactly what codegen already does implicitly (the reuse is defensive-copied, which is why `karac build`/`run` treat this diagnostic as advisory and compile it)", and the diagnostic ships a machine-applicable `.clone()` edit built around the program compiling. So `build` accepting it is correct and `check` exiting 1 was the defect.

FIX. `has_fatal_ownership_errors` inverted from an allowlist of one kind to a denylist of the two documented-advisory kinds (`RcFallbackNote`, `UseAfterMove`), so a NEWLY ADDED kind is fatal by default instead of silently advisory — the failure mode that produced this bug. `total_errors` (the `check` exit code) now filters through the SAME `is_fatal_ownership_kind` predicate, so the two lanes cannot drift apart again. Promoted by this change: ReassignToImmutable, MutateImmutableBinding, UseOfUninitialized, NoRcViolation, CaptureModeViolation, OwnershipCycle.

RENDERING FIXED TOO. Every ownership kind printed `error[ownership]`, so demoting `UseAfterMove` initially produced the contradiction of an `error[...]` line followed by `All checks passed.` The label now follows the same split — `error[ownership]` when fatal, `warning[ownership]` when advisory, matching the existing `warning[effect]` / `note[ownership]` convention. The advisory diagnostic is still RENDERED in both text and `--output=json`, and `karac fix` still applies its `.clone()` edit, so the Mend loop keeps the signal.

VERIFIED: check and build exit codes now agree on all four kinds above plus a clean-program and a type-error control. Suites green: cli 513, ownership 381, codegen 2680, typechecker 2122, interpreter 1351, effectchecker 409, resolver 335, raii_check 41.

title: `for x in <module-level Vec/Map/Set/String>` compiled to a zero-iteration loop (run-vs-build divergence)
resolution: Fixed in `src/codegen/control_flow_for.rs`: the `compile_for` Identifier arm's container dispatch now consults `module_bindings` in addition to `variables`. Verified the compiled output matches the interpreter on Vec/Map/Set/String module bindings, and `examples/shortener`'s `/stats` now reports real hit counts.

title: Mechanical diagnostics that name their own replacement carry no `karac fix` payload (`!` -> `not`, String -> StringSlice)
detail:
Writing `examples/shortener` blind-ish through the Mend loop produced two errors that state the exact replacement text and still cannot be auto-applied:

  1. `error[parse] E0001`: "the `!` operator is not used in Kāra; use `not` instead"
  2. `error[typecheck] E_MODULE_BINDING_HEAP_TYPE`: "module-level binding 'X' is declared with type 'String' which is heap-allocated ... use 'StringSlice' for static string data"

Both are single-token substitutions at a known span. `karac check --output=json` emits neither a `fix` nor a `resolution` field for either, and `karac fix` leaves the file untouched (it printed the diagnostic and applied nothing).

WHY THIS MATTERS DISPROPORTIONATELY. `!` -> `not` is the single most likely mistake a model writing Kāra will make — every C-family language spells it `!`, so an LLM emits it reflexively, and the Mend machine-fix rate is measured over exactly that blind authorship. A diagnostic that spells out its own repair but hands back no edit is pure lost rate. The contrast is visible in the same session: the ADVISORY use-after-move diagnostic on the same file did ship a machine-applicable `.clone()` edit, and `karac fix` applied it three times in a row to convergence.

SUGGESTED SHAPE: attach a machine-applicable replacement to both. `!` -> `not` is a literal token swap at the operator span. The module-binding one is a type-annotation span rewrite (`String` -> `StringSlice`), and is only valid when the initializer is a literal — which is the condition the check already establishes before firing.

SOURCE NOTE: found while authoring `examples/shortener/shortener.kara`; not a blind-LLM authoring run, so it does NOT count toward the machine-fix rate statistic.
resolution:
Both diagnostics now ship machine-applicable edits; `karac fix` applies them.

`!` -> `not` (src/parser/exprs.rs, `Token::Bang` prefix arm): a `TextEdit` over the `!` token span, hung on the existing `Parser::fix_edits` side-channel (the same channel the comma-separated-effect-clause recovery uses) and matched back to its diagnostic by span. `not` is a WORD operator, so the replacement is whitespace-aware: `!flag` -> `not flag` (replacement carries its own trailing space) but `! g` -> `not g` (existing space reused, not doubled). The parser holds no source text, so the gap is detected from the operand token's start offset versus the end of the `!` span. Scope is exactly the standalone prefix `!`: `!=` lexes as `BangEqual` and `vec![...]` is consumed on the postfix identifier path, so neither reaches the arm — pinned by a test.

E_MODULE_BINDING_HEAP_TYPE (src/typechecker/items.rs, both sites) via `type_error_with_fix_it`. The two sites need different edit shapes: the ANNOTATED form (`let X: String = "lit";`) rewrites the annotation span to `StringSlice`; the INFERRED form (`let X = "lit";`) has no annotation to rewrite, so it INSERTS `: StringSlice` after `name_span` (a zero-length edit whose offset differs from the diagnostic span, which points at the initializer — `FixIt` carries its own span, so the two decouple cleanly).

SAFETY GATE. Both fixes are attached only when the initializer is a bare string literal — exactly the condition the design.md §1284 coercion carve-out accepts for a StringSlice-declared binding. That is what makes the fix safe rather than merely plausible: applying it yields a program that PASSES. Verified the gate is load-bearing rather than over-cautious — `let J: StringSlice = "a" + "b";` fails with "expected 'StringSlice', found 'String'", so an ungated fix would trade one error for another. A non-literal initializer keeps the descriptive-only diagnostic.

REGRESSION COVER: tests/parser.rs (edit targets the `!` token; space added when absent; space reused when present; `!=` / `vec![]` untouched — each applying the edit and re-parsing clean), tests/typechecker.rs (annotated rewrite, inferred insertion, withheld-fix gate — the first two assert the PATCHED source typechecks, the third pins that the withheld fix genuinely would not), tests/cli.rs (end-to-end `karac fix` over a file carrying all four defects, then `karac check` passes).

title: E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING suggests renaming a single-uppercase-letter binding to itself
detail:
A module-level `let mut M: Map[String, i64] = Map.new();` is rejected with:

    error[resolve]: error[E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING]: module-level binding name `M` is Type-class but module-level `let` / `let mut` bindings introduce Const-class identifiers (SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE); consider renaming to `M`

The suggestion is the ORIGINAL NAME — "consider renaming to `M`" when the name is already `M`. Following the advice changes nothing, so the diagnostic is unactionable as written.

CAUSE (unverified, from the shape): a single uppercase letter is simultaneously valid Type-class (`M`) and the SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE-ization of itself, so the suggestion generator's Const-class transform is the identity on this input. Any all-caps single-letter name (`M`, `T`, `V`) should hit it; multi-letter names like `Foo` -> `FOO` presumably render fine.

SUGGESTED SHAPE: when the generated suggestion equals the original identifier, either suppress the "consider renaming to" clause entirely (the rule statement alone is still actionable — the user must pick a different name) or propose a distinguishing form. Cheap general guard: assert suggestion != original at the render site for this whole diagnostic family, since an identity suggestion is never useful.

SOURCE NOTE: hit while reducing B-2026-07-31-30 to a minimal repro (a scratch probe named its module-level map `M`).

SEVERITY RAISED low -> medium ON INVESTIGATION. Filed as a cosmetic message defect; it is actually a LIVENESS bug in the fix loop. The resolver hangs a machine-applicable rename off the same string it prints, so the identity suggestion also produced an identity EDIT. `karac fix` therefore reported `applied 1 fix(es)` on EVERY pass while the file stayed byte-identical and the error never cleared:

    $ for i in 1 2 3; do karac fix m.kara; done
    applied 1 fix(es) to m.kara
    applied 1 fix(es) to m.kara
    applied 1 fix(es) to m.kara
    $ head -1 m.kara      # unchanged
    let mut M: Map[String, i64] = Map.new();

A Mend driver that loops until 'no fixes applied' never terminates on such a file. The progress signal was not merely unhelpful, it was false.
resolution:
Root cause: `suggest_const_name` is a pure case transform with no idea whether its output satisfies the rule that prompted the diagnostic. For a name whose only letter is already uppercase it is the IDENTITY, while `classify_stripped`'s CN-7 arm classifies any single-letter name as Type-class regardless (so `T` / `K` / `V` read as type parameters). The two facts together make Const-class UNREACHABLE by capitalization for `M` — but the diagnostic suggested it anyway.

Fix: new `lexer::suggest_name_for_class(name, target) -> Option<String>`, which returns a suggestion only when it both differs from `name` AND actually `classify_ident`s as `target`. Checking the CLASS rather than merely `s != name` is what makes it general: it also declines `_M` -> `M`, a DIFFERENT string that is still Type-class and would have stalled the loop one step later.

Both call sites now use it. `src/resolver/collect.rs` (E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING) withholds the `suggestion` AND the `replacement` edit when it returns None — `karac fix` now prints `(no fixable diagnostics)` instead of claiming progress. `src/parser.rs` (`check_ident_class`, the shared struct/fn/const family) had the same identity-suggestion defect — `const M = 1;` advised renaming to `M` — but carries no edit, so it was useless rather than loop-inducing; same fix.

When no rename is reachable the message now explains WHY and what to do rather than naming a replacement: "a name with a single letter is always Type-class (so `T` / `K` / `V` read as type parameters), and no capitalization change can make it Const-class — use a name with more than one letter". Deliberately does NOT fabricate a distinct candidate (`M` -> `M_VALUE`): inventing the programmer's intent to satisfy a lint is worse than stating the constraint. Reachable renames are untouched — `maxRetries` still suggests and applies `MAX_RETRIES`.

REGRESSION COVER: tests/lexer.rs (helper declines M / M2 / M_2 / _M, returns validated renames otherwise), tests/resolver.rs (single-letter withholds both suggestion and edit while staying diagnosed and explanatory; digit-bearing single-letter names likewise — the case a `!=`-only guard would have missed; multi-letter rename unaffected), tests/parser.rs (const family, both directions), tests/cli.rs (three `karac fix` runs must not print 'applied' and must leave the file byte-identical, and the diagnostic must survive — pinning that withholding the edit did not silence the report).

tracker: src/resolver.rs (ResolveResult::error_fix_diffs, PendingBindingRename, attach_module_binding_renames, record_ident_ref, with_external_pub_refs), src/resolver/collect.rs (collect_module_binding), src/resolver/resolve_block.rs (Identifier/Path arms), src/cli.rs (cmd_fix, collect_diagnostics, resolve_errors_json/jsonl, package_root_of_member)
title: `karac fix` renames a module binding's DECLARATION only, breaking every use site
detail:
Found while fixing B-2026-07-31-32. E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING's machine-applicable rename (B-2026-07-06-3) spans `b.name_span` — the declaration identifier — and nothing else. Applying it to a binding that is actually USED turns a one-lint program into a broken one:

    $ cat n.kara
    let mut MyMap: Map[String, i64] = Map.new();
    fn main() { MyMap.insert("a", 1); println(MyMap.len()); }
    $ karac fix n.kara
    applied 1 fix(es) to n.kara
    $ karac check n.kara
    error[resolve]: undefined name 'MyMap', did you mean 'Map'?   (x2)

So the fix is DESTRUCTIVE, which is worse than B-32's no-op: the loop 'converges' on a program that no longer resolves. Any module binding referenced at least once is affected, which is essentially all of them.

WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED. `tests/cli.rs::test_fix_applies_module_binding_const_rename` pins the behavior with `pub let myConfig: i64 = 5;` — a binding with NO use sites — so it passes precisely by dodging the defect. Its comment says the rename applies "at the declaration site", and unlike its sibling `test_fix_applies_undefined_label_rename` ("and the program then compiles") it makes no claim that the result still builds.

WHY NOT FIXED WITH B-32. It needs a multi-span edit, which the pipeline cannot express today: `ResolveError::replacement` is a single `Option<Box<TextEdit>>`, and the diagnostic is emitted from `collect_module_binding` during COLLECTION — before use sites are resolved, so the reference spans are not yet known at the emission point. A real fix is structural: either a `Vec<TextEdit>` on the diagnostic (plus JSON + `cmd_fix` plumbing) with the naming check deferred to after reference resolution, or withdraw the machine-applicable edit and leave the diagnostic descriptive.

SUGGESTED SHAPE: prefer the multi-span rename — the edit is genuinely useful when complete. If that is deferred, withhold the edit per the B-2026-07-31-31 principle already adopted elsewhere in the compiler (offer a fix exactly when applying it yields a program that passes), and update the test above to assert the fixed program still checks, so the gap cannot reopen silently.

WIDER THAN FILED. The report covered same-file use sites. Verifying the fix surfaced a second, worse instance of the same class: a `pub` module binding can be read by SIBLING MODULES, and `karac fix` edits exactly one file. Renaming `pub let myConfig` in `src/helper.kara` left `src/main.kara`'s `helper.myConfig` dangling — the identical defect with a blast radius the single-file fixer cannot even see. Both are fixed here; a fix for only the in-file half would have been a fix for the easy half.
resolution:
Three-part fix.

(1) MULTI-SPAN RENAME. New `ResolveResult::error_fix_diffs` — the resolver-side twin of the field `OwnershipCheckResult` already carries — holds edit lists keyed by the owning diagnostic's span. The naming check still runs during collection (pass 1), but now parks a `PendingBindingRename` instead of synthesizing the edit; a new pass 3 (`attach_module_binding_renames`) runs after bodies resolve, when use sites exist, and decides among three outcomes: no use sites -> the declaration edit stands alone in `replacement` (unchanged behavior); use sites, all rewritable -> declaration + every reference go in the envelope and `replacement` is left EMPTY, so a consumer reading only the single-edit slot applies nothing rather than the declaration half that breaks the program; any reference not precisely locatable -> the whole edit is withheld and the diagnostic stays advisory.

(2) `resolutions` CANNOT DRIVE A RENAME — the non-obvious part. Its keys are whatever span the recording site had in hand, and for a method call that is the ENTIRE call: `MyMap.len()` resolves to `MyMap`'s symbol under a span covering all eleven bytes. An edit built from it would splice the new name over the call. So a second side table, `ident_ref_offsets`, records the START OFFSET of references written as a bare identifier (the `Identifier` and `Path` arms — a path's first segment is the resolved name and the span starts at it), with the length taken from the name. The sweep then requires the two records to agree EXACTLY before offering the rename: every reference `resolutions` knows about must also appear in `ident_ref_offsets`. That is what makes it fail closed on any reference shape this code does not model — a pattern position, future syntax — instead of silently skipping it. `ident_ref_offsets` is populated only while a rename is pending (known from pass 1), so the hot path pays nothing in the normal case.

(3) CROSS-MODULE GUARD. New `pub_refs_may_be_external` flag: set by `with_tree` (project mode — each module resolves in its own session, so an importer's references carry different symbol ids and are structurally invisible) and by the CLI via `with_external_pub_refs` when a single file sits inside a package's `src/`. When set, a `pub` binding gets the message and the suggestion but NO machine-applicable edit. Private bindings are module-local and keep the full rename, so the common case still fixes. The package-member test reuses the predicate behind B-2026-07-08-19's single-file-build refusal, extracted as `package_root_of_member` so both callers answer the question identically.

Also wired the envelope through the project-mode JSON emitters (`resolve_errors_json`/`_jsonl`), which previously rendered `replacement` only — without it a private-binding rename would have looked unfixable to an IDE simply because the file was compiled as part of a package.

REGRESSION COVER. tests/resolver.rs: the oracle test applies the envelope and RE-RESOLVES the result (asserting an edit count proves nothing); method-receiver and f-string cases pin that each edit covers the bare identifier and not the construct around it; a shadowing local must keep its name; no-use-sites keeps the single-edit slot. tests/cli.rs: end-to-end `fix` -> `check` passes and a second `fix` reaches a fixpoint; the JSON envelope is present AND `replacement` is absent; the package fixture pins pub-withheld + private-renamed + the importer still resolving. `test_fix_applies_module_binding_const_rename` — which passed only because its binding had no use sites — now asserts the fixed program checks, the missing assertion that let this hide.

title: 17 codegen-declared runtime symbols are absent from `__preserve_no_mangle_symbols` — each needs a per-symbol strip-risk verdict (async/net/TLS families). Pinned by tests/extern_keep_list.rs so the set cannot grow silently, but the pin is a placeholder for triage, NOT an approval.
fix: (no code change — verified not at risk)
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while building the keep-list drift guard (c500e84), itself a fallout of reviewing the `Codegen::new` extern-table proposal. MECHANISM: under `lto = "fat"` nothing inside the runtime crate calls the `karac_*` externs — only JIT'd/AOT'd Kara code does — so cross-module DCE may strip them from the staticlib. `runtime/src/lib.rs`'s `__preserve_no_mangle_symbols()` exists to take their addresses and defeat that; a symbol codegen emits calls to but the keep-list never names is therefore at risk. Codegen declares 284 `karac_*` symbols; the keep-list names 306; 17 declared symbols appear in no keep-list entry: karac_runtime_event_loop_register_fd_cancel, karac_runtime_http_builder_{new,free,add_header,set_body,set_timeout,send}, karac_runtime_http_response_header, karac_runtime_park_slot_{cancel_ptr,load_result,store_result}, karac_runtime_spawn_coro, karac_runtime_tcp_{connect,connect_start,connect_finish,shutdown,try_clone}. All are real `#[no_mangle] pub unsafe extern "C"` definitions (runtime/src/event_loop.rs, the tls-gated builder surface in runtime/src/lib.rs) sitting behind cfg-gated modules. WHY THIS IS OPEN RATHER THAN A BUG: a symbol reachable from other runtime code does not need a keep-list entry, so absence alone is not proof of risk — each of the 17 needs its own answer, which is why they were pinned rather than asserted either way. WHY IT MATTERS: the pre-existing detection for this class is INDIRECT — the E2E harness fails at link with `undefined reference to karac_*`, but only if some test program happens to exercise the symbol. Every one of these 17 is in the async/net/TLS surface, which has the thinnest E2E coverage in the suite, so a strip here is exactly the case least likely to be caught before a user hits it (the karac_realloc_or_panic shape, B-2026-07-12-22).
resolution: TRIAGED, NO CODE CHANGE NEEDED. All 17 are present in target/release/karac_jit_runner built under `lto = "fat"` — the one configuration the keep-list actually guards — and in both runtime archives. The six karac_runtime_http_builder_* are absent from the LEAN archive, which is correct by design (TLS-only symbols; the lean archive omits the TLS tree and codegen links the full archive for any program referencing them), not drift. METHOD CORRECTION — this entry's original next-step (`nm -g` on libkarac_runtime.a) is WRONG and was followed first: archive members retain their symbols by construction, so a strip can never show there. A second attempt, `nm` on target/DEBUG/karac_jit_runner, was also vacuous: `lto = "fat"` is set only on [profile.release], so a debug binary strips nothing. What redirected the investigation was noticing that karac_runtime_park_slot_store_result has ZERO internal references yet survives (killing the 'reachable from other runtime code' hypothesis) and that __preserve_no_mangle_symbols() is called from exactly two places — src/bin/karac_jit_runner.rs:141 and tests/codegen.rs:60 — both BINARIES, never the staticlib. That is why B-2026-07-12-22 manifested as a JIT 'Symbols not found' failure while AOT worked. NEGATIVE CONTROL (the step that makes the result meaningful): 348 karac_* fns are defined in runtime/src, 322 are exported by the release runner, so 26 come back absent — the feature-gated arrow/gpu surface and test-only helpers. That proves nm CAN detect a strip, so all-17-KEPT is a real finding rather than a check that cannot fail. Without it, the three all-KEPT runs would have been indistinguishable. The KNOWN_ABSENT pin in tests/extern_keep_list.rs stays as documentation and drift baseline; its doc comment now records the verification and the two dead-end methods so the next investigator skips them.

title: An eligible head-index deque in a function auto-par splits fails the BUILD: the __par_branch_* compile inherits the outer function's name-keyed head slots and loads another function's alloca (module-verifier 'Instruction does not dominate all uses')
detail: Regression introduced by 60733f7 (the B-2026-07-30-5 lowering), caught the same night by this session's probe battery: three ordinary two-deque / multi-deque programs (push loops + drains, no explicit par) failed `karac build` with `Module verification failed: "Instruction does not dominate all uses! %q.deque.head = alloca i64"`. ROOT CAUSE: emit_par_branch_fn saves/restores variables, var_type_names, loop_stack, cleanup frames and current_fn, but neither deque_head_slots nor current_fn_name — so inside a branch compile BOTH halves of is_head_index_deque still describe the outer function, and the branch's pop_front/len/is_empty arms load the outer function's head alloca. Auto-par emits branch functions for analysis groups it later DROPS (the dead functions still fail the verifier), which is why even guaranteed-sequential groups ICE'd. A second, silent hazard sat behind the ICE: a group that genuinely fans out while only READING the deque would execute with len-as-count semantics in the worker lane while the sequential lane runs len-as-end-index — after k fast-path pops the worker reads k dead elements (q.len() reporting 100 where 50 is live). FIX (three layers, uncertain => ineligible): (1) is_head_index_deque now requires the slot alloca's PARENT FUNCTION to be the function being emitted — a structural guard that makes every out-of-line emitter (par branches, closures, reduction/disjoint workers, sort comparators) fall back to the memmove lowering; (2) emit_par_branch_fn takes/restores deque_head_slots alongside its other saved state; (3) the materialization gate in compile_function drops any candidate MENTIONED in a statement that can genuinely fan out (parallel_groups minus groups with non-empty captured_container_mutations — those are unconditionally sequential per B-2026-07-15-2 — plus loop_reductions and disjoint_write_loops), with ordinal-vs-span alignment verified and any desync dropping every candidate. The gate is per-NAME: a blanket per-function gate was tried first and resurrected the B-2026-07-30-5 quadratic (25 s at n=400k) because the canonical push-then-drain main IS auto-par-analyzed. SIBLING FIX in the same commit: VecDeque was MISSING from concurrency.rs's collect_container_locals classifier (Vec/String/Map/Set/Sorted* only), so a par group mutating a captured VecDeque was not guaranteed-sequential — the same lost-branch-copy buffer orphan as B-2026-07-15-2, and the container-skip in layer 3 relies on the classifier seeing deques. Added. RESIDUAL: collect_move_hazard_locals' head_is_container still omits VecDeque (falls through to named_type_owns_heap = false for a builtin); untouched here, worth its own look. VERIFIED: the three ICE shapes compile with three-way interp/JIT/AOT parity and valgrind 0 errors; the read-only-group split-brain shape prints 50/50/50 on all three backends; drain stays linear (5/5/6/8 ms at 50k-400k) under the default build. Tests: the regression gate is tests/cli.rs build_deque_head_in_auto_par_split_fn_does_not_ice — it spawns the REAL karac binary on the minimal ICE shape (an eligible deque READ, println(e.len()), groupable with an independent tail whose only mutations are of an in-group-introduced binding, so captured_mutations is empty and the group is really emitted) and was verified FAILING with the fix stash-reverted and passing with it. TEST-INFRA NOTE: neither in-process E2E harness (tests/codegen.rs run_program, tests/par_codegen.rs run_program) reproduces the ICE even pre-fix — the same sources pass there with the fix reverted, so the in-process auto-par emission path diverges from the CLI's; the par_codegen pair test_e2e_deque_head_auto_par_split_function_compiles + test_e2e_deque_head_read_group_lane_consistency and the interp twin test_deque_head_read_group_lane_consistency are kept as behavior/lane-consistency pins, not regression proof. Big independent push/drain loops do NOT reproduce the ICE either (their groups carry captured container mutations and drop before emission). Also kept: KARAC_DUMP_IR_ON_VERIFY_FAIL=<path> env hook writing module IR on verifier failure (how this was root-caused; a verifier ICE is otherwise a one-line error with no module to inspect).

title: `karac build -o <path>` / `--out <path>` was PARSED BUT SILENTLY IGNORED for executable builds — the artifact always landed at `<stem>` in the CWD. No way existed to redirect a build, which is the root cause of the recurring stray-binary-at-repo-root class (7 instances).
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing the recurring stray-binary problem. A 7th stray (`g`) appeared DURING a full `cargo test --features llvm` run, which distinguished it from the earlier six: those came from manual bug-hunt builds, this one is produced automatically by the suite, for everyone, on every run. MECHANISM: `Command::Build`'s `out_path` field was threaded all the way into `cmd_build`, and the LIBRARY branch honored it (`let art_path = out_path.map(..).unwrap_or(default_name)`, src/cli.rs:6753), but the EXECUTABLE branch derived `exe_path` purely from the source stem (`if is_wasm { <stem>.wasm } else if windows { <stem>.exe } else { <stem> }`) and never consulted `out_path`. The flag therefore parsed cleanly — `-o/path` with no space correctly errors `unknown flag`, proving the parser knows it — drew no diagnostic, and wrote the artifact somewhere other than where the user pointed. Silent misdirection is worse than rejecting the flag: the user has no signal at all. CONSEQUENCE: there was NO way to redirect an executable build, so every `karac build` from the repo root left an artifact beside Cargo.toml where `git add -A` sweeps it into a commit. That is the entire stray-binary class: tup_vec, blockmin, pan, t, dc, uam, g. TEST LEG: tests/cli.rs's `ownership_gate_fixture` writes `g.kara` to a temp dir but the test invoked `karac build <tmp>/g.kara` with no `-o`; cargo runs tests with CWD = crate root, so the accepted cases dropped `g` into the repo on every suite run. ID NOTE: originally filed as B-2026-07-31-35; renumbered to B-2026-07-31-36 on rebase because a concurrent session had already pushed a different bug under -35 (the auto-par head-index deque build failure).
resolution: Added the `out_path` arm to `exe_path`, honored verbatim (cc -o style: no extension appended on any target, wasm included — an explicit path is the user's to name). Fixed the test leg to pass `-o <tmpdir>/g` so the fixture's artifact stays in its temp dir. Verified: the artifact now lands at the `-o` path and runs, no stray appears, the previously-leaking test is clean, and the full 558-test cli suite passes with zero untracked files afterward. NOTE this is the production-side fix; tests/no_tracked_binaries.rs (29f22c7) is the detection-side backstop for anything that still reaches a commit, and the two are complementary — the guard catches what is already tracked, this stops it being produced.

title: `a = b` on a struct binding runs b's user `impl Drop` body TWICE on every backend — and on a heap-bearing type codegen's second run reads the MOVED-FROM value, so the two backends print different numbers. The `let c = b;` form of the same move is correct, which is the bisect.

title: A binding moved into a variant constructor and then REASSIGNED never drops again on codegen: the ctor move retracts its UserDrop action permanently and the assign never re-arms it. The interpreter re-arms, so the two backends disagree.

Reassigning a struct binding never frees the OLD value's field heap — `let mut a = S{..String..}; a = S{..};` orphans the first String on every execution, for ANY heap-owning struct (no `impl Drop` required)
detail: Found while working B-2026-07-30-11's displaced-value leg; hidden until now because LLVM dead-codes the orphaned allocation in trivial probes (a never-read literal String field folds away entirely — 2 allocs / 2 frees, valgrind clean), so only an UN-ELIDABLE payload shows it: with runtime-varying f-string fields the probe loses 13 bytes definitely (valgrind), one displaced String per reassign, unbounded in a loop. ROOT CAUSE: the codegen Assign arm's identifier path had eager old-value reclamation for Vec/String vars, Map/Set vars (B-2026-07-15-25) and tensor vars, but NO struct-var case — B-2026-07-16-18 added only source-suppression for `a = b`, and a struct-literal/call RHS freed nothing. The binding's own StructDrop/UserDrop fire reads the slot AFTER the store, so it covers the new value and the old one simply vanishes. FIX: before the store, run the same cleanup scope exit would have run on the old slot contents — the karac_drop_<T> wrapper when the type has impl Drop (which also restores the missed user body, the B-2026-07-30-11 half), else emit_struct_drop_synthesis's __karac_drop_struct_<T> — gated on tracked non-shared struct, non-self-alias, NON-GENERIC type (per-instantiation cleanup would be needed, B-2026-07-11-35 — documented residual), and an RHS that does not mention the target (a moved-out old value must not be freed under the callee's feet; deque_head::expr_mentions_name_deep). The interpreter needs no memory fix (GC'd) — its half of the leg is the body timing, under B-2026-07-30-11. VERIFIED: the 13-byte definite loss is gone (valgrind 0 errors, 0 lost), `a = b` / `a = a` / `c = consume(c)` edge shapes free exactly once with three-way interp/JIT/AOT parity; the double-free direction is loud under asan_struct_reassign_displaced_value_freed_once; the leak direction is LSan-invisible for this shape (B-2026-07-31-27 blind spot) — valgrind is the authoritative check, and the body-side E2E e2e_struct_reassign_displaced_drop_semantics fails without the fix.

title: A Map introduced INSIDE an auto-par parallel group leaks whole (handle + buckets) at branch write-back — 344 bytes definitely lost per execution of the probe shape
detail: Found during B-2026-07-30-11's non-let probing (b3011_nonlet2 under the DEFAULT build; gone under KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0). valgrind: 344 (72 direct, 272 indirect) bytes definitely lost, karac_map_new called from __par_branch_0_3. The shape: `let mut m: Map[i64, Res] = Map.new(); let _ = m.insert(1, Res{7}); let _ = m.insert(1, Res{8});` grouped with adjacent statements — the map is INTRODUCED in-group, so `captured_mutations` excludes it (fresh let bindings flow through the return-slot write-back per the ParallelGroup doc) and captured_container_mutations does not force the group sequential. The branch creates the map; the write-back path evidently loses ownership of the handle (parent side never registers/frees it). Same family as B-2026-07-15-2 (lost branch-local container mutation) but for the in-group-INTRODUCED container the write-back is supposed to hand over. REPRO: scratchpad probe b3011_nonlet2.kara, default build, valgrind. Note VecDeque was added to collect_container_locals by B-2026-07-31-35's fix; Map was already classified, so this is NOT a classifier gap — it is the write-back/ownership-registration path for in-group intros. FIXED 06cbc7a: the write-back path was right, its bookkeeping was lossy — a Drop-VALUED map queues TWO transferable branch-side cleanup actions (its FreeMapHandle AND the B-2026-07-30-11 value-bodies UserDrop walker from register_map_val_bodies), and the slot-publish transfer's slot_ownership was HashMap<String, SlotOwnership> — one slot per binding — so the walker's SlotOwnership::User INSERT OVERWROTE the ::Map entry and the parent re-registered only the bodies walk: no karac_map_free* call existed ANYWHERE in the module (objdump-proven on the pre-fix object) and handle+buckets leaked. A scalar-valued map (single action) always transferred fine, which is the discriminator that localized it. FIX: slot_ownership becomes HashMap<String, Vec<SlotOwnership>> (push, not insert, in the retain loop — frame order preserved) and register_slot_ownership re-registers EVERY entry, so the parent's LIFO drain replays the branch's bodies-before-free sequencing. Both rebinding sites (auto-par dispatch in stmts.rs, compile_par_block Step 6) flow through unchanged. Probes: original repro + scalar/dropval/read-after-group/fn-wrapped variants all valgrind-clean (0 definitely lost; pre-fix fn-wrapped leaked 720B over 10 calls); interp/AOT output parity for the map legs (the E-section drop-timing divergence in the original probe is the separately-filed B-2026-07-31-41, unchanged). TESTS + a harness finding: the LSan harness CANNOT see this leak class — unoptimized code + parked pool threads leave stale copies of the handle pointer inside LSan-scanned stack regions, so the lost blocks classify reachable (the CLI's -O2 clobbers those slots, which is why valgrind catches shipped binaries). Regression is therefore pinned at the IR level: par_codegen test_ir_auto_par_ingroup_dropval_map_transfers_handle_free asserts a karac_map_free* CALL line exists (declare-only matched vacuously — the assert requires a call), with a premise-guard that fn work still forms a non-trivial group; proven failing pre-fix. Companions: test_e2e_auto_par_ingroup_dropval_map_output (output byte-parity), asan_auto_par_ingroup_dropval_map_freed (guards the double-free/UAF side of the transfer; doc states explicitly it cannot see the leak side).

title: User Drop timing diverges in auto-par lanes: under the DEFAULT build a displaced struct binding's body fires with the wrong id/time (drop 6 at the assignment, drop 5 after scope exit) while the sequential lanes on all three backends agree (drop 5 then drop 6)
detail: Found during B-2026-07-30-11's displaced-value leg. The E probe shape (`let mut x = Res{5}; x = Res{6};` inside a fn auto-par splits) prints `drop 5, drop 6, after overwrite` under interp, sequential AOT (KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) and JIT-on-nonsplit-fns — but the DEFAULT build (par lanes compiled for the same statements) prints `drop 6, after overwrite, ..., end, drop 5`: the displaced value's body fires at scope exit with the OLD id via a branch-lane copy, and the assignment-point fire covers the new value only. Same class as the branch-capture-by-value semantics B-27/B-28 documented — the branch's copy of the binding carries its own cleanup and the lanes disagree on which lane owns which fire. Pre-existing family (the pre-fix default build already fired drop 5 after end); the displaced-value leg (1276227) fixed the SEQUENTIAL semantics and did not touch lane ownership. REPRO: scratchpad b3011_nonlet2.kara E section, default build vs KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0. Likely wants a par-group gate for statements displacing user-Drop bindings (the captured_container_mutations analogue for Drop-bearing struct locals) or lane-aware fire ownership. FIXED dcb9b7a: took the par-group-gate option. MECHANISM PINNED first (analysis print + probes): the assignment `x = Res{6}` landed in a non-trivial parallel group with captured_mutations {x}; the group stayed parallel because x is never READ after it — but the parent's scope-exit DROP BODY is a hidden read the outside-reads set cannot see. The branch mutated its bit-copied env copy (a lost write), the lane's NLL fire printed the NEW value's body (drop 6) at the assignment, and the parent's scope-exit fire printed the stale pre-spawn value (drop 5) after end. This is EXACTLY the never-a-dead-write argument that created captured_container_mutations for containers (B-2026-07-15-2), so the fix widens that classification: collect_container_locals now also classifies locals whose type carries a user impl Drop (program.drop_method_keys lookup on the annotation head / pattern_binding_types name, plus a StructLiteral-RHS fallback for unannotated lets), so a captured mutation of a Drop-observable binding lands in captured_container_mutations and codegen's existing non-empty gate (stmts.rs group planner + functions.rs fan-out filter) forces the group sequential. Groups that merely INTRODUCE a Drop binding (no captured mutation) stay parallel — the B-2026-07-31-40 map tests pin that side and still emit __par_branch. Verified: the full b3011_nonlet2 probe now MATCHES interp on the default build (was drop 6 at assignment + drop 5 after end) and valgrind reports zero leaks; the isolated E shape (trivial groups, compiled inline) never diverged and still matches. Test: test_e2e_auto_par_captured_drop_mutation_sequential_semantics (proven failing pre-fix with the exact divergent output in the assert diff). RESIDUAL: wrapper types are not yet classified — a Drop payload inside a reassigned enum/Option/tuple binding (`let mut b = Box2.Full(Res{..}); b = Box2.Empty;` in a lane) has the same class of divergence but Box2 is not in drop_method_keys; needs a transitive drop-observable closure over declared struct fields / enum payloads (follow-on). RESIDUAL CLOSED fef9314: wrapper types now classify transitively. Probe-proven first: `let mut b = Box2.Full(Res{5}); b = Box2.Empty;` in a lane fired the stale pre-spawn payload body (drop 5) at parent scope exit while interp and KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 stay silent (the sequential enum-displacement body silence is a separate in-parity B-2026-07-30-11 residual — this fix makes default match sequential, it does not add the missing sequential fire). compute_drop_observable_types builds a fixpoint closure at ConcurrencyChecker construction: seed = drop_method_keys, admit any declared struct whose field (or enum whose variant payload) mentions a member through an OWNING type former (path head, generic args, tuples, arrays; refs/slices/weak/raw-pointers/fn types do not propagate). type_name_is_drop_observable and the StructLiteral-RHS fallback now consult the closure. Test: test_e2e_auto_par_captured_drop_wrapper_mutation_sequential_semantics (proven failing on the direct-gate-only tree — the stash diff shows the exact trailing 'drop 5'). Probes b41_wrap + b3011_nonlet2 MATCH interp on the default build, valgrind zero leaks. Remaining shapes outside the closure: locals typed by GENERIC instantiations whose Drop reaches through a type parameter (mono-level knowledge the analyzer's name-level closure cannot see) — unprobed, likely rare in group-captured mutation position.

title: The auto-par cost model has no notion of memory ACCESS PATTERN, only of statement count. Prism's `rotate` — the least arithmetic-heavy of its kernels — is the biggest fan-out win measured (3.52x) because its reads are transposed and latency-bound, and nothing in the model knows that. It cleared the gate by accident.
detail:
FOUND converting Prism's remaining kernels to the auto-par-eligible loop form (kara-katas 4f9ee6f). Measured at 12 MP on 4 cores, medians of 7, setup subtracted, every output identical to its KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 twin:

  rotate    117.4 -> 33.4 ms   3.52x
  adjust     94.9 -> 49.8 ms   1.91x
  flip       25.4 -> 19.2 ms   1.33x
  grayscale  29.3 -> 22.1 ms   1.32x
  crop       21.4 -> 19.7 ms   1.08x

The ordering is NOT predicted by anything the cost model measures. `adjust` is by far the most arithmetic-heavy body (f64 brightness/contrast/saturation, ~20 statements) and comes second. `rotate` does no arithmetic at all beyond index math — it is four byte copies per pixel, the same as `flip` and structurally the same as `crop` — and it wins by nearly 2x over the next kernel.

WHY: `rotate` reads TRANSPOSED. Each output row gathers from a different source column, so consecutive reads are `sw * 4` bytes apart and essentially every one is a cache miss. That makes it latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound, and latency is exactly what more cores hide well (more outstanding misses in flight). `crop` is the opposite extreme — a contiguous row memcpy already saturating bandwidth — and gains 1.08x. `flip` sits between: contiguous within a row, reversed or row-swapped across.

THE DEFECT is not the ordering, which is fine; it is that the model cannot see any of it. `CostEstimator` counts AST nodes, and `body_is_memory_bound` asks a yes/no question ("any index read, no substantial call"). Neither distinguishes a sequential stream from a strided gather, so:

  - `rotate` cleared the memory-bound carve-out on STATEMENT COUNT alone (the B-2026-07-31-10 correction: any body scoring >= 64 escapes). By the model's own reckoning it is a cheap memory-bound body that should have been declined. It fanned out by luck, and got the session's best speedup.
  - `crop` cleared the same gate the same way and got 1.08x — the case the gate nominally exists to prevent, waved through by the same accident.

So the gate is currently right for the wrong reason on the best case and wrong on the marginal one, and the two are indistinguishable to it.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THESE KERNELS: the memory-bound gate is under active question (see B-2026-07-31-10's calibration note — with the gate disabled entirely, kata-153's shape still declines via `declined_variable_k_param_bound`, so it may no longer be load-bearing). Any attempt to re-narrow or remove it will be reasoning about "memory-bound" as a single boolean when the measurements above span 1.08x to 3.52x within that one bucket. A stride/locality signal — even something as coarse as "is the innermost index affine in the loop var with unit stride, or not" — would separate the 3.52x case from the 1.08x case, which no amount of re-tuning the existing threshold can.

NOT ATTEMPTED HERE. It needs a new signal in the estimator plus a cross-machine calibration (these numbers are one 4-core Linux VM; the original gate was calibrated on an M5 Pro), which is a different slice from anything in flight. Filed so the observation is not lost in a session transcript. FIXED f56f958 (the coarse signal the row asked for — 'is the innermost index affine in the loop var with unit stride, or not'): par_cost.rs gains body_has_strided_gather, a nest-blind sibling of MemoryBoundDetector (same traversal, so the two predicates always describe the same top-level read set) that classifies each top-level index read against the fanout induction var — unit-stride = the var itself or var +/- loop-invariant (both pre-lowering Binary and post-lowering Call(Path([ty,'add'/'sub'])) forms); anything else that mentions the var (multiplied, nested index, computed) is a GATHER. fanout_verdict/_with_cost gain loop_var: Option<&str> (all four call sites — codegen reduce + disjoint_par, query-side effect_graph x2 — pass shape.loop_var, so `karac query concurrency` and the binary keep answering identically per B-2026-07-31-13). The DeclinedMemoryBound gate now lets a memory-bound body ESCAPE when its reads gather: latency-bound work is exactly what more cores hide. Nothing currently accepted changes — the escape only ADMITS bodies the gate used to decline, and the dispatch-cost thresholds still apply downstream. Calibration pins intact: kata-153's unit-stride stream still declines (memory_bound=true strided_gather=false, per_iter=14 < 64; test_ir_memory_bound_body_skips_par_reduce stays green). MEASURED on this 4-core Linux container: a stride-16 min-reduction over a 32 MiB Vec (100 reps, 7 runs, medians) — 137 ms sequential vs 47 ms fanned = 2.9x raw, ~4.9x with the common setup subtracted; per the row's own physics the sequential run is latency-serialized while 4 workers keep 4 miss streams in flight. KARAC_COST_DEBUG now also prints strided_gather. RESIDUALS, recorded: the signal is binary (no stride-magnitude model — a stride-2 read classifies like stride-16); the contiguous-copy overshoot the row noted (crop-like >= 64-unit bodies waved through, 1.08x) is left as-is — declining it risks the measured 1.3-1.9x unit-stride wins (flip/grayscale/adjust) that share the bucket, and needs the cross-machine calibration the row flagged. Tests: test_ir_strided_gather_escapes_memory_bound_gate (proven failing with src/ stashed — pre-fix the gate declined the strided shape and no par_reduce was emitted) beside the existing unit-stride decline pin. SOURCE NOTE: implemented from the row's own fix sketch, 2026-08-01 overnight session.

title: A chained method call on a fresh container-returning builtin receiver leaks the receiver temp: `let k = Env.args().len();` leaks the args Vec[String]'s element string(s) every execution — the receiver temporary is never registered for cleanup.
detail: Found while valgrinding the B-2026-07-30-11 discarded-temp probes: `fn main() { let k = Env.args().len(); println(f"{k}") }` shows `definitely lost: 19 bytes in 1 blocks` allocated by karac_runtime_env_args_into (the argv[0] string; the outer buffer IS freed). Control-probed as PRE-EXISTING and independent of the discard leg — the shape is a Binding-pattern let whose RHS is a method chain, none of the discard machinery runs. The two-statement form (`let args = Env.args(); let k = args.len();`) is clean: the bound Vec registers the full inner-string element walk. So the gap is the RECEIVER TEMP of a chained call on a fresh owned Vec[String]-returning builtin: `.len()` consumes the receiver as a borrow, the temp has no binding, and no owned-temp registration fires for the receiver position (the statement-discard chokepoints only see statement/wildcard-let tails, and the arg-position registrars only see call ARGUMENTS). Env.args() is the proven case; the class plausibly covers other fresh-receiver chains whose receiver type needs an element walk (a plain `mk_vec().len()` may be covered by existing method-receiver materialization in method_call.rs — scope unverified). SOURCE NOTE: valgrind control probe scratchpad/envargs_chain.kara, 2026-07-31 overnight session; ~19-21 bytes per execution of the statement, unbounded if looped. FIXED 53975c0: the class was GENERAL, not Env.args-specific — any fresh-owned call-result Vec receiver of len/is_empty/count with heap-bearing elements leaked them (mk(3).len() over runtime f-strings leaked all 3 element Strings, 93B; a Vec[Vec[i64]]-returning fn leaked both row buffers, 40B; is_empty identical; a literal-string Vec[String] probe was a VACUOUS pass — cap=0 statics). ROOT CAUSE: the parser gives a MethodCall its receiver's span, so a whole chain shares one span key and expr_types' last write (the outer scalar) evicts the receiver's Vec[T] — owned_temp_drops NEVER has an entry for a chained receiver, and materialize_owned_temp's documented degrade (outer buffer freed, elements leak) was the PERMANENT behavior at this intercept, not a rare fallback. FIX: new dedicated span-keyed table temp_recv_len_elem_types (typechecker records the receiver's element TypeExpr for len|is_empty|count on a call-shaped receiver, heap-bearing elements only: String / Vec[scalar] / user struct / user enum) + codegen try_track_len_family_recv_temp in the len-family intercept (user struct/enum elements thread vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr into track_vec_of_aggs_var; String/nested-POD-Vec ride the FreeVecBuffer vec-struct recursion), falling back to the chokepoint when absent. DEDICATED table on purpose: at a collided span temp_recv_elem_types describes the get-family receiver, a DIFFERENT value than the len-family receiver — sharing would type-confuse the element walk (analyzed against mk_rows().first().unwrap().len(): scalar elements deliberately unrecorded keep that shape off the new path). Scalar elements stay unrecorded — the outer-buffer free is already complete. Interp needs no twin (no manual heap); parity re-verified unchanged (Drop-struct element probe: bodies silent in BOTH backends — the known receiver-temp residual on B-2026-07-30-11's list, untouched). Tests: asan_len_family_fresh_recv_elements_freed (proven failing pre-fix with src/ stashed), e2e_len_family_fresh_recv_values; probes valgrind-clean incl. Env.args().len()/is_empty(), user-fn Vec[String], Vec[Vec[i64]], Vec[struct-with-String]; JIT parity spot-checked.

tracker: .github/workflows/ci.yml (the codegen-e2e job's explicit --test list; the `test` job's bare `cargo test --all`), docs/spikes/ci-test-coverage.md (Tier 1 scope)
title: 554 `--features llvm`-gated tests across 19 targets never run in CI — including par_codegen (220) and drop_differential (13). `cargo test --all` compiles them to nothing and reports green, and the LLVM jobs name their targets one by one, so the omission is invisible from a passing build.
detail:
SURFACE NOTE: the defect is in CI configuration, not a compiler phase, so `surface` is `other` — the enum has no test-infra value; `source` carries the real provenance.

SOURCE NOTE: found while deciding where to put an oracle for examples/shortener. The question "will this actually run in CI" turned out to have a general answer.

MECHANISM, and why it is silent. Every one of these test files is `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]` at the module level. The `test` job runs `cargo test --all` WITHOUT `--features llvm`, so the module compiles to an empty target and reports `ok. 0 passed` — a green tick for a file that ran nothing. The jobs that do enable the feature (`codegen-e2e`, `memory-sanitizer`, and the macOS/arm legs) name their targets explicitly (`--test codegen --test interpreter …`), so a test target is covered only if someone remembered to add it to a list. Nothing fails when they don't.

MEASURED 2026-07-31 (main @107a364), counting `#[test]` per llvm-gated target:
