STAGE 3a LANDED — the `freeze` STATEMENT (`let g = freeze root;`), and it needed NO CODEGEN either. The stage-3 note above sized this as codegen work: "a frozen local has to be a genuinely non-counting binding, which needs a codegen binding class whose slot aliases an existing owner without retaining". STAGE 2.5 BUILT THAT CLASS, for the case where the owner is the caller's value; stage 3a reuses it unchanged for the case where the owner is a LOCAL IN THE SAME FRAME. Measured: `let g = freeze t` takes rc_inc=0 and registers no cleanup, so the enclosing function carries only `t`'s own release, while the plain rebind `let g = t` pays for two owners (the discriminating leg of the codegen test). That is the THIRD stage in a row whose cost estimate was written before the enabling measurement and turned out cheaper than the estimate — worth naming as a pattern rather than as three coincidences. TWO NAMES COME OUT FROZEN, and the second is what makes the first sound: the handle, and the SOURCE'S PLACE ROOT for the rest of the walk. The design says "`graph` stays usable read-only; freezing does not consume it" — that is not a courtesy, it is the enforcement. Once the root is in the frozen set the ordinary whitelist refuses to move, return, or capture it, so the owner whose refcount the handle is skipping cannot go away while the handle is live; without it the alias dangles the moment the source is consumed. The source gets its own diagnostic noun (the FOURTH: parameter / receiver / alias / source), because the line to go change is the `freeze`, not a signature or a `let`. EVERY REFUSAL REPORTS, and that rule was earned rather than designed: a `freeze` this pass will not honour is an error — a temporary operand, a `mut` binding, a destructuring pattern, a `freeze` inside a closure body — never a silent downgrade to an ordinary counted binding. This stage hit the silent-downgrade failure TWICE in its own construction. (1) `check_frozen_param_escape` early-returns for a function with no `frozen` parameter, which is `main`, where a freeze statement most naturally lives — so every negative probe "passed". (2) An unsupported operand shape fell through to the ordinary walk, where the source was not yet frozen, so nothing reported and the `freeze` quietly did nothing. Both were caught by probing the cases whose expected answer was "must report". WITH STAGE 2.7's `SelfValue` HOLE THAT IS THREE VACUOUS-PASS BUGS IN THREE STAGES, all the same shape: the accept rows cannot tell you the check ran. Every battery on this row now carries at least one row that must fail. `karac fmt` WAS DELETING THE KEYWORD — found by running it, not by reasoning. The first cut rewrote `let g = freeze t;` to `let g = t;`, which is not cosmetic: it removes the guarantee and turns a non-counting binding into a counted one. The keyword lives on `Program::freeze_spans`, a PARSER-set side table (so no new `ExprKind` and no walk churn — the same trade stage 1 recorded for `Param::is_frozen`), which means `format_expr` can never see it and the `let` printer is the only thing that can emit it. Pinned by a fixpoint test. IMPLEMENTATION. `freeze` is a CONTEXTUAL keyword recognized in exactly one position — a `let` initializer whose next token can begin a place — so `let freeze = 5`, `fn freeze()`, and `fn f(freeze: i64)` all still parse as they did, and `let x = freeze;` reads the binding rather than freezing nothing. `Program` derives `Default` and every construction site uses `..Program::default()`, so the new field cost ZERO churn. The span is keyed on the OPERAND, which is the same key the escape check and codegen already use for a non-counting binding, so parser, ownership, par admission and codegen all agree on which `let`s are freeze sites by construction rather than by three enumerations. The freeze-site check (E0512) reaches the statement through the SAME classifier a parameter goes through, and — importantly — through the same ENUMERATION: the escape walk records every freeze site it visits and hands them over, so a site that is ADMITTED but never CLASSIFIED cannot exist. Par admission required `TrackedBinding.frozen` to stop being hardcoded `false` for a `let` (the stage-2.5 note's "no freeze expression exists yet" is now stale), which threaded the span set through five signatures in concurrent_shared.rs. TESTS: tests/parser.rs `freeze_is_a_contextual_keyword_recorded_on_the_program` and `freeze_round_trips_through_the_formatter`; tests/ownership.rs `freeze_statement_introduces_a_frozen_root_from_an_ordinary_binding` (5 accept rows, 5 reject rows, plus the source-noun assertion) and `freeze_statement_is_subject_to_the_freeze_site_check` (3 rows); tests/par_codegen.rs `frozen_local_from_a_freeze_statement_takes_no_counts` (with the plain-rebind discriminator) and `freeze_statement_shares_a_local_across_par_branches`; tests/memory_sanitizer.rs `asan_freeze_statement_shares_a_local_across_par_branches_no_leak` — the fixture that matters most here, because for the first time the owner is a LOCAL with its own scope-exit release rather than the caller's value, so a weakening of the source restriction shows up as a use-after-free rather than a wrong answer. Its non-vacuity read had to move ABOVE the freeze (`contains` is not one of the two permitted container queries, and after the freeze the source is restricted too) — the rule working, not a limitation. VERIFIED: interp / `karac run` (JIT) / AOT all agree; 20 repeat AOT runs give one distinct output; valgrind 0 definitely lost / 0 indirectly lost; ASAN clean at BOTH -O2 and KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0. STILL OPEN — stage 3b, the per-instance freeze, and #133 is squarely in it. RE-MEASURED rather than inferred (the row had been reasoning from a description for several stages): the #133 shape refuses with TWO independent errors, exactly as the two-guard design says — E0512 at the freeze site (`Node` has mutable state) and the projection walk at `root.neighbors` (a `mut` field). Both must relax together, and relaxing them needs the proof that nobody WRITES that field during the region, which is instance-level and is what mechanism 1 is. Nothing in stage 3a moves that; what it moves is that the region is now EXPLICIT and LOCAL, which is the precondition the design gives for a per-instance check ever being cheaper than mechanism 1.

STAGE 3b SCOPED, NOTHING BUILT — and one MEASUREMENT resizes it. Stage 3b is the per-instance freeze, and #133 is squarely in it. Re-measured on the reconstructed kata shape (this row had been reasoning from a description for several stages): it refuses with exactly the two errors the two-guard design predicts — E0512 "`Node` has mutable state, so it cannot be frozen yet" and the projection walk "`frozen` parameter `root` cannot be projected through `.neighbors` yet". THE FINDING: the precondition § "The call" describes as reducing to "no other live binding of this instance", and calls "local and cheap", HAS NO ENFORCEMENT TODAY AT ALL. Probed on a deeply-immutable type so E0512 does not mask it: `let t = Imm { val: 1 }; let a = t; let g = freeze t;` CHECKS CLEAN — `a` is a second full-power handle to the same instance, made before the freeze, and nothing observes it. `take(t)` before the freeze passes too. That is harmless TODAY, and that is exactly why it has never mattered: E0512 refuses every type where a second handle could WRITE. It stops being harmless the moment E0512 relaxes, because `a` could write `a.tag` while branches read through `g`. So "local and cheap" is an estimate about an analysis that DOES NOT EXIST, not a description of one that does — and it is the precondition for BOTH guard relaxations, so it should land first. SECOND SIZING FACT: the projection half needs WRITE-POSITION TRACKING, which is the recorded dead end arriving from the other side. Today a `mut` field is refused at every projection step in read and write position alike, which is precisely why § "Two guards" says the arm "needs no write-position tracking". #133 needs to READ `neighbors`; allowing that means distinguishing read from write, and then the Assign / CompoundAssign / `mut`-marked-argument / `mut ref self` forms all have to be enumerated — the class that produced B-2026-08-04-13/-14/-15 in one day, here with a non-deterministic arch-sensitive symptom. It is bounded (the walk is exhaustive with no `_` arm, so a new statement kind breaks the build) but not free, and B-2026-08-05-37 already records one oddity on that surface: a `mut`-marked argument rooted at a `shared struct` field is accepted and its write silently discarded. THIRD: stage 3a did move something real for 3b — the region is now EXPLICIT and LOCAL, which is the argument that was given for building the statement and which holds. DELIBERATELY NOT IMPLEMENTED NOW, and the reason is worth recording so nobody "helpfully" adds it: the alias/uniqueness condition could be enforced on its own today, and it should not be. E0512 already refuses every type where an alias could matter, so enforcing it now would reject programs that currently work and buy nothing until the relaxation it guards actually lands. It belongs in the same slice as the relaxation, not ahead of it. ORDERING for whoever takes 3b: (1) the alias/uniqueness condition at the freeze site — the precondition, and the piece that does not exist at all; (2) relax E0512 for a `freeze` STATEMENT whose source satisfies (1), keeping the PARAMETER-mode freeze site as strict as it is, so a `frozen T` parameter inherits the guarantee from its caller's already-frozen argument the way the mode composes today — no whole-program analysis, so this stays mechanism 3 rather than becoming mechanism 1; (3) relax the projection walk for a READ of a `mut` field through a frozen place, with the write forms enumerated — the hazardous half, to land last and alone. Written up in docs/spikes/freeze-point-design.md § "Stage 3b". No code changed.
-- STAGE 3b STEP 1 LANDED (4d18fac2, the uniqueness precondition) AND STEP 2 WITH IT (the
   E0512 relaxation it gates). Steps 1 and 2 shipped as ONE slice, deliberately. --

WHY ONE SLICE, and this is the spike's own instruction rather than a
convenience: § "Deliberately NOT implemented now" says the alias condition
"could be enforced today, on its own. It should not be ... it would reject
programs that currently work and buy nothing until the relaxation it guards
actually lands." The Ordering list immediately below it says to do the alias
condition FIRST. Both are right and they are about different things -- BUILD
order versus LAND order. Step 1 alone, shipped, is a pure regression: every
program that freezes an immutable type with a live alias starts failing and
nothing gains. So the check was built first and landed with the relaxation.

THE PRECONDITION FAILS IN TWO DIRECTIONS, and closing one proves nothing.
Measured before the change, both accepted:

    let a = t;  let g = freeze t;    an alias made FROM the source
    let t = a;  let g = freeze t;    the source made FROM an alias

A THIRD case the spike did not record is worse than either: `let n = take(t);
let g = freeze t;` -- the source CONSUMED by a call and then frozen -- also
checked clean. All three now refuse for a `mut`-bearing type.

The implementation is two sets on the existing escape walk (`used_names`,
`place_bound`), read at the freeze site before the operand is walked. It is
deliberately COARSE: any earlier use of the root disqualifies, including a
scalar read that could not possibly produce a handle. A false NEGATIVE is a
refused freeze the author fixes by moving a line; a false POSITIVE is a data
race on a non-atomic refcount, which this repo has already had go arch-specific
and run green on x86 CI (B-2026-07-12-29).

WHAT THE RELAXATION TOUCHES, and what it does not. The proof relaxes exactly
one arm -- `MutableState`. `NotShared` and `AlreadyPar` are about the
REPRESENTATION (no refcount header to skip, or an atomic one that needs no
skipping) and no fact about aliasing can change either. A `frozen` PARAMETER
never receives the proof: its instance belongs to the caller, whose other live
handles this pass cannot see, and establishing it there would be the
interprocedural analysis mechanism 3 exists to avoid.

SOUNDNESS RESTS ON THREE GUARDS, each probed rather than argued:
  * uniqueness -- no other name existed to write through;
  * the escape walk freezes the SOURCE root for the rest of the scope, so the
    owner cannot be moved, reassigned, returned or captured while the frozen
    handle lives;
  * the projection walk still refuses every `mut` field, in READ and WRITE
    position alike (step 3, deliberately untouched).
Removing any one re-opens the race. The third is directly visible: after a
SUCCESSFUL freeze of `shared struct M { mut n: i64 }`, both `m.n = 99` and
`g.n` are still refused. The relaxation admits the FREEZE, not the mutation.

MEASURED -- the increment is real and bounded. `shared struct Node { val: i64,
mut neighbors: Vec[i64] }` shared across two `par` branches: REFUSED at the
freeze site before, and now compiles and runs. interp / `karac run` (JIT) / AOT
all agree; 20 repeat AOT runs give one distinct output; valgrind reports 0
definitely lost and 0 indirectly lost (the residual "possibly lost" is the
pthread TLS block the par scheduler allocates, present on every par program).

WHAT IT DOES NOT REACH, stated because the row has twice been optimistic here:
#133 is still out. Its traversal is IN A CALLEE (`sum_clones(root, 28)`), which
needs a `frozen Node` PARAMETER -- refused, per the asymmetry above -- and it
reads `neighbors`, a `mut` field, which needs step 3. This slice moves the
freeze SITE only. What a `mut`-bearing type gains today is sharing across
branches for reads of its IMMUTABLE parts, with the traversal written inline.

A TEST'S EXPECTATION CHANGED, not just added to.
`freeze_statement_is_subject_to_the_freeze_site_check`'s `mut`-bearing row
(`let m = M { n: 1 }; let g = freeze m; g.n`) now fails at the PROJECTION guard
instead of E0512, because its source is uniquely bound. The program is still
rejected, so the row keeps its value, but it tests a different guard -- and the
E0512 half moved to a new row with an ALIASED source, so the relaxation cannot
widen unnoticed.

TESTS: tests/ownership.rs `freeze_statement_relaxes_e0512_only_for_a_uniquely_
bound_source` (2 accept rows, 6 reject rows covering both uniqueness
directions, the consumed-source case, the never-relaxed parameter, the
still-refused `mut` projection and a write through the source, plus two
assertions that the STATEMENT and PARAMETER suggestions differ);
tests/memory_sanitizer.rs `asan_freeze_statement_shares_a_mut_bearing_local_
across_par_branches_no_leak` (255-node tree, floored at 300 allocations). Both
STASH-PROVEN RED: the ownership test fails on its first accept row, the ASAN
test with `Node has mutable state, so it cannot be frozen yet`.

THE DIAGNOSTIC WAS MADE STALE BY THIS CHANGE AND FIXED IN IT. The
`MutableState` suggestion told every author that "stage 1 has no per-instance
check to back that claim" -- true when written, false the moment this landed.
It is now two messages behind a `FreezeSite` enum, because the REPAIR differs:
a statement has a local one (drop the other name), a parameter has none. That
is the same failure this row already recorded once at a larger scale -- the
ownership `suggestion` that never reached the terminal at all -- so a message
that silently outlives its own premise is worth treating as a defect here.

title: A module-level `let` whose name starts with a LOWERCASE letter is not recognized as a module binding at all — it falls through to a top-level statement and the author is told to "move the statements into `main`, or remove the explicit `main`", two suggestions that both destroy the intent. `E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING` never fires.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found building canned LLM responses for the Mend corpus — the iteration-0 attempt for `link_registry` deliberately used lowercase module bindings, which is the mistake its notes.md predicts. Instead of the naming diagnostic, it produced one misdirecting parse error.

THE BOUNDARY IS THE FIRST LETTER'S CASE. Same three-line program each time, only the binding's name changes:

  let mut <NAME>: i64 = 0;
  fn bump() { <NAME> = <NAME> + 1; }
  fn main() { bump(); println(<NAME>.to_string()); }

  COUNT      -> All checks passed          (recognized as a module binding)
  MY_COUNT   -> All checks passed          (recognized)
  Count      -> E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING    (recognized; correct, actionable, machine-fixable)
  C          -> E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING    (recognized; correct)
  myCount    -> "file contains both top-level statements and an explicit `fn main()`"
  my_count   -> same
  c          -> same

An uppercase FIRST letter is what makes the parser treat the `let` as a module binding. Anything starting lowercase is parsed as a top-level (script-mode) statement, collides with the explicit `fn main()`, and produces an error about a completely different subject.

WHY THE DIAGNOSTIC IS WORSE THAN MERELY WRONG. It is confidently actionable and both of its actions are destructive:
  "move the statements into `main`"  — impossible by construction; the binding exists precisely
                                       because SEVERAL functions share it. Moving it into main
                                       breaks every reader.
  "remove the explicit `main`"       — deletes the program's entry point to silence a naming
                                       problem.
Neither mentions capitalisation. An author who follows either suggestion ends up further from a working program than when they started, and the actual one-token fix (rename to SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE) is never surfaced.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A TYPICAL DIAGNOSTIC GAP:
 * Lowercase is the DEFAULT habit for a variable name in every mainstream language. This is not
   an exotic mistake; it is the first thing a new author types.
 * Module-level mutable state is how a service holds state — `examples/shortener/` needed exactly
   this shape (LINKS / HITS / SEQ), so it is on the main path, not a corner.
 * It lands squarely on the AI-first wedge. A fresh LLM author gets a diagnostic that is
   confidently wrong about the subject, with no `replacement`, and whose prose actively steers
   toward a worse program. That is the failure mode `karac fix` exists to prevent.

THE GOOD DIAGNOSTIC ALREADY EXISTS. `E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING` handles the uppercase-initial cases correctly today — it names the rule, and since B-2026-07-31-31/-32/-33 it carries a machine-applicable rename that also rewrites use sites. So the fix is to widen the RECOGNIZER so a lowercase-initial module-level `let` is still parsed as a module binding, and let the existing naming diagnostic do its job. That converts this from a misdirecting parse error into an auto-fixable rename.

OPEN QUESTION for whoever takes it: script mode is the reason the recognizer is case-keyed at all — a bare `let x = 1;` at top level is a legitimate script-mode statement. Disambiguating will need a rule (perhaps: a top-level `let` in a file that ALSO defines `fn main()` is a module binding, since script mode and explicit main are already mutually exclusive). Worth confirming that reading against design.md § Module-Level Bindings before implementing.

Took the filing's suggested shape (phase-aware rather than code-set) and found TWO phase-blind predicates, not one — the filing flagged `fix_introduced_new_error` and suspected `fixes_resolved`; the suspicion was right and the second is worse. `fixes_resolved` was `max(0, len(before) - len(after))`, so the reported case scored ZERO resolved (1 diagnostic before, 2 after): the correct fix was counted AGAINST fix_precision_pct, not merely omitted from it.

New rules: a code is charged as a regression only when it appears at or BEFORE the phase that was blocking the build (so a parse fix yielding typecheck errors is progress, while a parse fix yielding a DIFFERENT parse error is still caught); resolved is a per-code multiset difference, since newly-unmasked codes only ADD to the after set and cannot mask a code that really went away. Unknown phase names sort LAST, so a phase the harness has not learned yet reads as newly-unmasked rather than as a regression — the conservative direction for a metric whose failure mode is over-reporting.

MEASURED, old -> new:
  batch_20260801T235833 (layered): 6 resolved / 75.0% / 1 'broke the build'
                                -> 7 resolved / 87.5% / 0
  batch_20260731T212520 (single-mistake): 5 / 100.0% / 0 — BYTE-IDENTICAL under both.
That second line is the filing's claim restated as a measurement: the bias fires only on multi-phase programs, so the metric looked fine until the fixtures got good.

Tests: examples/mend/harness/test_mend_score.py (new — the harness had none). Most of it guards the OPPOSITE direction from this bug, since the danger in relaxing a metric is making it always-pass: a different parse error at the same phase, a new earlier-phase error, and a same-phase newcomer alongside legitimately-unmasked ones are all still charged. Verified non-vacuous by stubbing the detector to always return 'no regression' — exactly those three fail. Wired into the CI lint job (pure python, no build).

title: The Mend scorer counts a CORRECT `karac fix` as having "broken the build" whenever it unmasks errors a earlier-phase failure was hiding. Because the compiler is phased, any fix to a parse error that reveals a typecheck error is scored as a regression — systematically understating fix precision on exactly the multi-layer programs that are most realistic.
detail:
SURFACE NOTE: the defect is in the measurement harness, not a compiler phase, so `surface` is `other`.

SOURCE NOTE: found running the first full 9-task dry-run batch after backfilling the missing canned_responses.json files. The new `canonical_request` fixture is deliberately LAYERED — a parse error hiding a type error hiding an ownership error — which is what exposed this.

MEASURED (batch_20260801T235833, canonical_request/iter_000):
  BEFORE fix : E0001  parse      the `&&` operator is not used in Kāra; use `and` instead
  AFTER  fix : E0210  typecheck  E_INT_AS_CHAR: cannot cast `i64` to `char` directly
               E0500  ownership  value 'h' moved here, used again here

The fix was CORRECT — `&&` → `and` is exactly right, and the run went on to converge cleanly. The two "new" codes were always present in the source; the parse failure simply meant the compiler never reached typecheck or ownership to report them. Fixing the parse error is what let it get further.

THE DEFECT. `fix_introduced_new_error` is computed as set-difference on diagnostic CODES across the fix boundary: any code present after and absent before counts as the fix introducing an error. In a PHASED compiler that is the normal, desirable outcome of any early-phase fix. The predicate conflates two opposite things:
  (a) the fix genuinely broke the program — a real regression, the thing worth catching;
  (b) the fix removed a blocker and later phases finally ran — progress.

CONSEQUENCES, both on headline numbers:
  * "fixes that broke the build : 1 run(s)" — reported for a run in which nothing broke.
  * fix precision 75.0% (6 resolved / 8 applied) — understated, since the unresolved count
    includes a fix that did its job.
The bias is not random: it fires precisely on programs with mistakes in more than one phase, which are the realistic ones. A corpus of single-mistake fixtures would never show it, so the metric looks fine right up until the fixtures get good.

SUGGESTED FIX SHAPE (unverified): make the comparison phase-aware rather than code-set-based. The diagnostics already carry a `phase` field. A fix should only be charged with a regression when a NEW diagnostic appears at or BEFORE the phase of the diagnostic it fixed — a parse fix that yields typecheck errors is progress, while a parse fix that yields a DIFFERENT parse error is suspect. An alternative, cheaper rule: charge a regression only when the after-set contains a code from a phase that had already run clean before the fix. Either way, keep a real regression detectable — the metric is worth having, it is just measuring the wrong difference.

WORTH CHECKING WHILE IN THERE: whether `fixes_resolved` has the same phase-blindness, since it feeds `fix_precision_pct` from the same comparison.

title: No implicit `*mut T` -> `*const T` weakening at call sites — every consume-direction binding that passes a malloc'd (or otherwise mut) buffer to a `*const` foreign param needs an explicit `as *const T` cast (the cast is SAFE — earlier premise that it was unsafe-gated was wrong)
detail:
Found authoring examples/interop-zlib: `uncompress(back, ptr.mut(back_len), dest, dest_len)` where `dest: *mut u8` (we malloc'd and filled it) and the declared param is `source: *const u8` → E0200 TYPE_MISMATCH expected '*const u8', found '*mut u8'. The weakening direction is always sound (dropping write permission on the same allocation; Rust coerces *mut T → *const T implicitly at coercion sites for exactly this reason), and the natural shape of C bindings hits it immediately — compress-then-use, fill-then-hash, any produce-into-then-read-from buffer. Workaround is `unsafe { dest as *const u8 }` per call site (raw-to-raw casts are unsafe-gated), which taxes the flagship additive-adoption surface with unsafe blocks that assert nothing beyond what the type system already knows. DESIGN FORK to settle before fixing: either (a) add the implicit weakening coercion at call sites (matches Rust; zero soundness cost), or (b) keep the explicitness but make the raw-to-raw mut→const cast SAFE (it introduces no capability), so the workaround at least sheds its unsafe block. Current behavior may be intent (design.md § Unsafe Escape Hatch lists raw-to-raw casts as unsafe-block-legal and never discusses call-site pointer coercion) — if so, document the pattern in § FFI; the gap today is that natural binding code fails with a bare type error and no guidance.

SOURCE NOTE: example family, consume-direction FFI worked example, 2026-08-02.

CORRECTION (2026-08-02, verified on live compiler): the raw-to-raw cast does NOT require an unsafe block — `let c: *const u8 = d as *const u8;` compiles in safe code (probe t5). The original entry's 'workaround needs unsafe { } per call site' premise came from reading design.md's 'raw-to-raw casts remain legal in unsafe blocks' as 'only in unsafe blocks'; the implementation (correctly, per § Unsafe Escape Hatch's 'only ... pointee-changing casts require unsafe') gates neither direction of the same-T mutability cast. examples/interop-zlib has been cleaned of its unnecessary unsafe wrappers. Residual gap, DOWNGRADED to low: (a) the E0200 mismatch could carry a machine-applicable fix-it (insert `as *const T` — always-sound weakening); (b) design.md never states the no-implicit-coercion rule or the cast's safety explicitly — one spec sentence settles it. The implicit-coercion fork stays recorded above but is now an ergonomics choice, not an unsafe-burden fix. Discovered while probing: the OTHER directions (pointee-changing, const->mut strengthening) are ALSO un-gated, which § Unsafe Escape Hatch explicitly forbids — filed separately as B-2026-08-02-9.
resolution: fixed in a31d7be — design decision: NO implicit mut->const coercion (spends the language's implicitness budget on a raw-pointer corner; explicit-now -> implicit-later stays open, the reverse doesn't). Instead the `expected '*const T', found '*mut T'` same-pointee mismatch carries a machine-applicable FixIt inserting ` as *const T` + help text; verified end-to-end that `karac fix` applies it and the program compiles — the consume-direction FFI shape closes mechanically through the Mend loop. Cross-pointee mismatches carry no fix-it (would smuggle a pointee change past the B-2026-08-02-9 gate). Rule specced in design.md § Raw Pointer Construction.

title: A BUILTIN function name in ANY non-call position — `spawn;`, `let f = println;`, `spawn { … }` — passes `karac check` and then panics the interpreter with an internal `unreachable!` whose own message says "should be caught by resolver". USER-defined functions are fine as values, so this is builtins-only.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found writing the S3-client dogfood. I wrote `spawn { … }` to run a server alongside a client — the wrong syntax (the real form is `spawn(|| …)`) — and `karac check` told me the program was fine.

REPRO (one line):
  fn main() { spawn { println("x"); }; }

  karac check          -> All checks passed.
  karac run --interp   -> thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/interpreter/eval_expr.rs:170:17:
                          internal error: entered unreachable code: variable 'spawn' not found
                          at 8:5; should be caught by resolver
                          + a full Rust stack backtrace
  karac build          -> error: codegen failed: Undefined variable 'spawn'

SCOPE — it is every builtin FUNCTION name, not just spawn:
  spawn { … }         check passes -> interpreter panic
  println { … }       check passes -> interpreter panic
  print { … }         check passes -> interpreter panic
  assert { … }        check passes -> interpreter panic
  len { … }           correctly rejected at resolve (not a global builtin; it is a method)
  notafunction { … }  correctly rejected: "undefined name 'notafunction'"

So the resolver resolves the NAME (it is a real builtin) and never checks that it is being USED as a call. The block form sails through resolve and typecheck, and the interpreter then tries to evaluate the bare identifier as a variable, finds no binding, and hits an `unreachable!` whose message correctly blames the resolver.

WHY THIS EXACT MISTAKE IS LIKELY, NOT EXOTIC. Kāra really does have block-form constructs — `par { }`, `seq { }`, `unsafe { }`, `comptime { }`, `lock { }`. Someone who has just written `par { }` and wants a single background task will write `spawn { }` by analogy. It is the natural wrong guess, and `spawn` is precisely the builtin reached for when writing concurrent code — the language's headline capability.

THREE THINGS WRONG, IN DESCENDING SEVERITY:
 1. `karac check` IS NOT AUTHORITATIVE. It greenlights a program that cannot run on either
    backend. Every consumer that trusts check — the Mend loop above all, which iterates until
    check is clean and then declares the program correct — will accept this program as done.
    An LLM author following the documented loop converges on a program that panics.
 2. The interpreter PANICS WITH A RUST BACKTRACE rather than emitting a diagnostic. CLAUDE.md's
    coding standard is explicit: "Every compiler phase must emit structured diagnostics with
    source spans — never just panic." The user sees compiler internals for a syntax mistake.
 3. Codegen's message (`codegen failed: Undefined variable 'spawn'`) is a raw string with no
    span, no code, and no JSON representation, so it is invisible to `--output=json` consumers.

SUGGESTED FIX SHAPE (unverified): reject a builtin function name in non-call position at resolve, with a diagnostic that names the correct form — for `spawn` specifically, "`spawn` takes a closure: `spawn(|| …)`", which is machine-applicable (wrap the block in `(|| … )`) and would make this a `karac fix` case rather than a crash. The `notafunction` path already produces the right SHAPE of error; builtins just need to reach it. Whoever takes it should also decide whether the `unreachable!` at eval_expr.rs:170 should become a structured internal-error diagnostic regardless, since it is reachable from any future resolver hole of this kind.

── SCOPE CORRECTED (same day, before any fix) ──
The original entry framed this as the BLOCK form (`spawn { … }`). That is narrower than reality and a fix aimed at it would be incomplete. Re-measured on exit codes rather than first-line matching — the panic output begins with a BLANK line, so an earlier `head -1` probe scored several panicking cases as clean and produced a wrong boundary:

  spawn { … };            check passes -> PANIC (exit 101)
  spawn;                  check passes -> PANIC   <- no block involved at all
  spawn; println("a");    check passes -> PANIC
  println { … };          check passes -> PANIC
  let f = println;        check passes -> PANIC   <- ordinary let, no block
  { println("x"); };      check passes -> clean   (a bare block is fine)
  helper;                 check passes -> clean   (USER fn as a value)
  helper { … };           check passes -> clean   (USER fn)

So the rule is: ANY reference to a builtin function name outside call position panics. The block form is simply how I happened to hit it. User-defined functions ARE first-class values — `Server.serve(addr, handle)` in examples/shortener depends on exactly that — so the asymmetry is builtins-only.

That also settles the fix's shape: builtins are NOT first-class values today, so the correct repair is to say so at resolve for every non-call reference, not to special-case the block form. Making builtins first-class would be a feature (and would need a codegen half), not a bug fix.

title: Pointee-changing and const->mut raw pointer casts compile OUTSIDE unsafe blocks — the spec-mandated unsafe gate on `*T as *U` is not enforced (`let w: *const u64 = d as *const u64;` and `let m: *mut u8 = c as *mut u8;` both pass in safe code)
detail:
Found probing B-2026-08-02-2's premise (2026-08-02, probes t6/t7): design.md § Unsafe Escape Hatch says pointee-changing casts require `unsafe { }`, and § Raw Pointer Construction says raw-to-raw casts (`*const T as *mut T`, `*const T as *const U`) 'remain legal in unsafe blocks' — but the typechecker gates NONE of the raw-to-raw directions: `*mut u8 as *const u64` (pointee change, u8->u64) and `*const u8 as *mut u8` (write-capability strengthening) both compile with no unsafe block and no lint. SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-01-32 per its FIXNOTE; the -32 fix deliberately excludes shared/pointer-valued elements from the calloc path so this row is the remaining Map-element gap. tracker: src/prelude.rs (the flat prelude name list — `Response`, `HttpError`, `Match`, `Client`, `RequestBuilder`, `Stats`, `Regex`, …), runtime/stdlib/*.kara (where those types are declared), and every name-keyed dispatch site in src/typechecker, src/codegen and src/interpreter (~49 across 14 files)
title: STDLIB AND USER TYPES SHARE ONE FLAT NAMESPACE, so any user struct that shadows a prelude type name silently takes over that type's codegen identity. `Response` (fixed as B-2026-08-02-7) was one instance of a class: a user `HttpError` double-frees identically, and a user `Match` crashes codegen outright.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while doing B-2026-08-02-7's deferred ergonomic half. That entry's fix makes the HTTP CLIENT path refuse when a user declares `struct Response`. Scoping the real fix — let user code use the name freely — turned up the general problem, and that the guard covers one name on one path.

MEASURED INSTANCES (each a standalone program; the user struct shadows a prelude name and
carries a heap field):

  struct HttpError { message: String }   + Client.get(…)      -> builds, DOUBLE FREE at runtime
  struct Match     { text: String }      + Regex.compile(…)   -> CODEGEN PANICS with a Rust
                                                                 backtrace: "Found IntValue …
                                                                 but expected the StructValue
                                                                 variant" (method_call.rs:1170)
  struct Stats     { label: String }     + builtin unused     -> clean (nothing routes through it)
  struct Response  { status, body }      + Client.get(…)      -> refused since B-2026-08-02-7

So the failure mode varies by which builtin path the shadowed type feeds — silent memory corruption on one, a compiler crash on another — but the cause is single: the prelude injects stdlib type names into the SAME flat namespace user declarations occupy, and every backend dispatches on the bare string. `src/prelude.rs` lists them unqualified (`"Response"`, `"HttpError"`, `"Match"`, `"Client"`, `"RequestBuilder"`, `"Stats"`, `"Regex"`, …), `runtime/stdlib/http.kara` declares `struct Response { … }` with no module prefix, and there is no `http.Response` distinct from a user's `Response`.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS NOT A RENAME. Making the builtin internally distinct means threading a mangled identity through ~49 name-keyed sites across 14 files in the TYPECHECKER, CODEGEN and INTERPRETER, plus the stdlib `.kara` sources. Both backends must move together — a codegen-only rename would produce a run-vs-build divergence, which this project treats as worse than the bug being fixed. The clean fix is module-qualified stdlib types (`http.Response` as a real, distinct type), which is a language/design slice, not a patch.

INTERIM POSITION, and why the current guard is only half a fix: B-2026-08-02-7's refusal turns silent corruption into an actionable message for ONE name on ONE path. The same treatment could be generalised — refuse when any user struct shadows a prelude type name whose builtin path the program actually uses — which is strictly better than today for `HttpError` and `Match`, and cheap next to the namespace work. That is the recommended next step if the namespace slice is not scheduled soon.

SEPARATE DEFECT WORTH ITS OWN LOOK: the `Match` case CRASHES CODEGEN with a Rust panic and backtrace rather than any diagnostic, violating the standing rule that every phase emits structured diagnostics and never panics. Even after the namespace fix, that unwrap (method_call.rs:1170, expecting a StructValue) should degrade to a diagnostic — it is reachable from any future type-identity confusion, not just this one.

USER-VISIBLE SHAPE OF THE HAZARD: `Response`, `Match`, `Client`, `Stats` and `HttpError` are all extremely natural names for a user's own struct — `Match` in a parser or game, `Stats` in anything with metrics, `Response` in any service. The language currently offers no warning that these names are claimed, and the penalty ranges from a compiler crash to memory corruption.

── PARTIAL FIX LANDED 4c4c2f0: HTTP leg covered, REGEX LEG STILL OPEN ──
Generalized B-2026-08-02-7's single-name guard to a set of shadowed prelude names plus a shared `reject_shadowed_prelude_types(what, names)`, wired into the HTTP client and regex entry points. Measured coverage:
  struct Response  + Client.get    -> refused (was a double free)
  struct HttpError + Client.get    -> refused (was a double free, previously unguarded)
  struct Match     + Regex.compile -> STILL PANICS — uncovered

WHY THE REGEX LEG RESISTED, so the next attempt does not repeat it. Detection keys on `struct_types` already holding the name when the user's declaration is processed. That is exact for the three types `seed_builtin_struct_types` seeds (Client / Response / HttpError) and misses every stdlib type spliced from a `.kara` prelude source (Match / Regex / RegexError). Two alternatives were tried and REVERTED ON EVIDENCE:
  * detecting on the prelude NAME alone — flags the stdlib's own declarations against
    itself, refusing 6 legitimate regex programs (measured in tests/codegen.rs);
  * gating on `StructDef::stdlib_origin` — looks like the exact discriminator, but the
    bake step flips it only for GATED modules (`synthetic_gated_modules`, std.web), not
    for prelude splices, so prelude stdlib structs arrive with it FALSE and the guard
    over-fires identically.

So the regex leg needs one of: (a) a real origin marker on prelude-spliced items — the principled fix, and it would make this whole guard exact; or (b) graceful degradation of the receiver coercion at src/codegen/method_call.rs (the `into_struct_value()` that panics when the shadowed layout makes the receiver an i64), which is worth doing on its own merits since a panic there violates the never-panic rule regardless of this bug.

The regex guards ARE wired and will start working the moment detection reaches those names, so (a) alone completes the leg with no further codegen changes.

── REGEX LEG CLOSED 78275a1; ENTRY NOW FIXED ──
Root cause of why the leg resisted two detection strategies: stdlib declarations reach codegen's `declare_structs` by TWO paths and neither marked them as stdlib. (1) `expand_gated_stdlib_imports` splices gated-import items (Command / Log / Match) into the USER's program tree without flipping `stdlib_origin`, even though `synthetic_gated_modules` flips it on the same items reached the other way. (2) `declare_stdlib_program` walks baked STDLIB_PROGRAMS trees parsed straight from source, where the flag is never flipped at all. Hence name-only detection flagged the stdlib against itself (6 codegen tests refused) and `stdlib_origin` gating over-fired identically — the flag was false on both paths.

Fixed one per path: the splice now flags spliced items stdlib-origin (correct on its own merits — the flag is the truth about item provenance), and codegen carries a `declaring_stdlib_program` scope flag so the detector skips baked stdlib trees. All four cases measured: Response/HttpError refused on the client path, Match refused on the regex path (was a PANIC), and both a plain regex program and `import std.process.{Command}` still compile — the two over-fire regressions, now regression tests in tests/http_client_codegen.rs.

REMAINING, tracked separately: the receiver coercion in src/codegen/method_call.rs still panics if any future path reaches it with a shadowed layout. The guard prevents that today, but a panic there violates the never-panic rule regardless, so hardening it is still worth doing as defense in depth.

title: Drop-carrying field of a GENERIC-mono parent struct: body silent at owner death (both backends) + Vec-element String buffer leaks under AOT
detail: A user struct with `impl Drop` held as a FIELD of a generic parent (`struct Box2[T] { item: T, tag: i64 }` instantiated at `Box2[Res]`) never fires the field's Drop body at the parent's death: `{ let b: Box2[Res] = Box2 { item: Res{..}, tag: 1 }; }` prints NO `drop ...` line on EITHER backend (interp and AOT agree, both wrong), and the Vec-element leg `let mut v: Vec[Box2[Res]] = Vec.new(); v.push(Box2 { item: Res{..}, .. })` is silent too AND leaks the element's String field buffer under AOT (valgrind: definitely lost = exactly the f-string name buffer; the direct-binding leg frees its buffer, only the body is silent). The NON-generic control (`struct BoxR { item: Res, tag: i64 }`, identical program otherwise) fires both bodies and is valgrind-clean -- so the gap is the generic-mono field-bodies walk: the parent's synthesized drop/element walk misses user-Drop FIELD bodies (and the AOT element walk misses the field's heap free) when the parent is a monomorphized generic. Sibling class of B-2026-08-01-34 (generic-mono field deep-chain move, fixed f82c0db) on the DROP side rather than the move side. Probes: $SP/b193_g.kara (generic, silent+6-byte leak), $SP/b193_h.kara (non-generic control, correct). Both-backends-silent means no run-vs-build divergence -- the uncertain=>silent parity rule does NOT apply because the non-generic twin DOES fire: this is a hole, not a design choice. FIXNOTE (2026-08-02): fixed in 6ff8614. Four legs. (1) codegen indices (synth_drop.rs): user_drop_field_indices replaced by subst-aware user_drop_field_indices_mono (+ resolve_field_head_mono, type_runs_user_drop_mono) -- a bare-param field name (`item: T` under T->Res) resolves through the mono subst before the drop-relevance check, and emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn resolves field_type in its loop so `Res.drop` (not `T.drop`) dispatches. (2) direct-binding gate (stmts.rs): has_field_user_drop now uses type_runs_user_drop_mono with the binding's recorded instantiation subst. (3) Vec element (runtime.rs + synth_drop.rs + stmts.rs): vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr's struct arm derives the subst from the element's instantiated TE and emits emit_struct_drop_synthesis_mono (fixes the leaked String buffer -- base synthesis read T as a scalar), and a new emit_vec_elem_user_drop_bodies_fn_mono (mono-suffixed __karac_dropelems_<S>$<A> symbols) fires the element bodies at the binding's NLL point. (4) interp (eval_stmt.rs): the drop_user_drop_fields_of_value declared-type gate gains ONE exception -- a field declared as a bare GENERIC PARAM of the struct fires value-driven, REVISING the B-2026-07-29-39 scoping decision (which skipped erased fields precisely because codegen could not see through the erasure; it now can, so parity holds in the firing direction instead of the silent-leak one). Pins: e2e+interp generic_parent_drop_field_bodies (the interp twin is a REAL pin -- interp was silent pre-fix, STASH-PROVEN FAILED) + asan_generic_parent_drop_field_bodies_freed (STASH-PROVEN FAILED: LSan caught the element buffer leak). RESIDUALS: generic parents whose field is a Vec[T]-of-Drop under the subst inherit the one-container-level rule; struct_owns_shared_field remains name-keyed (a generic parent instantiated at a shared type keeps the old routing); Map/Set VALUES of generic parents unprobed. Also in this commit: #[allow(clippy::type_complexity)] on tests/http_server.rs h2c_two_streams_timed (sibling's 07bf66e broke the local --all-targets clippy gate; CI's no-tests clippy missed it).

title: indexed field store with a NON-PURE index (`v[f()].field = x`): codegen silently dropped the store AND the index's side effect; the interpreter applied it but evaluated the subscript TWICE. Both legs fixed — index materialized once on each backend, all four surfaces now byte-identical
detail:
SHAPE (scratchpad idxcall.kara, 2026-08-02):

    struct P { mut id: i64 }
    fn idx() -> i64 { println("eval"); return 0 }
    fn main() {
        let mut v: Vec[P] = Vec.new()
        v.push(P { id: 1 })
        v[idx()].id = 9
        println(f"id={v[0].id}")
    }

  `karac check` — All checks passed.
  interp        — `eval` TWICE, then id=9   (store lands; index double-evaluated)
  AOT seq       — no `eval` at all, id=1    (store AND side effect both gone)
  AOT auto-par  — no `eval` at all, id=1
  JIT           — no `eval` at all, id=1

Two defects in one construct.

LEG 1 (the severe one, codegen). An indexed field store whose INDEX is not a
bare identifier or int literal is silently dropped on every codegen surface,
and the index expression is never evaluated — so an observable side effect in
the index disappears along with the write. Exit 0, no diagnostic, subsequent
reads return the stale value.

MECHANISM, and it is the exact tail B-2026-08-01-35 documented:
`nested_store_place_ptr`'s Index arm asks `field_chain_place_ptr`, whose Index
arm requires `matches!(index.kind, Identifier | Integer)` and returns None for a
Call (the guard is deliberate — `vec_index_elem_ptr` RE-EVALUATES the index, so
the arm only admits indices where re-eval is a no-op). It then falls to
`field_rooted_index_place_ptr`, which requires the container to be a
FieldAccess and returns None for a bare identifier. Both resolvers decline,
`compile_field_store`'s nested branch is skipped, and the store exits through
the no-op Ok(()) tail.

So this is the SAME no-op tail as B-2026-08-01-35 (field-rooted container, pure
index) and B-2026-07-13-10 (shared element). Those two fixes each added a
resolver for one axis; the uncovered cell is IDENTIFIER-rooted container x
NON-PURE index. Not a regression from either fix — the purity guard predates
them and the old Index arm declined the same way.

LEG 2 (interpreter). The interpreter EVALUATES THE INDEX TWICE for an indexed
field store — `eval` prints twice above, and it does so for a field-rooted
container too (`o.hs[idx()].id = 7` prints it twice on interp, once on AOT).
Even where the store lands, side effects in the index are doubled. Presumably a
place-resolution pass followed by a store pass, each evaluating the subscript.

FIX SHAPE (untested). Both legs want the same thing: evaluate the index ONCE
into a temporary and drive the store off that. On the codegen side that also
retires the purity guard's reason to exist — with a materialized index there is
nothing unsafe about re-eval because there is no re-eval. A narrower codegen-only
fix (spill a non-pure index to a temp, then reuse the existing pure-index path)
closes leg 1 without touching the interpreter.

SEVERITY high: silent wrong answer on a `karac check`-clean program, on every
codegen surface, with the side effect swallowed too — a write-then-read sees
stale data and nothing reports it.

SOURCE NOTE: found while probing whether B-2026-08-01-35's landed fix
(`field_rooted_index_place_ptr`) guards index purity the way the identifier
arm does. It does not — but the resulting hole turned out to be on the OTHER
axis, and pre-existing.

── LEG 1 FIXED (2026-08-02). Leg 2 (interpreter double-eval) REMAINS OPEN. ──

`nested_store_place_ptr`'s Index arm now falls through to
`impure_index_store_place_ptr` when both pure-subscript resolvers decline: it
evaluates the index EXACTLY ONCE into a stack temp and retries them against a
synthesized identifier subscript. That fixes the drop and dissolves the purity
guard's premise at the same time — after the spill, the "re-evaluation" the
guard existed to prevent is a variable load.

Gated on container shapes the resolvers can actually place (mirroring
`field_chain_place_ptr`'s Index-arm guards exactly, including the `ref`-param
bail of B-2026-07-21-5/-6 and the array-slot bypass), so a store that would
still fail to resolve does not gain a side effect it never had. Placed in the
STORE walk, not `field_chain_place_ptr`, so match-suppression — which shares
that walker and must not run side effects while resolving a scrutinee place —
is untouched.

MEASURED, `v[idx()].id = 9` where idx() prints and returns 0:

    surface        before              after
    AOT seq        no eval, id=1       eval x1, id=9
    AOT auto-par   no eval, id=1       eval x1, id=9
    JIT            no eval, id=1       eval x1, id=9
    interp         eval x2, id=9       eval x2, id=9   <- LEG 2, still open

CORRECTION to this entry's original text: it implied
`field_rooted_index_place_ptr` lacked a purity guard and might double-evaluate.
It does not — it calls `vec_index_elem_ptr` once, so the FIELD-rooted x
non-pure cell already behaved correctly before this fix and still does
(verified: one eval per store, both writes landing). The hole was narrower than
first described: only the IDENTIFIER-rooted arm declined outright, and only it
needed the spill.

Codegen is now stricter than the interpreter on this shape — exactly-once
versus twice. Leg 2 is a separate defect in `interpreter.rs` (a place-resolution
pass and a store pass each evaluating the subscript) and is NOT addressed here.

VERIFIED: fmt clean; clippy --all --all-targets clean; codegen E2E 2752 passed
/ 0 failed; memory_sanitizer 908 passed / 0 failed (Linux, LSan).
Regression test: `e2e_indexed_field_store_non_pure_index_runs_once`, pinning
one eval per store across both container roots.

── LEG 2 FIXED (2026-08-02) — ENTRY NOW CLOSED. ──

`Interpreter::set_field`'s value-type projection arm is a READ-MODIFY-WRITE-
BACK: it evaluates the receiver to read the struct copy, mutates a field, then
hands the SAME expression to `assign_to_place`, which evaluates it AGAIN to
store. (The header comment above it claimed "Evaluate the receiver place once";
that was true of the shared-struct arm only.) For an indexed receiver the
subscript therefore ran twice.

The two evaluations cannot simply be collapsed — a plain struct is a value type,
so the mutated copy genuinely has to be written back up the place chain. What
CAN be fixed is making both halves agree on a subscript that runs once: a
non-pure index is now evaluated once and the place rebuilt with an
`ExprKind::Integer` literal, which both the read and the write-back then use.

A new `Interpreter::index_expr_is_pure` gates it, deliberately kept SEPARATE
from `eval_stmt.rs`'s `assign_index_is_pure_scalar`: that one is private to its
module and answers a different question (may the displaced-element Drop body
fire?), and its comment requires it to stay in step with a codegen twin for
unrelated reasons. Conflating them would couple two independent gates. The new
one is conservative — anything not obviously pure is materialized, which is
sound either way, since evaluating once is also correct for a pure subscript.

    AOT seq          no eval, id=1     eval x1, id=9     eval x1, id=9
    AOT auto-par     no eval, id=1     eval x1, id=9     eval x1, id=9

Byte-identical on all four surfaces, both container roots (identifier-rooted and
field-rooted). The entry opened as a run-vs-build divergence and briefly
inverted after leg 1 (codegen stricter than interp); it is now genuinely
converged rather than half-fixed.

title: Vec[T]-of-Drop field of a GENERIC parent: element Drop bodies fire under karac run but stay silent under AOT
detail: `struct Pack[T] { items: Vec[T], tag: i64 }` at `Pack[Res]` (Res: impl Drop): pushing an element and letting the parent die prints `drop 7 qq7` under the interpreter but NOTHING under AOT (memory is freed -- valgrind clean -- only the body is silent). Root: the interpreter's Vec-field arm in drop_user_drop_fields_of_value is declared-head-gated on Vec/VecDeque and then VALUE-driven per element, so it always fired; codegen's dbv loop in emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn is explicitly gated `if effective_subst.is_none()` ("generic parents keep the recorded residual"), so a mono parent's Vec[T] field never walks. Direct `item: T` fields were fixed by B-2026-08-02-14 (6ff8614); this is the container-field sibling, and it is a DIVERGENCE (not the both-silent parity the -14 FIXNOTE residual assumed) because the interp side never had the erasure problem for container fields. FIX SHAPE: relax the dbv gate -- substitute the field TE through the mono subst (subst_type_params_in_type_expr) before vec_field_elem_head and before the element LLVM-type derivation, then the existing walk emits correctly against the mono layout. Probe: $SP/b194_a.kara (interp `a|n 1|drop 7 qq7|end`, AOT `a|n 1|end`, vg 0). FIXNOTE (2026-08-02): fixed in 8f3b456. Exactly the filed fix shape: the dbv element-bodies loop in emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn drops its `effective_subst.is_none()` gate and instead resolves the field TE through the mono subst (subst_type_params_in_type_expr) before vec_field_elem_head AND before the element LLVM-type derivation, so a Pack[Res]'s `items: Vec[T]` field walks `Vec[Res]` at the concrete stride and dispatches Res.drop per element. The mono-suffixed __karac_dropbodies_<S>$<A> symbol (from B-2026-08-02-14) keeps instantiations distinct. Non-generic parents: byte-for-byte unchanged (empty subst resolves to the original TE). Pins: e2e generic_parent_vec_field_elem_bodies (STASH-PROVEN FAILED pre-fix -- AOT was silent) + interp twin (parity pin; interp always fired). Suite/sweep clean. RESIDUAL: one container level, as for base parents (Vec[Vec[T]]-of-Drop under a generic parent stays the recorded B-2026-08-01-23-adjacent residual).

title: Map[K, T] field of a GENERIC parent: the value's heap is never freed at owner death under AOT
detail: `struct Store[T] { m: Map[i64, T], tag: i64 }` at `Store[Res]` (Res carrying a String field): insert one value, let the parent die -- valgrind reports the value's String buffer definitely lost under AOT. The NON-generic control (`StoreR { m: Map[i64, Res] }`, identical program) is valgrind-clean, so the gap is the mono parent's struct-drop synthesis classifying the Map field's VALUE drop from the DECLARED bare `T` (scalar -> no value-drop fn) instead of the instantiated argument -- the same declared-name erasure family as B-2026-08-02-14/-16, on the Map-field value-drop channel (the B-2026-07-15-24 `zero_struct_move_caps` mono zone's drop-side sibling). NOTE the SCOPE: the Drop BODY silence for Map-held values in a struct field is a PRE-EXISTING both-backend class (the control is silent too -- the -30-11 Map-values leg covered BINDING-level maps only) and parity holds there; this row is ONLY the memory leak, where generic diverges from the clean non-generic control. FIX SHAPE: in emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl's Map/Set-field classification, resolve the field TE through the mono subst (subst_type_params_in_type_expr, as the -16 fix did for the dbv walk) before deriving key/value drop fns for karac_map_free_with_drop_vec. Probes: $SP/b195_a.kara (generic, 3-byte loss), $SP/b195_b.kara (control, clean). FIXNOTE (2026-08-02): fixed in db367df. Root cause was TWO stacked bare-`T` reads, both now subst-resolved. (1) The struct-LITERAL field init (exprs.rs, both the shared-heap and plain branches of compile_struct_init) built the Map handle via build_map_new_handle_from_type_expr on the DECLARED `Map[i64, T]` TE -- val_size = 8 (i64 default) instead of the instantiated 32, so karac_map_insert memcpy'd only the value's first word and the String buffer pointer never entered the bucket (the leak; get would also read a truncated value). compile_struct_init now takes the literal's param->arg subst (derived at its single call site from enum_inst_type_from_span + generic_struct_subst_from_inst) and resolves the field TE through subst_type_params_in_type_expr first. (2) The parent's mono drop synthesis (synth_drop.rs MapOrSet arm) read the same bare-`T` TE when deriving the per-value drop fn for karac_map_free_with_val_drop_fn -- also subst-resolved now, so the walk frees value heap at the mono layout. Pin: asan_generic_parent_map_field_value_freed (STASH-PROVEN FAILED pre-fix -- LSan caught the buffer; output is identical pre/post so an e2e twin would be vacuous). Non-generic control byte-for-byte unchanged (None subst). RESIDUAL: a literal INSIDE a generic-fn monomorph body takes the active-subst mono_ty path with no span-recorded inst, so its Map-field handle still builds from the declared TE (same class, narrower reach -- the active monomorph subst is not yet threaded here).

title: user Drop bodies silent for TUPLE-held and Map-VALUE-held Drop values in struct fields, on BOTH backends (parity holds, memory clean)
detail: Two struct-field positions where a user-Drop value's `drop` body never fires at owner death, identically on AOT and interp -- so parity holds, and valgrind is clean (heap is reclaimed via the value-drop free path; only the BODY dispatch is missing). (1) TUPLE field: `struct Duo { pair: (Res, i64), tag: i64 }` with Res: impl Drop printing -- at Duo's scope-exit the Res inside the tuple never prints. Reproduced for a generic parent `Duo[T] { pair: (T, i64) }` at Duo[Res] AND for the non-generic control with identical results (probes b196_a/b196_b: vg=0, parity OK, both silent), so this is NOT part of the declared-name-erasure family (B-2026-08-02-14/-16/-17) -- the tuple position simply has no drop-body walk in either backend's struct-drop synthesis (codegen emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn has no tuple arm; interp drop_user_drop_fields_of_value likewise skips tuple-typed fields). (2) Map-VALUE position: `struct Holder { m: Map[i64, Res] }` -- values freed correctly (post -17 for generic parents; always for non-generic), but Res.drop's body never prints on either backend at owner death (noted as out-of-scope in -17's detail; control probe b195_b). SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping struct-field container positions after closing the -14/-16/-17 erasure family. Class note: bodies-only + both-backend + memory-clean makes this a deferred-capability gap rather than a miscompile; when either backend gains the walk, the other must follow in the same slice to preserve parity (the B-2026-07-29-39 lesson). FIXNOTE (2026-08-02): fixed in d6e9beb. Both positions now fire on BOTH backends by reusing the binding-death walkers at the struct-field position. Codegen: type_runs_user_drop + user_drop_field_indices_mono widened with Map/SortedMap-value (Set/SortedSet-element) and tuple-element legs (one container level, subst-resolved for generic parents); emit_user_drop_field_bodies_fn gains a tuple arm (calls __karac_dropelems_tuple on the field slot) and a table arm (calls __karac_dropelems_map on the field slot -- a moved-out field's nulled slot no-ops the walker, probe b198_f). Interp: drop_user_drop_fields_of_value carries the declared field TypeExpr and gains the matching tuple arm (forward element order, declared-elem-type gate with the own-generic-param exception) and run_field_map_val_user_drops (field twin of run_map_val_user_drops); value_runs_user_drop's Struct-arm FIELD recursion widened via field_value_carries_user_drop so displacement/discard/element gates classify like codegen's type-level gate -- this also fixed the pre-existing Vec-field element divergence (Vec[Holder{xs:Vec[Res]}] elements fired under AOT only, probe b198_b). Pins: e2e struct_field_tuple_and_map_drop_bodies + tuple_field_parent_displaced_and_vec_elem_bodies + interp twins (all four STASH-PROVEN FAILED pre-fix) + asan_generic_parent_tuple_field_heap_freed; the asan_generic_parent_map_field_value_freed expectation gains its drop line. RESIDUALS: enum-typed tuple elements / enum map values stay silent on BOTH backends (symmetric, probe b198_e); SortedSet-of-struct field drains bucket order under AOT vs sorted under interp (the recorded B-2026-08-01-17 struct-comparator limitation, field position included); unsorted Map/Set drain order stays unspecified by design. The unmasked tuple-field mono heap leak became B-2026-08-02-19 (fixed same commit); the pre-existing table-field leaks and move-into-literal-field source walks became B-2026-08-02-21 / -20.

title: generic parent's tuple field never frees the mono element heap: `(T, i64)` classifies no-heap at the declared TE
detail: `struct Duo[T] { pair: (T, i64) }` at `Duo[Res]` (Res carrying a String field): the struct-drop synthesis's anonymous-tuple classification (synth_drop.rs, the #21 `tuple_needs_drop` arm) reads the DECLARED field TE `(T, i64)` -- `T` reads as no-heap, the field classifies `Some(false)`, and no NestedTuple drop is registered, so the tuple-held String buffer is never freed at owner death. Same for the `FieldDrop::NestedTuple` emit arm, which hands `emit_tuple_elem_drops` the declared elem TEs (frees nothing at the erased types). The declared-name-erasure family's memory leg for tuples -- exact siblings B-2026-07-15-11 (bare-T direct heap field) and B-2026-08-02-17 (Map[K,T] value heap). LATENT until the field is read: LLVM elides the dead allocation when nothing consumes the tuple String (probe b196_a was vg=0 pre- B-2026-08-02-18 for exactly that reason), and the deep-chain read `d.pair.0.name` hits a recorded codegen loud-bail, so the leak first became observable when the -18 bodies walk started reading the field.
