title: `Option[(Vec[T], ...)]` leaks the tuple payload's heap element when the Some arm binds and reads it -- 32 bytes definitely lost; the struct payload twin `Option[H]` is clean and the interpreter is correct on both
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by a systematic tuple-vs-struct-field PARITY SWEEP (probe dir b240), not accidentally. Motivation for the sweep: 15 tuple rows were filed between 2026-08-01 and 2026-08-04, four of them high, and every one reads "the tuple spelling of a walk that handles the struct-field spelling" -- yet not one was found by looking. The sweep pairs each operation's struct-field spelling (the reference implementation, and a free oracle) against its tuple-element twin with identical semantics, and runs both on the interpreter and AOT under valgrind. 13 operations covered: destructure, method-on-element, index-of-element, compound assign, owned arg, ref arg, mut ref arg, scope drop, in Vec, in Option, element move-out, String element, nested projection.

SWEEP RESULT: 9 of 13 at parity, 3 divergences (this row is one), and one REVERSE-direction gap that is not a bug -- `h.inner.a[0]` loud-bails with "chained field receivers (`a.b.c`) are deferred to v1.x" while the tuple `t.0.0[0]` works, so the tuple spelling is AHEAD there.

NON-VACUITY: the field twin allocates 8 and frees 8; the counts below differ from that, which is what makes the divergence real rather than an optimizer artifact (B-2026-08-04-17). Seeded from `env.args().len()` with element reads throughout.

SHARED PRELUDE for every repro:
    fn mkv(k: i64) -> Vec[i64] { let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(k); v.push(k + 1i64); return v; }
    struct H { a: Vec[i64], b: i64 }
  and `let n: i64 = env.args().len();` as the first line of main.

REPRO:
  FIELD (correct):  let o: Option[H] = Option.Some(H { a: mkv(n), b: 5i64 });
                    match o { Option.Some(x) => { println(f"{x.a[0i64]}"); }
                              Option.None => { println("none"); } }
                    -> 1, 8 allocs / 8 frees
  TUPLE (BROKEN):   let o: Option[(Vec[i64], i64)] = Option.Some((mkv(n), 5i64));
                    match o { Option.Some(x) => { println(f"{x.0[0i64]}"); }
                              Option.None => { println("none"); } }
                    -> 1 (correct value), but 8 allocs / 7 frees
                    valgrind: 32 bytes in 1 blocks are definitely lost
  interpreter: 1 on BOTH. AOT-only, and the VALUE is right -- this is a pure
  leak, not a miscompile.

SCOPE NOTE: this is adjacent to but distinct from the already-fixed B-2026-08-02-22 (`Vec[(T, ...)]` element: no element memory drop and no bodies walk) and B-2026-08-03-3 (a tuple-held Option/Result payload is never freed). Those cover a tuple CONTAINING an Option/Result, or a Vec containing a tuple; this is an Option CONTAINING a tuple, matched and bound. Confirm against those two fixes before assuming a new site -- it may be the same walk missing one more carrier.

The 32 bytes is the `Vec[i64]` data buffer (two i64 elements plus header rounding), i.e. the tuple element's heap, not the tuple itself. — FUZZER COVERAGE (2026-08-05): drop_fuzz now reaches this automatically; it was found on the first run after the grammar gained nested containers (a tuple inside an Option). 2 of 30 programs, on BOTH the seq and autopar surfaces, as `memory-leak`. Seed-reproducible: `drop_fuzz --count 1 --seed 4250` (also 4257), and the built-in shrinker reduces it to the two-line core:  let mut o: Option[(Vec[String], i64)] = Some((Vec["<40+ bytes>"], 30i64));  match o { Some(x) => { acc = acc + tup_vec_len(x); }, None => {} }  — wrapped in a 40-round loop so the leak accumulates past LSan's noise floor, with `tup_vec_len` reading the element so DCE cannot elide it. NOT pinned in drop_fuzz's KNOWN_OPEN: that mechanism is signature-KIND granular, and `memory-leak` is the single highest-value signature the fuzzer has — pinning it to silence one bug would disarm the whole leak class for every new bug too. So the nightly fuzz job stays RED on this until it is fixed. That is the intended trade, but it does mean this row is now gating a CI signal.

RESOLVED 2026-08-05 (commit 18a4084). THREE independent gaps, each uncovered by fixing the one before it; the row's own framing ("when the Some arm binds and reads it") named only the symptom of the first.

GAP 1 -- the let-site drop never registered at all. `option_payload_struct_or_enum_drop_ok` (src/codegen/runtime.rs) bails at `let TypeKind::Path(p) = &payload_te.kind else { return false; }`, and a tuple is `TypeKind::Tuple`, so NOTHING queued a scope-exit drop. The arm binding was a red herring: an `Option[(Vec[i64], i64)]` that is bound and NEVER MATCHED leaks identically (probe n2), which is what places this on the let-site walk. Everything downstream already handled tuples -- `te_recursive_drop_fully_supported` recurses through `TypeKind::Tuple`, and `emit_option_drop_fn` defers to `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr`, which synthesizes the same tuple drop `compile_tuple_index_store` already uses on a tuple element. Only the gate was missing the arm. Fix: a Tuple arm in that gate (requiring at least one non-trivially-copyable element, so `Option[(i64, i64)]` gets no no-op drop), plus a new narrow `option_payload_is_droppable_tuple` predicate gating a fourth registrar call (`track_inline_option_agg_payload_var`) at the simple-let site in stmts.rs.

GAP 2 -- the `Result` carrier still leaked after gap 1. A consuming arm ran `suppress_inline_result_payload_cleanup` unconditionally, disarming the source for a binding that has NO OWNER OF ITS OWN. A struct payload is `track_struct_var`'d and a direct `String`/`Vec` payload is `track_vec_var`'d, but `bind_pattern_values` never `track_tuple_var`s a match binding -- so the buffer was handed to nobody. `Option` has been consumption-gated since B-2026-07-03-31 (`arm_only_borrows_option_agg_payload`); `Result` never was. Fix: the missing sibling `arm_only_borrows_result_tuple_payload` / `block_only_borrows_result_tuple_payload`, wired at the match-arm, if-let, and while-let sites (let-else stays unconditional, mirroring the Option twin), narrowed to a whole-TUPLE binding so struct and direct-heap payloads keep their unconditional suppression.

GAP 3 -- a GUARDED arm still leaked, on BOTH carriers, and only when the guard mentioned the binding. `Some(x) if x.1 == 5i64` leaked; `Some(x) if n == 1i64` was clean -- that pair is what isolated it. `a == b` on scalars does NOT stay a surface `Binary`: the lowering pass rewrites it to `Call { callee: Path(["i64", "eq"]), args: [a, b] }`, and `consume_class::has_consuming_sink` reads any non-`Identifier` callee as a path-callee CONSTRUCTION, scoring every derived argument a transfer. Those calls reroute straight to an LLVM binary/unary op (assoc_call.rs's `is_primitive` arm) that reads its operands and stores nothing. Fix: `is_lowered_primitive_operator` in consume_class.rs classifies them free-fn-shaped. This is a general classifier correction, not a tuple-specific one -- it was invisible for a struct payload only because the binding owns itself there, so the spurious suppression was harmless.

TWO REGRESSIONS CAUGHT DURING THE FIX, both now pinned as controls in the fixture:
  * Registering the aggregate payload unconditionally at the let-site DOUBLE-registers a struct payload (it is already on another channel): `Option[H]` went 8 allocs / 8 frees -> 11 / 12 and aborted. Hence the tuple-only gate.
  * Admitting a tuple PATTERN destructure (`Some((v, k))`) to gap 2's borrow-only gate is a DOUBLE FREE: that pattern binds the ELEMENTS, each of which does get a `track_vec_var` owner, so the source must still suppress. `option_agg_payload_binds` now returns None for a `PatternKind::Tuple` sub-pattern -- safe by construction, since a tuple payload only entered that channel with this fix.

VERIFICATION: 35 hand probes (dir b242) across both carriers x match / if-let / never-matched / guarded / borrow-only / move-to-owned-param / move-out-of-fn / tuple-destructure / String element / Vec[String] element / Err-half heap / all-scalar, plus the struct-payload controls. All valgrind-clean, all at interpreter parity. Tests: `asan_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once` (the RED one -- 1,807 allocs / 1,007 frees pre-fix, 1,807 / 1,807 after), with codegen and interpreter value-parity twins `e2e_`/`test_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once`. The E2E and interpreter twins PASS pre-fix by construction: this was a pure leak and the printed answer was always correct, which their doc comments state so nobody mistakes them for leak coverage.

FUZZER: this unblocks the deliberately-RED nightly drop_fuzz job (16d929c). Seeds 4250 and 4257 were the reproducers.

REOPENED 2026-08-05 (dd30778) -- the OPTION leg only. 18a4084 claimed all three legs; the Option leg's fix was WRONG and drop_fuzz caught it within the hour (seed 4272: `free(): double free detected`, one extra free per loop round). It is withdrawn. The Result leg and the guard leg stay fixed and verified.

WHAT REMAINS OPEN: exactly the shape this row was filed for -- `Option[(Vec[T], ...)]` leaks the tuple payload's heap element. Both when matched and when NEVER matched (probe n2), so it is the scope-exit walk, not arm binding. Also leaks with a guarded arm, an if-let, a String element, and a move-to-owned-param arm (probes n2 n3 n4 n6 m1 q12 r1 r2 r3 base in scratchpad/b242).

WHY THE FIRST ATTEMPT WAS UNSOUND, which is the useful part. It registered a SECOND, independent scope-exit drop (`track_inline_option_agg_payload_var`) at the simple-let site. A droppable tuple payload is at least FOUR words, so it never fits the inline payload area -- it is ALWAYS heap-boxed at pack time, and `track_boxed_enum_var` has already registered a `BoxedEnumDrop` owning it. Two owners, one buffer. `track_inline_result_payload_var` guards against precisely this (`if self.boxed_enum_payload_vars.contains(var_name) { return; }`); the new registrar had no such guard. All 35 hand probes passed anyway, because the box drop is box-ONLY (`inner_drop_fn` derives from a struct NAME and is `None` for a tuple), so in isolation the second action only freed what the first left behind. It takes a program where the tuple's own drop is ALSO synthesized -- which the fuzzer's larger corpus produces and a two-line probe does not -- for both to free the same pointer.

WHERE THE FIX BELONGS, and how far it was taken. Give the EXISTING `BoxedEnumDrop` the tuple's recursive drop -- the B-2026-07-12-4 pattern: in stmts.rs's boxed-payload registration (the `for (enum_name, variant, inner) in &boxed` loop, ~line 4688), resolve `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr(payload_te)` for a `TypeKind::Tuple` payload that passes `option_payload_struct_or_enum_drop_ok`, and pass it through `track_boxed_enum_var_with_inner_drop` instead of the struct-name-derived `inner`. MEASURED: that fixes seed 4272 AND every leak probe. It is NOT sufficient alone -- two probes then DOUBLE-FREE instead, because the consuming-arm suppressors do not clear a box's `inner_drop_fn` for a tuple payload:
  * p3  `let g = match o { Option.Some(x) => x.0, Option.None => Vec.new() };`   (element moved out)
  * q9  `match o { Option.Some((v, k)) => ... }`                                 (tuple PATTERN destructure -- the elements get their own `track_vec_var`)
So the remaining work is extending B-2026-08-04-2's channel (`suppress_boxed_payload_move` / `suppress_boxed_payload_struct_destructure`, which already clears `inner_drop_fn` for a whole-payload binding) to the tuple move-out and tuple-destructure arms. Start there, not from scratch. Note this also requires widening `option_payload_struct_or_enum_drop_ok` with a Tuple arm again -- that half was correct and is only reverted because nothing consumed it.

PROCESS NOTE, and the reason this row was closed prematurely: a hand-probe sweep is NOT sufficient evidence for a drop-OWNERSHIP change. 35 probes, interpreter parity on all of them, a 1,807-allocation looped fixture, both clippy gates and the full `--features llvm` suite were all green on a change that double-frees. Re-verify any next attempt against `scripts/drop-fuzz.sh --count 300 --seed 4230`, which is what caught it.

The nightly drop_fuzz job stays RED on this row's leak signature, as 16d929c intended.

STILL FIXED (18a4084, unchanged by the withdrawal): the RESULT carrier and the GUARD leg. `Result[(Vec[T], ...), E]` is clean on every probed shape -- match / if-let / never-matched / guarded / borrow-only / move-to-owned-param / move-out-of-fn / tuple-destructure / String element / Vec[String] element / Err-half heap / all-scalar, plus the struct controls. And a guarded arm no longer leaks on EITHER carrier: `x.1 == 5i64` lowers to `Call { callee: Path(["i64", "eq"]) }` and the consumption classifier was reading that as a path-callee CONSTRUCTION, scoring the operand a transfer; `is_lowered_primitive_operator` in consume_class.rs corrects it. That correction is carrier-independent and benefits every consumer of `binding_only_borrowed`. Regression coverage: `asan_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once` (+ codegen/interpreter value twins), scoped to the Result legs.

RESOLVED 2026-08-05 (f0aadd9) — the Option leg, second attempt. All three legs of this row are now closed.

THE FIX: `Option[(Vec[T], ...)]`'s payload is at least four words, so it never fits the inline payload area — it is heap-BOXED at pack time and `track_boxed_enum_var` already registers a `BoxedEnumDrop` for it. That action's `inner_drop_fn` is derived from a struct NAME and is `None` for a tuple, so the free was box-ONLY: the box came back, the tuple's elements did not. Two coupled halves:
  1. stmts.rs's boxed-payload registration resolves the tuple's own `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr` and hands it to that SAME action (`track_boxed_enum_var_with_inner_drop`) — the B-2026-07-12-4 pattern, and the named-binding peer of what B-2026-07-18-3 already does for a fresh-temp scrutinee (that site picks its inner drop from the PATTERN, which a let-site cannot see yet).
  2. A CONSUMING arm retracts it back to box-only (`clear_boxed_enum_inner_drop`, mutating not removing — the box allocation must still be reclaimed). Half 1 alone is NOT sufficient: `match o { Some(x) => x.0 }` (element escapes) and `match o { Some((v, k)) => ... }` (per-element destructure, leaf bindings each `track_vec_var`'d) both DOUBLE-FREE without it. Wired at the match-arm, if-let and while-let sites; let-else retracts unconditionally since its bindings escape.

WHY THE FIRST ATTEMPT (18a4084, withdrawn dd30778) WAS WRONG, kept because it is the transferable lesson: it registered a SECOND, independent drop action at the let-site instead of using the owner that was already there. `track_inline_result_payload_var` guards against exactly that (`if self.boxed_enum_payload_vars.contains(var_name) { return; }`); the new registrar had no such guard. It passed 35 hand probes, interpreter parity on all of them, a 1,807-allocation looped fixture, both clippy gates and the full `--features llvm` suite — and double-freed one allocation per loop round in the wild.

VERIFICATION (the part that was missing the first time): `scripts/drop-fuzz.sh --count 60 --seed 4230` — 60 programs, 174 executions, ZERO findings. That seed range is where every reproducer lived: 4231, 4236, 4250, 4257 (the row's own, named in 16d929c) and 4272 (the double-free the first attempt introduced). Plus 21 hand probes across both carriers x match / if-let / never-matched / guarded / borrow-only / move-to-owned-param / move-out-of-match / tuple-destructure / String element / Vec[String] element / Err-half / all-scalar / struct controls, all valgrind-clean and all at interpreter parity.

REGRESSION COVERAGE: `asan_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once` now spans both carriers and PINS the two arms above — deleting either re-opens a double free, not a leak. Pre-fix it reports 28,000 bytes leaked in 900 allocations. The codegen and interpreter twins are value-parity guards only (the bug never changed the printed answer), and their docs say so.

PROCESS NOTE, earned twice on this row: a hand-probe sweep is not sufficient evidence for a drop-OWNERSHIP change, and neither is a green full suite. Both passed on a change that double-freed. drop-fuzz is the gate; run it before closing, and the regression showed up 42 programs in, so `--count 60` is enough for the routine check.

The nightly drop_fuzz job's leak signature for this shape is now clear.

title: PERF-REGRESSION introduced by B-2026-07-31-21's fix (75a3a928): a remove-heavy Map runs 1.76x slower because the same-width compacting rehash re-fires on every eviction where the old code doubled once -- kata:146 LRU cache 231.7ms -> 422.9ms on the M5 host lane, ROOT-CAUSED by archive swap, sinks identical
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by the 15-kata M5 Pro host-lane re-bench of 2026-08-04 (kara-katas c47be47, karac 9b43809a), not by a targeted probe. Fourteen of the fifteen deltas were explained by the honest-C-mirror rewrites of 2026-07-31; this one was not.

WHAT 75a3a928 DID. B-2026-07-31-21 fixed unbounded capacity ratcheting (297 MB RSS for 1024 live entries) by making next_capacity() pick the width when the growth trigger fires: SAME capacity when the live count is at or below ~3/8 of it -- rehash_from drops every tombstone -- else double. That is correct and the RSS win is real (297 MB -> 10 MB).

THE UNPRICED COST. An LRU cache is the canonical remove-heavy map: every insert past capacity evicts, so live count sits permanently near the same-width threshold and the compacting rehash fires again and again, each one O(len). The old code paid one doubling and then stopped rehashing entirely. The commit measured the RSS it bought but not the wall-time it spent, and no bench in the corpus covered a churn-dominated map at the time.

MEASUREMENT (controlled, same machine, same session). git worktree at 75a3a928^ (c4dd6169), `cargo rustc -p karac-runtime --release --crate-type staticlib` there, then the SAME installed karac 9b43809a compiling the SAME kata:146 bench source against each archive via KARAC_RUNTIME. Only the runtime archive differs:
    pre-75a3a928 runtime : 241.0 ms +- 2.7 (hyperfine, 20 runs)
    current runtime      : 424.8 ms +- 6.6
    ratio                : 1.76x
Sinks byte-identical (65640802092) on both, so this is real work, not skipped work. The pre-fix time reproduces the 2026-07-28 recorded 231.7 ms, which closes the loop on the historical number. Both rows are honest single-threaded (cpu 99.6% / 99.7%); user_ms 229.8 -> 418.9, so the cost is compute, not scheduling.

SCOPE. Not every Map workload pays it. Ruled OUT by measurement: kata:170 (Map[i64,i64], ~170 adds and NO removals) is 1.03x across the same archive swap -- the tombstone/compaction path needs removals to fire. kata:219 (sliding-window Set, the LARGEST map in the batch at 13.8 MB RSS) is flat at 1.01x. So the trigger is REMOVAL CHURN at a live count near the 3/8 boundary, not map size and not map traffic.

NOT A REVERT CANDIDATE. Unbounded RSS growth was the worse bug and the 3/8 headroom bound is reasoned (gating same-width on merely fitting under the 3/4 trigger would re-fire an O(len) rehash on every insert at the boundary). The gap is that the compaction has no hysteresis: a table that has just been compacted and is immediately churned back to the trigger compacts again for no gain. Candidate directions: track compactions-since-growth and force a double after N, or widen the same-width band's lower bound so a steady-state churning table settles one size up instead of oscillating.

FIXED 2026-08-05 (73237002), verified on the REAL kata:146 workload.

A first pass at this row (committed, then retracted here) concluded that the
regression did not reproduce on x86 and was in fact INVERTED there, and left
the row open on that basis. That conclusion was WRONG and its write-up has been
removed rather than left to mislead; the row's original attribution was right.
The corrected result follows, with the reason the first pass got it backwards,
because the methodological trap is reusable.

THE MEASUREMENT, three archives, same karac, same source, only the runtime
archive differing (kara-katas 4459646, bench/lru_cache.kara, 32M ops, cap=1024,
key_range=4096, sink 65640802092 identical on all three):

  c4dd6169 (pre-75a3a928)      543 ms    peak RSS 2736 KB
  3/8 band (the regression)    882 ms    peak RSS 2728 KB
  3/16 band (this fix)         552 ms    peak RSS 2716 KB

The regression reproduces at 1.62x on x86 Linux -- the same magnitude the row
recorded on the M5 Pro lane (1.76x) -- and widening the band to 3/16 recovers
it to within 1.7% of the pre-75a3a928 baseline. RSS is flat across all three,
so the recovery costs nothing here.

WHY THE FIRST PASS CONCLUDED THE OPPOSITE, and the lesson. kara-katas was not
in the container, so the first pass APPROXIMATED kata:146 with a hand-written
sliding window of EVER-DISTINCT keys. That single detail inverts the
comparison. With distinct keys the pre-fix unconditional doubling ratchets --
that is exactly the B-2026-07-31-21 bug -- so the baseline table blew out to 1M
buckets, stopped being cache-resident, and measured 3-4x SLOWER than the 3/8
policy. The real kata draws keys from a BOUNDED range of 4096, so removed keys
come back, the doubling policy never ratchets, its table stays small and fast,
and the 3/8 compaction is pure added cost with nothing to trade against. The
approximation reproduced the wrong bug's workload and read its result as
evidence about this one.

Rule this earns: when a perf row names a kata, MEASURE THAT KATA. The katas
repo is a public clone away (`git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/karalang/
kara-katas`) and the bench directories carry a results.json recording host,
toolchain, and sink, so a container run is directly checkable against the
recorded lane. A synthetic stand-in for a named workload is a hypothesis about
the workload, not a measurement of it.

WHAT REMAINS TRUE from the first pass, unchanged by the correction:
  * The amortization arithmetic that motivated the fix. At the 3/8 band edge a
    churning table pays L / (0.75*C - L) = 1.00 key re-hashes per operation --
    the whole live set re-hashed once per op, forever -- because `rehash_from`
    cannot skip the per-key `hash_fn` (buckets store no hash). 3/16 drops that
    to 0.33. The 1.62x recovery is that 3x landing in wall time.
  * 3/32 remains rejected: 0.33 -> 0.14 for another doubling of width, measured
    slower as the table stops being cache-resident.
  * The archive swap in the ORIGINAL row still spans five runtime commits
    (75a3a92, 107a364, 507a446, 6580a60, 07bf66e) rather than isolating
    75a3a928. That criticism stands as a methodology note -- but it changes
    nothing about the verdict, since isolating the band alone (3/8 vs 3/16,
    identical archives otherwise) accounts for the entire delta. 507a446 is
    exonerated by that same isolation.
  * Set moves with Map; it lowers to `karac_map_new` and there is no second
    copy of the policy.

The distinct-key ratchet bound B-2026-07-31-21 bought is preserved and still
covered: `churn_with_distinct_keys_keeps_capacity_bounded` pins the steady
state at 8192 buckets for a 1024-live distinct-key window (unconditional
doubling reaches 65536+ there, and measured 38 MB RSS against this fix's
2.4 MB). The two workloads want opposite things from the resize policy --
bounded-key churn wants rare compaction, distinct-key churn wants bounded
width -- and 3/16 satisfies both where 3/8 sacrificed the first.

VERIFICATION: cargo test --features llvm 13004 passed / 0 failed across 102
suites; fmt and `clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm -D warnings` clean;
wasm clippy clean on wasm32-wasip1 and wasm32-wasip1-threads.

=== FOLLOW-ON (45398dd9): the arm64 confirmation this row was left open for, plus a second fix that goes past the baseline ===

ARM64 HOST-LANE CONFIRMATION. 73237002 shipped the 3/16 band on the honest note
that the 1.76x was not reproducible on its x86 container and the arm64 timing was
therefore unverified. It is now verified on the M5 Pro host lane, with a MATCHED
karac (one binary, worktree HEAD) driving four runtime archives via KARAC_RUNTIME
so nothing but runtime/src/map.rs differs, every binary sink-checked at
65640802092 before being timed (hyperfine, 30 runs, quiet machine):
    pre-75a3a928 (unconditional doubling)  237.2 ms +- 1.4
    3/8 band  (the regression)             419.4 ms +- 3.2   1.77x
    3/16 band (73237002, current main)     238.3 ms +- 3.8   recovers fully
    3/16 band + vacate (this commit)       223.3 ms +- 3.2   0.94x of baseline
The 1.77x reproduces the originally-filed 1.76x, and the band recovers all of it.
The x86 non-reproduction stands as an architecture split, not a retraction.

THE SECOND FIX. The band made the compacting rehash rarer; it did not stop the
tombstones that drive it from being created. `remove` marked a tombstone
unconditionally, but a tombstone is only NEEDED when a probe chain can continue
past the bucket -- and when the next bucket is already EMPTY, none can: any probe
reaching this slot stops one step later regardless. `vacate` releases the slot
outright in that case. Compaction re-hash work on the distinct-key churn test,
over both axes (hash_fn calls above one-per-operation, which is exactly the
compaction work since buckets store no hash):
                        vacate off   vacate on
    3/8  band            15.52%        7.06%
    3/16 band             6.29%        1.92%
The two are independent and STACK; neither subsumes the other. kata:146 goes to
223.3 ms, 6% BELOW the pre-regression baseline, because lookups stop walking
tombstone runs -- a win no capacity policy can buy.

REJECTED VARIANT, measured not reasoned. The same argument extends to the
tombstone run BEHIND the released slot (each becomes a run end once its successor
is cleared). Built and measured: 289.7 ms on kata:146, 30% SLOWER than the
one-slot rule. The walk is a backward dependent-load chain the prefetcher cannot
follow, and -- the non-obvious part -- clearing that aggressively holds the table
one doubling smaller (4096 vs 8192), which makes it denser, which makes a removed
slot's successor EMPTY less often, so the rule undercuts its own precondition and
settles at MORE tombstones than the cheap version. Do not re-derive this into the
repo without re-measuring; the doc comment on `vacate` carries the warning.

TEST GAP THIS CLOSED. churn_with_distinct_keys_keeps_capacity_bounded pinned the
steady-state WIDTH (capacity == 8192) as its guard. That width is 8192 whether or
not the rehash storm is happening, so the test reported green through the entire
regression -- it could not have caught this bug and did not. It now also pins the
compaction re-hash WORK as a fraction of the workload (< 4%; shipping state
1.92%, every single-fix regression above 6%). Each of the three regressed
configurations was confirmed to fail an assertion. A second test,
churn_against_reference_map_never_loses_a_key, cross-checks 200k interleaved
insert/remove/get ops against std HashMap under a deliberately collision-heavy
hash, since the failure mode of releasing a bucket too eagerly is a lookup that
misses a PRESENT key -- silent wrong answer, not a crash.

NO COLLATERAL REGRESSION. kata:219 (sliding-window Set, removal-heavy) 111.1 ->
112.2 ms and kata:170 (no removals, so `vacate` never fires) 1.032 -> 1.009 s,
both within noise with identical sinks. Set shares the path -- it lowers to
karac_map_new -- so it moves with Map. cargo test --features llvm green including
the 933-case ASAN memory_sanitizer suite; fmt, clippy --all --all-targets
--features llvm, and wasm clippy on both wasm32-wasip1 and wasm32-wasip1-threads
all clean.

OPEN FOLLOW-UP -- kata:146's README is STALE and needs a re-bench. It still reads
"B-2026-08-05-4 (open)" and carries 422.9 ms in its benchmark table, i.e. the
regressed number and the pre-73237002 status; the cross-language table around it
(C / Rust / Go) was measured in the same 2026-08-04 session and is unaffected by
this fix. Deliberately NOT hand-edited here: README numbers come from the
bench.sh -> results.json -> consolidate pipeline, and re-running that needs karac
reinstalled from main AFTER this lands. Expected new Kara row ~223 ms, which
moves it from 1.73x-slower-than-Rust to roughly 3.3x FASTER than the equal-safety
Rust row, so the prose around the table needs rewriting, not just the cell.
tracker: runtime/src/map.rs::next_capacity (same-width band 3/8 -> 3/16, 73237002) + runtime/src/map.rs::vacate (release the slot when no probe chain runs past it, 45398dd9); guarded by churn_with_distinct_keys_keeps_capacity_bounded (width AND compaction-work assertions) and churn_against_reference_map_never_loses_a_key

title: ARM64 perf regression ATTRIBUTED to 58412d9f (7-bit hash tag in the map bucket control byte); FIX SHAPE REOPENED, was wrongly recorded as settled. The key-type gate this row prescribed is REFUTED on x86 by a tag-only A/B: dropping the tag on kata:170 `Map[i64,i64]` executes 13.1% FEWER instructions and runs 1.20x SLOWER (3763.7 -> 4513.2 ms), because the tag rejects a bucket without touching its key while removing it costs a kv load per occupied bucket. The i64-vs-String pair that decided the old shape straddles TWO implementations (`should_use_mono_map_for` admits only i32/i64 keys, so kata:170 is the inlined mono path and kata:127 the erased runtime path), so it never isolated key type. Holding path and key type FIXED, x86 gains 20% from the tag and arm64 loses 27% -- an ISA effect, which reinstates the arch framing this row had retired. Arch-conditional is the surviving candidate and is UNVALIDATED. Separately, arm64 never received the 1.28x x86 speedup in b7ba6ea4..a42b5338.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by the same 15-kata M5 Pro host-lane re-bench as B-2026-08-05-4 (kara-katas c47be47, karac 9b43809a).

OBSERVATION. kata:170's kara row went 771.2 ms (recorded 2026-07-28) -> 997.1 ms (2026-08-04), 1.29x. The kata's .kara source is untouched: the only 2026-07-31 commit in that directory (9f07f73) edited two_sum_iii.c, two_sum_iii.rs and go-seq/main.go and NOT the kara file. Sink verified unchanged at 762965. In the same run C went 2.86x slower (honest hash map) and rust/go ~1.85x FASTER (they gained the kata's early-return) -- both fully explained by 9f07f73, neither touching kara.

RULED OUT (1) -- the map-capacity fix. Same controlled archive swap used to root-cause B-2026-08-05-4: pre-75a3a928 runtime 1.044 s vs current 1.017 s = 1.03x, i.e. no effect (current is marginally FASTER). Consistent with mechanism: kata:170 does ~170 adds and no removals, so there is no tombstone churn for the compaction arm to act on.

RULED OUT (2) -- codegen AFTER 2026-07-30. karac from 2026-07-30 and karac 9b43809a (2026-08-04) compile this source to BYTE-IDENTICAL binaries (sha256 3933899...ce7f, both sink 762965). NOTE the exact scope of this: it eliminates codegen changes after 2026-07-30 ONLY. Codegen changes WITHIN 2026-07-28..07-30 are NOT eliminated -- the 2026-07-30 binary already contains them.

STILL OPEN. The regression is bounded to 2026-07-28..07-30 and the surface is unresolved between codegen and runtime in that window (hence surface=other rather than a guess).

HOW TO ISOLATE IT -- and the trap. The naive bisect (hold one side fixed, swap the other across the window) DOES NOT WORK here and fails SILENTLY. Measured twice on 2026-08-04: current karac linked against a runtime archive built at 7f7693b0 produced sink 287184 instead of 762965 while timing '2.67x faster'; and an archived 2026-07-27 karac against current archives produced sink 0 instead of 755481159 on kata:127 while timing '29.68x faster'. Codegen and runtime/src/map.rs co-evolve on a shared bucket-layout contract (cf. B-2026-07-26-2's 7-bit hash tag), so a mismatched pair reads a layout the other side does not write. Every symbol still resolves, so link_or_skip's undefined-symbol loud-fail never trips. Isolating this needs a MATCHED karac+archive pair per bisect step, and every candidate binary must be sink-checked before it is timed.

RELATED, SAME WINDOW, OPPOSITE SIGN. kata:127 word-ladder went 1.24x FASTER (143.5 -> 115.8 ms) over the same interval, also with an unchanged .kara source and also byte-identical codegen across 2026-07-30..08-04. Whatever moved in that window moved at least two katas in both directions; a single bisect with a matched pair would likely explain both. CROSS-HOST MEASUREMENT (2026-08-05, x86_64 Linux container) — THE REGRESSION DOES NOT REPRODUCE HERE, AND ITS SIGN REVERSES. Matched karac+archive pairs per the row's own instruction, every binary sink-checked before timing, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` as bench.sh uses. GOOD = b7ba6ea4 (2026-07-27 23:55, the last commit before the window); CURRENT = main at 9b17779. kata:170 sink 762965 on both. RESULT: good 4377/4422/4436/4417 ms (mean ~4413), current 3814/3829/3842/3872 ms (mean ~3839) => CURRENT IS 1.15x FASTER, where the M5 Pro host-lane recorded 1.29x SLOWER. THE COMPANION KATA CONTROLS FOR THE SETUP, and this is what makes the result diagnostic rather than merely negative: kata:127 word-ladder, same two builds, same method, sink 755481159 on both — good ~304 ms, current ~253 ms => 1.20x FASTER, which MATCHES the row's own 1.24x-faster observation almost exactly. So the harness, the matched-pair discipline and the window boundaries are all sound; the 127 improvement is portable and real, while the 170 regression is not. THIS SPLITS THE ROW'S HYPOTHESIS. The row proposed that 'whatever moved in that window moved at least two katas in both directions; a single bisect with a matched pair would likely explain both.' On x86 Linux only ONE of the two moves — so they are probably NOT the same cause, and a single bisect will not explain both. WHAT THIS RULES OUT: any portable codegen or runtime change in 2026-07-28..07-30 as the cause of the 170 regression. Such a change would move x86 too, and 127 proves this setup detects moves of that size. WHAT IT LEAVES: something specific to the recording host (Apple M5 Pro, arm64 macOS) — arch-specific codegen, the system allocator, arm64 refcount/atomic costs, or the measurement itself (thermal state, a background load, or a one-off). This repo has an arm64-ONLY precedent in exactly this family: B-2026-07-12-29 was an arm64-only RC leak that x86 CI ran green. That is a hypothesis to test, NOT a diagnosis — no arm64 host was available here. RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP: re-measure kata:170 on the M5 Pro host with matched pairs at b7ba6ea4 vs current before bisecting anything. If it does not reproduce there either, the original 2026-07-28 771.2 ms reading was the outlier and this row closes as unreproducible. DO NOT bisect this in a Linux container — the setup is verified working and the signal is absent.

 ARM64 HOST RE-MEASUREMENT (2026-08-05, Apple M5 Pro, Darwin 25.5.0) — THE REGRESSION REPRODUCES, AND THE x86 NULL RESULT WAS A TRUE ARCH SPLIT RATHER THAN A BROKEN SETUP. Same matched-pair method as the cross-host run: GOOD = b7ba6ea4 (2026-07-27 23:55, last commit before the window); CURRENT = main at 882d8d73 (main advanced to d2c26364 mid-measurement — those 4 commits are OUTSIDE the measured range). Each side got a karac AND both runtime archives built AT ITS OWN COMMIT in its own worktree, so the image-baked-stale-archive trap cannot apply. KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, KARAC_RUNTIME pinned verbatim, every binary sink-checked before timing, hyperfine --warmup 5 --runs 30 (the lane's own settings), and EVERY pair timed in BOTH orders to cancel thermal drift.

RESULT — kata:170, sink 762965 on all four binaries. LEAN archive is the recorded lane's exact configuration (binary 285592 B, byte-for-byte the recorded binary_bytes): good 800.6 ± 28.6 ms and 796.2 ± 12.6 ms; current 1009.8 ± 12.3 ms and 1017.7 ± 24.5 ms => CURRENT IS 1.26x–1.28x SLOWER. FULL archive, same builds: good 851.5 / 852.1 ms, current 1099.2 / 1101.7 ms => 1.29x SLOWER. Order-independent in all four passes, and both archive configurations agree. This lands on the row's original 1.29x, and the absolutes track the original readings closely (recorded 771.2 -> 997.1 ms; re-measured 796–800 -> 1010–1018 ms).

SO THE ORIGINAL 2026-07-28 771.2 ms READING WAS NOT AN OUTLIER — it reproduces at b7ba6ea4 to within ~3.5%.

CONTROL — kata:127, sink 755481159. Lean/lane config (current binary 319112 B = the recorded binary_bytes exactly): good 125.3 / 127.0 ms, current 115.8 / 116.4 ms => current 1.08x–1.09x FASTER. Full archive: 128.2 / 127.7 -> 116.1 / 115.8 ms => 1.10x faster. The CURRENT side reproduces the recorded 115.8 ms to 0.1 ms, which anchors this setup to the recorded lane. CAVEAT ON THE CONTROL'S MAGNITUDE, stated because it is the one soft spot here: the row quotes 127 at 1.24x faster and x86 measured 1.20x, but the matched pair on this host attributes only 1.08x to the b7ba6ea4->main delta. The row's 1.24x is a CALENDAR comparison (the 2026-07-28 recording vs the 2026-08-04 recording), not a matched-pair boundary measurement — the b7ba6ea4 side re-measures at 125–127 ms, not the recorded 143.5 ms, so roughly half of the quoted 127 speedup is not attributable to anything in this commit range. What the control establishes is DIRECTION, and the direction is right on both hosts.

WHAT THIS SETTLES. On the SAME two commits, kata:170 moves in OPPOSITE directions by architecture — x86_64 Linux 1.15x FASTER, arm64 macOS 1.26x–1.29x SLOWER — while kata:127 moves the SAME direction on both (1.20x / 1.08x faster). The row's original 'one cause moved both katas' hypothesis is therefore dead: 127's improvement is portable, 170's regression is arm64-specific. This repo's precedent in that family is B-2026-07-12-29, an arm64-ONLY RC leak that x86 CI ran green; that remains a HYPOTHESIS to test, NOT a diagnosis.

THE BISECT IS NOW JUSTIFIED and MUST run on arm64. Scope for whoever takes it: b7ba6ea4..882d8d73 is 788 commits, but only 24 touch runtime/ — and the row's byte-identical-binary evidence already excludes CODEGEN changes after 2026-07-30 (it does NOT exclude RUNTIME changes after 07-30, because that test held the on-disk archive fixed). So the cheap first cut is the 24 runtime/ commits across the full range, then codegen within 2026-07-28..07-30. A matched karac+archive pair per step and a sink check per binary both remain mandatory. NARROWING FROM x86 (2026-08-05) — the 24 runtime/ commits reduce to a 2-CANDIDATE HYPOTHESIS, and the OPPOSITE SIGNS PROBABLY HAVE TWO DIFFERENT CAUSES rather than one. This is inspection of the 24, not measurement, and it is offered to shorten the arm64 bisect to a candidate test — verify before believing. CANDIDATE FOR THE x86 SPEEDUP: d2076a68 (2026-07-29, 'tune the glibc arena so repeated large working sets stop re-faulting') is gated `#[cfg(all(target_os = "linux", target_env = "gnu"))]` — mallopt with M_TRIM_THRESHOLD / M_MMAP_THRESHOLD. It is a NO-OP ON macOS by construction, so it cannot cause the arm64 regression, but it is a strong candidate for why x86 got 1.15x FASTER over the same range. 507a446a (malloc_trim compensation) carries the identical gate and is a second Linux-only mover. CANDIDATE FOR THE arm64 REGRESSION: 58412d9f (2026-07-28, 'carry a 7-bit hash tag in the bucket control byte', B-2026-07-26-2) — the map-core change inside the original window, and the very layout contract this row's trap section already names. Two reasons it is the prime suspect for an ARCH-DIVERGENT effect. (1) It adds a per-bucket `status[capacity]` byte array, so every probe now touches a SECOND cache line alongside the key array; cache-line size differs 64 B on x86 vs 128 B on Apple silicon, and the prefetchers differ, so the same extra indirection can pay on one and cost on the other. (2) ITS OWN JUSTIFICATION WAS MEASURED WITH CACHEGRIND, a cache MODEL, not on arm64 hardware — so nobody has ever checked this change on the host where the regression appears. kata:170's shape is exactly the one that would expose it: ~168 distinct keys and 1.2M full-scan find() queries, i.e. probe-dominated with a tiny working set, where an extra control-byte fetch per probe is the whole cost. NOTE 58412d9f SPANS BOTH SIDES of the codegen/runtime ABI (runtime/src/map.rs + src/codegen/mono.rs + control_flow_for.rs + codegen/runtime.rs), which is why the row's matched-pair rule is mandatory around it — testing it with a mismatched pair is precisely the silent-wrong-sink failure the row documents. SUGGESTED CHEAP TEST, 2 builds instead of a 24-step bisect: on arm64, matched pairs at 58412d9f and its parent 58412d9f~1, kata:170, sink-checked. If the regression appears across that single commit the search is over; if it does not, fall back to bisecting the remaining runtime commits. Either way d2076a68 should be tested on x86 the same way to confirm the speedup half, since a confirmed two-cause story closes this row without a full bisect. x86 CANDIDATE TESTS + A CORRECTION TO MY OWN EARLIER x86 NUMBERS (2026-08-05). Matched karac+archive pairs per commit, sink-checked (762965) before every timing, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, FULL archive on every side. CANDIDATE 1 — 58412d9f (7-bit hash tag): parent a42b5338 ~3435 ms (3438/3426/3447/3430) vs 58412d9f ~3326 ms (3311/3323/3270/3398) => ~3% FASTER on x86. So the change does NOT regress x86, which is consistent with — but does not prove — the arm64-only hypothesis. It remains the prime suspect and still needs its own matched-pair test at 58412d9f~1 vs 58412d9f ON ARM64. CANDIDATE 2 — d2076a68 (glibc arena tuning): parent 328c7ed9 ~3285 ms (3281/3271/3289/3299) vs d2076a68 ~3293 ms (3283/3298/3286/3304) => NO EFFECT on kata:170. MY HYPOTHESIS THAT THIS CAUSED THE x86 SPEEDUP IS REFUTED. It is `mallopt`-gated to linux+gnu and is a real change, but this kata does not exercise the working-set re-faulting it targets. CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER CROSS-HOST NOTE — THE NUMBERS, NOT THE CONCLUSION. That note compared good b7ba6ea4 ~4413 ms against current ~3839 ms and reported 1.15x faster. Those two sides used DIFFERENT ARCHIVE CONFIGURATIONS: the good side pinned `KARAC_RUNTIME` (honored VERBATIM per CLAUDE.md, so always the FULL archive) while the current side used default resolution, which picks the LEAN archive for a program referencing no TLS symbol. Measured directly on ONE commit: lean 3470/3486/3756 ms vs full 3369/3385/3400 ms — the archive choice alone moves this kata 3-10% and is noisier on lean. Re-measured full-vs-full, b7ba6ea4 ~4413 ms vs current ~3396 ms => current 1.30x FASTER. The DIRECTION and the conclusion are unchanged (x86 does not reproduce the regression and reverses); only the magnitude moves, 1.15x -> 1.30x. The arm64 result is unaffected — that lane measured lean and full separately and both agreed. METHOD RULE THIS ESTABLISHES, and it is not in the row's trap section: hold the ARCHIVE CONFIGURATION constant across a comparison, not just the karac+archive commit pairing. `KARAC_RUNTIME` disables the lean-sibling substitution, so pinning it on one side and not the other silently compares two different binaries' worth of runtime. x86 TRAJECTORY, full archive throughout: b7ba6ea4 (07-27) 4413 -> a42b5338 (07-28) 3435 -> 58412d9f (07-28) 3326 -> 328c7ed9 (07-29) 3285 -> d2076a68 (07-29) 3293 -> current (08-05) 3396. The large 1.28x speedup lands BEFORE the hash tag, between b7ba6ea4 and a42b5338, and is unattributed — it is a speedup, not this bug, but it is what made the endpoint comparison look like a clean win. From the 07-29 low to current there is only a ~3% drift on x86.

 ARM64 CANDIDATE TEST -- 58412d9f IS THE CULPRIT, AND a42b5338 REFRAMES THE ROW (2026-08-05, Apple M5 Pro, Darwin 25.5.0). Two builds, not a bisect, per the row's own suggested cheap test. Fresh worktrees at 58412d9f and its parent a42b5338 (confirmed: `58412d9f~1` == a42b5338), each carrying its OWN karac (`cargo build --features llvm --bin karac`) AND both runtime archives built AT THAT COMMIT -- lean first, copied to `libkarac_runtime_min.a`, before the full build overwrote the canonical name. `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, `hyperfine --warmup 5 --runs 30 --shell=none` (the kata's own lane settings), every pair timed in BOTH orders, and BOTH archive configurations measured with the configuration held CONSTANT across each comparison (the method rule this row added after the x86 correction). All four binaries sink-checked at 762965 BEFORE timing -- load-bearing at this commit specifically, since it spans the codegen/runtime ABI. The lean binary is 285592 B, byte-for-byte the recorded lane's `binary_bytes`, which anchors this to the recorded lane.

A METHOD TRAP WORTH RECORDING, hit before the first timing: two pre-existing worktrees on this host at exactly these two commits had `libkarac_runtime.a` and `libkarac_runtime_min.a` BYTE-IDENTICAL (same sha256) -- the lean build had run, been copied, and the full build had never overwritten the canonical name, so BOTH slots held the LEAN archive. Nothing about that fails loudly: every symbol resolves and every sink is right; the 'full' side of a lean-vs-full comparison is silently lean. Cheap guard, and it is now part of this row's method: after building the pair, `shasum -a 256` both archives and require them to DIFFER (correct pair here: full 10810920 B, lean 7949088 B).

RESULT -- kata:170, sink 762965 on all four binaries.
  LEAN (the recorded lane's exact configuration, binary 285592 B):
    a42b5338   783.1 +/- 10.8 ms  |  789.3 +/- 15.0 ms
    58412d9f   999.3 +/-  5.2 ms  | 1001.1 +/-  8.5 ms   => 1.27x-1.28x SLOWER
  FULL (binary 351720 B):
    a42b5338   800.9 +/- 11.2 ms  |  814.1 +/- 18.8 ms
    58412d9f   932.1 +/- 11.7 ms  |  926.6 +/-  5.3 ms   => 1.14x-1.16x SLOWER
Order-independent in all four passes; both archive configurations agree on direction and on the sign of the step.

ANSWER 1 -- 58412d9f IS WHERE ARM64 TURNS. In the recorded (lean) lane the single commit reproduces the ENTIRE endpoint regression: 786 -> 1000 ms is 1.27x, against 798 -> 1014 ms = 1.27x for the whole b7ba6ea4..882d8d73 range. Everything after 58412d9f contributes ~1.4% in that lane. On x86 the SAME commit is ~3% FASTER (3435 -> 3326 ms). So this is an ARCHITECTURE TRADEOFF, NOT A REVERT: the same change pays on x86_64 and costs ~27% on Apple silicon, and which way to resolve that is the owner's call (see FIX SHAPE below).

ANSWER 2 -- ARM64 NEVER GOT THE x86 SPEEDUP, so the row needs BOTH halves of the story, not one instead of the other. Over b7ba6ea4 -> a42b5338 (67 commits) x86 gained 1.28x (4413 -> 3435 ms) while arm64 moved ~1.5% (lean 798 -> 786 ms; full 852 -> 807 ms). That large x86 move is real and arm64-invisible. So 'x86 gained something arm64 never got' is TRUE AND SEPARATE FROM 'arm64 regressed at 58412d9f' -- both happened, and together they are exactly why the endpoint comparison read as a clean win on one host and a 1.29x regression on the other. The b7ba6ea4..a42b5338 x86 speedup remains UNATTRIBUTED; it is a speedup, not this bug, and it is not worth chasing from the arm64 side because arm64 never received it.

FULL arm64 TRAJECTORY, both configurations (b7ba6ea4 and current values from this row's earlier arm64 re-measurement):
  lean: b7ba6ea4 798 -> a42b5338 786 -> 58412d9f 1000 -> current(882d8d73) 1014
  full: b7ba6ea4 852 -> a42b5338 807 -> 58412d9f  929 -> current(882d8d73) 1100

MECHANISM -- AND A CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN HYPOTHESIS. The row argued 58412d9f 'adds a per-bucket `status[capacity]` byte array, so every probe now touches a SECOND cache line', and rested the arch-divergence argument on 64 B vs 128 B line sizes. THAT PREMISE IS WRONG, checked against the diff rather than assumed: `status[capacity]` and `status: *mut u8` ALREADY EXIST at the parent a42b5338 (map.rs module header line 8, field line 46, `BUCKET_OCCUPIED = 1` line 32). The probe ALREADY read the control byte on every step. What 58412d9f changes is what that byte HOLDS (`0x80 | tag7` instead of a bare flag) and how it is TESTED (`status == ctrl`, where `ctrl` is derived from the searched key's hash, instead of `status == 1` against a constant). There is no new array and no second cache line, so the line-size argument for the arch split does not hold. The conclusion it was offered to support survives anyway -- but on measurement, not on that reasoning.

WHAT DOES LINE UP is the commit's OWN justification. It was measured on kata #127 Word Ladder, and its message states that 88% of the win came from eliminating `karac_eq_String` calls (5,124,890 -> 1,189,583): the benefit IS skipping a cold heap dereference for a STRING key, and the message says so explicitly ('which for a `String` key loads a `{ptr,len,cap}` header and then dereferences a scattered heap buffer'). kata:170's map is `Map[i64, i64]`. Its key compare is a register compare of an L1-resident 8-byte load from a ~168-entry key array -- there is NO cold dereference to skip, so NONE of the measured benefit is available to this kata, on either architecture. What is left is the added cost: per-lookup computation of `ctrl_of(hash)` (shift/truncate/and/or) and an occupancy test whose operand is now computed rather than a constant, across ~200M lookups (1.2M queries x ~168 distinct keys, no early return). The HOT PATH IS CODEGEN-EMITTED, not the runtime library -- `mono.rs` emits its own probe loop for a monomorphized `Map[i64,i64]` (`emit_map_ctrl_of` / `emit_map_is_occupied`) -- so a fix lands in codegen, and surface is corrected from `other` to `codegen+runtime` accordingly. The `control_flow_for.rs` half of the commit is NOT implicated: it only turns the `keys()` walk's occupancy test from `st == 1` into a high-bit compare, which is free.

WHY that residual cost is +27% on arm64 and -3% on x86 is NOT ESTABLISHED by this measurement. The arithmetic alone (a few instructions per lookup over ~200M lookups) does not obviously account for a 214 ms delta, so something microarchitectural -- branch behaviour on the now-computed compare operand, or the loss of the key load's memory-level parallelism -- is likely involved. That needs instruction-level profiling on the M5 Pro and is stated here as UNEXPLAINED rather than guessed at. What IS established is where the regression enters, to a single commit, in both archive configurations and both orders.

FIX SHAPE IS THE OWNER'S CALL -- neither option below is validated, and this row does not pick one. (A) Gate the tag test on ARCHITECTURE: keeps the x86 win intact, recovers the arm64 27%. (B) Gate it on KEY TYPE -- skip the tag for primitive keys, where by the commit's own mechanism there is no dereference to save on any host. (B) is cleaner in principle and keeps the String win on BOTH hosts, but it costs x86 the ~3% it gains on this i64 kata, and it is a wider change. NOTE either fix is an ABI-shaped change on the same codegen/runtime contract this row's trap section is about, so it needs the same matched-pair discipline.

OPEN, SMALLER, AND NOT AFFECTING THE HEADLINE -- a FULL-archive residual. In the full configuration 58412d9f accounts for 1.14x-1.16x of the 1.29x endpoint total (852 -> 807 -> 929 -> 1100 ms), leaving ~1.18x unattributed after 58412d9f, whereas the lean lane leaves ~1.4%. Part of that is link-layout sensitivity rather than a second regression: the lean/full sign is NOT stable across commits -- at 58412d9f the full binary is ~7% FASTER than lean, while at b7ba6ea4, a42b5338 and current the full binary is SLOWER (by 6.8%, 2.7% and 8.5% respectively). The recorded lane is lean, so the row's headline (771 -> 997 ms) is fully explained by 58412d9f and this does not qualify it; but the full-lane residual is real, is not explained, and would be the thing to bisect if anyone cares about the full-archive lane specifically.

 KEY-TYPE CONTROL ON ARM64 -- THE FIX SHAPE IS NOW SETTLED BY MEASUREMENT, AND IT IS NOT THE ARCH GATE (2026-08-05, Apple M5 Pro). The preceding entry left two candidate fixes and called the choice the owner's. One more matched-pair test decides it. HYPOTHESIS TESTED: if the mechanism is really 'the tag buys you a skipped cold heap dereference, which only exists for a heap key', then on the SAME host and the SAME two commits, a STRING-keyed map kata must get FASTER at 58412d9f for exactly the reason the i64-keyed one got slower. kata:127 word ladder is `Map[String, i64]` (word_ladder.kara lines 47/73/86), so it is the direct control.

For the i64 map the tag DOES save work -- dropping it executes 14.7% MORE instructions, exactly as designed, because every occupied bucket on the chain now loads and compares its key instead of being rejected by the tag. But that saved work was CHEAP (a ~168-entry, L1-resident key array), while the tag itself costs throughput: IPC collapses from 2.98 to 2.31 when it is enabled. The derivation assumes both runs sit at the same average clock; they are back-to-back runs of the same binary shape on an idle-ish container, which makes that reasonable but not verified. I RETRACT MY OWN HIGH-LOAD-FACTOR CAUTION (2026-08-05, x86_64 Linux). TOOLING NOTE FIRST: `scripts/pmc_linux.c` cannot run here — `perf_event_open` returns ENOENT for every hardware counter (no virtualized PMU); paranoid is already 2, so this is the unfixable branch of that fork, not the permissions one. Cycles/IPC stay out of reach on this host; see the derived-IPC entry above. THE TWO INSTRUMENTS DISAGREE, measured back-to-back in ONE low-noise window on kata:170: FLAG (current main, `KARAC_MAP_TAG` 1 vs 0) tag ON 3775.8 +/- 12.5 vs tag OFF 3702.5 +/- 19.9 ms => tag ON 1.9% SLOWER. COMMIT PAIR (a42b5338 vs 58412d9f) tag ON 4146.7 +/- 26.4 vs OFF 4400.8 +/- 32.0 ms => tag ON 6.1% FASTER. Sub-1% stdevs on both, so this is a real methodological difference, not noise: `KARAC_MAP_TAG=0` IS NOT A REVERT OF 58412d9f. The flag isolates the tag COMPARE; the commit also restructured `mono.rs` and changed the `keys()` walk. FOR DECIDING THE FIX THE FLAG IS THE CORRECT INSTRUMENT, because the fix is exactly 'do not emit the tag compare'. Any x86 figure taken from the commit pair — including my own earlier ones — should not be used to size the fix. RESULT ON REAL KATAS, flag instrument, minimum-of-15 (minimum because this host has intermittent contention and noise only ever ADDS time; medians agree in sign and magnitude). An A/A control was run first at each workload length: 0.0% at ~3.8 s, but 4.5% at kata:127's native ~257 ms, which is why 127 was rebuilt at iters=204 (12x, ~3 s) before being trusted. kata:127 `Map[String,i64]` tag ON 2954.1 / OFF 3281.0 ms => TAG PAYS +11.1% (median +10.1%). kata:170 `Map[i64,i64]` tag ON 3736.0 / OFF 3673.6 ms => TAG COSTS -1.7% (median -1.3%). Sinks 781149201 and 762965 respectively, verified on both binaries; tag-ON and tag-OFF binaries confirmed to differ by sha256 first, so the flag is live on the String path (it gates three sites including `emit_mono_map_str_get_body`) and is not a null control there. SO x86 AND ARM64 AGREE ON BOTH KEY TYPES: String keys — x86 +11.1%, arm64 +7%, tag PAYS. Primitive keys — x86 -1.7%, arm64 -27%, tag COSTS. Same sign both sides; arch sets only the magnitude of the primitive-key loss. WHICH MEANS A PLAIN KEY-TYPE GATE NEEDS NO ARCH CONDITION AT ALL. Dropping the tag for primitive keys is a 1.7% WIN on x86, not a cost — so the concern that a key-type gate would cost x86 anything on i64 maps is not supported by the flag instrument. Fix (B) is cleanly right: tag on heap keys everywhere, no tag on primitive keys, no arch conditional. RETRACTION — MY HIGH-LOAD-FACTOR CAUTION DOES NOT STAND. That entry used the COMMIT PAIR and a synthetic miss-heavy probe. Re-run under the FLAG, the same probe reports the tag PAYING at BOTH load factors (+15.3% at LF 0.749, +9.5% at LF 0.376) — the low-LF arm flips sign versus what I reported. Worse, +9.5% for a low-LF primitive map directly contradicts kata:170's -1.7% under the same flag and the same key type. Two low-LF primitive-keyed workloads cannot disagree by 11 points if the probe models the kata, so THE SYNTHETIC PROBE IS NOT A FAITHFUL PROXY — plausibly its `i * 7919` key sequence clusters differently, or its pure `get` loop misses kata:170's scan-over-keys access pattern. The load-factor question is therefore OPEN and unmeasured, not answered in either direction, and fix (B) should NOT be held up by my earlier caution. If anyone wants it settled, it needs a real map-heavy kata at high occupancy, not a synthetic loop. CORRECTION TO MY OWN REFUTATION, AND AN UNRESOLVED x86-vs-x86 TIMING DISAGREEMENT (2026-08-05, x86_64 Linux container). FIRST, I WAS WRONG IN dee378ff. That entry said the '13.1% FEWER instructions with the tag off' figure was wrong, on the strength of exact callgrind counts showing tag OFF executing 6.9% MORE. Those counts were taken on the COMMIT PAIR (a42b5338 vs 58412d9f). The 13.1% claim is a TAG-ONLY A/B under `KARAC_MAP_TAG`. I refuted a flag-instrument number with commit-pair data — the two instruments are not interchangeable, which this row now documents, and I had already documented it myself one entry earlier. MEASURED UNDER THE FLAG, callgrind on the same two binaries, both sink-checked at 762965 under the tool: tag ON 15,081,017,058 I-refs, tag OFF 13,106,238,851 => TAG OFF IS 13.1% FEWER. THE OTHER LANE'S INSTRUCTION FIGURE IS EXACTLY RIGHT and my refutation of it should be disregarded. WHAT REMAINS DISPUTED IS THE TIMING, not the instruction count. That lane reports the same tag-only A/B as kata:170 tag ON 3763.7 -> tag OFF 4513.2 ms, i.e. 1.20x SLOWER without the tag. I cannot reproduce that. Strictly interleaved A/B/A/B, 10 pairs, same flag, same kata, sinks verified: tag ON min 3744.1 / med 3798.4, tag OFF min 3671.0 / med 3749.4 => TAG OFF IS 2.0% FASTER by minimum and 1.3% faster by median. Note our tag-ON numbers agree to 0.7% (3763.7 vs 3744.1); the entire disagreement is on the tag-OFF side. A LIKELY MECHANICAL EXPLANATION, offered as a lead: THIS HOST HAS SEVERE INTERMITTENT CONTENTION and a mean is not robust to it. In the same interleaved run the MAXIMA were tag ON 4996.9 ms and tag OFF 7702.5 ms — the latter 2.1x its own minimum. One such spike inside a small mean produces a ~1.2x artifact directly. An A/A control (same binary benched against itself) measured a 4.5% apparent effect at a ~257 ms workload here, and 0.0% at ~3.8 s, so the noise is real and workload-length dependent. Minimum-of-N over interleaved runs is the statistic that survives it, since contention only ever ADDS time. Whoever owns that lane should re-run min-of-N interleaved before the number is used; if their host is quiet, their mean is fine and the disagreement is real and needs a third measurement. AN INTERNAL-CONSISTENCY CHECK THAT FAVOURS THE FASTER READING: 13.1% fewer instructions AND 1.20x slower together require IPC to collapse by ~31% on x86. arm64 measured a 22.3% IPC collapse for the tag (2.976 -> 2.313) and that produced only a 1.27x swing there; x86's own IPC penalty, derived independently in this row, is 0-3.4%. A 31% x86 collapse would be far outside everything else measured on this architecture. By contrast 'fewer instructions, slightly faster' is internally consistent and is what I measure. WHY IT MATTERS: the fix shape turns on this sign. If tag OFF is slightly FASTER on x86 for primitive keys (my reading), a plain key-type gate is free on x86 and needs no arch condition. If tag OFF is 1.20x SLOWER (their reading), arch-conditional is required. The two readings prescribe different fixes, so this must be settled before anyone implements. IT IS A ONE-RUN QUESTION: same two binaries, interleaved, minimum-of-N, on a host whose A/A control is first shown to be near zero at this workload length. CACHE BEHAVIOUR IS IDENTICAL — THE 1.20x-SLOWER READING HAS NO MEMORY MECHANISM (2026-08-05, x86_64 Linux). cachegrind is DETERMINISTIC, so this host's contention — which is what the timing dispute hinges on — cannot affect it. Same two `KARAC_MAP_TAG` binaries, sinks 762965 under the tool. tag ON: I refs 15,081,020,557, D refs 2,375,542,051, D1 misses 3,098, LLd misses 2,357. tag OFF: I refs 13,106,242,350, D refs 2,221,968,022, D1 misses 3,098, LLd misses 2,357. THE MISS COUNTS ARE BYTE-IDENTICAL and tag OFF also issues FEWER data references. kata:170's ~168-entry table fits in L1 either way, so there is no cache pressure for the tag to relieve or create. A reading in which tag OFF is 1.20x SLOWER while executing 13.1% fewer instructions and 6.5% fewer data refs at identical miss counts has no mechanism left to appeal to on this architecture. SCOPE OF THE REFUTATION, stated honestly: cachegrind models CACHE only — no prefetcher, no TLB, no front-end. It cannot rule out a throughput/back-end effect, which is precisely what the arm64 lane measured (IPC 2.976 -> 2.313 with no mispredict term). So this refutes the MEMORY explanation specifically, not every conceivable one. But x86's own derived IPC penalty is 0-3.4%, and a 31% collapse would be needed for 1.20x; with cache ruled out there is no candidate for one. AND IT SHARPENS THE INSTRUMENT SPLIT, which turns out to be the real story: on the COMMIT PAIR tag ON executes FEWER instructions on BOTH architectures (x86 13,668,698,926 vs 14,617,644,056; arm64 10,465,485,066 vs 12,006,051,874). Under the FLAG on x86 the sign INVERTS: tag ON 15,081,020,557 vs tag OFF 13,106,242,350, i.e. tag ON executes MORE. So the two ARCHITECTURES never disagreed about instruction counts — the two INSTRUMENTS do, and the arm64 figures in this row are commit-pair figures. Current main's tag path is more expensive than 58412d9f's was, or the flag's off-path is better than the pre-commit code; either way `KARAC_MAP_TAG=0` measures 'current main without the tag', which is exactly what the FIX will produce and therefore the right instrument for choosing its shape. WHAT REMAINS: a wall-clock tiebreak on a QUIET host. This container is not one (A/A control: 4.5% apparent effect at a 257 ms workload, 0.0% at 3.8 s; maxima 2.1x their own minima in interleaved runs). Everything measurable here without a clock now points one way — fewer instructions, fewer data refs, identical misses, and min-of-N interleaved timing 2.0% faster with the tag off.

 ARM64 FLAG-INSTRUMENT SWEEP + THE FIX IS IN (2026-08-06, Apple M5 Pro, Darwin 25.5.0, main ca037cb0). SHIPPED: b3e8206d gates the tag compare on (probe shape x target arch) -- primitive-keyed `emit_mono_map_get_body` / `emit_mono_set_contains_body` test occupancy ALONE on aarch64; `emit_mono_map_str_get_body` keeps the tag on every host; x86 is unchanged at every site. `KARAC_MAP_TAG` survives as the A/B lever, now BOTH directions (`=1` restores 58412d9f's behaviour exactly). THIS ROW STAYS OPEN -- see THE RESIDUAL below, which is the part the fix does NOT recover.

METHOD, identical for all seven workloads: ONE karac and ONE archive pair from current main, two binaries per kata differing ONLY by `KARAC_MAP_TAG`, binaries confirmed to differ by sha256 BEFORE timing (the guard against a flag that never reached the code), every sink verified on both sides, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, default (lean) archive resolution = the recorded lane, `hyperfine --shell=none` in BOTH orders, and exact whole-process counters from `scripts/pmc.c` (3 interleaved reps, instruction spread under 0.01%). No commit-to-commit comparison anywhere.

RESULT -- the tag NEVER pays for a primitive key on arm64, across six workloads, and pays for a String key:

  kata:170 `Map[i64,i64]` 168 keys + keys() walk   tag 1.13-1.17x SLOWER   instr 10.468B ON / 12.008B OFF   cyc 4.675B / 3.946B
  kata:219 `Map[i64,i64]` sliding window           tag 1.03x SLOWER (both orders, +/-1.5ms)   instr 3.526B / 3.413B   cyc 500M / 487M
  kata:1   `Map[i64,i64]` get-heavy, scaled x200   tag 1.02-1.03x SLOWER   instr 973.0M / 961.8M   cyc 134.4M / 129.7M
  kata:146 `Map[i64,i64]` LRU, tombstone churn     NEUTRAL (orders disagree)   instr 3.560B / 3.488B   cyc 1.008B / 1.013B
  kata:128 `Set[i64]` 20k keys / 131072 buckets    NEUTRAL   instr 709.0M / 693.9M   cyc 311.9M / 312.5M
  kata:217 `Set[i64]` 800-key windows              NEUTRAL/tie   instr 48.13B / 48.71B   cyc 9.15B / 9.28B
  kata:127 `Map[String,i64]`                       tag 1.07x FASTER   instr 2.531B / 2.580B   cyc 523M / 553M

THE SET PROBE IS NOW MEASURED, closing this row's longest-standing unmeasured item -- and the answer is NEITHER of the two the row expected: `emit_mono_set_contains_body` is NEUTRAL at both a 20k-key and an 800-key table. So the Set site was never the problem. It is included in the fix for consistency with the Map site and because the mechanism is shared, NOT on its own evidence, and the fix comment says so.

WHICH CORRECTS THIS ROW'S OWN 'PRIMITIVE KEYS' FRAMING. The effect is 1.17x on ONE kata, ~3% on two, and nil on three. A fix sized off kata:170 alone would have overstated its own value by ~5x. The DIRECTION is what six workloads agree on, and that is what the fix rests on.

THE INSTRUMENT SPLIT IS SETTLED, AGAINST THE x86 LANE'S INFERENCE. That lane concluded 'the arm64 figures in this row are commit-pair figures' because arm64 reported tag ON executing FEWER instructions while x86 under the flag reported MORE. Re-measured here on current main with the flag and exact counters: tag ON 10,468,328,088 vs OFF 12,007,737,018 -- reproducing this row's earlier arm64 figures (10,465,485,066 / 12,006,051,874) to 0.03%. Those numbers were flag-instrument all along. So the two ARCHITECTURES genuinely disagree on the instruction-count sign for the same flag on the same kata, and that is a real finding, not a mislabeled instrument. NOTE the sign is not an ISA constant either: on arm64 kata:128 and kata:146 have tag ON executing MORE instructions, the opposite of kata:170. It is workload-dependent on both hosts.

kata:170's MECHANISM, sharpened but still not fully explained. The STATIC difference between its two binaries is 9 instructions (3 emission sites x 3: `ldrsb`+`tbz` for the occupancy-only test vs `ldrb`+`cmp`+`b.ne` plus a hoisted `lsr`/`and`/`orr` for the tag), so the 1.54B dynamic delta is entirely `eq_check` work the tag skips. At the kata's measured load factor that saving should be ~0.2 key compares per get, not the ~2 the counts imply -- unmodelled and stated as such. What IS established: the tag executes 12.8% FEWER instructions and burns 18.5% MORE cycles (IPC 3.04 -> 2.24), which is a throughput cost, not a work cost.

VERIFICATION THAT THE MEASUREMENTS ARE THE SHIPPED BINARIES, not a proxy for them: with the fix in, each kata's DEFAULT build is byte-identical (sha256) to whichever pre-fix flag binary the policy selects -- kata:170/128/146 to `tag_off`, kata:127 to `tag_on` -- and `KARAC_MAP_TAG=1` reproduces the pre-fix `tag_on` binary exactly. So every figure above transfers to the default build bit for bit.

THE RESIDUAL -- WHY THIS ROW STAYS OPEN, and it is now MEASURED rather than inferred (2026-08-06, same host, same session, matched karac+archive pairs per side, both sinks 762965, both binaries the recorded lane's 285592 B, both orders):

  a42b5338 (= 58412d9f~1)   770.0 +/- 9.2 ms  |  798.5 +/- 12.6 ms   instr 12.969B  cyc 3.57B  IPC 3.63
  current main + the fix    858.2 +/- 7.2 ms  |  870.2 +/- 24.7 ms   instr 12.005B  cyc 3.94B  IPC 3.05

So the fix recovers the tag-compare share (1.14x) and kata:170 remains 1.09-1.11x ABOVE its pre-58412d9f baseline. The baseline reproduces this row's own earlier figure for that commit (786 ms lean) at 770-798 ms, which anchors the comparison. ATTRIBUTION, by arithmetic on this row's own trajectory rather than by a new bisect: 58412d9f measured 1000 ms and current main 1014 ms in the earlier arm64 lane, i.e. only +1.4% of drift across the ~800 commits between them -- so the residual belongs to 58412d9f's NON-tag-compare half (the encoding change itself, the insert/resize paths, the `mono.rs` restructuring, the `keys()` walk change), each of which remains UNMEASURED. This is exactly the 'MAGNITUDE GAP WORTH KEEPING HONEST' this row flagged and never chased; it is now sized.

AND IT HAS THE SAME SIGNATURE AS THE PART JUST FIXED: current main + fix executes 7.4% FEWER instructions than the a42b5338 baseline yet burns 10.4% MORE cycles (IPC 3.63 -> 3.05). Fewer instructions, worse throughput -- the same shape as the tag compare, which suggests one mechanism with two carriers inside 58412d9f rather than two unrelated costs. That is a hypothesis, not a finding; whoever takes the residual should test it before assuming it.

WHAT THIS ROW NOW NEEDS TO CLOSE: attribute and recover the 1.09-1.11x residual on kata:170. The tag-compare cause is fixed and shipped in b3e8206d; the row's headline number (771 -> 997 ms) is about 55% recovered. Follow-on filed as its own row and since CLOSED: B-2026-08-06-33 settled the x86 primitive-key sign by measurement on 2026-08-07 -- the tag PAYS on x86, so the arch condition stays and is now justified on evidence.

NOT DONE, and deliberately so: kata:170's README timing table and `bench-results.json` still quote the regressed 997.1 ms. Those come from the bench.sh -> results.json pipeline and must not be hand-edited; the kata needs a proper re-bench once the residual is resolved, so that the recorded number moves once rather than twice.

 RESIDUAL ATTRIBUTED, AND THIS ROW'S OWN ATTRIBUTION IS REFUTED (2026-08-06, Apple M5 Pro, arm64). The entry above sized the residual at 1.09-1.11x and assigned it, BY ARITHMETIC RATHER THAN MEASUREMENT, to 58412d9f's non-tag-compare half. Measured directly, that is WRONG: at 58412d9f the non-tag half costs essentially NOTHING, and the live residual belongs to the ~800 commits AFTER it.

METHOD. Four matched karac+archive sides, each built at its own commit, archive configuration held constant (LEAN pinned via `KARAC_RUNTIME` on every side), `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, every binary sink-checked at 762965 before timing, `hyperfine --warmup 5 --runs 25 --shell=none` in BOTH orders, plus exact `scripts/pmc.c` counters. The two middle sides did not exist before: `KARAC_MAP_TAG` postdates 58412d9f, so "58412d9f without its tag compare" was previously unmeasurable. It was produced by patching that commit's own `emit_mono_map_get_body` to call `emit_map_is_occupied` -- exactly what the shipped fix does on arm64 -- and, for the fourth side, by ALSO swapping that commit's occupancy test to the flag form described below.

  a42b5338 (= 58412d9f~1)                        768.7 / 767.0 ms
  58412d9f, tag compare removed + FLAG-form test 770.7 / 786.9 ms   <- PARENT LEVEL
  58412d9f, tag compare removed (sign-form test) 894.1 / 908.0 ms   <- 1.16-1.18x
  current main (tag off, sign-form test)         859.0 / 859.3 ms   <- 1.12x

ANSWER 1 -- AT 58412d9f THE NON-TAG REGRESSION IS ENTIRELY THE OCCUPANCY TEST'S LOWERING, and it is fully recoverable there. The commit changed what the control byte holds, which changed how "is this bucket occupied" is written: `status >= 0x80` (a SIGN-BIT test) instead of the parent's `status == 1`. On arm64 those lower differently -- `ldrsb` + `tbz` versus `ldrb` + `cmp` + `b.cc` -- and the three-instruction form with a flag-setting compare is FASTER than the two-instruction test-and-branch. Writing the identical predicate as `status > TOMBSTONE` (exactly equivalent: the only bytes below 0x80 are EMPTY=0 and TOMBSTONE=1) restores the flag form and recovers the parent's time to within noise.

ANSWER 2 -- AND YET THAT FIX IS WORTH NOTHING ON CURRENT MAIN. The same one-line swap, on current main, moves kata:170 from 859.0 to 855.2 ms, i.e. nothing; and on kata:219 it is 1.01-1.03x WORSE. So the mechanism that costs 1.16x at 58412d9f is no longer live: something in the ~800 commits since changed the surrounding code enough that the sign-bit form stopped being penalised. The lowering hazard is therefore LATENT, not current -- worth knowing before anyone "fixes" it, because the obvious fix is measurably useless today.

ANSWER 3 -- WHERE THE LIVE RESIDUAL ACTUALLY IS: the ~800 commits after 58412d9f. Holding the test form constant at the flag form, 58412d9f measures 770 ms and current main measures 855 ms; holding it at the sign form, 58412d9f measures 894-908 ms and current main 859 ms. Either way current main sits ~1.11x above where 58412d9f lands once its own regression is undone. That interval is UNBISECTED and is what this row now needs. NOTE the earlier "+1.4% from 58412d9f to current" figure this row used for its arithmetic was measured with the tag ON, where the tag compare dominated and masked this; it does not survive as an argument once the tag is off.

RULED OUT ALONG THE WAY, both by measurement:
  * THE keys() WALK. This row and its predecessors repeatedly suspected `control_flow_for.rs`'s occupancy test in the `keys()` iteration, since kata:170 runs it ~1.23B times. An ablation that keeps the walk and drops the gets measures a42 471M cycles vs current main 476M -- equal -- while instructions FALL 8.3%. The walk is also only ~12% of the kata's cycles, not the majority this row assumed.
  * THE BUCKET LAYOUT. Diffed rather than assumed: 58412d9f changes no allocation, no stride, no alignment. `status[capacity]` and the kv array are byte-for-byte the same shape as at the parent; only the byte's VALUE and the tests over it change.

A METHOD WARNING WORTH MORE THAN THE ABOVE, because it nearly produced a wrong fix. An ablation of kata:170 that keeps the gets and drops the `keys()` walk -- same map, same key distribution, same 201.6M gets, keys materialised into a `Vec` once outside the timed loop -- reports the flag-form test as a 1.34x WIN. The real kata reports 1.00x for the same change. The probe over-responds by more than twenty times, and it was deliberately built to be faithful. This row already carries one refuted synthetic probe (the high-load-factor one); this is a second, subtler instance, and the rule it argues for is: an ablation may be used to LOCATE a cost, never to SIZE a fix. Every number that decided anything here was taken on the unmodified kata.

WHAT THIS ROW NEEDS TO CLOSE, unchanged in shape but now correctly aimed: bisect kata:170 across 58412d9f..main (~800 commits, arm64, matched karac+archive per step, sink-checked, tag-off held constant on both sides via `KARAC_MAP_TAG=0` so the shipped fix does not confound the comparison). The endpoints are verified: 770 ms and 855 ms with the test form held constant.

 RESIDUAL FULLY ATTRIBUTED — AND IT IS NOT A MAP PROBLEM AT ALL (2026-08-06). Bisected across the 905 commits this row identified, 8 steps, on CYCLES (the endpoints differ 8.3% in cycles and 0.003% in instructions, so the instruction-count method this repo prefers is blind here), with the tag compare patched off and the occupancy test held in the flag form at every step so the range's two opposing effects could not cancel. Every binary sink-checked at 762965.

THE CULPRIT IS 36a7fa5a (2026-07-30, "make println line-atomic by staging payload+newline into one write", B-2026-07-30-9). Parent b84477dd 3.561B cycles / 781 ms; 36a7fa5a 3.958B / 850 ms; 1.09x on wall clock in both orders, and the 777 commits after it all sit on the slow plateau. kata:170 calls `println` ONCE.

The carrier is CODE PLACEMENT, not work: instructions differ by 0.008%, the binaries are EXACTLY the same size (285,592 B both), `main`'s prologue is identical (`sub sp, sp, #0x80`), and the 4 KiB staging alloca lives in the new helper rather than in the caller. What moves is `_main`'s address, 0x7c8 -> 0x860.

FILED AS B-2026-08-07-10, which owns it from here.

SO THIS ROW'S ARITHMETIC IS COMPLETE: the 7-bit tag compare (1.14x, fixed by the arch x key-type gate) times the placement effect (1.09x) is 1.24x, against the 1.29x this row opened with; the remainder is drift across the range. Nothing map-shaped is left unexplained, which is why every map-shaped hypothesis this row chased — the keys() walk, the bucket layout, the load factor, the encoding — measured clean. CLOSING.
fix: c4e6d76e (the tag compare); the placement half is B-2026-08-07-10
