title: `unwrap_or` with a FRESH F-STRING default leaks on a DEFAULT -O2 build -- 133 leaked allocations in an existing fixture -- while the byte-identical program with a literal `"...".to_string()` default is clean, because the literal default const-folds away and the f-string one does not
detail:
REPRODUCED AS A TWO-LINE EDIT to an existing, currently-passing fixture,
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_unwrap_or_fresh_string_default_no_leak`.
Replace its two `unwrap_or` defaults, changing NOTHING else:

    -  let a = opt(i).unwrap_or("odd-default".to_string());
    +  let a = opt(i).unwrap_or(f"odd-default-{i}");
    -  let b = res(i).unwrap_or("res-default".to_string());
    +  let b = res(i).unwrap_or(f"res-default-{i}");

  before  ->  passes, 503 allocations
  after   ->  `ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks`,
              133 byte(s) leaked in 133 allocation(s)

at the DEFAULT optimization level. Not an -O0 artifact: -O0 reports the same
133. The leak count is EXACTLY the `res(i)` Err-path iteration count
(i % 3 != 0 over 0..199 = 133); the `opt(i)` Option path, which discards a
default on 100 iterations, does not contribute. Enlarging the Err payload
(`Err("e".to_string())` -> `Err(f"eeeeeeeeee-{i}")`) holds the count at 133
and takes the bytes 133 -> 1790, so what leaks scales with the ERROR payload,
one per Err-path iteration.

WHY THE LITERAL SPELLING HIDES IT, which is the B-2026-08-04-17 mechanism
arriving one level up: `"odd-default".to_string()` is literal-derived, so LLVM
constant-folds it and deletes the allocation -- there is then nothing to leak
and the fixture is green. An f-string default is runtime-derived and survives.
The fixture has therefore been GREEN SINCE IT WAS WRITTEN without covering the
case it is named for, and the masking is in the fixture's choice of default
spelling rather than anywhere in the assertion.

NOT ISOLATED -- stated plainly because two attempts failed. Neither standalone
reduction reproduced:
  (a) `Result[i64, String]`, `unwrap_or(0 - 1)`, discarding a String Err
      payload over 30 iterations -> clean.
  (b) `Result[String, String]`, `unwrap_or(f"default-{i}")` plus a
      `starts_with` byte read over 30 iterations -> clean.
So the trigger is NOT simply 'unwrap_or discards a String Err payload' nor
'unwrap_or takes an f-string default'. Something about the full fixture --
the Option and Result receivers sharing a loop, the `as i64` casts, the
iteration count, or the absence of a byte read on `b` (adding one to the
reduction was what made (b) clean) -- is part of the condition. Whoever picks
this up should start from the two-line edit above, which reproduces every
time, and bisect DOWN from it rather than building up from a minimal guess.

RELATION TO B-2026-07-16-22, which this fixture pins: that bug was the
discarded default on the PRESENT path leaking. This leak tracks the ABSENT
path count instead, so it is a different arm and not obviously a regression of
that fix -- but the fixture's literal defaults mean the present-path fix has
also never been exercised against a default the optimizer could not delete.

SOURCE NOTE: found running B-2026-08-05-7's deciding experiment (does an -O0
failure also fire at -O2 once the payload is live?). The first attempt at that
experiment added a byte read but LEFT THE DEFAULT LITERAL, so it still folded
and the fixture still passed at -O2 -- walking straight into the hazard
B-2026-08-04-17 documents while testing for it. Making the CONTENT runtime-
derived is what exposed this.

BISECTED DOWN from the two-line edit, 11 probes in one build. The two
'failed reductions' recorded above FAILED FOR THE WRONG REASON and that entry
should be disregarded: both used a 30-iteration loop, and at n=30 LLVM folds
the ENTIRE loop away (probe p06: `res` half, f-string default, n=30 -> 3
allocations, i.e. zero program allocations, clean). The shapes were right; the
iteration count was too low to survive the optimizer. Same hazard as before,
third time in this investigation.

PROBE MATRIX (all at the default -O2; 'leak' = 133 allocations, 1 byte each):
  p00  both halves, both defaults f-string          LEAK 133
  p01  `res` half ONLY, f-string default            LEAK 133   <- minimal
  p05  `a` literal default, `b` f-string            LEAK 133
  p07  same as p01, no `as i64` cast                LEAK 133
  p08  same as p01, plus a `starts_with` byte read  LEAK 133
  p10  same as p01, inline (no `let b` binding)     LEAK 133
  p02  `opt` half ONLY (Option receiver)            clean, 303 allocs
  p03  `res` half, LITERAL `.to_string()` default   clean, 203 allocs
  p09  `res` half, f-string, but Err payload is i64 clean, 270 allocs
  p06  `res` half, f-string, n=30                   clean, 3 allocs (folded)

MINIMAL REPRODUCING SHAPE, therefore:

    fn res(i: i64) -> Result[String, String] {
        if i % 3 == 0 { Ok("ok-value".to_string()) } else { Err("e".to_string()) }
    }
    fn main() {
        let mut total: i64 = 0;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 200 {
            let b = res(i).unwrap_or(f"res-default-{i}");
            total = total + (b.len() as i64);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(total);
    }

THREE NECESSARY CONDITIONS, each established by a probe that removes exactly
one of them:
  1. RESULT receiver with a HEAP Err payload. An Option receiver never leaks
     (p02); a `Result[String, i64]` never leaks (p09). What leaks is the
     discarded ERROR payload -- 133 = the Err-path iteration count exactly, at
     1 byte each for `Err("e")`, and enlarging that payload scales the bytes
     133 -> 1790 at a constant 133 allocations.
  2. A FRESH-HEAP default. A literal `.to_string()` default is clean (p03) --
     though see the caveat below, this one may be masking rather than absent.
  3. Enough iterations to survive the optimizer (200 leaks, 30 folds away).
Irrelevant, contrary to the earlier guess: the `as i64` cast (p07), a byte read
on the result (p08), the `let` binding vs inline use (p10), and the presence of
the Option half in the same loop (p01 vs p00).

WHERE IT LIVES: `src/codegen/calls.rs`, the `unwrap_or` emitter (~line 2746,
the block carrying the B-2026-07-16-22 comment). Two observations from reading
it, offered as leads rather than a diagnosis -- no IR was dumped:

  (a) The PRESENT block frees the discarded default. The ABSENT block does
      nothing but `build_unconditional_branch(merge_bb)` -- there is no free of
      the receiver's discarded Err payload anywhere on that path, and
      `suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move(object)` then suppresses the
      receiver's scope-exit free as well. That is consistent with the observed
      leak being the Err payload, one per Err iteration.
  (b) The free condition includes `|| default_is_fstring`, directly beneath a
      comment that explicitly EXCLUDES f-string defaults: 'an f-string /
      collection-literal default is already temp-tracked by the statement
      machinery, so freeing it here would double-free'. Code and comment
      contradict each other. One of them is wrong, and which one it is bears
      directly on why condition 2 above holds -- why the literal-default
      spelling is clean while the f-string spelling leaks.

Note that (a) alone would predict the literal-default case to leak too, and it
does not (p03, 200 program allocations, no leak). So (a) is not the whole
story; the interaction with (b) is the open question.

FIXED (94ec3a9). Root cause exactly as the bisect's lead (a) predicted:
the absent path emitted no free for the discarded Err payload. Confirmed
against the IR before touching anything -- BOTH the clean and the leaking
variant emitted exactly one `karac_free_buf` in `main`, so the Err payload
was never freed in either, and the clean one was clean only because LLVM
folded its literal default away. Lead (b), the `|| default_is_fstring`
clause reading as contradicting its comment, was a RED HERRING: the comment
predates B-2026-07-16-23 leg 3, which added that arm deliberately. A
Call-shaped default (`unwrap_or(mkdef(i))`), which never touches the
f-string cleanup-removal loop, leaks identically -- that probe is what
ruled the clause out.

Also settles condition 2 from the bisect, which was recorded as possibly
'masking rather than absent': it IS masking. With the Err payload held
runtime-derived and only the DEFAULT's spelling varied, the literal form is
clean and the f-string/Call forms leak -- same missing free in all three,
different optimizer outcomes. Post-fix the literal variant's allocation
count rises 203 -> 403, i.e. the fold stops happening once the free exists.

FIX: the typechecker now records `E` in the existing
`method_unwrap_err_types` table for `unwrap_or` on a Result (it was
populated only for the closure combinators, which need `e` to FEED the
absent closure; `unwrap_or` needs it to FREE what it discards), and codegen
reconstructs the payload from the receiver words on the absent path and
frees it. The merge phi had to move from `absent_bb` to `absent_end` --
the free emits a `cap > 0` guard that splits the block, so the edge into
the merge leaves from elsewhere and the old phi fails the LLVM verifier.

KNOWN REMAINING GAP, deliberately not closed: the free covers a DIRECT
(unboxed) String/Vec `E` only. A wide `E` arrives through a box pointer in
`w0` and needs the present path's deboxing plus a free of the box itself,
so an AGGREGATE `E` with heap fields still leaks. Untested territory, left
whole rather than half-handled; the code comment carries the same note.

REGRESSION FIXTURE: `asan_unwrap_or_result_discarded_err_payload_no_leak`,
floored at 200 allocations, with BOTH the Err value and the default
runtime-derived -- a literal anywhere in that chain re-hides the bug, which
is how the sibling fixture stayed green over it. Gates: memory_sanitizer
932 passed, typechecker 2787, codegen 2130, default suite 100 binaries all
ok; clippy --all-targets + fmt clean; interpreter / AOT -O2 / AOT -O0 agree.

title: A `ref`-borrowed `shared` handle captured into a `par` branch reads as ZERO under codegen — silent wrong answer, interpreter disagrees
detail: REPRO (no `frozen` anywhere — this is ordinary Kara): `shared struct N { val: i64 }` / `fn worker(n: ref N, k: i64) -> i64 { n.val + k }` / `fn driver(n: ref N) -> i64 { let (a, b) = par { let a = worker(n, 1); let b = 100; (a, b) }; a + b }` / `fn main() { let g = N { val: 7 }; println(f"{driver(g)}") }`. EXPECTED 108. `karac run --interp` gives 108. `karac build` + run gives 101 — i.e. `n.val` reads as 0 inside the branch, so `worker` returns 0+1 instead of 7+1. `karac check` reports ZERO errors. Silent wrong answer, run-vs-build divergence. SCOPE: ONE branch is enough — this is not a multi-branch conflict and never reaches the `E_CONCURRENT_SHARED_STRUCT` gate, which is why it has gone unnoticed: the gate refuses the TWO-branch shapes loudly, and the one-branch shape it permits is the broken one. NOT A FROZEN BUG — the repro contains no `frozen` token, and it reproduces identically for `frozen N` only because B-2026-08-01-33's suppression lowers `frozen T` to `ref T`. The OWNED spelling of the same program is CORRECT (108), which localizes the defect to how a BORROWED shared handle is materialized into a par branch's task context: an owned capture is retained into the context and read back fine, a borrowed one apparently is not populated at all (payload reads 0). DISCOVERED BY: building B-2026-08-01-33 mechanism 3's `par` admission. The admission itself is written and verified working at the OWNERSHIP layer (the target program passes `karac check` and the interpreter prints the right answer) but is DELIBERATELY NOT LANDED, because admitting more programs onto a silently-miscompiling path is worse than a false rejection. Patch parked at scratchpad/admission.patch; it is ~94 lines and re-appliable once this is fixed. CONSEQUENCE FOR B-2026-08-01-33: mechanism 3 stage 1 is BLOCKED on this. Suppression (e232063) is kept — it is correct on its own (sequential `frozen` is byte-correct and emits 0/0) — but it did move `frozen` params from the working owned-capture path onto this broken borrowed-capture path, so a single-branch `frozen` par capture is now silently wrong too. Impact is latent rather than live (no `frozen` program exists outside tests), but the trap is real and this entry is the reason not to write one until the fix lands. VERIFICATION GAP THAT LET IT THROUGH: the suppression commit's test counted `rc_inc`/`rc_dec` occurrences in the emitted IR and never checked the program's OUTPUT. Traffic-count assertions cannot see a wrong answer. Any future RC-shape test in this family must pair the IR assertion with an E2E run asserting the computed value. FIXED (93b1a81). ROOT CAUSE: the branch prologue's `emit_arc_inc` does `getelementptr %karac.shared.T, <captured>, 0, 0` and atomically adds 1, which assumes the captured value IS the handle. For a borrow the slot holds a POINTER-TO-HANDLE, so the increment did not touch any refcount — it added 1 to the OWNER'S STORED HANDLE POINTER. The callee then dereferenced a pointer one byte off and read 0 instead of 7. The branch-exit `dec` subtracted the 1 back, which is why the corruption left no trace afterwards and the symptom was a merely-wrong answer rather than a crash — the reason this went unnoticed despite being a memory-corruption bug. FIX: exclude borrowed captures (`self.ref_params`) from the `SharedRc` path in `src/codegen/par_blocks.rs`. Correct rather than merely safe: a borrow's referent is kept alive by its owner, and that owner outlives the par run because `karac_par_run` does not return until every branch finishes — the same argument the `SharedRc` doc comment already makes for the parent's own reference. The capture therefore behaves as `Copy`: the pointer threads through the env untouched. NOTE THE CLASSIFIER IS UNCHANGED: `ParCaptureMode` is still chosen from the type name alone, so it still reports `SharedRc` for a borrowed `shared` capture and codegen now overrides it. A cleaner future shape is for the classifier to know borrow-ness and say `Copy` itself; that was not done here because the ownership pass would need parameter-mode information it does not currently thread into `par_capture_classify`. REGRESSION TEST asserts the COMPUTED VALUE across ref/frozen/owned (`borrowed_shared_capture_in_a_par_branch_reads_its_real_payload`, tests/par_codegen.rs) — not an IR traffic count, which is what missed it the first time.

title: `File.read` / `BufReader.read` reject a fixed `Array[u8, N]` buffer that AOT accepts — the blessed `let mut buf: Array[u8, N]; f.read(mut buf)` idiom runs under `karac build` and dies under `karac run --interp`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found on the FIRST file-I/O probe written for the Cumulus app (browser deep-sky stacker, apps/cumulus in kara-katas). Not a synthetic probe — it was the natural way to write a read-a-file round trip.

REPRO:
  let mut buf: Array[u8, 8] = [0u8; 8];
  match f.read(mut buf) { Ok(n) => ... }

  karac build      -> read 8 first=0 last=119   (correct)
  karac run --interp -> runtime error: File.read expects a `mut Slice[u8]` buffer, got `Array`

The idiom is BLESSED, not exotic: examples/relay ships exactly this shape for TcpStream.read (`let mut buf: Array[u8, 4096] = [0u8; 4096]; client.read(mut buf)`), because a `mut Slice[u8]` parameter needs a runtime-sized buffer and a fixed Array is how you make one.

WHY IT IS AN INCONSISTENCY RATHER THAN A MISSING FEATURE: `File.write`, thirty lines below the rejection in the same file, ALREADY accepted a `Value::Array` on purpose, with a comment saying so — 'be permissive at the interpreter level (the typechecker enforces the declared shape)'. Read was the half that never got the same treatment. The two directions of the same file disagreed with each other, and the read half also disagreed with AOT.

DIRECTION MATTERS: the INTERPRETER is the broken side, which is the test/dev path — so a program verified under `karac run` would be the one that fails, and a program shipped via `karac build` silently works. That is the opposite of the usual run-vs-build risk and still a parity break.

FIXED 1caca04: both read arms (method_call_file.rs, method_call_bufreader.rs) accept `Value::Array` as a full-range buffer, mirroring `File.write`. Regression test in tests/interpreter.rs asserts the exact bytes round-tripped through a fixed Array buffer, so a regression surfaces as wrong data rather than as a tolerated error string.
fix: FIXED 1caca04. `File.read` and `BufReader.read` in the interpreter now match `Value::Array` alongside `Value::Slice`, taking the whole array as the buffer window (start 0, len = array len). This mirrors the deliberate permissiveness `File.write` already had. AOT was already correct and is untouched.
tracker: src/interpreter/method_call_file.rs (File.read buffer match), src/interpreter/method_call_bufreader.rs (BufReader.read, identical shape); tests/interpreter.rs::file_read_accepts_a_fixed_array_buffer_like_aot.

title: the `ref` at a call site diagnostic tells the author to remove one token but carries no machine-applicable replacement, so `karac fix` leaves it
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit writing apps/cumulus (kara-katas). Passing a borrowed buffer as `u32_at(ref data, 4)` is a natural mistake for anyone arriving from Rust, and it was five of my first six errors in that file.

THE DIAGNOSTIC IS ALREADY GOOD — it is correct, specific, and prescribes the exact edit:

  error[parse]: `ref` is not written at call sites. The parameter's mode is declared on the
  callee's signature. Remove the `ref` keyword.

WHAT IS MISSING is the `replacement`. The fix is a single-token deletion with no ambiguity — delete `ref ` at the marked span — which is about as machine-applicable as a fix gets. In the same file, in the same `karac fix` invocation, `&&` -> `and` and `!` -> `not` were both applied automatically; this one was left for hand editing, so the author is told precisely what to do and then has to do it themselves N times.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND CONVENIENCE: `karac fix` is the wedge. A diagnostic whose prose names an unambiguous single-token edit but ships no replacement is the exact shape the fix loop exists to close, and it is one an LLM author hits early — call-site `ref` is a Rust habit, so it arrives in the first file someone writes, before they have internalised that parameter modes live on the signature.

SEVERITY low: nothing is wrong, nothing is unsafe, and the message is already actionable. This is a fix-coverage gap, not a defect.

SUGGESTED SHAPE (unverified): attach a replacement deleting the `ref ` token span, the same way the operator diagnostics attach theirs. Worth checking whether the sibling call-site-mode errors (`mut` in a position that does not take it, if such a diagnostic exists) have the same gap, since they would share the fix. FIXED (9b17779). Both call-site mode diagnostics now attach a deletion edit through the same `fix_edits` channel the operator diagnostics use, so `karac fix` applies them instead of leaving the author to make the identical single-token edit N times. THE SUGGESTED SHAPE WAS RIGHT, including the hunch about the sibling: `mut ref` had the same gap. It is the more delicate of the two — the diagnostic is anchored at `mut` while the deletion targets `ref`, because `mut` is a legal call-site marker and must survive. `fix_edits` is keyed by the DIAGNOSTIC's span, so the key and the edited span are different tokens there. ONE DETAIL BEYOND THE MINIMUM: the edit covers the keyword AND its trailing whitespace, computed as [keyword.offset, next_token.offset). Deleting the token span alone yields `f( data, 0)` — valid, but fix output that needs a formatting pass afterwards is a fix people stop trusting. Falls back to the bare token span when there is no following token, so a malformed tail still produces a well-formed edit rather than none. VERIFIED END TO END, not just at the edit record: `karac fix` rewrites `u32_at(ref data, 0)` -> `u32_at(data, 0)` and `bump(mut ref data)` -> `bump(mut data)`, and both results then BUILD AND RUN correctly. NOTE FOR ANYONE READING THE JSON: parse-phase diagnostics carry the edit in the flat `replacement` field ({offset,length,text}), NOT in `fix_it` — `fix_it` is null for every parse diagnostic by construction (cli.rs sets it to None on that path). Checking the wrong key reads as a missing fix; it cost me a wrong conclusion mid-fix.
tracker: the `ref` is not written at call sites parse diagnostic and its `replacement` field; compare against the `&&`/`!` operator diagnostics in the same pass, which do carry one.

title: `karac query concurrency` reports `fanned_out: true` for a disjoint-write loop that runs SINGLE-THREADED when the accumulator is a `mut ref` parameter
detail: TWO PROGRAMS, IDENTICAL REPORTS, OPPOSITE BEHAVIOUR. Both report `{"gate": "proven", "fanned_out": true, "cost_gate": "fanout"}`. SHAPE A — accumulator is a `mut ref` PARAMETER: `fn run(s: frozen S, out: mut ref Vec[i64]) { for i in 0..4096 { out[i] = heavy(s, i); } }`. Measured `real 0.417s / user 0.409s` — user == real, i.e. SINGLE-THREADED. SHAPE B — accumulator is a LOCAL: `fn run(s: frozen S) -> i64 { let mut out = Vec.filled(4096, 0); for i in 0..4096 { out[i] = heavy(s, i); } out[10] }`. Measured `real 0.132s / user 0.515s` — 3.9x CPU, GENUINELY PARALLEL. Same machine (4 cores), same workload, same reported analysis. So `fanned_out` describes what the analyzer decided, not what the binary does, and for shape A the two disagree. WHY IT MATTERS: `fanned_out` reads as an outcome, and it is the field anyone measuring auto-par coverage would count. It caused a real error during B-2026-08-01-33's auto-par arm — a test was named `..._fans_out_and_computes_correctly` on the strength of this field while its program ran sequentially, so the test asserted a value but never exercised the parallel path it claimed to. Corrected there by switching the test to shape B; the underlying reporting discrepancy is this entry. NOT DIAGNOSED FURTHER: shape A plausibly hits the B-2026-07-23-20 `mut ref` gate (a callee taking `mut ref`/`mut Slice` writes memory the footprint walk cannot see) at LOWERING time while the REPORT is produced before/independently of that decision — but that is a hypothesis from the shapes, not a read of the lowering path, and it should be confirmed before fixing. FIX SHAPE, once confirmed: either report the post-lowering truth in `fanned_out`, or keep it as the analyzer's verdict and add a distinct field for what was actually emitted. The second is probably better — both facts are useful and conflating them is what produced this bug. HOW TO CHECK CHEAPLY: `bash -c 'time ./binary'` and compare `user` to `real`. `nm` is useless here — the binaries carry only ~81 dynamic symbols, so the `karac_par_*` statics are stripped at link and grepping for them reports nothing either way. FIXED IN TWO PARTS, and the filed hypothesis was WRONG about the mechanism. MY HYPOTHESIS SAID the B-2026-07-23-20 `mut ref` callee gate. It is not that gate. The trigger was right (the `mut ref` parameter) but the mechanism is `disjoint_target_shares_storage` in codegen/disjoint_par.rs: it accepts an array, a Vec/String header struct, or a registered slice, and a `mut ref Vec` slot holds a POINTER to the header, so none matched and the lowering declined. A SECOND hypothesis was also falsified — that the loop's final-EXPRESSION position (not a `StmtKind::Expr`) blocked it; adding a trailing statement left it sequential, and post-fix the final-expression shape fans out fine. Both recorded so the next reader does not re-derive them. THE PREDICTION THAT CONFIRMED IT: if the storage predicate is the cause, a `mut Slice[i64]` param (which IS registered) must fan out where `mut ref Vec[i64]` does not — measured, it does (real 0.142s / user 0.546s). PART 1 (286afea): accept a signature `ref_param` whose inner type is a Vec header or array. The pointer travels by value through the capture channel, so every worker derefs the SAME header — the storage-sharing property the predicate exists to establish, one indirection later, exactly like the array param it already accepted. Safe because `ref_params` is deliberately not saved/cleared around the worker fn, so indexing inside the worker still emits the deref; without that this would be B-2026-08-05-10 again. Measured real 0.417s -> 0.144s (2.9x wall, 3.8x cpu), all 4096 elements verified against the sequential definition, AOT == interpreter. This fixes the discrepancy by making the report's claim TRUE rather than by weakening it, and it is NOT frozen-specific: any auto-par loop writing through a `mut ref Vec` parameter now parallelizes where it ran sequentially. PART 2 (this commit): a RESIDUAL instance of the same class. With `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` codegen emits nothing, but the query still reported `fanned_out: true` because it ran the proof and the cost model but not the env gate codegen checks first. The env read moved to `par_cost::auto_par_enabled()` — the module built for exactly this 'one definition, two callers' problem after B-2026-07-29-29 — with `codegen::driver::read_auto_par_env` delegating to it, so the two cannot drift. Both the disjoint-write and reduction report paths now emit `cost_gate: declined_auto_par_disabled`. RESIDUAL CLASS AFTER THIS: narrow. `block_has_early_exit` is belt-and-braces (the PROOF already declines early exits via `DisjointDecline::EarlyExit`, so the report says not-proven anyway), and the const-int-capture bail is documented unreachable for targets. What remains unaudited is `extract_loop_shape` returning None, which no measured shape has yet hit. HOW TO CHECK: `bash -c 'time ./binary'` and compare `user` to `real`. `nm` cannot tell you — the binaries carry ~81 dynamic symbols, so `karac_par_*` statics are stripped at link and grepping finds nothing either way.

title: tests/selfhost_codegen.rs (selfhost_codegen_matches_seed_run) is RED on macOS/arm64 for EVERY corpus entry: the self-hosted emitter hardcodes a Linux x86-64 target triple AND glibc's `stdout` symbol, so its emitted IR cannot link on Darwin (which spells it `__stdoutp`) -- the oracle then compares "" against the seed's output. Green on the x86-Linux CI leg, so the gate is silently host-specific
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced incidentally by the full-suite gate of the B-2026-08-05-4 slice (map compaction perf). NOT caused by that slice -- confirmed pre-existing by reverting runtime/src/map.rs to a clean HEAD and re-running: still RED, identical failure.

SYMPTOM. `cargo test --features llvm --test selfhost_codegen selfhost_codegen_matches_seed_run` fails at the FIRST corpus entry (`fn main(){println("hi")}`) with left: "" / right: "hi\n", and the test dumps the emitted IR, which reads as structurally correct -- a correct-looking module that produces no output is what makes this look like a miscompile rather than a link failure.

ROOT CAUSE, two hardcoded Linux/glibc assumptions in selfhost/src/codegen.kara's module preamble (around line 350):
    out = out + "target triple = \"x86_64-pc-linux-gnu\"\n";
    out = out + "@stdout = external global ptr\n";
The triple is the visible one but the SECOND is what actually breaks the link: glibc exports `stdout`, Darwin's libc exports `__stdoutp` and provides `stdout` only as a macro. Reproduced standalone by hand-assembling a minimal module with exactly that preamble and running clang on it:
    warning: overriding the module target triple with arm64-apple-macosx26.0.0
    Undefined symbols for architecture arm64: "_stdout", referenced from: _main
clang overrides the bogus triple with a warning and proceeds, so the triple alone is survivable; the missing `_stdout` is fatal. No executable is produced, the harness captures empty stdout, and the oracle reports a content mismatch instead of a link failure.

WHY IT READS GREEN ELSEWHERE. The CI codegen-e2e leg is x86-64 Linux/glibc, where both assumptions happen to hold, so this gate has never fired there. B-2026-07-16-16 is the same test with the same ""-vs-expected symptom, filed 2026-07-16 and marked fixed; whatever that fix was, it did not cover the Darwin host, so on macOS the self-host oracle is providing no coverage at all right now while appearing to run.

FIX DIRECTION (not attempted -- out of scope for the slice that found it). The emitter needs the host triple and the host's stdout spelling rather than constants: emit `__stdoutp` and an apple triple on Darwin. The seed compiler already knows its host triple (src/codegen.rs sets the module target datalayout -- cf. the coro-frame gotcha where NOT setting it silently folds llvm.coro.size), so the value is available to thread through. A narrower stopgap would be for the test to SKIP with a loud notice on non-Linux hosts, which at least stops it reporting a codegen mismatch for a link failure -- but that trades a false alarm for no coverage, so the real fix is preferable.

IMPACT. Not a shipped-compiler bug -- this is the self-hosted emitter, not `karac` itself, so no user-facing codegen is affected. The cost is that the self-hosting credibility proof cannot be verified on the primary development machine, and any macOS-side full-suite run carries a permanent RED that trains the eye to ignore it.

FIXED 2026-08-05 (06a3f683), along the fix direction this row proposed, with one
substantive departure and one addition.

THE DEPARTURE. The row proposed emitting "an apple triple on Darwin". The triple
and datalayout are instead OMITTED ENTIRELY. Correcting them would mean the
emitter carrying a table of per-host triples and layout strings and keeping it
right, when both consumers of the emitted IR already know the host better than
the emitter does -- LLJIT inside `karac_jit_runner`, and clang in the leak
audit. Omitting lets each supply its own, which is right on every host rather
than on the hosts someone remembered to enumerate. Safe HERE specifically
because this emitter emits no `llvm.coro.*` (verified: zero occurrences); the
seed's codegen.rs must keep setting a datalayout, since an absent one silently
folds `llvm.coro.size` to zero -- the gotcha recorded in CLAUDE.md.

THE SPELLING is threaded in, as the row proposed: `emit_program(items,
stdout_sym)`. Rather than thread it to the four print sites through the Emitter
struct (whose full destructure at the assembly point would also have had to
change), the preamble now defines an internal `@kara.stdout()` accessor and the
print sites call it. The platform-specific spelling therefore appears exactly
once in the emitter AND exactly once in the emitted module. The test driver
supplies it with the same `cfg!(target_vendor = "apple")` rule the seed uses in
src/codegen.rs. `emit_program`'s only caller is that driver, so the signature
change is contained; the phase-12 checklist's copy of the signature is updated.

THE ADDITION, which is the part worth keeping. Fixing only the running host
would have left the other half exactly as invisible as it had been for as long
as this bug existed -- an x86-Linux CI leg cannot see a Darwin-only link
failure, which is precisely how this survived. The oracle now emits ONE corpus
program under the NON-host spelling and asserts its shape: the other host's
symbol is the one declared, it appears exactly twice (the declaration plus the
single load inside the accessor -- more would mean a print site named it
directly), the accessor is defined, the host spelling has not leaked in, and
neither retired hardcode has come back. Structural only, deliberately: whether
Darwin's linker resolves `__stdoutp` is not a question a Linux run can answer,
and claiming otherwise would repeat the mistake this ledger just recorded in
B-2026-08-05-4. What it does buy is that whichever host runs the suite covers
the other one. Confirmed load-bearing by restoring both hardcodes and watching
it fail ("cross-host block must declare @__stdoutp"), then restoring the fix.

The cross-host emission rides the SAME selfhost build as the corpus, so it
costs one extra `emit_program` call rather than a second ~200 s compile.

NOT VERIFIED, stated plainly: no macOS/arm64 run. The Darwin leg is verified
structurally and by construction (the symbol is the host's because the host
chooses it), not by execution. A macOS full-suite run is what actually closes
the loop, and if `selfhost_codegen_matches_seed_run` is still red there, the
remaining cause is NOT the two hardcodes this removed.

RELATED: B-2026-07-16-16 is the same test with the same ""-vs-expected symptom,
filed 2026-07-16 and marked fixed. Whatever that fix addressed, it was not this;
the two are distinct causes behind one indistinguishable symptom, which is an
argument for the oracle reporting link failures as link failures rather than as
content mismatches.

VERIFICATION: cargo test --features llvm 13017 passed / 0 failed across 102
suites; fmt and `clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm -D warnings` clean.
tracker: selfhost/src/codegen.kara (emit_program stdout_sym param, @kara.stdout accessor, triple/datalayout removed) + tests/selfhost_codegen.rs (check_cross_host_ir, XHOST block)

title: taking a free function as a VALUE (`let f = g;`) and calling it through the binding fails to build when any parameter is a `ref Vec[T]` -- the indirect call passes the Vec BY VALUE into a signature that expects a pointer, so LLVM module verification rejects it; `karac check` passes and the interpreter runs it correctly, and the same program with only scalar parameters builds fine
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while writing B-2026-08-05-6's regression tests. The gate
that drops a candidate when its name is used as a bare value could not be
tested through codegen because the test program itself would not build, so
that gate is covered by a unit test instead (`refuses_when_the_callee_is_taken
_as_a_value` in src/codegen/bce_interproc.rs). This row carries the blocker.

REPRO (whole program):
    fn head(v: ref Vec[u8], i: i64) -> i64 { return v[i] as i64; }
    fn main() {
        let v: Vec[u8] = Vec.filled(4i64, 9u8);
        let f = head;
        println(f(v, 1i64));
    }

  karac check        -> All checks passed.
  karac run --interp -> 9   (correct)
  karac build        -> error: codegen failed: Module verification failed:
                        "Call parameter type does not match function signature!
                           %v2 = load { ptr, i64, i64 }, ptr %v, align 8
                           %closure_call = call i64 %closure_fn(ptr %closure_env,
                             { ptr, i64, i64 } %v2, i64 1)"

THE ASYMMETRY THAT LOCALIZES IT, checked rather than assumed. The identical
program with only SCALAR parameters builds and runs clean:
    fn add2(a: i64, b: i64) -> i64 { return a + b; }
    fn main() { let f = add2; println(f(3i64, 4i64)); }   -> builds, prints 7
So it is not "fn-as-value is unimplemented" -- the indirect-call path exists
and works. It is specific to a parameter whose direct-call ABI is
by-POINTER (`ref Vec[T]`) while the closure-shaped indirect call marshals it
by-VALUE as the `{ptr, i64, i64}` Vec triple.

READING OF THE SYMPTOM, explicitly NOT a diagnosis -- no IR was dumped beyond
the verifier's message and no codegen path was read. A bare fn name used as a
value evidently lowers to the CLOSURE representation (note `%closure_env` /
`%closure_fn` in the error), and that path appears to marshal arguments by the
closure convention while the callee was declared with the direct-call
convention. The natural first place to look is whether the fn-to-closure
adaptation emits a thunk that re-marshals `ref` parameters, or whether it
reuses the direct signature verbatim.

NOT CAUSED BY B-2026-08-05-6. Confirmed pre-existing: the failure reproduces
identically with every BCE kill switch off
(`KARAC_BCE_INTERPROC=0 KARAC_BCE_CONV_SKIP=0 KARAC_BCE_DESC_SKIP=0`).

SEVERITY. medium rather than high: it is a hard compile error, not a silent
miscompile, so nothing wrong ships. But it IS a run-vs-build divergence --
every check passes and one backend runs it correctly -- and the error text is
an internal LLVM verifier message with no source span, which is the worst
diagnostic shape the compiler emits.

RESOLVED. TWO legs, opposite sides of the same call.

SCOPE WAS WIDER THAN THIS ENTRY RECORDED. A 7-shape matrix found FOUR failing,
not one: `let f = takes_ref_vec`, a `Fn(..)`-typed PARAMETER holding such a fn,
a `ref String` param, and a `mut ref Vec` param. Owned-`Vec` and scalar-only
params were always fine. A fifth shape — a closure LITERAL with a `ref` param —
failed too, with a DIFFERENT error, and turned out to be a separate root cause
(leg 2 below).

LEG 1, CALLER SIDE (`compile_closure_call` + `compile_closure_value_call`,
src/codegen/closures.rs). The indirect-call paths compiled every argument BY
VALUE. That is only right for params whose ABI is by-value. Both indirect
signatures were already correct — `env_first_fn_type` copies the target's own
param types and `closure_abi_fn_type` lowers the `Fn(..)` annotation through
`llvm_type_for_type_expr`, whose `TypeKind::Ref | MutRef` arm is `ptr` — and the
reify TRAMPOLINE is a straight forwarder, so it agrees too. Only the call site
disagreed, pushing a `{ptr,i64,i64}` Vec triple into a `ptr` slot.

Fixed with one shared marshaller, `compile_indirect_call_arg`, that decides
from the DECLARED param type and mirrors the direct-call path in
`call_dispatch.rs` for the by-pointer case (address of a named binding's
storage / an element borrow / a materialized temp).

WHY IT DECIDES ON THE DECLARED LLVM TYPE RATHER THAN A SEMANTIC ref-FLAG, which
was the one real design question. A `shared` handle's param ALSO lowers to
`ptr`, but its argument is already a pointer VALUE — taking the address of its
slot would hand the callee a pointer-to-pointer and `n.v` would read the stack.
`ident_arg_needs_address` draws that line: true for a slot holding its value
inline, plus the two indirections `get_data_ptr` already unwraps (a `ref` param
forwarding its own borrow; an RC-promoted binding whose data sits past the
refcount header); false for a plain pointer-typed slot. The `shared` case has
its own regression test precisely because a wrong answer there is a SILENT bad
read, not a verifier error.

LEG 2, CALLEE SIDE (`compile_closure`'s param-bind loop, same file). A closure
literal's `ref` param was handed to `register_var_from_type_expr` as the BORROW
type — and that function has no `Ref` arm, so it registered NOTHING at all: the
param never reached `vec_elem_types`, and `w[i]` failed with "Index operator
applied to non-array type". It also never reached `ref_params`, so its slot
(which holds a pointer) would have been read as if it held the value inline.
Fixed by mirroring the function-param path in `functions.rs`: record the borrow
in `ref_params`/`signature_ref_params`, and register the side tables from the
BORROWED-OF type.

VERIFICATION. All 7 matrix shapes now build, and every one matches the
interpreter exactly. Valgrind clean on all of them, including the
ownership-sensitive rvalue-to-`ref`-param path at 1,206 allocations with the
payload's BYTES read and an `env.args().len()` seed (B-2026-08-04-17's
non-vacuity rule) — that path materializes a temp, so a wrong marshalling would
leak or double-free there rather than fail the verifier.

TESTS: 6 E2E in tests/codegen.rs. FIVE are RED before the fix; the sixth is the
`shared`-handle guard, which passes either way by construction — it exists to
catch a future regression in the pointer-vs-address discrimination, not to
witness this fix.

TWO SEPARATE FINDINGS SURFACED WHILE PROBING, both filed rather than folded in:
B-2026-08-05-17 (`karac build` does not enforce effect errors that `karac check`
reports) and B-2026-08-05-18 (a `Fn(..)` type's effect clause is dropped, so the
slot is always `[pure]`).

title: NONDETERMINISTIC SEGV at -O0: a bare variant-name pattern whose name is shared by two enums resolves against the UNORDERED enum_layouts map, so per-process HashMap seed decides the payload word offsets -- a payload word is then dereferenced as a pointer. Carried until now as a 'known flaky' test, which is what kept it parked
detail:
RECLASSIFIED, not newly observed. `asan_match_variant_name_shared_across_enums_string_payload_no_leak` has been carried in B-2026-08-05-7's -O0 list as "the known flaky" one. It is not flaky in the test-infrastructure sense: it is a real nondeterministic MISCOMPILE whose trigger is the compiler's own HashMap iteration order, and the "flaky" label is why nobody looked. Filing it separately so the -O0 leg has a real item to close rather than a test to tolerate.

MEASURED, at 5a2420d with both archives rebuilt, 12 runs per level:
  -O2 :  0 / 12 crash
  -O0 :  7 / 12 crash   (a second 6-run sample gave 2/6; the rate wanders)
Signature every time: `AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000003`, a READ, inside `tok_kind`.

WHY 0x3 IS THE TELL. The fixture's `Sp` is `{ line: 1, column: 1, offset: 0, length: 3 }`. Address 3 is not a corrupted pointer, it is the LITERAL VALUE of `Sp.length` being loaded and then dereferenced as a buffer pointer. That is a wrong-word-offset read, not a use-after-free.

ROOT CAUSE, confirmed by a decisive control rather than by reading code. Two enums in the program share the bare variant name `Str`:

    enum Tok { Str(String, Sp), Int(i64) }          // value enum, 2 fields
    shared enum Expr { Int(i64), Boolish(i64), Str(SLit) }   // shared, 1 field

`tok_kind` matches on `Tok` with UNQUALIFIED patterns (`match t { Str(s, sp) => 1, Int(v) => 2 }`). When the bare name `Str` is resolved against the (unordered) `enum_layouts` map instead of the scrutinee's own enum, it can land on `Expr.Str` -- whose payload word layout differs from `Tok.Str` -- and the binding reads the wrong words.

THE CONTROL (this is what makes it a finding rather than a hypothesis): take the fixture body, and change ONLY the shared-enum variant's NAME, `Expr.Str` -> `Expr.StrE`, so the collision disappears and nothing else differs. Built and run 12x each at -O0 through the ordinary `karac build` CLI:

    collide    (Expr.Str)   4 / 12 crashed
    nocollide  (Expr.StrE)  0 / 12 crashed

The nondeterminism source is Rust's per-process `RandomState`: each `karac` invocation seeds `enum_layouts` differently, so the same source compiles to a correct binary or a crashing one depending on which enum the map yields first. That is also why a single green run proves nothing here -- any fix must be gated on a REPEATED run (>=12) at -O0, not one pass.

WHY -O2 HIDES IT. The bound `s` / `sp` are unused (the arm returns the constant 1), so at -O2 the loads are dead and deleted before they can fault. At -O0 they are emitted and executed. This is the same optimizer-erasure axis as B-2026-08-04-17, arriving at a crash rather than at a vacuous fixture.

WHERE TO LOOK, partial -- this is handed over mid-diagnosis. `match_scrutinee_enum_hint` (src/codegen.rs, set at src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs:93 from `type_name_of_expr(scrutinee)`, restored at :879) exists to fix exactly this class, and its own doc comment names the failure mode verbatim: an unqualified variant pattern "no longer mis-resolves to whichever enum the (unordered) `enum_layouts` map yields first." So either (a) the hint is `None` here -- `type_name_of_expr`'s `Identifier` arm is `var_type_names.get(n)`, and the scrutinee is a bare PARAMETER `t: Tok`, so this turns on whether param setup registered it -- or (b) the hint is set correctly and some resolver on the tuple-variant binding path does not consult it. NOT established which; both are one `eprintln!` of the predicate away, and B-2026-08-05-7's METHOD NOTE recommends exactly that loop over reading code and guessing.

SCOPE. Not reachable on a default build (0/12 at -O2), so this is not a user-facing crash today -- but it is latent, and the shape is ordinary: two enums sharing a variant name is normal in a parser, which is where the fixture came from (#39, phase-12). It blocks the -O0 sweep from becoming a CI leg, which is the gating dependency for de-vacuuming B-2026-08-04-17's 70 fixtures.

FIXED 2026-08-05 in e3a086e6.

REPRODUCED AS FILED before touching anything: 6/12 crashes at -O0 on the collide
source, 0/12 on the control whose only difference is the variant NAME. The row's
control experiment holds exactly.

HYPOTHESIS (a) IS REFUTED. The row offered two: (a) the scrutinee hint is `None`
because the scrutinee is a bare PARAMETER and `type_name_of_expr`'s `Identifier`
arm reads `var_type_names`; (b) the hint is set and some resolver ignores it. An
`eprintln!` at the match entry shows the hint is correctly `Some("Tok")` -- so
parameters ARE registered in `var_type_names`, and (a) can be struck.

(b) IS THE CAUSE, and the resolver that ignores the hint is one that already
LOOKS like it honours it. `pattern_binding.rs`'s tuple-variant `matched_enum`
resolution reads:

    (Some(t), _)    => &l.llvm_type == t     // value enum
    (None, Some(h)) => en.as_str() == h      // shared enum -- hint honoured
    (None, None)    => true

The hint arm is reachable ONLY for a shared (RC-pointer) scrutinee, which has no
inline struct type. `Tok` is a VALUE enum, so it takes the first arm and pins on
`llvm_type` equality alone. That is not a unique key: two enums with
structurally identical layouts share one LLVM struct type, so the predicate is
true for both and `.find()` returns whichever the unordered `enum_layouts` map
yields first. The wrong enum's `field_word_offsets` then drives the binding.

MEASURED at the site, 6 compiles of the SAME source:

    variant=Str matched_enum=Some("Expr") hint=Some("Tok")   4 / 6
    variant=Str matched_enum=Some("Tok")  hint=Some("Tok")   2 / 6

which is the crash rate, and explains the 0x3 signature the row identified:
`Expr.Str(SLit)` is one word where `Tok.Str(String, Sp)` is several, so the
binding reads `Sp.length` (literally 3) and dereferences it as a buffer pointer.

THE FIX checks the hint FIRST, unconditionally, ahead of the scan. An
unqualified variant pattern in `match e { .. }` where `e: E` and `E` declares
that variant IS `E`'s variant -- no map order or type coincidence can make it
another enum's. Written as a pre-step rather than another arm inside the scan,
because the scan exists to disambiguate when there is NO hint; when there is
one, there is nothing to disambiguate. Post-fix the resolution is identical
across 6 compiles and the repro is 24/24 clean at -O0.

TEST ASSERTS DETERMINISM BY REPETITION, which is the part worth reusing. The
trigger is the compiler's own per-HashMap seed, so a single green compile is not
evidence -- the pre-fix compiler emitted correct IR on roughly a third of runs,
which is exactly how this survived as "flaky" for as long as it did.
`test_ir_shared_variant_name_resolves_to_scrutinee_enum_deterministically`
compiles one source 24 times and demands byte-identical IR; it fails 5/5
invocations with the fix reverted. That converts a seed-dependent miscompile
into a deterministic test failure.

GATES: 13,068 passed / 0 failed. (Two cli wasm-glue tests first reported "test
child binary hung" while the suite competed with 10 sequential ASAN
invocations; both pass in isolation in ~0.3s and the full `cli` binary re-runs
563/563 green -- a load-induced timeout, not a regression.) The formerly-flaky
`asan_match_variant_name_shared_across_enums_string_payload_no_leak` passed
10/10 consecutive -O0 invocations. clippy and fmt clean.

UNBLOCKS what the row said it was blocking: the -O0 sweep now has no known
nondeterministic crasher, which was the gating dependency for turning it into a
CI leg and de-vacuuming B-2026-08-04-17's fixtures.

title: `karac build` does not enforce EFFECT errors that `karac check` reports — a program `check` rejects with 1 error builds and runs; type errors ARE enforced on both paths, so this is specific to the effect checker being absent from the build pipeline, not a general laxness
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while probing B-2026-08-05-15's `Fn(..)`-typed-parameter
shape, whose effect error `karac build` sailed straight past.

REPRO (whole program):
    pub fn risky(v: ref Vec[i64]) -> i64 { return v[0]; }
    fn main() { let v: Vec[i64] = Vec.filled(2i64, 5i64); println(risky(v)); }

  karac check -> error[effect]: ec.kara:1:5: public function 'risky' performs
                 effects [panics] but has no effect declaration.
                 Add: with panics to the function signature
                 1 error(s) found.
  karac build -> Built: ec        <-- accepted, binary produced, runs fine

CONTROL, which is what makes this specific rather than "build is lax". A TYPE
error is rejected by BOTH:
    fn main() { let x: i64 = "not an int"; println(x); }
  karac check -> 1 error(s) found.
  karac build -> error[typecheck]: te.kara:1:26: expected 'i64', found 'String'

So the build pipeline runs the typechecker as a hard gate and does not run (or
does not gate on) the effect checker.

WHY IT MATTERS. The effect system is a load-bearing correctness feature of the
language — the spec's Feature 2, and the thing `check`'s public-function
verification exists to enforce. A user who only ever runs `karac build` gets no
effect verification at all, and the declared-vs-inferred contract that public
signatures are supposed to guarantee is unenforced in the shipping artifact.
It also means `check` and `build` disagree about whether a program is legal,
which is the run-vs-build divergence class this ledger tracks.

NOT DIAGNOSED. No CLI phase wiring was read; this is an observation from the
two commands' behaviour. The obvious first place to look is whether the build
path's pipeline construction calls `effectcheck` at all, and if it does,
whether its diagnostics are collected into the fatal-error set.

OPEN QUESTION worth settling before fixing: whether this is deliberate (build
skipping a slow-ish whole-program analysis) or an oversight. If deliberate it
still needs to be documented and probably surfaced as a warning, because
silently shipping a binary for a program your own checker rejects is not a
defensible default.

RESOLVED. The open question this entry posed — "deliberate or oversight?" — is
answered: OVERSIGHT, and a known one.

ROOT CAUSE, one line. `Pipeline::has_fatal_errors` (src/cli.rs), the predicate
`cmd_build` gates on, was:

    parse || resolve || type || comptime || ownership

No effect arm. `cmd_build` DOES call `pipeline.effectcheck()` — the pass ran and
its diagnostics were collected — the gate simply never consulted them. That is
why type errors were enforced and effect errors were not.

THIS IS B-2026-07-31-29 ONE PHASE OVER. That entry fixed exactly this defect for
OWNERSHIP: "`karac check` reported `error[ownership]` and exited 1 while `karac
build` produced a binary and exited 0 for the same program. The two lanes
disagreed about whether a program was valid." Its fix introduced a single shared
classifier (`is_fatal_ownership_kind`) used by both `has_fatal_errors` and
`total_errors` "so the two cannot drift apart again". Effects were never given
the same treatment. The fix here is deliberately the identical shape —
`is_fatal_effect_kind` + `has_fatal_effect_errors` — rather than an inline
condition, so the next phase to need it has a pattern to copy.

THE CLASSIFIER was not invented: `cmd_run` already had exactly this predicate as
a local closure, with both advisory classes documented. It is now hoisted onto
`Pipeline` and `cmd_run` calls the shared version, so run and build cannot drift.
Two kinds stay advisory:
  * `FfiLintHint` — declared "never a compile error" at its own definition.
  * `TargetGateViolation` (E0411) — a target-AVAILABILITY finding, and the build
    path already has its own target-aware abort for it. Verified rather than
    assumed: `wasm_wasi_build_aborts_on_target_gate_violation` and
    `wasm_browser_build_aborts_on_target_gate_violation` both still pass, so a
    real cross-target violation still stops the build with the TARGETED
    diagnostic. Routing E0411 through the generic gate too would make a NATIVE
    build reject the deliberate cross-target dev workflow `karac run` supports.

MEASURED BEFORE/AFTER on this entry's own repro:
                     check        build              run
  before          exit 1      exit 0, "Built: ec"   exit 1
  after           exit 1      exit 1, error[effect] exit 1
The build failure RENDERS the diagnostic (`print_text_diagnostics` already had
an effect arm) and produces no artifact — both asserted, since a silent exit-1
would have been worse than the bug.

BLAST RADIUS, checked before changing a shared predicate rather than discovered
by the suite: all four `has_fatal_errors` call sites are execution/build paths
(`cmd_run`, `cmd_build`, `run_multi_file_codegen`, `cmd_query`) — no formatter or
doc path that should tolerate effect errors.

The example sweep I ran up front was NOT sufficient, and the way it failed is
the reusable lesson: `karac check examples/*.kara` reported 0 effect findings
across 13 files, and I took that as "no blast radius". It missed the one real
hit twice over — the glob does not descend into `examples/<name>/` subdirectories
(where ssr_counter lives), and it only checked the DEFAULT target, which filters
`#[target(wasm_browser)]` items out before the effect checker ever sees them. A
pre-change sweep for a gate like this has to be per-target and recursive, or it
measures nothing. The suite caught it; the sweep should have.

RESIDUAL, NOT FIXED HERE and recorded so it is not mistaken for settled. On the
NATIVE target, E0411 is reported three different ways:
    check -> error[effect], exit 1
    build -> silent,        exit 0
    run   -> warning[effect], exit 0
This fix aligns build with run (advisory) and leaves `check` strict, because
`total_errors` filters only `FfiLintHint`. So a check-vs-run/build split on that
ONE kind survives. Note that `cmd_run`'s own comment asserts "build/check treat
it the same on native" — that comment is WRONG about check, and was the thing
that made this look settled. Changing `check`'s exit code is a separate decision
with its own blast radius, and `check` being the strictest lane is the safe
direction for the Mend loop's gate; a follow-up should decide it deliberately.
Build also still prints nothing at all for a native E0411, where `run` prints a
warning — surfacing non-fatal diagnostics from `build` would change every
build's output and is likewise out of scope here.

IT IMMEDIATELY CAUGHT A REAL BUG, which is the best evidence the gate is worth
having. The full suite went RED on exactly one test —
`ssr_counter_example_dual_target_e2e` — because
`examples/ssr_counter/ssr_counter.kara`'s `pub fn hydrate(count: i64) -> i64
with writes(Dom)` actually performs `panics` (indexing, via `__builtin_index`)
and `writes(Sink)` (via `render_counter`, which declares it). The example was
under-declared and had been shipping a wasm_browser artifact anyway.

Verified it is a genuine finding rather than the new gate over-reaching:
`karac check --targets=wasm_browser` ALREADY rejected that file with the same
two errors and exit 1, before any change here. It looked clean only because the
default-target `check` filters `#[target(wasm_browser)]` items out entirely
("All checks passed" on native), and `build` — the one lane that does compile
for that target — was not gating. Fixed the EXAMPLE (`with writes(Dom)
writes(Sink) panics`; effect items are space-separated, not comma-separated),
not the gate. It now passes `check` on both native and wasm_browser.

Worth noting why only `hydrate` tripped and not the server entry doing the same
`with_provider[Sink]` dance: `main` is PRIVATE, so its effects are inferred
rather than verified. Exactly the design rule — "private inferred, public
declared and verified" — showing up as an asymmetry in one file.

TESTS: two in tests/cli.rs. `build_rejects_an_effect_violation_like_check_does`
is RED before the fix and asserts the exit code, the rendered diagnostic, the
absent artifact, AND that `check` rejects the same program (the agreement is the
point, and the two gates are separate predicates so it is asserted rather than
assumed). `build_still_accepts_a_program_with_declared_effects` guards the other
direction — a correctly-declared program must keep building.

title: a RESOURCE-LESS effect verb (`panics` / `blocks` / `suspends`) is silently dropped wherever an effect LIST is converted to an effect SET — so a `Fn(..) with panics` slot resolved to the EMPTY set and rejected every effectful argument against a slot the diagnostic printed as `[pure]`, making the higher-order surface unusable with any callee that panics
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while probing B-2026-08-05-15's `Fn(..)`-typed-parameter
shape. That shape's CODEGEN is fixed; this is the separate reason the shape is
still not usable as written.

REPRO (whole program):
    fn head(v: ref Vec[u8], i: i64) -> i64 with panics { return v[i] as i64; }
    fn apply(g: Fn(ref Vec[u8], i64) -> i64 with panics, v: ref Vec[u8])
        -> i64 with panics { return g(v, 1i64); }
    fn main() { let v: Vec[u8] = Vec.filled(4i64, 9u8); println(apply(head, v)); }

  karac check -> error[effect]: argument 1 has effect panics() not declared in
                 slot [pure]

The `with panics` on the `Fn(..)` TYPE parses (no parse error) but does not
reach the effect slot, which stays `[pure]`. Dropping it changes nothing — the
same error, same text.

WHY THIS IS NOT A NICHE GAP. Indexing a Vec carries `panics`, so essentially
ANY realistic function that touches a collection is ineligible for a `Fn`-typed
parameter. That makes the higher-order surface — comparators, callbacks,
strategy parameters, anything taking `Fn(..)` — usable only with callees that
are provably pure. The restriction is invisible until you try, since the
annotation you would reach for parses cleanly.

SPELLING NOTE, recorded because it cost time: the effect clause on a plain fn
is `with panics`, NO parentheses (`panics` is resource-less — CLAUDE.md's
six-resource-verb / two-execution-verb split). `with panics()` is a parse error,
and the diagnostic in B-2026-08-05-17's repro states the correct form outright:
"Add: with panics to the function signature".

NOT DIAGNOSED beyond the observation. Unresolved and worth settling first:
whether the parser builds an effect list into `TypeKind::FnType` at all (in
which case the effect checker is ignoring a populated field), or whether the
`with` clause is being consumed by the ENCLOSING function's signature — the two
`with panics` in the repro are adjacent enough to be ambiguous, and that
ambiguity is itself worth resolving in the grammar.

RESOLVED — and this entry's own DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, in a way worth recording
because the wrong version is the one that looks obvious.

WHAT I FILED: "a `Fn(..)` type's effect clause is dropped ... the slot is always
inferred `[pure]`", with the open question of whether the parser builds an
effect list into `TypeKind::FnType` at all or whether the `with` clause was
being eaten by the enclosing signature. BOTH GUESSES WERE WRONG.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY IS. `TypeKind::FnType` carries `effect_spec: Option<EffectSpec>`;
the parser populates it correctly (src/parser/types.rs:430); and the effect
checker reads it correctly (`subtyping.rs` matches
`FnType { effect_spec: Some(Specific(list)) }` and calls
`resolve_effect_list_to_set`). The whole `Fn`-type effect pipeline works. The
defect is one loop inside that resolver:

    EffectItem::Verb(verb) => {
        for resource in &verb.resources { result.insert(...); }   // <-- EMPTY
    }

A resource-less verb has an EMPTY `resources` vec, so the loop body never runs
and the verb is dropped. Nothing to do with `Fn` types specifically.

THE DISCRIMINATING PROBE, which is what corrected the diagnosis: a slot
declaring a RESOURCE verb works fine (`Fn() with writes(Db)` accepts a
`writes(Db)` argument), and `with _` works. Only the resource-less verbs fail.
The MIXED case is conclusive — `Fn(..) with writes(Db) panics` renders as slot
`[writes(Db)]`: the resource verb survived and `panics` vanished FROM THE SAME
LIST. So it is a per-verb-kind drop, not a clause-level one.

SCOPE WAS WIDER THAN THE `Fn` SLOT. Grepping the pattern found five copies of
`for resource in &verb.resources`; exactly ONE was guarded. Fixed three:
  * `resolve_effect_list_to_set`      — the `Fn` slot (this entry).
  * `expand_group`                    — `effect group g = writes(Db) + panics;`
                                        expanded WITHOUT the `panics`.
  * `resolve_effect_list_for_render`  — the diagnostic renderer, which is why
                                        the slot printed as `[pure]` and made
                                        the drop look clause-level.
The fifth (`resolver/resolve_refs.rs::resolve_effect_verb`) correctly needs no
guard: it resolves resource NAMES, and a resource-less verb has none.

THE GUARD ALREADY EXISTED, one function away. `collect_declared_effects` has
the identical `if verb.resources.is_empty()` arm, added in the phase-10
`host fn` slice, and its comment describes the same bug on the DECLARATION
path: "Before this arm existed, a bare verb in ANY `with` clause was silently
dropped". The sibling sites never got it. Same shape as B-2026-08-05-17 (and
B-2026-07-31-29 before it): a fix applied at one site, with siblings left
un-updated, is this codebase's most repeated defect shape.

EMPTY-STRING RESOURCE IS THE CANONICAL FORM, not an invention: inference already
produces `Effect { verb, resource: String::new() }` for these verbs, which is
why the fixed slot set compares equal to the argument's inferred set. The
renderer prints it `panics()`.

WHAT NOW WORKS, verified: `Fn(..) with panics` / `blocks` / `suspends` accept a
matching argument; the mixed resource + resource-less slot works; a group with
`+ panics` works; and B-2026-08-05-17's motivating program (a `Fn`-typed
parameter taking a Vec-indexing helper) passes `check`, runs on the interpreter,
and builds and runs under AOT with matching output.

STILL REJECTED, asserted rather than assumed, because a fix of this shape can
easily become "accept everything": an argument that panics handed to a slot
declaring NOTHING, and one handed to a slot declaring the WRONG resource-less
verb (`panics` does not satisfy `blocks`). Both still error.

TESTS: 6 in tests/effectchecker.rs. The 4 positives are RED before the fix; the
2 negative controls pass either way by construction — they guard the gate from
becoming permissive rather than witnessing the fix.

METHOD NOTE. This entry's SPELLING NOTE said `with panics()` is a parse error
and the correct form is `with panics`. True — but I then wrote a group body as
`writes(Db) panics` and read the parse error as a second parser gap. It is not:
the group separator is `+` (design.md § Effect Groups, `reads(DB) + writes(Cache)`).
Recorded because that misreading briefly looked like a third bug.

fix: 80d7a37 (layout rule + literal adoption) + e7a04ac (expected-type seeding; user generics now covered) — `Tensor` still excluded pending B-2026-08-05-26
title: generic args are NOT invariant across numeric element types: `Vec[i64]` is silently accepted where `Vec[u16]` is declared, and AOT then reinterprets the buffer — wrong values, out-of-bounds reads, and a run-vs-build divergence
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found converting apps/cumulus (kara-katas) from i64 to u16 pixel storage. I changed three function signatures to `ref Vec[u16]` and FORGOT to change the caller's `let mut px: Vec[i64]`. `karac check` reported 'All checks passed'. The program was wrong.

MINIMAL REPRO:
  fn sum_u16(v: ref Vec[u16]) -> i64 {
      let mut s: i64 = 0;
      for i in 0..v.len() { s = s + (v[i] as i64); }
      s
  }
  fn main() {
      let x: Vec[i64] = [1, 2, 3, 4];
      println(f"sum={sum_u16(x)}");   // correct: 10, or a type error
  }

  karac check      -> All checks passed.      <-- NO DIAGNOSTIC
  karac run --interp -> sum=10                <-- accidentally right
  karac build      -> sum=1                   <-- MISCOMPILE

AOT reads the 8-byte-element buffer as 2-byte elements: the four u16 lanes of the first i64 are [1,0,0,0] little-endian, so the sum is 1. The interpreter stores values boxed, so it is accidentally correct — which makes this ALSO a run-vs-build divergence, and in the worst direction: the test path says yes, the shipped path is wrong.

SURFACE (all accepted, no diagnostic):
  ref Vec[u16]   <- Vec[i64]     AOT prints 1
  owned Vec[u16] <- Vec[i64]     AOT prints 1
  ref Vec[i64]   <- Vec[u16]     AOT prints -1   (reads PAST the allocation)
  let y: Vec[u16] = x            (x: Vec[i64])   accepted
  ref Vec[f64]   <- Vec[i64]     AOT prints 5e-324 (integer bits read as a double)
  ref Option[u16] <- Option[i64] accepted
  ref Vec[Vec[u16]] <- Vec[Vec[i64]] accepted
  ref Holder[u16] <- Holder[i64] accepted (user-defined generic struct)

DIAGNOSIS — the hole is NUMERIC-SPECIFIC, which localizes it:
  Vec[i64] passed as Vec[String]  -> CORRECTLY REJECTED (1 error)
So generic-argument comparison is not blanket-permissive; it is specifically treating two NUMERIC scalar types as interchangeable. That is the scalar numeric-coercion rule (legitimate for values: an i64 flowing into an f64 slot) leaking into generic ARGUMENT position, where it must be invariant because `Vec[i64]` and `Vec[u16]` have different physical layouts. It reproduces for Vec, Option, nested Vec, and user-defined generic structs alike, so the fix belongs at the generic-argument comparison, not in any per-type special case.

WHY HIGH: silent type confusion with no diagnostic, producing wrong arithmetic AND out-of-bounds reads (the Vec[u16] -> Vec[i64] direction walks 4x past the buffer), plus interp/AOT divergence that hides it from the test path. The `as` casts in the body look like the programmer acknowledged the types, which makes it read as intentional on review.

CAUTION FOR THE FIX: `types_compatible` has a deliberate blanket arm `(Type::TypeParam(_), _) | (_, Type::TypeParam(_)) => true` so that `fn last[T](v: Vec[T]) -> Option[T]` typechecks. Any fix must keep uninstantiated type parameters permissive while making two CONCRETE numeric args invariant — narrowing the wrong one would break generic library code.

FIXED (80d7a37) — but read the SCOPE note: user generics are deliberately
still permissive, so this row's `Holder[u16] <- Holder[i64]` line is NOT
closed. Reopen or split if that matters.

THE RULE IS LAYOUT IDENTITY, NOT TYPE EQUALITY. Signedness is deliberately
excluded: `i64` and `u64` occupy the same eight bytes, so a container of one
read as the other reinterprets nothing — only the value's meaning changes,
which is the ordinary integer coercion the language allows at scalar
positions. The first attempt gated on 'any two differing numeric types' and
rejected `fn find[T](..) -> Option[u64] { .. return Some(i); }` with `i: i64`,
which is a TESTED shape (`enum_payload_push_does_not_change_integer_coercion`)
— that test is what caught the miscalibration. What must be invariant is
width, and int-vs-float at equal width (`Vec[i64]` into `ref Vec[f64]` printed
5e-324).

LITERAL ADOPTION WAS THE HARD HALF. Unsuffixed integer literals default to
`i64`, so closing the hole rejected a pile of legitimate code until each
literal position learned to adopt its context first:
  * collection literals now adopt BEFORE `check_assignable`, not after. The
    existing re-record block asserted 'acceptance semantics are unchanged —
    check_assignable above already ruled', which was true only while the check
    was permissive about numeric width.
  * `Array[T, N]`-typed PREFIX literals adopt too — the dedicated check-mode
    arm recognised only `ArrayLiteral`, so `first(Array[10, 20, 30])` against
    `Array[i32, 3]` slipped past it.
  * an `Option`/`Result` payload that is an unsuffixed int literal pushes the
    slot inward (`let o: Option[u16] = Some(3)`). LITERALS ONLY: `Some(i)`
    with a variable stays in synthesis mode, which is precisely the case the
    surrounding comment warned a blanket push would break.
Range checking is unaffected — `let v: Vec[i8] = [200]` and `Some(300)` into
`Option[u8]` are still rejected.

SCOPE, and why: enforced for the LAYOUT-BEARING containers (Vec, VecDeque,
Option, Result, Map, Set). A USER generic keeps the old permissive behaviour,
because enforcing it there rejects `let b: Box[i32] = Box.new(5)` — the
literal seeds `T = i64` through generic inference and never sees the
annotation. Fixing THAT needs expected-type SEEDING of a generic call's type
params, which is a real change of its own and was not attempted at the end of
this session. Three tests pin the gap (`test_copy_bound_generic_method_callable_on_primitive`, `test_volatile_cell_copy_bound_*`,
`test_tensor_body_annotation_generic_shape_param_ok`) — they pass today only
because user generics are excluded.

A LIVE INSTANCE WAS FOUND IN THE BOOK. `docs/book/src/ch01b-two-surfaces.md`
passes an unannotated `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]` (`Vec[i64]`) to a
`ref Vec[i32]` parameter. It MISCOMPILES today: interp `found at index 3`,
AOT `found at index 6`. `tests/book_snippets.rs` was asserting that snippet
compiles, so the suite was actively guarding the bug. Annotated the literal;
both backends now agree. Worth noting the shape — an unannotated collection
literal flowing into a narrower-element param — is the most likely way a real
user meets this, and it was in the FIRST chapter that shows a function call.

SCOPE GAP CLOSED (e7a04ac) — user generics are no longer exempt, so this
row's `Holder[u16] <- Holder[i64]` line is now REJECTED along with the rest.

The blocker was `let b: Box[i32] = Box.new(5)`: the literal seeds `T = i64`
through generic inference and never consults the annotation. Unifying the
instantiated return `Box[?T]` against the expectation `Box[i32]` binds
`?T = i32` BEFORE arguments are solved, so the literal is then checked against
`i32`. Call-side twin of `infer_struct_literal_expected`'s existing `seeded`
arm (B-2026-07-18-17).

TWO CALIBRATIONS, both found by measurement after a wrong first guess:
  1. The seed gates on the instantiated RETURN carrying a metavar, NOT on the
     callee's formal-generics list. For `impl[T] Box[T] { fn new(..) }` the
     `T` belongs to the IMPL, so the fn's formals list is empty while the
     return is `Box[?0]` — gating on formals left exactly the target case
     unseeded, and a trace of the seed site is what showed it.
  2. The expectation is published only for a PATH-callee call. A bare
     `ExprKind::Call` gate LEAKED it into a nested call inside an argument:
     `let b = Bag { items: [..] }` is unannotated, so its expectation is an
     unsolved metavar, and the first inner call bound that metavar instead —
     after which `T` failed to infer at all. The comment I had written
     claiming the `take()` prevented this was simply wrong; the existing test
     `test_generic_struct_literal_infers_param_from_container_field` caught
     it. Both cases are now pinned by tests.

ONE EXCLUSION REMAINS, by name: `Tensor`. Enforcing invariance there rejects a
tested, correct program because tensor arithmetic infers an f64 element for an
f32 operand pair — filed as B-2026-08-05-26 with the reasoning that excluding
one name is narrower and more honest than leaving EVERY user generic
permissive to hide it. Remove the exclusion when that row closes.

The allowlist is now an inverted denylist for exactly that reason: an
allowlist could never have closed this row, since the reported surface
explicitly included a user-defined generic struct.

title: A whole-value binding-to-binding move of a BOXED-payload `Option` (`let b2 = body;`) double-frees at -O0 -- deterministic, no destructure involved, and it SURVIVES B-2026-08-05-7's leak-B fix
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while reducing B-2026-08-05-7's leak B, as the control that was supposed to show a whole-value move behaving correctly. It does not. Re-verified at 486f655 (i.e. WITH leak B's fix f380a8f in place), so it is a distinct defect and not a leftover of that row.

REPRO, minimal and complete. `Wide` is 4 words, wider than the seeded `Option` payload area of 3, so the payload is heap-BOXED:

    struct Wide { tag: i64, payload: String }
    fn mk_wide() -> Wide {
        Wide { tag: 7, payload: "boxed-option-payload-string-long-enough-aaaa".to_string() }
    }
    fn read2() -> i64 {
        let mut body: Option[Wide] = None;
        body = Some(mk_wide());
        let b2 = body;                       // <-- the whole-value move
        match b2 { Some(w) => { w.tag + (w.payload.len() as i64) } None => 0 }
    }
    fn main() {
        let mut acc = 0i64; let mut i = 0;
        while i < 50 { acc = acc + read2(); i = i + 1; }
        println(acc);
    }

  KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 -> ASAN `attempting double-free`. Deterministic: 8/8 at
                       239c5e4, 4/4 again at 486f655.
  KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=2 -> clean, but see the SCOPE caveat below.

DELETE the `let b2 = body;` line and match `body` directly: CLEAN. That single line is the whole trigger.

INDEPENDENT OF ANY DESTRUCTURE, which is what separates it from B-2026-08-05-7's leak A. The variant above has no destructure at all and fails; the sibling that also destructures the payload in the arm (`Some(w) => { let Wide { tag, payload } = w; ... }`) fails identically. Both still fail after leak A (02f5562) and leak B (f380a8f) landed.

HYPOTHESIS, explicitly NOT verified -- stated so the next person starts from a measurement rather than from this paragraph. Both `body` and `b2` may end up owning the box: the let-site registers a `BoxedEnumDrop` for each (`track_boxed_enum_var` inserts both names into `boxed_enum_payload_vars`), and the suppressor that would disarm the source, `suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move`, DOES consult `boxed_enum_payload_vars` and zero the slot -- but its call sites are struct-literal field inits, call arguments and method receivers (src/codegen/{call_dispatch,calls,exprs,channel}.rs). A plain binding-to-binding `let b2 = body;` is not among them. Confirm with an `eprintln!` at the suppressor's entry before writing anything; B-2026-08-05-7's METHOD NOTE recommends that loop over reading code and guessing, and this row's own first mechanism guess (a consuming-callee ownership story, offered for the b04_7/b31 regressions) was WRONG -- the real cause there was an unresolvable inner-drop name, which f380a8f's filter fixes.

SCOPE CAVEAT, honest about what was and was not measured: -O2 is clean HERE, but the payload in this reduction is read only through `.len()` and a scalar field, which is exactly B-2026-08-04-17's dead-payload masking. Whether a program that genuinely reads the payload bytes aborts on a DEFAULT build has NOT been measured. That is the first thing to check, and it decides whether this is an -O0-only nuisance or a user-facing abort; severity is set high on the assumption it is the latter, and should be lowered if measurement says otherwise.

REPRODUCE with the probe added alongside this row:

    KARAC_PROBE_SRC=<file>.kara KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 cargo test --features llvm \
      --test memory_sanitizer -- --ignored --exact \
      memory_sanitizer_tests::asan_probe_from_env --nocapture

Check the `PROBE <n> allocations` line appears before trusting a clean result -- two false CLEANs during this reduction came from invocations that never ran (wrong cwd; a `git stash` that took the probe test with it), and a run that produces no output greps identically to a run that passed. Match all three ASAN signatures too: grepping only for `byte(s) leaked` reports a DOUBLE FREE as clean, which cost a wrong conclusion here before it was caught.

FIXED 2026-08-05 in e7023333.

SEVERITY WAS UNDER-RATED, and this row named that as the first thing to check.
The SCOPE CAVEAT asked whether a program that genuinely reads the payload aborts
on a DEFAULT build. Measured across every level, on the reduction verbatim AND
on a variant whose payload is consumed byte by byte:

    OPT=0   rc=139  SIGSEGV
    OPT=1   rc=139  SIGSEGV
    OPT=2   rc=134  glibc `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
    OPT=3   rc=134  same

Both variants, identically. So the row's "-O2 -> clean" is wrong: this is a hard
crash on a default `karac build`, not an -O0 nuisance. The clean -O2 reading
came from running the reduction under a path that never exercised it; the row's
own suspicion (B-2026-08-04-17 dead-payload masking) was the right thing to
check but was not what happened -- the ORIGINAL reduction aborts at -O2 too.

MECHANISM CONFIRMED BY INSTRUMENTATION, per this row's instruction to start from
a measurement. Temporary `eprintln!` at both ends of the hypothesis:

    PROBE track_boxed_enum_var name=body enum=Option variant=Some
    PROBE track_boxed_enum_var name=b2   enum=Option variant=Some
    (no `suppress_called_on=body` anywhere in the run)

Two `BoxedEnumDrop` registrations on one box, and the suppressor never reached
the source. That is the row's stated HYPOTHESIS, now measured rather than
inferred.

THE FIX applies the suppressor that already existed.
`suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move` zeroes the moved-from box word and
is called at every OTHER move site -- call arguments, struct-literal field
inits, method receivers, channel sends. A plain `let` initializer was simply not
among its call sites, exactly as this row predicted. One call added in the `let`
arm, after the destination registers and after the value is stored, so the store
lands on a source whose bytes are already copied out. Self-gated on
`boxed_enum_payload_vars`.

NOT A NEW MECHANISM: the same `let` arm already performs the container-bodies
equivalent, whose comment reads "or the body fires twice". This is that
retraction's boxed-enum peer, which had been missing.

TEST: `asan_whole_value_move_of_boxed_option_frees_the_box_once`. Its payload is
consumed BYTE BY BYTE rather than through `.len()`, deliberately: reading via
`.len()` is what let the original reduction look -O2-clean, so a fixture written
that way could pass against a compiler that still aborts. Stash-proven RED with
the fix reverted. AOT matches the interpreter oracle at every opt level
(2550 / 217350).

GATES: full `--features llvm` suite 13,067 passed / 0 failed / 0 skips on the
merged tree (re-run after rebasing onto five commits that touched
