tracker: src/codegen/bce_interproc.rs + bce_length_pin.rs (the proven-in-bounds fact); the overflow-check emitter for integer `+` on an index expression
title: The INTEGER-OVERFLOW check on an index add `v[base + i]` is still emitted after BCE has PROVEN `0 <= base + i < v.len()` -- a fact that already entails the add cannot overflow. The check sits on the loop-carried critical path, so on kata #246 it, not bounds checking, is the entire residual 1.23x vs C: removing the bounds checks moved the kata only 3%, while adding an equivalent overflow check to the C mirror lands C exactly on Kara's time. Writing the same loop over a `Slice` row-view reaches full C parity today (35.07 vs 35.16 ms), because the row view removes the add entirely.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found re-measuring kata #246 after B-2026-08-05-6's interprocedural
fix (c87f488) landed, to check whether the kata's headline number finally moved.
It did not, and chasing why produced this. Supersedes B-2026-08-04-8's
attribution -- see the CORRECTION appended to that row.

THE CLAIM, PRECISELY. `bce_interproc.rs` proves a callee's index precondition and
discharges it at the call sites, so for the punch loop in #246 the compiler
establishes `0 <= base + lo < corpus.len()`. `corpus.len()` is an i64 that fits
in memory, so that fact ENTAILS `base + lo` does not overflow i64. The bounds
check is dropped on the strength of it; the overflow check on the very same add
is not. The fact needed to kill the `jo` is already computed -- it is simply not
consumed by the overflow-check emitter.

DISASSEMBLY, x86 container, karac 239c5e4f, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`. The #246 punch
loop, which both binaries fully inline into `main`:

  BCE off (KARAC_BCE_INTERPROC=0)   21 insns   2x (lea; cmp $0x9c400; jae panic)
  BCE on                            18 insns   0 bounds checks, but keeps
                                               `mov %rax,%r13; add %r15,%r13; jo panic`
  C (clang -O3)                     15 insns   neither

So the elision removed exactly 3 of the 6 excess instructions, and the remaining
3 are the checked add: a `mov`+`add` that C does not need (it indexes with one
addressing mode) plus the `jo`.

MEASURED, hyperfine, --warmup 10 --runs 80, min-of-80 (the mean is outlier-prone
on this container; the ordering is the same either way):

  C ptr-folded (as shipped)            35.16 ms   1.00x
  C base+idx, UNCHECKED                35.15 ms   1.00x   <- the address form is free
  C base+idx + __builtin_add_overflow  43.04 ms   1.23x   <- the check is the cost
  kara base+idx, BCE ON                43.71 ms   1.25x
  kara base+idx, BCE OFF               45.12 ms   1.29x
  kara Slice row-view                  35.07 ms   1.00x   <- full parity

Read it as three separate results. (1) BCE ON vs OFF is the value of
B-2026-08-05-6 on this kata: 1.29x -> 1.25x, about 3%. Real, sound, and nearly
worthless here -- and note 3% does NOT clear this lane's ~1.15x noise floor on
its own; it is quoted only because the elision is confirmed in the disassembly,
so the timing is pricing a change already known to have happened. (2) The middle
pair is the control that identifies the residual: rewriting C to Kara's
`base+idx` shape costs NOTHING (35.15 vs 35.16), and adding only the overflow
check moves it to 43.04 -- landing on Kara's 43.71 within 1.6%. So the residual
is the check, not the addressing, and not codegen quality. (3) The Slice row-view
row shows the gap is reachable in the language as it stands.

WHY RUST DOES NOT PAY IT, which corroborates the mechanism from another angle:
this kata's lane has both `rust` (23.03 ms) and `rust_ovf`
(`-C overflow-checks=on`, 23.21 ms) and they are a tie. Rust's mirror indexes a
row SLICE by `lo` alone, so there is no `base + i` add for the check to apply
to. Overflow checking is not intrinsically expensive here; checking an add that
only exists because the row was addressed by offset is.

THE `Slice` SPELLING, and why it is evidence rather than a workaround. Written as
`fn is_strobogrammatic(row: Slice[u8], len: i64)` called with
`corpus[i*len .. i*len + len]`, the punch loop compiles to 15 instructions with
NO bounds check and NO overflow check -- instruction-for-instruction C's loop --
and runs at 35.07 ms. VERIFIED SOUND rather than assumed: a probe that hands the
helper an 8-element row view while claiming `len = 40` traps correctly on BOTH
backends (AOT `panic ... vec index out of bounds`, interpreter
`index 39 out of bounds (len 8)`), so the checks are proven away in the honest
program, not skipped. The kata KEEPS the `base+idx` form -- that is the surface
that exposes this gap and must not be rewritten away; the slice form is committed
ALONGSIDE it as `bench/strobogrammatic_slice.kara`, per the kata rule to probe
every canonical spelling. Both agree on the sink (325454619) across interp, JIT,
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` build and default auto-par build.

FIX DIRECTION. Where BCE has established `0 <= base + i < v.len()` for an index
expression, mark that add non-overflowing and let the overflow-check emitter skip
it. This is narrower than a general overflow-elision pass: it reuses a fact the
BCE pass has already proven and applies only to the add feeding the index. The
soundness argument is the same one the bounds skip already rests on, so it lives
or dies with a mechanism that is now gated by the codegen-E2E + memory_sanitizer
x86 AND arm64 suites. It should carry its own kill switch, like its siblings.

BREADTH. Every flat/row-major traversal addressed as `base + i` -- matrix scans,
fixed-stride record buffers, per-row two-pointer checks. Exactly the population
B-2026-08-04-8 identified, which is unsurprising: this is that entry's real
finding, arrived at by measuring instead of inferring.

NOT A CORRECTNESS ISSUE: the check is sound and Kara is right to check by
default. The gap is that it is provably dead on this path and emitted anyway.

METHOD NOTE, since it is the reusable part. B-2026-08-04-8 concluded the gap was
bounds checking from an experiment that added bounds checks to C and reproduced
the magnitude. That establishes sufficiency in C, not causation in Kara -- two
different checks with similar per-iteration cost are indistinguishable by that
test. The discriminating experiment is to remove the suspect from the SUBJECT
(here, `KARAC_BCE_INTERPROC=0` vs on) rather than add it to the CONTROL. Both
halves are cheap; only one of them can falsify.

FIXED 2026-08-05 in 72f9fd7d. The elision is gated on `index_sum_var_pair` --
the index is literally `<ident> + <ident>` -- plus `index_bounds_already_proven`
returning `(true, true)`. `compile_proven_index_expr` (collections.rs) wraps the
six call sites that already had the shape
`index_bounds_already_proven(..)` then `compile_expr(index)`, and arms
`accum_overflow`'s existing one-shot latch around the index compile.

WHY THE ARMING IS PRECISE, both halves needed. (1) `<ident> + <ident>` compiles
to exactly ONE add, so the latch cannot leak onto an unrelated, unproven add --
the same argument B-2026-07-26-1 rests on. (2) A `(true, true)` on that shape
can ONLY have come from the SumIndex fact: the other path through
`index_bounds_already_proven` runs `index_var_and_offset_sign`, which requires
one operand to be an integer LITERAL (`idx ± k`) and therefore returns None --
hence `(false, false)` -- for two identifiers. So the proof backing the elision
is always the one that literally states `0 <= base + idx < len`. That second
half is not obvious from either function alone and is recorded in the doc
comment.

NO NEW SOUNDNESS SURFACE. The elision consumes the SAME fact the bounds skip
consumes, and is wrong exactly where that skip would already be an OOB access.
If the underlying analysis is ever wrong, the OOB is the bug and this is a
symptom of it.

REUSED rather than duplicated: `accum_overflow`'s latch is the single place a
checked add becomes plain, and it stays that way. The new producer
SAVE/RESTORES instead of clearing, so it can neither consume nor destroy an
arming owned by the accumulator pass -- strictly safer than the previous
unconditional set. (Audited first: the accumulator pattern requires a bare-ident
target and a `<ident> + <literal>` RHS, so no index expression is ever compiled
while that latch is armed. The save/restore is belt-and-braces.)

MEASURED, kata #246, x86 container, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, hyperfine min of 80:

  kara, KARAC_BCE_OVF_SKIP=0   44.22 ms   1.26x
  kara, fix ON                 35.22 ms   1.00x
  C clang -O3                  35.39 ms   1.01x
  kara Slice row-view          35.07 ms   1.00x

The punch loop is now 15 instructions -- instruction-for-instruction clang's --
with neither a bounds check nor an overflow trap. So the residual this entry is
about is CLOSED: the base+index spelling now measures the same as the row-view
spelling and the same as C. The kill switch reproduces the pre-fix binary.

TESTS. 2 IR tests written as a DIFFERENTIAL against the reordered (unproven)
variant of the same program: both carry the same five adds, so the assertion is
"exactly two fewer `sadd.with.overflow`" rather than an absolute count that
would rot if the fixture gained an add. The same test asserts the UNPROVABLE
adds (`lo + 1`, `i + 1`, `acc + ..`) keep their checks -- a zero count would
mean the elision fires far too widely, which an absence-assertion would have
called success. 2 E2E: correct addresses on an odd-width exact-size buffer, and
an `i64::MAX` base whose bounds are unproven and which must therefore still trap
`integer overflow`. 1 ASAN over 1009x63 rows (odd width, prime row count, exact
size) so the elided add runs at many magnitudes with no slack at the buffer end.

`--all --all-targets --features llvm -D warnings` clean; fmt clean. One

title: A fresh-temp aggregate ARGUMENT whose heap lives only behind `Option` fields registered no caller-side cleanup and leaked one payload per call -- 7492 B / 200 allocs on a DEFAULT -O2 build once the payload is read. Both ownership signals are Option-blind: `aggregate_has_heap_field` walks the LLVM type where an Option is erased i64 words, and `type_expr_has_drop_heap` excludes Option by design because bindings free it -- which a temp argument is not. (This row's original title blamed destructuring; that was wrong and is corrected in the detail.)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: reached while picking up `b27_option_enum_undestructured_drop` (432 B x12), the largest remaining -O0 failure. The first hypothesis -- that an ENUM payload leaks where a STRUCT payload does not, because `boxed_enum_payload_variants` cannot name an enum's inner drop (the same filter f380a8f made load-bearing for B-2026-08-05-7 leak B) -- is WRONG, and the 2x2 that killed it is the finding.

THE 2x2, at b404ddd, -O0, 6 iterations, 40-byte payload strings:

                        Vec-sourced        fresh-temp source
                        (`for a in xs`)    (`use_a(mk())`)
    enum payload  Val     CLEAN              360 B / 10 allocs
    struct payload Inner   CLEAN              200 B / 5 allocs

The SOURCE is the axis. Payload kind is not: both leak on a fresh temp, both are clean when the struct arrives as a moved-in owned param out of a Vec. So this is not the unresolvable-inner-drop-name family at all.

THE PASSING SIBLING WAS PASSING FOR THE WRONG REASON. `b27_option_struct_undestructured_drop_no_leak` carried ONLY the Vec-sourced half, while its enum sibling carries both that and a fresh-temp source. It never ran the broken path. Its doc comment nonetheless described the pair as covering the same ground, which is how the gap survived: the two fixtures read as a matched enum/struct pair and were not. Closed in this commit by adding the `use_a(mk())` half; it now fails at -O0 exactly like the enum one, taking the -O0 leg 10 -> 11 real failures. That is the gate getting MORE honest, not a regression.

WHY -O2 IS NOT EVIDENCE HERE, and why the added half is deliberately NOT floored with `assert_clean_asan_run_min_allocs`: `match value { Some(_) => 1, None => 0 }` never reads the payload, so this is squarely B-2026-08-04-17's DISCARD-shaped family, where LLVM at -O2 deletes the allocation REGARDLESS of whether it is freed. Both halves read clean at -O2 on the current compiler, and would read clean on a broken one too. A min-allocs floor would therefore fail at -O2 against a CORRECT compiler, which is why that row's conclusion for this family is that the -O0 sweep is the only lever and the fixture should not be contorted to chase -O2. The -O2 suite stayed green at 938/0 with the added half, so CI is unaffected.

WHERE TO LOOK, and stated as a starting point rather than a diagnosis -- this row's first mechanism guess was already wrong once, and B-2026-08-05-7's METHOD NOTE is explicit that the `eprintln!`-the-predicate loop beats reading code and guessing. In `finish_owned_struct_destructure` (src/codegen/stmts.rs) the two sources diverge at `fresh = expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp(value)`: a fresh temp takes `callee_owned_src = None`, so the `zero_struct_field_move_cap` disarm never runs, while the Option-field branch's own `source_owned` gate is `fresh || <non-ref identifier>` and so is TRUE for both. Whether the leak is a missing registration on the fresh path or a registration that fires against an already-freed source has NOT been established. Reproduce either half with the probe:

    KARAC_PROBE_SRC=<file>.kara KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 cargo test --features llvm \
      --test memory_sanitizer -- --ignored --exact \
      memory_sanitizer_tests::asan_probe_from_env --nocapture

The four 2x2 programs are four lines apart -- swap `Val`/`Inner` for the payload and `for a in build()` / `use_a(mk())` for the source.

FIXED 2026-08-05 (this commit), and THIS ROW'S OWN TITLE AND MECHANISM WERE WRONG -- corrected here rather than quietly rewritten.

THE DESTRUCTURE IS NOT INVOLVED AT ALL. This row was filed saying a fresh-temp struct source leaks when its `Option` field is DESTRUCTURED. Reducing further killed that: the callee can ignore its parameter entirely --

    fn use_a(a: A) -> i64 { 1 }        // no destructure, no match, no read
    fn main() { ... use_a(mk()) ... }  // still leaks, 200 B / 5

-- and it still leaks. A named binding instead of an inline temp (`let a = mk(); use_a(a);`) is CLEAN. So the trigger is a fresh-temp aggregate ARGUMENT, and everything about destructuring in the title above was a property of the fixtures I happened to reduce from, not of the bug.

THE REAL BOUNDARY, measured one variable at a time:
  struct P { s: String }                     fresh-temp arg -> CLEAN
  struct Q { v: Vec[i64] }                   fresh-temp arg -> CLEAN
  bare String temp arg                       fresh-temp arg -> CLEAN
  struct A { value: Option[String] }         fresh-temp arg -> LEAKS 200 B / 5
  struct A { value: Option[Inner] }          fresh-temp arg -> LEAKS 200 B / 5
  struct A { value: Option[Inner], tag: String }              -> CLEAN
The last row is the whole diagnosis in one line: adding ANY plain heap field makes it clean, because that field is LLVM-visible and the temp then gets its drop for an unrelated reason, with the Option payload riding along. A struct whose heap lives ONLY behind `Option` fields gets no caller-temp cleanup at all.

ROOT CAUSE, confirmed by instrumenting the predicate rather than by reading code (the method note's loop, after this row's first guess was wrong). At the call-argument site both ownership signals are blind:
  * `aggregate_has_heap_field` walks the LLVM TYPE, and an `Option` field lowers to erased `i64` payload words (or a box pointer), never a `{ptr,len,cap}`. This is the same blindness the enum-leaf case beside it already documents.
  * the source-level fallback then asks `type_expr_has_drop_heap`, which returns FALSE for `Option`/`Result` BY DESIGN -- its own comment says "their inline payloads are freed by the let-binding machinery". True for a binding. A fresh-temp ARGUMENT has no binding.
Measured directly: `llvm_heap=false copy_supported=true any_drop_heap=false -> NEEDS=false` for the leaking shapes, and `llvm_heap=true -> NEEDS=true` for the clean one. The IR confirms it: the struct's drop fn IS synthesized and IS called in the callee, but `main` never calls it for the temp (1 call vs 2 in the clean variant).

FIX: `option_field_te_has_drop_heap` (synth_drop.rs), a narrow companion to `type_expr_has_drop_heap` that reports true for an `Option`/`Result` field whose payload is something a drop would actually free, joined into the call-argument site's source-level fallback. `Option[i64]` stays false, so no spurious cleanup is registered. `type_expr_has_drop_heap` itself is UNCHANGED -- it is consulted in many places and its carve-out is correct for all of them; only this one caller must not inherit it. The change stays under the existing `copy_supported` gate, so the ownership argument is untouched: the callee entry-copies a copy-supported struct, so the caller temp is an independent buffer nothing else frees.

SEVERITY WAS UNDERSTATED: this is a DEFAULT-BUILD leak, not -O0-only. The row was filed at medium on the strength of an -O0-only reproduction, but that reproduction used `Some(_)`, which never reads the payload -- B-2026-08-04-17's discard masking, again. Give the payload a runtime-derived value and a byte-level read and it leaks 7492 B in 200 allocations at DEFAULT -O2, identical at -O0, through the ordinary `karac build`. Raised to high.

GATES: -O0 sweep 11 -> 9 real failures, closing BOTH b27 fixtures (the enum one and the struct one whose missing fresh-temp half this row added). -O2 memory_sanitizer 939/0, codegen E2E 2800/0, par_codegen + interpreter + typechecker green, fmt + clippy clean.

REGRESSION: `asan_fresh_temp_arg_option_only_heap_no_leak`, written to B-2026-08-04-17's three rules so it cannot go vacuous -- `env.args().len()` seed, runtime-derived payload content, `starts_with` byte read -- and floored at 100 allocations. Proven live rather than inert: it FAILS against the unfixed compiler with the full 7492 B, and passes with the fix.

tracker: tests/selfhost_codegen.rs (run_ir + RUNNER_ERR guard), tests/lljit_e2e.rs (jit_run_program guard), and the status Display argument in the seven selfhost binary oracles
title: the JIT/selfhost oracles report a module that NEVER RAN as an output mismatch: run_ir discarded karac_jit_runner's stderr, so an unresolved external surfaced as `left: "" / right: <expected>` beside correct-looking IR -- the presentation that cost B-2026-07-16-16 and B-2026-08-05-14 -- and the seven build-and-run oracles printed only stderr, so a SIGSEGV rendered as an empty message
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: not found by a probe -- surfaced twice by the COST of not having it.
B-2026-07-16-16 (2026-07-16) and B-2026-08-05-14 (2026-08-05) are different bugs
with an identical presentation in `tests/selfhost_codegen.rs`: `left: "" /
right: <expected>`, printed beside an IR dump that reads as structurally
correct. Both were LINK failures -- the emitted module named an external symbol
the host could not resolve -- and in both cases the oracle had the information
to say so and threw it away.

THE GAP, three separate shapes across the JIT/selfhost oracle family.

(1) `tests/selfhost_codegen.rs::run_ir` captured the runner's stdout and exit
    code and DISCARDED stderr. When LLJIT cannot resolve a symbol it prints
    `karac_jit_runner: ...` / `JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ ... ]`
    there and produces no stdout, so the oracle's first assertion -- stdout
    parity against the seed -- fired on `""` and reported a MISMATCH. The
    module never ran at all. Reading that as a miscompile means auditing
    correct IR, which is what both bugs above cost.

(2) `tests/lljit_e2e.rs::jit_run_program` had the same shape: stderr dropped, a
    failed run reaching the caller as `("", nonzero)` so every one of its
    ~16 tests would report `assert_eq!(out, "42\n")` failing on an empty
    string rather than "the module did not link".

(3) The seven selfhost oracles that build a Kara binary and run it
    (`selfhost_lexer` / `parser` / `parser_items` / `parser_types` /
    `resolver` / `typechecker` / `codegen`) asserted `run.status.success()`
    and printed ONLY stderr. A binary that dies by SIGNAL writes nothing to
    stderr, so the entire failure message rendered as the literal text
    "<name> exited nonzero:" followed by a blank line. Live example: with
    02f5562 on main, `selfhost_parser_matches_rust_parser_items` and
    `selfhost_resolver_matches_rust_resolver` both fail exactly that way, and
    the message does not distinguish a segfault from a clean `exit(1)`.

FIX. (1) and (2) discriminate on the `karac_jit_runner:` prefix, which every
harness-level failure inside the runner carries and which a program's own
failure never does -- `emit_panic` lowers to `printf` + `exit(1)`, unprefixed
-- so tests that legitimately expect a nonzero exit are unaffected. A match
fails with an explicit "FAILED TO RUN -- this is a link/JIT failure, NOT an
output mismatch" plus the runner's stderr, BEFORE any output comparison. (3)
adds `run.status` to the message; `ExitStatus`'s Display renders
"signal: 11 (SIGSEGV)" or "exit status: 1", which is the whole difference
between a crash and a clean nonzero exit.

VERIFIED by reproducing the Darwin failure ON LINUX: handing the emitter the
non-host `stdout` spelling makes the corpus modules unresolvable here, and the
oracle now reports

    emitted IR for corpus[0] ("fn main() { println(\"hi\") }") FAILED TO RUN
    -- this is a link/JIT failure, NOT an output mismatch. ...
    JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ __stdoutp ]

which is B-2026-08-05-14 diagnosed from the failure text alone. Shape (3) was
verified against the live 02f5562 regression, where the message went from an
empty stderr to `signal: 11 (SIGSEGV)` -- i.e. from "something went wrong" to
"the binary is crashing, look for memory corruption".

NOT A COMPILER BUG. Nothing shipped is wrong; this is test-harness
diagnosability. Filed because the class has now cost two multi-hour
misdiagnoses and the information was present and discarded both times, which
is the same shape as B-2026-08-04-17 (a fixture hazard that made green runs
meaningless) rather than a style preference.

FIXED 2026-08-05 (9e25bfaa) in the same slice that filed it -- the fix is three
assertions and one extra format argument, so splitting the file from the fix
would have cost more than it documented.

WHAT IS NOT COVERED: the discrimination is on the runner's stderr PREFIX, so a
future harness-level failure inside `karac_jit_runner` that prints without the
`karac_jit_runner:` prefix would fall through to the old behaviour. That is a
convention the runner already follows at every one of its error sites, but it
is a convention, not a type.

title: `main` is RED: tests/cli.rs::wasm_browser_rich_exports_marshal_e2e fails a typecheck since 80d7a37c (B-2026-08-05-19, generic args invariant across numeric LAYOUTS). Its inline fixture writes `Result.Err(0 - 1)` in a fn returning `Result[i32, i32]`, which the new invariance rule correctly rejects as `Result<T, i64>` -- so this looks like a FIXTURE that the typechecker fix outgrew, not a regression in the fix. Gated behind --features llvm, which is why it survived the authoring run.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while re-running the full `--features llvm` suite after rebasing
B-2026-08-05-21's codegen work onto a `main` that had advanced 6 commits. Not
my change: ATTRIBUTION VERIFIED by stashing the codegen diff and running the
single test on clean origin/main (e39a0f83), where it fails identically.

THE FAILURE:

  error[typecheck]: richlib.kara:19:24: expected 'Result<i32, i32>',
                    found 'Result<T, i64>'
     |
  19 |     if b == 0 { return Result.Err(0 - 1); }

`0 - 1` is integer-literal arithmetic that infers i64; the enclosing function
returns `Result[i32, i32]`. Before 80d7a37c that flowed; the invariance rule now
refuses it. On the face of it the RULE is right and the FIXTURE is stale -- the
literal wants to be written at i32 -- but that call belongs to the author of
80d7a37c, which is why this is filed rather than patched from under them.

WHY IT SURVIVED: `tests/cli.rs` is `--features llvm`-gated, so a plain
`cargo test` never builds it. The same gate that hides codegen regressions hides
this one.

NOTE ON THE RUN THAT FOUND IT: cargo stops at the first failing test BINARY, so
the initial post-rebase run reported only 1,769 tests and never reached
`codegen` / `memory_sanitizer` at all. Re-running with `--no-fail-fast` gave the
real picture (13,056 passed, this one failure). Worth remembering -- a truncated
run looks like a much smaller suite, not like an aborted one.

FIXED 2026-08-05 in 8d6d1b92 -- and the diagnosis in this row's TITLE was WRONG,
which is the part worth keeping.

IT IS NOT A STALE FIXTURE. Filed as "looks like a FIXTURE that the typechecker
fix outgrew", on the reasoning that `0 - 1` infers i64 and the new invariance
rule correctly rejects it. Probing before touching anything showed the real
shape:

    Some(1)             OK        Option.Some(1)        REJECTED
    Some(-1)            OK        Option.Some(-1)       REJECTED
    Ok(1) / Err(-1)     OK        Result.Ok(1)/.Err(-1) REJECTED

The BARE constructor adopts its expected payload type; the QUALIFIED one does
not. Position is irrelevant (return, let-annotated and tail all behave the
same) -- the axis is the spelling, which the language treats as equivalent
everywhere else. So `main` was red on a genuine typechecker gap, not on a
fixture that needed updating.

ROOT CAUSE, one line: the check-mode adoption block in
`typechecker/exprs.rs` is entered under `if let ExprKind::Identifier(ctor) =
&callee.kind`. `Option.Some(..)` is an `ExprKind::Path` with segments
`["Option", "Some"]`, so it never reached the block and its literal stayed i64.

NOT A REGRESSION FROM 80d7a37c -- that commit REVEALED it. While generic
arguments were permissive about numeric width, `Option<i64>` against
`Option<i32>` was simply tolerated, so the missing adoption had no visible
effect. B-2026-08-05-19 closed that hole and the latent gap became a hard error.
Worth recording because the obvious reading -- "the typecheck fix broke this" --
is wrong and would have led to weakening a sound rule.

WHAT 80d7a37c DID ANTICIPATE: it added
`generic_numeric_arg_same_layout_and_literals_still_accepted`, whose comment
says "unsuffixed literals must still adopt their context", and it covers
`let o: Option[u16] = Some(3)`. Every case in it uses the BARE spelling, so the
qualified arm went untested. The new test asserts the two spellings in PAIRS
for exactly that reason.

THE FIX derives the constructor name from either an `Identifier` callee or a
two-segment `Option`/`Result` path. The existing `(ctor, expected)` match
already pairs `Some` with `Option` and `Ok`/`Err` with `Result`, so a
mismatched qualifier (`Result.Some`) still falls through to `None` -- no new
acceptance beyond making the spellings agree.

TESTS: `qualified_enum_ctor_literal_adopts_expected_type_like_bare` asserts
bare/qualified in pairs across return, let and tail position, plus the narrow
element type (`Option[u16]`), plus TWO negatives that pin the fix from becoming
"believe the expectation" -- `Option.Some(300)` into `Option[u8]` must still be
out of range, and `Result.Ok(1)` into an `Option[i32]` must still error.
Stash-proven RED with the fix reverted. Full `--features llvm` suite 13,059
passed / 0 failed; clippy and fmt clean. `main` is green again.

tracker: src/typechecker/exprs.rs — the check-mode enum-payload adoption block (`payload_is_unsuffixed_int`)
title: A constant integer EXPRESSION payload does not adopt its expected type in an enum constructor: `Result.Err(0 - 1)` into `Result[i32, i32]` is rejected as i64, while `Result.Err(-1)` is accepted. Affects the bare and qualified spellings identically (since B-2026-08-05-24), so this is a payload-SHAPE limit, not a spelling one: adoption fires for an unsuffixed literal but not for arithmetic over literals.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out while fixing B-2026-08-05-24. The red `main` fixture wrote
`Result.Err(0 - 1)`; making the qualified spelling adopt (8d6d1b92) fixed the
spelling half but `0 - 1` still does not adopt, so the fixture was moved to the
natural `-1`.

THE SHAPE, after 8d6d1b92 -- symmetric in both spellings, which is the point:

    Some(1)        OK      Option.Some(1)        OK
    Some(-1)       OK      Option.Some(-1)       OK
    Some(0 - 1)    REJECTED  Option.Some(0 - 1)  REJECTED

So `-1` adopts and `0 - 1` does not. Both are compile-time constants and both
are natural spellings; a reader has no way to predict which one the checker
accepts.

WHY IT IS FILED RATHER THAN FIXED, and why the obvious fix is not obviously
right. The adoption predicate is deliberately narrow. The code comment above it
records the reason: pushing the expected type at EVERY payload changes integer
handling -- `return Some(i)` with `i: i64` into an `Option[u64]` then
check-mode-coerces and trips the i64->u64 narrowing diagnostic where synthesis
mode accepted it, which `book_snippets_compile` caught on ch08's `find[T]`.
Extending from "unsuffixed literal" to "constant expression over literals" is a
smaller step than a blanket push, but it is the same class of change and needs
its own regression pass over the book snippets and the kata corpus, not a
one-line predicate widening.

SEVERITY low: the workaround is to write the constant directly (`-1`) or to
suffix it (`0i32 - 1i32`), and the diagnostic, while not pointing at the real
issue, does name both types. It is filed because the accept/reject line between
`-1` and `0 - 1` is arbitrary from the outside, and because a const-folding step
before the adoption check would likely subsume it.

FIXED (895ea26). The cause was an ASYMMETRY I INTRODUCED in B-2026-08-05-19:
expected-type seeding fired only for a PATH callee, so `Option.Some(0 - 1)`
adopted `i32` while bare `Some(0 - 1)` kept the literal's `i64`.

THAT CORRECTS THIS ROW'S OWN CLAIM. It states the bug 'affects the bare and
qualified spellings identically … so this is a payload-SHAPE limit, not a
spelling one'. Measured, the qualified spelling ALREADY WORKED and only the
bare one failed — it was a spelling asymmetry after all, sitting on top of the
payload-shape limit the row correctly identified. Either half alone would have
hidden the other.

The bare constructors now seed too. Narrow on purpose: `Some`/`Ok`/`Err` are
constructors rather than arbitrary calls, so admitting them does not reopen
the nested-call leak the Path restriction exists for. And the case this row
flags as the reason not to widen — `return Some(i)` with `i: i64` into an
`Option[u64]` — is untouched, because seeding binds the RETURN type and the
payload is then an ordinary scalar assignment where numeric coercion stays
permissive. Verified against both spellings; the row's caution was right about
the risk and wrong about this particular route avoiding it.

ONE GUARD HAD TO BE TIGHTENED, and an existing test caught it rather than
review: the seeding guard rejected inference METAVARS only, but an unannotated
generic struct literal checks its field against the DECLARED slot
(`Option[T]` with a bare `T`), so seeding bound the payload to the parameter's
own name and `T` then could not be inferred at all
(`let b = Boxed { v: Some("x".to_string()) }`). It now rejects an
un-instantiated `TypeParam` as well.

REGRESSION PASS, which this row explicitly asked for rather than a one-line
widening: book_snippets 1 passed, typechecker 2136, codegen 2805,
memory_sanitizer 943, clippy --all-targets and fmt clean.

title: tensor arithmetic infers an f64 element for an f32 operand pair: `let p: Tensor[f32, [D]] = a * k` with `a: ref Tensor[f32, [D]]` and `k: f32` types the product `Tensor[f64, ..]`, which only stayed invisible because generic args were permissive about numeric width
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by B-2026-08-05-19, which made generic arguments
invariant across numeric LAYOUTS. `Tensor` had to be excluded BY NAME from
that rule to keep a tested program compiling — this row is that exclusion's
reason, recorded so the exclusion can be removed once it is fixed rather
than becoming permanent by default.

REPRO (`tests/typechecker.rs::test_tensor_body_annotation_generic_shape_param_ok`
is the existing coverage):

    fn scale[D](a: ref Tensor[f32, [D]], k: f32) -> f32 {
        let p: Tensor[f32, [D]] = a * k;   // product types as Tensor[f64, [D]]
        p.sum()
    }

Both operands are f32 — the tensor's element and the scalar — so the product
has no f64 anywhere to come from. With numeric generic args held invariant
the annotation then reports `expected 'Tensor<f32, [3]>', found
'Tensor<f64, [3]>'`.

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: `types_compatible` treats any float pair as
compatible, so `Tensor[f64]` silently satisfied a `Tensor[f32]` annotation.
The mis-inference has presumably always been there; only the check that
would notice it is new.

NOT DIAGNOSED: no attempt was made to find where the f64 enters — the
tensor binop element rule, a literal-typed scalar operand defaulting to
f64, or the shape-generic instantiation are all candidates. What IS known is
that it is element inference and not variance, because the annotation names
the element explicitly and is still not honoured.

WHETHER IT MISCOMPILES IS UNTESTED. If the product really is computed and
stored as f64 while the binding claims f32, that is the same
layout-reinterpretation class as the parent row and would be high, not
medium. If the f64 is only a typing artifact that codegen ignores, it is a
diagnostics-quality issue. Deciding that is the first step for whoever picks
this up — build the repro with an f32 annotation and compare against an
interpreter run.

FIXED (a64e931) — AND THIS ROW'S OWN DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG. Corrected here so
nobody re-runs the dead end.

IT IS NOT TENSOR ARITHMETIC. The element-wise binop propagates the tensor's
own element type correctly and was never involved. The f64 comes from
`Tensor.from`: unsuffixed float literals default to `f64`, and
`infer_tensor_from` took its element from `infer_expr(leaves[0])` with no
expected-type input, so

    let x: Tensor[f32, [3]] = Tensor.from([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]);

typed `Tensor[f64, [3]]` and never consulted the annotation.

TWO SIGNALS THAT SHOULD HAVE CAUGHT THE MISDIAGNOSIS EARLIER, both available
when the row was filed: the error's POSITION was the `Tensor.from` call, not
the multiply; and writing `1.0f32` made it pass, which is the signature of
literal adoption rather than an arithmetic rule. The row was written from the
test's failure message without reducing it.

So this is the same class as the integer-literal work in B-2026-08-05-19, at
a site that pass missed. The fix reuses the expectation that seeding already
publishes for a path-callee call: `Tensor.from` adopts the expected element
and CHECKS each leaf against it, so literals adopt while a genuinely wrong
leaf still errors, and with no expectation the first leaf still drives
inference.

CONSEQUENCE FOR B-2026-08-05-19: its last carve-out is gone. Both exemptions
that arm carried — user generics and `Tensor` — are removed, so numeric-layout
invariance now applies to EVERY generic with no denylist, and
`layout_bearing_generic` plus its permissive sibling were deleted rather than
left as no-ops.

NOT FIXED, and filed as B-2026-08-05-31: with the type now correctly `f32`,
the INTERPRETER still computes tensor elements in f64 while AOT uses a packed
f32 buffer, so `0.1 * 3` over a `Tensor[f32]` prints differently on the two
backends. That is a separate, pre-existing representation gap
(`Value::Tensor` holds boxed f64 `Value`s), not a typing question.

title: The surface-concat RECEIVER gap is only closed for the len-family: `("p:".to_string() + s).starts_with(..)` still leaks the concat on a DEFAULT -O2 build (8200 B / 200 allocs). The len leg's fixture reads `.len()` only, which masks the same class at -O2
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the residual half of B-2026-08-05-7's `surface_binary_string_concat_temp` leg, carved out when the len-family receiver gate was fixed. Everything below is measured on this container, not argued.

WHAT WAS FIXED, for context. A string concat the `String.add` desugar skips stays an `ExprKind::Binary`, and `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` matches `Call`/`MethodCall` only -- so every gate built on it declines the concat. B-2026-07-21-12 admitted the shape on the ARGUMENT side; the len-family RECEIVER gate (method_call.rs, the `len`/`count`/`is_empty` arm) now admits it too via `expr_is_fresh_owned_string_concat`. That closes `("p:".to_string() + s).len()` and the fixture named for it.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN: every OTHER receiver-side gate of the same shape. Measured with a byte-reading receiver instead of `.len()`:

    match v.first() {
        Some(s) => { if ("p:".to_string() + s).starts_with("p:elem") { acc = acc + 1; } }
        None => { }
    }

  KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=2 (DEFAULT) -> 8200 byte(s) leaked in 200 allocations
  KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0           -> identical
Both BEFORE and AFTER the len-family fix -- it is a different gate, so the fix does not touch it. Confirmed through the ordinary `karac build` CLI, not just the harness.

SEVERITY IS HIGH BECAUSE THIS IS A DEFAULT-BUILD LEAK, and that is the substantive finding here. The len leg reads the concat through `.len()` only, which touches the length word and never the bytes -- so at -O2 the buffer is a dead allocation LLVM deletes, and the leg reads CLEAN at -O2 while leaking at -O0. That is B-2026-08-04-17's masking, and it is why the whole `surface_binary_string_concat_temp` fixture looked like an -O0-only curiosity. Give the concat a byte-level read and the same class leaks on the surface a user actually builds. The existing fixture is not wrong, but it cannot see this half.

WHERE IT LIVES. `starts_with`/`ends_with` are compiled in `compile_vec_method` (vec_method.rs), which receives a materialized receiver POINTER rather than the receiver EXPRESSION -- so the len-family's expression-level gate has no analogue there, and whoever materialized the receiver is the one that must free it. The other receiver-side gates on `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp(object)` are method_call.rs 2697 / 13582 / 13740 / 13888 / 14067 and expr_ops.rs 855 (that last one is field access, not a String method). Each needs its own look; they are NOT obviously one edit.

DELIBERATELY NOT SWEPT ALL AT ONCE. This row's parent has had THREE over-broad ownership widenings reverted (freeing the box in `reconstruct_payload_value`; `ptr_has_any_registered_cleanup`; the unfiltered boxed-payload swap), each of which fixed its target and broke something else. Widening `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` itself would reach all these gates in one line and is exactly the shape that keeps failing -- it is consulted by the destructure-ownership paths too, where a Binary receiver means something different. The len-family fix instead added a NARROW companion predicate at one call site, which is why it gated clean (-O2 940/0, -O0 8 real failures, codegen E2E 2804/0).

FOR WHOEVER PICKS THIS UP: `expr_is_fresh_owned_string_concat` (runtime.rs) is the predicate to reuse -- expression shape AND a `llvm_ty_is_vec_struct` value check, the second half being what keeps it off scalar `a + b`. Reproduce with the probe, and note the two traps this reduction hit: a `.len()`-only read masks the leak at -O2, and a grep that matches only `byte(s) leaked` scores a double-free as clean.

FIXED 2026-08-05 (this commit).

THE CONTROL THAT LOCALIZED IT, run first because it decides the shape of the fix: a CALL receiver of the same method was already CLEAN.

    fn mk(k: i64) -> String { ... }
    mk(i).starts_with("p:elem")                  -> CLEAN at -O2 and -O0
    ("p:".to_string() + s).starts_with("p:elem") -> 8200 B / 200 allocs, both levels

So the free machinery was correct and simply never reached for a Binary receiver -- this was a predicate gap, not a missing free, which is why the change is one disjunct rather than new cleanup code.

WHERE: the fresh-temp String receiver materialization in method_call.rs stores a non-identifier receiver into a synthetic slot, dispatches through compile_vec_method, then frees the intermediate buffer -- gated on `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp || expr_is_fresh_owned_string_slice`. Both decline an `ExprKind::Binary`. Added `expr_is_fresh_owned_string_concat` (the predicate the len-family leg introduced) as a third disjunct. The result-aliasing analysis that follows is UNCHANGED and still decides whether the free is safe: `starts_with` / `contains` return a bool, so they are receiver-independent; a heap-struct result from a borrowing method stays conservatively un-freed exactly as before.

VERIFIED ACROSS THE FAMILY, at both -O levels: `starts_with`, `contains`, and the len-family shape from the parent leg all clean; the let-bound and plain-String-operand controls stay clean (they never entered this path); the Call-receiver twin stays clean, so the added disjunct introduces no double-free.

GATES: -O2 memory_sanitizer 941/0, -O0 8 real failures (unchanged -- this shape had no fixture before, so the count does not drop; the new one passes), codegen E2E 2804/0, fmt + clippy clean.

REGRESSION: `asan_surface_concat_byte_read_receiver_no_leak`, floored at 100 allocations and proven live -- it fails against the unfixed compiler with 12000 B / 400 allocations. It pins at -O2, unlike its len-consuming sibling, and the fixture comment explains why the pair differs: `.len()` never touches the bytes, so at -O2 that buffer is a dead allocation LLVM deletes.

SEPARATE GAP FOUND WHILE PROBING THE FAMILY, filed as B-2026-08-05-28: the String-to-String xform methods do not COMPILE on a Binary receiver at all -- `to_uppercase` and `trim` both fail with "no handler for method on non-identifier receiver". Pre-existing (verified against the unfixed compiler), unrelated to ownership, and it is why those two shapes could not be included in the sweep above.

tracker: src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs (dual-write of method_callee_types under SpanKey::for_method_call) + src/codegen/method_call.rs (callee_key tries method_call_key then the receiver span)
title: a String-to-String xform does not compile when its RESULT is itself a method RECEIVER — `("p:".to_string() + s).to_uppercase().len()` fails with "no handler for method on non-identifier receiver"; NOT the missing dispatcher arm this row first diagnosed (the arm exists, which is why the standalone form always worked) but SPAN CLOBBER, the outer call evicting the inner receiver's String type
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while sweeping the receiver-method family for B-2026-08-05-27 (the surface-concat receiver leak). Not an ownership bug and not caused by that fix -- verified by building the same programs against the unfixed compiler, where they fail identically.

REPRO, either method:

    match v.first() {
        Some(s) => { acc = acc + ("p:".to_string() + s).to_uppercase().len(); }
        None => { }
    }

    error: codegen failed: codegen: no handler for method 'to_uppercase' on
    non-identifier receiver (method dispatch fell through; this is a codegen
    bug -- add a dispatcher arm in compile_method_call ...)

`trim` is identical. The diagnostic is the compiler's own "this is a codegen bug" fall-through message, so it is self-identifying rather than a deliberate rejection.

WHAT WORKS on the same receiver shape, which bounds it: `starts_with`, `contains`, and `len` all compile and (since B-2026-08-05-27) free correctly. So a surface-Binary receiver reaches dispatch fine for the predicate and len families, and only the String-to-String xform family falls through.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ERGONOMICS: the fresh-temp receiver free logic has a dedicated branch for exactly this family -- it treats trim / to_lowercase / to_uppercase / the split family as allocating an INDEPENDENT copy and therefore safe to free the receiver behind. That branch is currently unreachable for a Binary receiver, so whoever adds the dispatcher arm should re-run the -O2/-O0 sweep on these two shapes rather than assume the ownership half already works: it has never executed.

NOT A REGRESSION and NOT URGENT -- a let binding is an obvious workaround (`let t = "p:".to_string() + s; t.to_uppercase()`), and that form compiles today.

RESOLVED, with BOTH this entry's diagnosis and its scope corrected.

DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG. "add a dispatcher arm in `compile_method_call`" — the
arm is already there, in `try_compile_nonident_collection_method`, and it
lists `to_uppercase` / `trim` / `split` by name. That is precisely why
`("p:".to_string() + s).to_uppercase()` compiles today. The self-
identifying "this is a codegen bug" fall-through message is accurate that
something is wrong and misleading about what.

SCOPE WAS WRONG TOO, in the direction that matters: this is NOT specific
to a surface-concat receiver, and not even to a non-identifier one.
Measured, all failing identically before the fix:
    ("p:".to_string() + s).to_uppercase().len()   Binary root
    "p:".to_string().to_uppercase().len()         MethodCall root
    f"p:{s}".to_uppercase().len()                 f-string root
    s.to_uppercase().to_lowercase()               IDENTIFIER root
    ("p:".to_string() + s).split(":").len()       `split`, same family
The last one is the tell: an identifier root fails too, so "non-identifier
receiver" describes the diagnostic's wording, not the defect. The actual
predicate is: the xform's own result is used as a RECEIVER.

ROOT CAUSE, instrumented rather than reasoned about. The parser gives a
MethodCall its RECEIVER's span, so in a chain the inner and outer calls
share one span key and the outer wins both tables the dispatch consults:
`method_callee_types` resolves to the outer call's `Type.method` (the
`m == method` filter then rejects it, yielding None) and `expr_types`
records the outer `i64`, evicting the inner `String`. A temporary eprintln
showed the identical receiver at the identical span (134, 20) reporting
    standalone: key=Some("String.to_uppercase")  is_str=true
    chained:    key=None                         is_str=false
Two independent String signals, both span-keyed, both clobbered by the
same mechanism — which is why adding a second span-keyed signal would not
have helped.

FIX: a third signal that is span-FREE — the method name. Restricted to
methods that exist ONLY on String (`to_uppercase`, `to_lowercase`, the
trim family, `starts_with`/`ends_with`, `replace`/`replacen`, `repeat`,
`split`/`split_whitespace`/`lines`). `sorted`, `contains` and `len` are
shared with Vec and are deliberately ABSENT, so a Vec receiver can never
take this path. A non-String receiver bearing one of these names would
already have failed the typechecker, which is what makes the name
sufficient evidence rather than a guess.

WHY NOT FIX THE CLOBBER AT THE SOURCE: considered and rejected for this
slice. A per-(span, method) side table would work and is the more general
answer, but it is typechecker + lowering + codegen plumbing for a defect
one predicate closes, and the span-sharing convention is load-bearing
elsewhere (the effect checker relies on the inner key resolving first —
see the comment at method_call.rs's `dispatch_key`). Recorded as the
principled follow-up if this class recurs on a method set where the name
is NOT discriminating.

OWNERSHIP SWEEP, which this entry explicitly asked for because the
fresh-temp receiver free has a dedicated branch for this family that "has
never executed": six shapes x {-O0, -O2} under
`valgrind --leak-check=full --error-exitcode=99`, ALL CLEAN, at 410–1214
allocations with an opaque `env.args().len()` seed so the loop cannot be
const-folded away (B-2026-08-04-17's non-vacuity rule). The branch works;
it simply had never been reachable. Fourteen probed shapes also match the
interpreter exactly on both backends.

TESTS: one E2E in tests/codegen.rs covering four roots (Binary,
MethodCall, f-string, identifier-with-two-xforms) plus `split`, so the
"non-identifier" mis-scoping cannot creep back into the coverage. RED
before the fix, failing on the first assertion with the original message.

FIXED 2026-08-05 (7f067c28). The row's diagnosis was HALF right and the wrong
half changes the fix, so both are recorded.

WRONG: "the String-to-String xform methods do not COMPILE on a surface-concat
receiver", with the prescription "add a dispatcher arm in compile_method_call".
The UNCHAINED form compiles today and always did:

    println(("p:".to_string() + b).to_uppercase());        -> P:Y
    let t = "p:".to_string() + b; t.to_uppercase().len();  -> fine

The trigger is the CHAIN, not the concat receiver, and no dispatcher arm was
missing. The row's own repro happens to be chained (`.to_uppercase().len()`),
which is why the concat looked like the variable.

RIGHT, and the reason it looked like a dispatch gap: the failure IS in dispatch,
just not for want of an arm. The parser sets `MethodCall.span = receiver.span`
(src/parser/exprs.rs), so every link of `x.a().b()` carries ONE span.
`method_callee_types` is span-keyed, so the outer link's insert clobbers the
inner's. At the inner call the lookup returned `String.len`, whose method
segment is not `to_uppercase`, and the pre-existing "the key must name THIS
method" filter correctly rejected it -- leaving no dispatch key, so the
String-receiver materialization declined and dispatch fell through to the
self-identifying error. `len` was unaffected because it has its own earlier arm;
`starts_with` / `contains` because they are the OUTERMOST link and win the
clobber.

This is the same class as B-2026-07-29-7 (`v.reduce_sum().to_string()`) and
B-2026-07-14-18 (`a.matmul(b).transpose()`), each previously worked around
per-feature with a collision-immune side table or a method-NAME match.
`crate::token::method_call_key` / `SpanKey::for_method_call` already exist for
exactly this and already back the `method_unwrap_*` tables (Slice 1 of the
span-collision fix). `method_callee_types` had simply never been migrated.

THE FIX IS A DUAL WRITE, and the first attempt is worth recording because it
failed instructively. MOVING the producer key to the closing paren broke SIX
tests -- four in `use_classifier`, plus `ownership_errors_gate_build_and_check_
identically` and a migrate-tool test -- because this table has many
collision-AWARE consumers whose workarounds are calibrated to today's clobbering
(`use_classifier` even documents the aliasing it relies on). So the receiver-span
insert is left verbatim, clobbering and all, and the closing-paren key is added
ALONGSIDE. No existing read changes. The two keys coincide for an unchained
call, where the second insert is idempotent. Codegen tries the disambiguated key
first and falls back to the receiver span, which also leaves the two producers
with no `args_close_span` in scope (BoundedChannel, `String.to_cstring`)
untouched. A fallback that lands on a sibling link's entry stays safe: the
method-segment filter turns a wrong hit into NO key -- today's behaviour --
never a mis-dispatch.

MEMORY, which the row asked for explicitly rather than assumed. The fresh-temp
receiver free has a dedicated branch treating the String-to-String xform family
as allocating an independent copy (so the receiver is safe to free behind), and
that branch had NEVER EXECUTED for a Binary receiver, because the call could not
be compiled. Now that it runs: valgrind clean at both KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and the
DEFAULT -O2, 200 iterations, 1001 allocs / 1001 frees, no leak and no invalid
access. Two buffers per iteration are at stake -- the concat receiver and the
fresh xform result.

TESTS: `chained_string_xform_on_concat_receiver` (codegen E2E) pins the chained
AND unchained forms, since only the first was broken and a fix that regressed
the second would otherwise pass; proven RED against the unfixed compiler.
`asan_surface_concat_chained_xform_receiver_no_leak` floors at 100 allocations
and is written to B-2026-08-04-17's rules.

OBSERVED WHILE VERIFYING, filed as B-2026-08-05-35: the ASAN helper SKIPS on a
codegen failure ("setup failed -- skipping"), so that regression test passes
vacuously against the unfixed compiler. Its liveness here rests on the
allocation floor and the measured 1001 allocs, not on a RED run.

STILL OPEN, deliberately: the underlying span collision. Every consumer of a
span-keyed method-call table still needs its own workaround or its own migration
to `method_call_key`. This slice migrates one table's READ path and adds one
key; it does not retire the class.

tracker: src/cli.rs: Pipeline::target_skipped (captured from filter_inactive_items), target_skip_note (text), target_skipped_json (--output=json)
title: a single-target `karac check` silently omits `#[target(T)]`-gated bodies: they are stripped before any pass, so `check` prints "All checks passed" and `--output=json` an empty `diagnostics` over source it never examined, with nothing naming the omission -- the capability to check them (`--targets=`, `[build].targets`) already existed and works
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-05-24. That row's fixture had a real
type error (`Result.Err(0 - 1)` at i64 in a fn returning `Result[i32, i32]`)
that `karac check` reported as clean. The interesting question was not the
literal but WHY nothing caught it, and this is the answer.

REPRO, three commands on one file:

    #[target(wasm_browser)]
    pub fn blatantly_wrong(a: i32) -> i32 {
        let s: String = a;
        return s;
    }
    fn main() {}

    karac check gate.kara                      -> All checks passed.
    karac build gate.kara -o gate.bin          -> Built: gate.bin
    karac build gate.kara --target=wasm_browser
        -> error[typecheck]: gate.kara:3:21: expected 'String', found 'i32'
           error[typecheck]: gate.kara:4:12: expected 'i32', found 'String'

Two errors that any first-year typechecker catches, in a function the default
`check` walks straight past. The body is not merely unchecked for
target-specific reasons -- it is not checked AT ALL. The third command proves
the errors are perfectly catchable; nothing about them is target-dependent.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A STALE FIXTURE. `karac check --output=json` is the
front door of the Mend loop, and CLAUDE.md makes it the verification path for
all new Kara. For any `#[target(...)]`-gated code that front door reports
success on source it has not examined. An LLM author following the documented
loop gets "All checks passed" on a file with hard type errors in it, and finds
out only if someone later builds that exact target -- which for `wasm_browser`
means a CI leg with a wasm sysroot, a wasm runtime archive, and (see
B-2026-08-05-30) a wasm-tools install. B-2026-08-05-24 is the worked example:
the error sat in `main` until a typechecker change made some OTHER build path
notice it.

NO WAY TO ASK FOR IT EITHER. `karac check --target=wasm_browser` is rejected
with `error: unknown flag '--target=wasm_browser'`, so even an author who KNOWS
the gap exists cannot check a gated body short of a full cross-target build.
That is the smaller half of the fix and probably the first half: `check` should
take `--target`, and plausibly should check every gated body under its declared
target by default, since a `#[target(T)]` annotation names the target to check
against.

NOT VERIFIED: whether the same hole applies to the other gated surfaces
(`#[cfg]`-like attributes, `#[target(wasm_wasi)]`, feature gates) or only to
`#[target]`. The mechanism -- exclude from the build, therefore exclude from
the check -- suggests it generalises, but only `#[target(wasm_browser)]` was
measured.

CORRECTED AND FIXED 2026-08-05 (e865f233). This row as filed OVERCLAIMED, and the
correction matters because it changes what the fix is.

WHAT THE ROW GOT WRONG: "`karac check` has no `--target` flag to reach it". The
flag is `--targets` (plural), it has existed since the phase-10 multi-target
work, and it does exactly the right thing. Measured on the row's own repro:

    karac check gate.kara --targets=all
      -- target: native --        All checks passed under target 'native'.
      -- target: wasm_browser --  error[typecheck]: expected 'String', found 'i32'
                                  error[typecheck]: expected 'i32', found 'String'

The manifest route works too, and needs no flag at all: with
`[build] targets = ["native", "wasm_browser"]` in kara.toml, a bare
`karac check src/main.kara` runs the matrix and reports both errors. design.md
line 10165 specifies all of this -- per-target passes that "re-parameterize not
just the provided-resource set but also `#[target(...)]` absence filtering", the
`--targets=<list|all>` override, the manifest discovery rule, and cross-target
dedup. It was designed, built, and works. The row was written after testing
`--target=wasm_browser`, getting `unknown flag`, and concluding too much from it.

WHAT SURVIVES, restated accurately and narrowly: the DEFAULT single-target
check is silent about what it skipped. `filter_inactive_items` strips gated
items before any pass runs and records a tombstone map for each -- the compiler
knows precisely which bodies it did not examine -- and then nothing says so.
Text mode prints "All checks passed"; `--output=json` prints
`"diagnostics":[]`. Neither is distinguishable from a file that was fully
checked and clean. That silence is the whole of what let B-2026-08-05-24's
fixture -- two plain type errors in a `#[target(wasm_browser)]` fn -- sit in
`main`: the author had the tool and no reason to reach for it.

SEVERITY accordingly drops high -> medium. Nothing is unsound and nothing is
unreachable; a documented flag and a manifest field both work. The defect is
that the default output does not distinguish "checked and clean" from "not
looked at", which is a diagnostics gap, not a missing capability.

THE FIX is therefore the note, not the flag. A single-target check now ends
with, before the verdict line it qualifies:

    note: 1 item NOT checked -- gated away from target 'native': gated (wasm_browser)
          Their bodies are stripped before any pass runs, so nothing above covers
          them. Check them with `--targets=all` (or declare `[build] targets` in
          kara.toml).

and `--output=json` grows a peer field to `diagnostics`:

    "target_skipped":[{"name":"gated","gated_for":"wasm_browser"}]

which is the half that matters for the Mend loop, since that loop reads the
JSON and would otherwise see a clean bill of health on unexamined source.

DELIBERATELY A NOTE, NOT A WARNING, and the exit status is unchanged: gating an
item away is correct behaviour and an author building only for native has no
reason to be nagged. What was missing was the fact plus the flag that acts on
it. The `--targets=` matrix does NOT carry the note -- each pass there checks
its own target's active set, so the note would fire on the pass that skipped a
body while a sibling pass was checking it.

TESTS: four in tests/cli.rs. Two accept (the text note names the item, its gate,
and `--targets=all`; the JSON field names the item) and two controls (a file
with nothing gated carries no note and an EMPTY-not-absent `target_skipped`; the
`--targets=all` matrix omits the note AND still catches the error). The two
accept tests were confirmed RED against the pre-fix compiler; both controls pass
either way, which is what a control should do.

NOT ADDRESSED, and left deliberately: the gated body is still unchecked by
default. Making the default check every gated body under its declared target is
a real option -- typechecking never consults the active target, so it would be
safe from the typechecker's side -- but the effect checker's target gate IS
target-sensitive, and the stripping comment states bodies "may reference
target-specific names". So it is a design change with a real blast radius, not
a bug fix, and design.md already prescribes the matrix as the answer.

SECOND AND THIRD LEGS (192947f, aa38d78) — the "NOT ADDRESSED, and left
deliberately" paragraph above is now addressed. Landed from a different
session working the same row concurrently; recorded here rather than as a
new id because it is the same defect, and because the COLLISION is itself
the most useful thing on this entry.

THE DEFERRAL'S REASONING, and why it does not apply to what was built.
Above: "the effect checker's target gate IS target-sensitive, and gated
bodies may reference target-specific names — a design change with real
blast radius." Both facts are true, and both are reasons not to check a
gated body under the WRONG target. The landed change checks it under its
OWN declared target: for a `#[target(wasm_browser)]` item the extra pass
runs with wasm_browser active, so the gate is the right gate and the
target-specific names are the ones that exist. The annotation names the
target; the check follows it.

WHAT LANDED (192947f). With no `--targets` flag and no manifest
`[build].targets`, `check` now covers the ACTIVE target plus every target
named by a `#[target]` attribute in the file. Ungated files keep the
single-pass path and pay nothing, and so does a negated gate the base
already admits (`not(gpu)` on native needs no second pass — the ordinary
pass reads the body). The discovery shares `item_attrs_and_name` and
`TargetSpec::is_active_on` with `filter_inactive_items` itself, so the
two cannot drift about what "gated" means.

KEYED ON THE ACTIVE TARGET, NOT ON `native` — a real bug caught before
landing. The non-llvm `karac build --target=T` fallback degrades into
`cmd_check` with T already active; a discovery hardcoded to `native`
would have turned that explicit one-target request into a native+T
matrix. Verified against a real non-llvm karac binary.

Also: `check` now accepts `--target=` (singular) as the one-target
spelling of `--targets=`, sharing its validation. That closes the
discoverability half this entry's CORRECTION identified — the capability
existed, the spelling `build` teaches did not work, and dying on
`unknown flag` is what made "no way to ask for it" look true.

THE COLLISION, and the reconciliation it forced (aa38d78). The note from
e865f233 fires only on the SINGLE-PASS path, by design: an item one pass
gates away is usually an item a sibling pass is checking, so firing
per-pass in a matrix would be noise. Correct rule — but once gated files
route through the matrix by default, that rule left the note with no
reachable trigger for the case it was written for. A green suite in each
session, red on `main` the moment both landed.

Reconciled by moving the note one level up rather than weakening either
fix: it now fires on the INTERSECTION of the per-pass skip maps — items
NO requested target admitted. e865f233's rule survives intact (an item
some pass checked is still never mentioned), and it closes a hole that
rule did not cover: `--targets=native,wasm_wasi` over a `#[target(gpu)]`
item checks it nowhere and said nothing, which is the same silence the
note exists to break, one level up. The `target_skipped` JSON field gains
a peer in the multi-target envelope, same `{name, gated_for}` shape.

The two accept tests from e865f233 now request `--target=native`
explicitly where they used a bare `karac check`, and one assertion
relaxes from `"All checks passed."` to `"All checks passed"` because the
per-target driver words it `... under target 'native'.`. Their subjects
are unchanged — only the invocation that reaches the path under test.

METHOD NOTE, the reason this is worth the words: two sessions took the
same open row, each shipped a defensible fix, each ran a green suite, and
the composition was red — because one fix changed which CODE PATH the
other's feature sits on. Neither test suite could have caught it alone.
The tell was cheap and was missed twice: `git log` on the row id before
starting. Worth doing on any row that has been open long enough for
someone else to pick up.

RESIDUALS after all three legs:
  * `karac fix` still builds its own single-target (native) pipeline, so
    it cannot propose fixes inside a gated body. Verified, not assumed.
  * Discovery reads the ENTRY FILE's top-level items. A `#[target]`
    inside an IMPORTED module is not found — that file falls to the
    single-pass path, where e865f233's note covers it. The two fixes
    compose here rather than overlapping.
  * For a gated file, `check --output=json` now emits the per-target
    envelope by default instead of the flat one. That shape already
    occurred for any `--targets`/manifest run, but it is a DEFAULT-path
    change and a consumer that only ever saw the flat shape will notice.

TESTS for these legs: 5 in tests/cli.rs (default check catches it; JSON
carries it; `--target=` accepted; ungated stays single-pass; a
native-admitted `not(gpu)` gate stays single-pass), 6 unit tests on the
discovery rule in src/target.rs, and 1 for the matrix-blind-spot note.
THREE of the five cli tests are RED before the fix; the two single-pass
guards pass either way by construction — they exist to catch this
default becoming a matrix for everyone, which is how it would regress.

tracker: tests/cli.rs::wasm_build_skip_reason (the `wasm-tools not found` arm) and its call sites, which consult it BEFORE out.status.success()
title: the wasm E2E tests skip on a SUCCESSFUL build: `wasm_build_skip_reason` matches the string `wasm-tools not found`, which the browser-bindings path emits as a size-optimization NOTE on a build that succeeded, and the predicate is consulted before `out.status.success()` -- so wasm_browser_rich_exports_marshal_e2e reports ok while asserting nothing
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-05-24's fix end-to-end rather than
through the test.

THE MECHANIC. Every wasm E2E test runs the build, then:

    let stderr = String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stderr);
    if let Some(reason) = wasm_build_skip_reason(&stderr) { ...skip... }
    assert!(out.status.success(), "wasm browser build failed: {stderr}");

The skip predicate is consulted BEFORE the success check, and one of its arms
is `stderr.contains("wasm-tools not found")`. For `--bindings component` that
string accompanies a genuine failure -- componentization shells out to
wasm-tools. For `--bindings browser` it is a NOTE on a SUCCESSFUL build:

    note: wasm-tools not found -- emitted .wasm retains debug info (install
    wasm-tools for ~10x smaller modules, or set KARAC_WASM_KEEP_DEBUG=1 ...)
    Built: fixed.wasm + fixed.js + fixed.d.ts

So the browser tests skip on a build that produced all three artifacts, purely
because a size hint mentioned the tool.

MEASURED, not inferred. On this container (node v22.22.2 present,
wasm32-wasip1 installed, libkarac_runtime_wasm.a built, wasm-tools ABSENT):
`wasm_browser_rich_exports_marshal_e2e` reports `test result: ok` and prints
`skip: ... wasm-tools not installed` under --nocapture. Building the same
fixture by hand succeeds, and running the test's OWN JS against the emitted
glue under node passes all eight assertions (mk / area / checked_div hit+none /
safe_div ok+err / shout / squares). The test could have run in full and chose
not to.

WHY IT IS WORTH A ROW. This is the B-2026-08-04-17 shape: a green run that
asserted nothing. The marshalling surface it covers -- structs to JS objects,
`Option[T]` to `T | null`, `Result[T,E]` to `{ok}|{err}`, `Vec[T]` to arrays --
has no other E2E coverage, and B-2026-08-05-24 sat in `main` partly because the
one test that exercises it was skipping. Any environment without wasm-tools
gets zero browser-marshalling coverage while reporting success.

FIX DIRECTION (not attempted): consult `wasm_build_skip_reason` only when the
build FAILED -- infrastructure skips exist for builds that could not run, and a
successful build is by definition not one of those. That is a one-line reorder
at each call site, but it will UNSKIP wasm tests wherever the sysroot and
archives are present, so it should land with a full wasm-family run behind it
rather than as a drive-by. Narrower alternative: match the wasm-tools arm on
the component-path error text instead of the bare tool name.

RESOLVED — and the fix this entry RECOMMENDED would have been a
regression. Recording that first, because the recommendation is the
obvious one and it is wrong.

WHAT THIS ENTRY PROPOSED: "consult `wasm_build_skip_reason` only when the
build FAILED — infrastructure skips exist for builds that could not run,
and a successful build is by definition not one of those." The premise is
right for six of the seven walls and FALSE for the seventh.

THE COUNTEREXAMPLE, measured rather than reasoned about: a karac built
WITHOUT `--features llvm` does not fail on `karac build --target=wasm_*`.
It degrades to a type check, prints `note: karac build requires the llvm
feature; falling back to type check`, and EXITS 0. Built a non-llvm karac
into a separate CARGO_TARGET_DIR to confirm — exit 0 on both wasm_wasi and
wasm_browser. Under plain `cargo test` (which is how CI's non-llvm tiers
and every default local run execute tests/cli.rs) that wall fires 87
times. A blanket status gate would have converted all 87 clean skips into
hard failures — turning a vacuous-pass bug into a can't-run-the-suite bug.

THE FIX is therefore a SPLIT, not a gate: the llvm-feature wall is checked
first, status-independently, and the six aborting walls moved behind
`!status.success()` into `failed_wasm_build_skip_reason`. The split is the
documentation — the one exception is visibly the exception, with the
exit-0 reason stated at the call site.

SECOND HALF, defense in depth: the wasm-tools arm now matches the
COMPONENTIZER's own text ("wasm-tools not found (`--bindings component`")
rather than the bare phrase. The status gate alone would have fixed
today's bug, but the strip note can also ride along on a build that fails
for an UNRELATED reason, and then the bare phrase turns a real regression
into a skip. Two independent walls now stand between the note and a false
skip.

MEASURED IMPACT in this container (node present, both wasm archives built,
both rustup targets installed, wasm-tools absent — the configuration that
exposes the bug):

    before      52 skips
    after       11 skips
    delta       41 tests newly EXECUTE, 0 newly skip, all 41 pass

The 41 are not a long tail of near-duplicates: they include the entire
`wasm_threads_*` event-delivery family (17), the `fathom_*` / `plume_*`
example E2Es (6), the simd128 lowering pair, the bindings-emission pair,
`ssr_counter`'s client leg, and `wasm_browser_rich_exports_marshal_e2e`
itself — this entry's motivating case and, as it noted, the only E2E
coverage of the JS marshalling surface (structs → objects, `Option[T]` →
`T | null`, `Result[T,E]` → `{ok}|{err}`, `Vec[T]` → arrays). Every one of
them was reporting `ok` while asserting nothing.

The 11 that still skip all report `wasm-tools not installed`, and all 11
genuinely require it: the six `wasm_wasi_component_exports_*` tests, the
two other componentization tests, byte-reproducibility, the debug-strip
test (whose subject IS the missing tool), and the toolchain-pin test.
`concurrent_same_stem_wasm_builds_do_not_collide` is in that set because
`wasm_wasi` defaults to `--bindings component`, so its probe build really
does abort.

NOTHING NEWLY FAILED. The row asked for "a full wasm-family run behind
it rather than as a drive-by" precisely in case unskipping exposed real
breakage; it did not. `wasm_browser_rich_exports_marshal_e2e` passes on
its own terms, matching the entry's own observation that hand-running its
JS under node satisfied all eight assertions. Full `--features llvm`
suite green, and the non-llvm `cargo test --test cli` leg green too (523
passed) — that second run is the one that proves the llvm arm survived.

TESTS: `wasm_skip_predicate_discriminates_notes_from_walls`, a unit test
over the predicate itself. It synthesizes an `Output` for each of the five
cases — successful build + strip note (must be None), failed build +
componentizer error (must skip), exit-0 llvm note (must skip), an aborting
wall, and a plain typecheck error (must NOT skip) — so the three-way
discrimination is pinned without needing a container that happens to lack
wasm-tools. RED against the old predicate on the first assertion.

Testing the test harness is unusual and deserves its justification: a
wrong answer here makes tests report `ok` while asserting nothing, which
is strictly worse than a failure, because a failure gets looked at and
this does not. This bug survived in the tree until someone noticed a test
that "passed" too fast.

METHOD NOTE worth carrying forward. The check that made the fix safe was
mechanical, not judgemental: before touching the signature, a script
confirmed all 73 `wasm_build_skip_reason(&stderr)` call sites are preceded
by `let stderr = String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stderr)` — 73/73 with the
`Output` bound to `out` — so the rewrite was a sed plus two hand-fixed
specials (`probe`, `web`), with the compiler verifying every site. Widening
a predicate's input type is the cheap way to make a whole call-site class
provably consistent.

title: the interpreter computes `Tensor[f32]` elements in f64 while AOT uses a packed f32 buffer, so an f32 tensor gives DIFFERENT ANSWERS on the two backends -- 0.1*3 prints 0.30000000000000004 under `karac run --interp` and 0.30000001192092896 from `karac build`
detail:
REPRO:

    fn main() {
        let a: Tensor[f32, [1]] = Tensor.from([0.1]);
        let b: Tensor[f32, [1]] = a * 3.0;
        println(b.sum());       // interp 0.30000000000000004
                                // AOT    0.30000001192092896
        let s: f32 = 0.1;
        println(s * 3.0);       // BOTH   0.30000000000000004
    }

AOT is the one honouring the declaration: `0.30000001192092896` is what
`0.1f32 * 3` actually is. The interpreter is wrong.

CAUSE, structural rather than a slip: `Value::Tensor { dims, data }` holds
`Vec<Value>` — one BOXED value per element — and a float `Value` is f64.
There is no f32 representation in the interpreter at all, so the declared
element width is simply not modelled. Codegen, by contrast, packs a real
f32 buffer for a tensor.

NOTE THE SCALAR CONTROL, which localizes this to tensors: a plain
`let s: f32` computes in f64 on BOTH backends, so scalars agree with each
other (while arguably not honouring `f32` either — that is a separate
question, and NOT a divergence). Tensors are the case where codegen narrows
and the interpreter does not, which is why only they diverge.

PRE-EXISTING, not introduced by B-2026-08-05-26. That fix corrected the
TYPE (`Tensor.from([1.0])` under a `Tensor[f32]` annotation now yields
`Tensor[f32]` rather than `Tensor[f64]`); the interpreter still computes in
f64 with the type unambiguously f32, which is what shows the element width
is ignored regardless of what the typechecker says.

SEVERITY medium, not high: it is a precision divergence, not memory
unsafety, and it needs f32 specifically. But it is a genuine run-vs-build
divergence in the direction this repo treats as worst — the interpreter is
the test path and it disagrees with the shipped one — so an f32 tensor
kernel validated under `--interp` is not validated.

FIX SHAPE, unattempted: either narrow on store/compute for f32 tensors in
the interpreter (round through `as f32` at element writes and after each
element-wise op), or give `Value` a genuine f32 carrier. The first is
narrower and probably enough; the second is what would also settle the
scalar question.

FIXED (2bfece1). `Value::Tensor` now carries the declared element WIDTH, and the
sites that PRODUCE element values round through it: element-wise
tensor-tensor and tensor-scalar ops, unary negation, and matmul. Matmul
matters and is easy to miss — it accumulates sums of products, so it drifts
exactly like the binops if left unrounded. Shape-only operations (reshape,
permute, transpose, slice, squeeze, iter_axis) carry the width through
WITHOUT rounding, because they move existing elements rather than computing
new ones; rounding there would be harmless but is not the contract.

The width comes from the `Tensor[Elem, …]` annotation the interpreter already
consults for `zeros`/`ones` fills — `TensorElemFill::Float` now carries it
rather than collapsing every float into one variant, which that type's own
doc comment had recorded as a known limitation ('the interpreter's `Value`
can't represent the distinction'). It can now, for tensors.

SCOPE, deliberately narrow: `f16`/`bf16` keep the f64 path (no Rust-stable
carrier, and no codegen narrowing to match against), and an Arrow IPC stream
decodes to f64 slots and claims no narrowing.

THE SCALAR QUESTION IS UNCHANGED AND STILL OPEN. A plain `let s: f32` is
computed in f64 on BOTH backends, so it does not DIVERGE and is not what this
row was about — the regression test keeps it as the control line precisely to
pin that. Whether scalar `f32` should narrow at all is a separate question
this fix does not answer and does not foreclose.

Gates: interpreter 1450, typechecker 2135, codegen 2804, memory_sanitizer
942, default suite 0 failures; clippy --all-targets and fmt clean.

title: A struct with a DIRECT `shared` field, bound to a LOCAL and passed BY VALUE, never rc-decs the box -- it leaks on a DEFAULT -O2 build (288 B / 8 allocs). The drop IS registered and then never emitted. The fresh-temp form is already fixed, so the b28 fixture's "pre-existing residual" note points at the wrong half
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: reached by decomposing `b28_option_shared_and_direct_shared_struct_drop_no_leak` (324 B x8), the largest remaining -O0 failure, into its six constituent shapes and running each separately. Five are clean; the leak is one shape, and it is NOT the one the fixture's comment flags as the known residual.

THE TRIGGER, isolated to one line. A struct with a DIRECT `shared` field, bound to a LOCAL, passed BY VALUE to a function:

    shared enum Val { Nothing, Ident(String), Num(i64) }
    struct DirH { value: Val }
    fn ignore_dir(h: DirH) -> i64 { 1 }          // body is irrelevant
    ...
    let d = DirH { value: Val.Ident(pay(i)) };
    t = t + ignore_dir(d);                       // <-- this line

  KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=2 (DEFAULT) -> 288 B / 8 allocations over 8 iterations
  KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0           -> 608 B / 16 allocations
Confirmed through the ordinary `karac build` CLI, so this is a DEFAULT-BUILD leak, not an -O0 curiosity. The -O2 count is lower because the String payload is never read and LLVM deletes it; the RC BOX leaks at both levels. The callee body does not matter -- a callee that ignores its parameter entirely leaks identically to one that matches on it.

FOUR CONTROLS, each one variable away, all CLEAN:
  * `Option[shared]` field instead of direct (`OptH { value: Option[Val] }`),
    same local-then-pass shape                                    -> CLEAN
  * DirH as a FRESH-TEMP arg (`ignore_dir(DirH { .. })`)          -> CLEAN
    (this is B-2026-07-04-9(b), already fixed -- and it is what the b28
    fixture's own comment calls a "separate PRE-EXISTING residual...
    deliberately not exercised". That characterisation is now stale: the
    fresh-temp form is fixed and the LOCAL form is the one that leaks.)
  * DirH local moved to another LOCAL (`let e = d;`), never passed -> CLEAN
  * DirH local never passed at all (scope-drop only)              -> CLEAN

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED ABOUT THE MECHANISM, by instrumentation rather than reading:
  * The drop IS registered. `track_struct_var_inst` fires exactly once for
