    `DirH` with `owns_shared=true`, so it takes the B-2026-07-03-28 combined
    path (value drop + `emit_nested_struct_shared_rc_decs`) and returns a real
    drop fn.
  * It is never CALLED. `main`'s IR contains ZERO
    `call void @__karac_vec_elem_full_drop_DirH`, against 2 for the
    moved-to-local control and 1 for the fresh-temp control. So the action is
    armed and then not emitted -- not a missing registration.
  * It is not the drain. `drain_top_frame_with_emit` skips only `UserErrDefer`.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: where the armed action goes. Grepping for a retract / suppress / moved-binding filter on `CleanupAction::StructDrop` found nothing that fits, so the next step is an `eprintln!` at the emit site keyed on the DirH alloca, not more reading -- the same loop that settled the other rows in this family.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT PROBABLY EXPLAINS IT, offered as a hypothesis and not a finding: `DirH` is NOT copy-supported (`field_copy_supported` bails on a direct `shared` field), so its by-value param is CALLER-RETAINS -- the callee never entry-copies and so never rc-incs or rc-decs. Passing a local by value presumably suppresses the caller's scope drop as a move. For the copy-supported `OptH` that suppression is balanced by the callee's entry-copy rc-inc/dec pair, which is why the `Option[shared]` control is clean; for `DirH` nothing takes over and the box is stranded. If that is right, the fix is to keep the caller's drop when the callee is caller-retains for a shared-owning struct -- i.e. the LOCAL-arg mirror of what B-2026-07-04-9(b) did for the fresh-temp arg, which registers `src_shared_owning` at the struct-literal arg site precisely because nothing else owns that temp.

CAUTION FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: this row's family has had three over-broad ownership widenings reverted, and an rc-dec that fires twice aborts rather than leaks. Gate any change on BOTH the -O2 suite (must stay 0 failures) and the -O0 sweep, and re-run the four controls above -- the `Option[shared]` and fresh-temp ones are exactly the shapes a too-broad fix would double-dec.

FIXED (17b58f4). The hypothesis in this row was RIGHT, and the site is
`move_declined_copy_struct_arg` (call_dispatch.rs, B-2026-07-28-4): it
retracts the caller's `StructDrop` whenever copy-support declines, so the
argument becomes a true move.

The key point is that copy-support declines for TWO unrelated reasons and the
move semantics only follow from one of them:
  * a self-referential `struct N { edges: Vec[N] }` declines because the
    per-element copy has no finite emission (B-2026-07-28-3). The callee gets
    an ALIAS it may STORE into an owning container, so the caller must give up
    its drop or both free the same buffers. This retraction was written for
    exactly that.
  * a direct `shared` field declines because `field_copy_supported` bails on
    it. Nothing is stored or aliased: the callee is caller-retains, so it
    never entry-copies, never rc-INCs and never rc-DECs. The binding's drop is
    the box's ONLY rc-dec.
Gating the retraction on `struct_owns_shared_field` keeps the first case and
restores the second. It cannot double-dec precisely because caller-retains
means there is no second owner — the same reasoning B-2026-07-04-9(b) already
applies to the fresh-TEMP form, whose comment claiming the let-bound sibling
"is already covered by `track_struct_var` at its binding site" was true only
until this retraction removed it.

All four controls in this row were re-run and stay CLEAN, and three of them
are now in the regression fixture, since a too-broad fix double-decs exactly
there and a double rc-dec ABORTS rather than leaks.

GATES: -O2 memory_sanitizer 943 / 0 failures; the -O0 sweep 10 -> 7 remaining.
Three fixtures cleared, including this row's source `b28_option_shared_and_
direct_shared_struct_drop`.

ONE CORRECTION TO THIS ROW, offered because it affects severity: the reported
288 B / 8-alloc leak on a DEFAULT -O2 build did NOT reproduce. The reduction
above is -O2 CLEAN and leaks only at -O0 (320 B / 8), including a variant
where the callee reads the payload so the optimizer cannot delete it as dead.
The missing rc-dec is real either way and the fix is unchanged, but the
default-build claim should be treated as unconfirmed unless someone
reproduces it — possibly it needed the surrounding shapes of the original b28
fixture rather than the isolated one.

fix: 13a6f9ed fixed (a) by registering the by-value param drop at its DECLARED instantiation (enum_inst_var_types) instead of by bare name. 126180fb fixed (b); 17b58f4 fixed (c).
tracker: src/codegen/param_own.rs::make_aggregate_param_callee_owned_inst (the own-by-transfer arm) + src/codegen/functions.rs (threads the param's recorded generic instantiation) + src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs::move_declined_copy_struct_arg (the caller-side retraction it stays in lockstep with)
title: LAW, not one fixture: a by-value aggregate param that is CALLER-RETAINS is owned by nobody and leaks once per call on a DEFAULT -O2 build. Three predicates reach it -- generic-erased field (2400 B/40), Map-bearing field (26400 B/160), and direct `shared` field (B-2026-08-05-32, which is therefore a special case of this row, not its own bug)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: reached from `generic_struct_field_receiver_param_indexed_no_leak` (68 B x39), picked off the -O0 list because its allocation COUNT was the highest. Decomposing it produced a law rather than a fixture fix, so it is filed as its own row.

THE LAW: a by-value aggregate PARAM that is CALLER-RETAINS has no owner on either side, and its heap leaks once per call. The callee never entry-copies (that is what caller-retains means), and the caller's scope drop is suppressed because the argument was moved in. Nobody frees it.

THREE INDEPENDENT PREDICATES all land there, and each was measured separately. Every one is a DEFAULT -O2 leak, confirmed through the ordinary `karac build` CLI, not just the ASAN harness:

  (a) GENERIC-erased field -- `struct Box[T] { v: T }`, `fn sink(b: Box[String])`
      2400 B / 40 allocations. Copy-support bails on the erased `T`
      (`field_copy_supported`'s conservative `_ => false`), and
      `try_make_generic_struct_param_callee_owned` needs an ACTIVE MONOMORPH
      SUBST that a CONCRETE fn taking `Box[String]` never has.
  (b) MAP-bearing field -- `struct MapH { m: Map[i64, String] }`
      26400 B / 160 allocations. `make_aggregate_param_callee_owned`'s own
      comment says Map-bearing aggregates are "left on caller-retains".
  (c) DIRECT `shared` field -- `struct DirH { value: Val }`, filed separately as
      B-2026-08-05-32 (288 B / 8 at -O2). `field_copy_supported` bails on a
      direct shared field.

So B-2026-08-05-32 IS NOT ITS OWN BUG -- it is this law seen through predicate (c). Whoever fixes either row should know that, because a fix aimed only at the shared predicate leaves (a) and (b) live, and three separate narrow fixes at the same site will conflict.

CONTROLS, each one variable away, all CLEAN:
  * the same struct NEVER passed (scope-drop only)          -> clean, all three
  * a NON-generic twin of (a) (`struct BoxS { v: String }`) -> clean (it IS
    copy-supported, so the callee entry-copies and drops)
  * the callee IGNORING its parameter                       -> leaks identically,
    so the callee BODY is irrelevant
  * (a) as a FRESH-TEMP arg rather than a local             -> leaks too, so the
    ARGUMENT FORM is irrelevant here. NOTE this differs from (c), where the
    fresh-temp form is CLEAN because B-2026-07-04-9(b) special-cased it at the
    struct-literal arg site. That asymmetry is a symptom of the piecemeal
    fixing, not a real difference in the shapes.

MECHANISM, established rather than assumed: for (a), `sink`'s IR contains NO
free/drop call of any kind, and no `__karac_drop_struct_Box*` is defined at all
-- the drop synthesis sees the erased `T`, classifies the field as no-heap, and
returns None. The caller emits the same two `karac_free_buf` calls as the
never-passed control, i.e. nothing extra for the moved-in value. For (c),
B-2026-08-05-32 records the mirror observation: the drop IS registered there and
then never emitted.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A UNIFIED FIX: the correct rule is one sentence -- if the
callee is caller-retains for a by-value aggregate, the CALLER must keep its
drop, because the callee provably never took ownership. That is the same
conclusion B-2026-07-04-9(b) already reached for one narrow case (a
direct-shared struct as an inline fresh-temp arg, where it registers
`src_shared_owning` precisely because nothing else owns the temp). The general
form is that special case with the predicate widened from "shared-owning" to
"not copy-supported".

CAUTION, and it is the reason this row does not carry a fix: an rc-dec or free
that fires twice ABORTS rather than leaks, and this family has already had three
over-broad ownership widenings reverted. Any fix must be gated on BOTH the -O2
suite (must stay at 0 failures) and the -O0 sweep, and must re-run the
copy-supported controls above -- `BoxS`, and the `Option[shared]` sibling in
B-2026-08-05-32 -- since those are exactly the shapes that a predicate widened
one step too far would double-free.

NOT FIXED HERE deliberately: B-2026-08-05-32 is being worked by someone else at
what is very likely this same site, so a second edit would collide. This row
exists so that work is scoped to the law rather than to predicate (c).

ATTEMPTED AND REVERTED 2026-08-05 — the LAW AS STATED IS INCOMPLETE, and the
counterexample is recorded here so the next attempt does not rediscover it.

WHAT WAS TRIED, exactly the fix this row prescribes: replace the
B-2026-08-05-32 guard in `move_declined_copy_struct_arg` (`if
struct_owns_shared_field { return }`) with the general predicate, retracting the
caller's drop ONLY for the SELF-REFERENTIAL decline and keeping it for every
other one. Implemented as a new `struct_is_self_referential` walking field
TypeExprs through tuples, Vec/VecDeque elements and generic args — the cycle
guard trips iff the struct reaches itself, so asking that directly is
equivalent to "the decline was the self-referential one" and independent of how
the copy-support walk is later refactored.

IT WORKS ON BOTH LIVE PREDICATES. Confirmed through the ordinary CLI at the
DEFAULT -O2, under valgrind:
    (a) generic-erased  `struct Box[T]{v:T}` / `fn sink(b: Box[String])`
        1,360 B / 40 blocks lost  ->  0 leaks, 0 invalid, output unchanged
    (b) Map-bearing     `struct MapH{m:Map[i64,String]}`
        25,360 B / 40 blocks lost ->  0 leaks, 0 invalid, output unchanged
and it FIXES this row's own source fixture: with the change,
`asan_generic_struct_field_receiver_param_indexed_no_leak` goes from FAILING to
passing on the -O0 sweep. The full -O2 suite stayed at 13085 passed / 0 failed,
so nothing there catches it.

AND IT INTRODUCES A DOUBLE FREE, which only the -O0 sweep caught — exactly the
outcome this row's CAUTION predicted. -O0 memory_sanitizer went from 5 failures
to 5 failures with a DIFFERENT SET: it fixed the fixture above and broke
`asan_generic_wrapper_accessor_and_move_no_double_free` (B-2026-07-15-11).
Comparing the two callees is the whole lesson:

    fn sink(b: Box[String]) -> i64 { b.v.len() }        // my probe — READS
    fn sink(b: Box[String]) -> i64 { let s = b.v;       // that test — MOVES
                                     s.len() }           //   the field OUT

Both take the SAME caller-retains by-value aggregate param. The second consumes
the field's heap and frees it through `s`, so the caller keeping its drop is a
second free of the same buffer.

SO THE LAW NEEDS A THIRD CLAUSE. "The callee never entry-copies, therefore it
never took ownership" does not follow: a caller-retains callee can still MOVE a
field out of the aggregate and own that field. Caller-retains constrains how the
param ARRIVES, not what the body does with it. The correct condition is
something like "caller-retains AND the callee does not consume any heap-owning
field of the param", and the second half is an interprocedural fact that does
not exist today — `OwnershipCheckResult` exposes `param_modes` /
`elidable_ref_params`, and both callees above are simply `own`, so nothing
currently distinguishes them.

TWO ROUTES, neither a predicate tweak:
  * Plumb a "callee consumes an aggregate field" fact from ownership into
    codegen and gate the retained drop on it. Keeps the caller-side shape of
    this row.
  * Or fix the CALLEE side instead: teach `field_copy_supported` to duplicate a
    Map-bearing and a generic-erased field so those params become callee-owned
    and balance the ordinary way. That removes the caller-retains state that
    creates the ownerless value at all, rather than patching who frees it. It is
    the larger change — the Map case is why the comment says such aggregates are
    "left on caller-retains" — but it is the one that makes the law true instead
    of conditional.

METHOD NOTE for whoever picks this up: the -O2 suite is NOT sufficient to gate a
change here. It stayed fully green across a change that introduces a double
free; only `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 cargo test --features llvm --test
memory_sanitizer` saw it, and only by DIFFING the failure SET rather than the
count, which was 5 both before and after. Baseline set on this commit:
generic_struct_field_receiver_param_indexed, generic_struct_heap_field_move_out,
nested_option_pattern_boxed_payload_lifecycle, shared_payload_view_optres_field_
call_arg_copy, tensor_lifecycle.

STAYS OPEN. Predicates (a) and (b) still leak on a default build; only (c) is
fixed (17b58f4).

PREDICATE (b) FIXED 2026-08-05 (126180fb) — and by the OTHER SIDE than this row
proposed, which the failed first attempt is what identified.

THE ROW PRESCRIBED a caller-side fix: keep the caller's drop, because "the
callee is caller-retains and therefore never took ownership". That is the
half-truth recorded in the previous note — a caller-retains callee can still
MOVE a field out and free it, so keeping the caller's drop double-freed
`asan_generic_wrapper_accessor_and_move_no_double_free`.

THE CALLEE SIDE HAS NO SUCH AMBIGUITY. The caller has already retracted its drop
by the time the callee runs, i.e. the value was MOVED in, so the callee can take
the original buffers outright. A copy was never the point:
`deep_copy_struct_heap_fields_in_place` exists to leave the CALLER's original
intact, and there is no original to protect once ownership transferred. So
`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned`'s non-copy-supported arm now registers the
drop (`track_struct_var`) WITHOUT the copy — the copy-supported path's own
pairing minus its first line. A field the body moves out is excluded by the same
cap-zeroing move-suppression the copy-supported path already relies on, which is
exactly why `let s = b.v` balances here and did not on the caller side.

LOCKSTEP WITH THE CALLER'S RETRACTION is the safety argument, and it dictates
the two exclusions: a shared-owning struct (B-2026-08-05-32 made the CALLER keep
its drop, so owning here too rc-decs twice) and a self-referential struct (the
callee may store the alias into an owning container, B-2026-07-28-3, so a param
drop could free what the container now owns). `struct_is_self_referential` was
added for the second: the copy-support cycle guard trips iff the struct reaches
itself, so asking that directly is equivalent to "the decline was the
self-referential one" and independent of how that walk is later refactored.

MEASURED: `struct MapH { m: Map[i64, String] }` by value goes 25,360 B / 40
blocks lost -> valgrind CLEAN at the default -O2, output unchanged. Regression
`asan_map_bearing_struct_by_value_param_no_leak`, floored at 100 allocations,
proven RED unfixed (LeakSanitizer fires).

PREDICATE (a) STILL LEAKS, and the reason is now established rather than
inferred. `track_struct_var` fires for `struct Box[T] { v: T }` taken as
`Box[String]` — the transfer arm reaches it — but it is a NO-OP, because the
drop SYNTHESIS emits nothing: it sees the erased `T`, classifies the field as
no-heap, and returns None. This row's own MECHANISM paragraph said as much ("no
`__karac_drop_struct_Box*` is defined at all"); what is new is that the fix must
attack the SYNTHESIS, not the ownership decision, which is already correct for
(a) now.

NEXT STEP for (a), concrete: the field type IS available without a monomorph
subst — the param's own TypeExpr is `Box[String]`, so `T = String` is
recoverable from the declared parameter type. That is the same information
`try_make_generic_struct_param_callee_owned` currently demands from an ACTIVE
MONO SUBST (which a concrete fn never has), and it is why that path declines.
Resolving the struct's generic args from the param TypeExpr would serve both the
drop synthesis and that helper.

STILL OPEN for (a). (b) fixed here, (c) fixed at 17b58f4, and the
self-referential leak remains deliberately untouched.

PREDICATE (a) FIXED 2026-08-06 (13a6f9ed). The ownership decision was already
correct after 126180fb; what was missing was a DROP TO RUN.

THE ONE-LINE CAUSE, as the previous note predicted: `track_struct_var` is keyed
by NAME, so the synthesizer read `Box`'s DECLARED field `v: T`, classified the
erased type as no-heap, and returned None -- no `__karac_drop_struct_Box` was
emitted at all, and the registration silently did nothing. The transfer arm had
been reaching this shape since 126180fb and freeing nothing.

THE FIX is to register at the param's DECLARED INSTANTIATION instead of its bare
name. `track_struct_var_inst(type_name, slot, inst)` already accepts one and
already resolves fields through it (`generic_struct_subst_from_inst` ->
`emit_struct_drop_synthesis_mono`); the machinery to classify a bare-`T` field
bound to a heap type, and to GEP it at the widened mono layout, has existed since
B-2026-07-15-11 / -24. It was simply never handed the binding.

WHERE THE BINDING COMES FROM, and why this is not a new fact anyone has to
compute: `enum_inst_var_types[param_name]` is ALREADY seeded with `Box[String]`
at the param-registration site in `compile_function` (B-2026-07-15-20 added it,
for field-receiver method dispatch), several lines ABOVE the
`make_aggregate_param_callee_owned` call. The fix threads that existing record
down through a new `_inst` overload. The previous note framed the recovery as
parsing the param's TypeExpr; the table was already built.

WHY A CONCRETE FN NEEDED THIS AT ALL. Every mono-aware path here
(`mono_struct_type_from_active_subst`, `subst_monomorph_type_params`) reads the
ACTIVE monomorph subst, which a concrete `fn sink(b: Box[String])` never has --
it is not a monomorph, it just happens to name one. That is the same reason
`try_make_generic_struct_param_callee_owned` declines this shape, and it is what
made the generic-erased predicate outlive the Map-bearing one.

MEASURED at the DEFAULT -O2 under valgrind, through the ordinary CLI:
  * `struct Box[T] { v: T }` / `fn sink(b: Box[String])`
    1,360 B / 40 blocks lost -> 0 leaks, 0 invalid, output unchanged.

PROBES, each one variable away from that, all CLEAN at -O2 AND -O0:
  * mid-position bare-T heap field (`Multi[T] { a: i64, v: T, w: Vec[i64] }`)
    -- the offset leg: the declared layout erases `v` to one i64 word while the
    instance is the widened `{ptr,len,cap}`, so a name-keyed drop would GEP the
    trailing Vec at the wrong offset (a wild free, not a leak)
  * two type params (`Pair[A, B]` at `String, Vec[i64]`)
  * `T` bound to a non-heap type (`Box[i64]`) -- no-op, as before
  * `T` bound to `Vec[i64]` / `Vec[String]` / `Option[String]`, to a heap ENUM
    (`Wrap.Full(String)`), and to a nested STRUCT (`Inner { s: String }`)
  * nested (`Box[Box[String]]`)
  * two instantiations of one wrapper in one program (symbol collision)
  * a generic struct with a CONCRETE Map field (`Gmap[T] { m: Map[i64, T] }`)
  * callee MOVES the field out (`let s = b.v`) -- the double-free shape below --
    and the CONDITIONAL form, one branch reading and the other moving
  * callee STORES the param into an owning container (`sink.push(b)`)
  * callee RETURNS the param (tail-return move)
  * callee IGNORES the param
  * the non-generic twin `BoxS { v: String }` -- unchanged, still clean
  * the self-referential control -- unchanged at 5,120 B / 40 (deliberate)

THE PAIRED DOUBLE-FREE RISK, and why it does not fire.
`asan_generic_wrapper_accessor_and_move_no_double_free` (B-2026-07-15-11) is the
test whose callee MOVES the field out -- `fn sink(b: Box[String]) { let s = b.v;
s.len() }` -- and it is the exact shape that killed the earlier caller-side
attempt at this row. It now runs against a param drop that actually FIRES, and
stays clean at both opt levels: the whole-move and field-move-out suppressions
resolve through the same `enum_inst_var_types` record, so the source's caps are
zeroed at the mono offsets and the drop no-ops on what was moved out. The two

  #8  atoi        11x i32, 5x u8 53.9 / 54.4 ms    57.4 / 57.3 ms     1.059x SLOWER

ATTRIBUTION IS COMPLETE FOR #9 AND PARTIAL FOR #8, stated separately because they differ. #9's 1.123x across this ONE commit IS its entire endpoint regression (218dd7d7 -> 688865b4 measured 1.124x). #8's endpoint regression is 1.113x and this commit supplies 1.059x of it, leaving a ~1.05x RESIDUAL still unattributed somewhere in the window -- a second, smaller mover exists and has not been chased.

MECHANISM, from the diff rather than inferred. `compile_narrow_int_binop` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs) now lowers every narrow-int (`i8/i16/i32/u8/u16/u32`) ARITHMETIC op (`+ - * / %`) as: zext/sext both operands to i64, compute at i64, then range-check the i64 result against the declared width's `[lo, hi]` with two `icmp`s plus an `or`, then a conditional branch to a trap block. Bitwise and shift ops skip the check (their results always fit). So the cost is roughly four extra instructions and a branch PER NARROW ARITHMETIC OP, which is why it shows up as a large relative cost in tight integer loops and nowhere else.

THE NEGATIVE CONTROL IS THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE. #11 container has exactly one `i32` in its source and is FLAT to 0.1% across the same pair, while the two narrow-int-dense katas both move. Note the magnitudes do NOT rank by token count (#8 has 16 narrow tokens to #9's 16 yet moves half as much) -- expected, since what matters is how hot the narrow arithmetic is inside the loop, not how often the type is spelled. Presence/absence predicts the effect; density does not predict its size.

THIS IS A CORRECTNESS FIX AND IS NOT A REVERT CANDIDATE. It resolves B-2026-06-08-1 (narrow arithmetic previously computed at the operand's true LLVM width and WRAPPED or TRUNCATED the wider operand) and implements design.md's "traps ... at the declared width". Its own commit message reads 'Zero corpus impact: all flagged katas (reverse-integer, atoi, palindrome, decode-ways, utf-8-validation, valid-number, KMP) build and run correctly -- no spurious traps'. That verified CORRECTNESS on exactly the katas that regressed and never measured their COST, which is precisely how a 1.06x-1.12x hit landed unnoticed. The cost is the unoptimized price of real narrow-int semantics; the follow-on is to make it cheaper, filed as B-2026-08-05-38.

A per-op widen + two compares + a branch costs on any architecture; nothing in the lowering is arch-conditional. title: the ASAN harness SKIPS on a CODEGEN failure ('setup failed -- skipping'), so a memory_sanitizer test written for a shape that does not yet compile reports ok rather than red -- the same vacuous-green class as B-2026-08-04-17, and it makes a leak regression test unprovable against the compiler it was written for
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while proving B-2026-08-05-28's regression tests live. The
codegen E2E went RED against the unfixed compiler as expected; the ASAN test
passed. It was not passing -- it was skipping:

    [surface_concat_chained_xform_receiver] compile_to_object failed: codegen:
      no handler for method 'to_uppercase' on non-identifier receiver ...
    [surface_concat_chained_xform_receiver] setup failed -- skipping

WHY IT MATTERS. A soft skip is right for MISSING INFRASTRUCTURE -- no archive,
no `cc` with -fsanitize=address -- which is what the pattern was built for. A
CODEGEN FAILURE is not missing infrastructure, it is the defect under test. The
practical consequence is that a memory test authored for a not-yet-compiling
shape can never be shown RED, so its liveness has to be argued from an
allocation floor instead of demonstrated, and a future regression that breaks
COMPILATION (rather than ownership) turns the test green instead of red.

`common::link_or_skip` already discriminates -- an undefined-symbol link failure
PANICS with a rebuild recipe rather than soft-skipping, precisely because it
always means staleness rather than absent infrastructure. A codegen failure is
the same kind of signal.

setup absence. Cheap to state, but it will convert any currently-skipping ASAN

title: a `mut ref` PARAMETER given a PLACE argument silently DISCARDS the callee's write on every backend — `bump(mut g.val)` / `bump(mut t.0)` / `bump(mut vs[0].v)` / the forwarding `bump(p.v)` all print the PRE-call value, with no diagnostic at any phase; only a bare identifier argument worked
detail:
SHAPE, minimal:

    struct P { val: i64 }
    fn bump(x: mut ref i64) { x = x + 1; }
    fn main() { let mut g = P { val: 7 }; bump(mut g.val); println(g.val); }

`karac check` passes; every backend prints 7.

MEASURED MATRIX at 7d00f32, `bump(mut PLACE)` with the answer 8 expected in every row:

  place                                    AOT   interp   jit
  bare identifier `a`                        8      8       8   (the only working form)
  struct field `g.val`                       7      7       7
  nested field `g.q.v`                       7      7       7
  tuple element `t.0`                        7      7       7
  Vec element `v[0]`                         8      7       8   <- the only DIVERGENT row
  field of a Vec element `vs[0].v`           7      7       7
  whole struct payload `setq(mut g.q)`       7      7       7
  f64 field / bool field                     7      7       7
  forwarding `bump(p.v)`, p: mut ref P       7      7       7
  generic callee `setg(mut g.v, 8)`          7      7       8

WHY IT SURVIVED. Both backends were wrong by DIFFERENT mechanisms and therefore AGREED on the wrong answer, so the run-vs-build oracle this repo leans on stayed silent. Codegen handed the callee a pointer to a shallow COPY of the place; the interpreter's CICO write-back matched only `ExprKind::Identifier` and `continue`d on every projection. The single divergent row (`v[0]`) is an accident of codegen having an unrelated `ref_arg_index_borrow_ptr` arm.

THE FORWARDING ROW IS THE WORST OF THEM, because the compiler DIRECTS AUTHORS TO IT: writing `bump(mut p.v)` inside `fn go(p: mut ref P)` is rejected with error[typecheck] "this argument is already a mut-ref; drop the `mut` marker", and the spelling it names — `bump(p.v)` — was the one losing the write.

THE GENERAL FORM OF TWO EARLIER ONE-SHAPE FIXES. B-2026-07-12-1 (struct field) and B-2026-08-05-2 (tuple element) both taught the ref-argument path to borrow in place, but gated it to a `{ptr,len,cap}` element — 'so a scalar or enum element keeps the existing path'. That scoping was RIGHT for what those rows had measured: only a heap element can DOUBLE FREE, which was their symptom. The lost-write half is not type-specific, and B-2026-08-05-2's own text predicted exactly this: 'a lost `mut ref` write on a shape with no bounds-checked read after it is a SILENT wrong answer.' Nobody went looking. So the lesson is not that the earlier gates were wrong, it is that a fix whose row NAMES a second failure mode should carry a probe for it.

FIX. The gate is now the PARAMETER MODE rather than the payload type. Codegen gains `fn_param_mut_ref` (the mutate-through subset of `fn_param_ref`) and a place-pointer arm on BOTH call paths — the direct call in call_dispatch.rs and the generic mono call in mono.rs, which needed its own (without it a generic callee kept losing the write under AOT while the interpreter, keyed on the same flags, performed it). `mut_ref_place_arg_ptr` is mostly `field_chain_place_ptr` with ONE deliberate difference: it FOLLOWS a `ref` / `mut ref` parameter root instead of bailing, which is what closes the forwarding row; that walk bails there by design for its other callers, so the borrow is followed locally rather than by widening it. A `shared` / `par` struct place is refused EXPLICITLY (its slot holds a handle, not the aggregate — GEPing it as the struct would write past the 8-byte slot), rather than relying on the `struct_types` lookup happening to miss.

The interpreter stores through `assign_to_place`, the same walk `g.val = x` uses. Restricted to places whose RE-EVALUATION is a no-op, because the store runs after the callee's scope is popped: an impure subscript (`bump(mut v[next(mut c)])`) is skipped rather than evaluated twice, which would double the side effect and pick a different slot than the one the callee borrowed. That leaves the impure-subscript shape at the pre-fix behaviour (write lost, and AOT-vs-interp divergent) rather than wrong in a new way; pinned by `test_mut_ref_place_writeback_skips_impure_subscript` so a later widening is a deliberate act.

READ-ONLY `ref` PARAMS ARE UNTOUCHED, deliberately: a copy is a correct borrow for a reader, and the existing arms do type-specific work on that path (the `Option[shared T]` field RC-inc, the declared-`ref` field forward) that has its own regression history.

TESTS: `e2e_mut_ref_place_argument_writes_back` (tests/codegen.rs) and `test_mut_ref_place_argument_writes_back` (tests/interpreter.rs) — twelve place/payload shapes each, both STASH-PROVEN RED against the unfixed compiler (10 of 12 arms wrong; the two heap controls the earlier fixes bought stay correct in both directions). Suites: non-llvm 8633 pass, codegen E2E and memory_sanitizer clean, clippy and fmt clean.

PROVENANCE. This row previously described only the `shared struct` field spelling, found while sweeping the negatives for B-2026-08-01-33's stage-2 `frozen` projection rule. Widening the probe to plain structs showed the shared case was a SUBSET of a much larger bug, so the row was re-scoped to the general one. The `shared` leg is NOT fixed here and is filed separately.

RESIDUALS FOUND BY THE SAME SWEEP, all pre-existing, all now filed: B-2026-08-05-39 (AOT loses a `mut ref` heap-param REASSIGNMENT, e.g. `x = x + "c"` on a `mut ref String`, for ANY argument form including a bare identifier), B-2026-08-05-40 (`mut Slice[T]` given a Vec-FIELD argument), B-2026-08-05-41 (the `shared struct` field leg, which also bypasses the immutable-field write gate).

fix: CLOSED AS ANSWERED 2026-08-06, owner call, no further code change. What did land under this row: ac79f284 (div/mod check elision — 16.7% at -O0, nothing at -O2, which is what the row is about). title: [CLOSED — NOT A LOWERING DEFECT; both proposed fixes measured and refuted] The narrow-int width trap is emitted UNCONDITIONALLY on every `i8/i16/i32/u8/u16/u32` arithmetic op -- zext/sext to i64, two icmps, an or, and a conditional branch per op -- costing 1.06x-1.12x on narrow-int-dense loops (kata #9 palindrome, #8 atoi) with no range analysis to elide provably in-range checks
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: isolated by the arm64 bisect recorded in B-2026-08-05-34, which attributed that row's real signal to a12a1a69 (2026-06-09, 'narrow-int arithmetic traps at declared width'). This row is the OPTIMIZATION follow-on, not a correctness complaint: a12a1a69 is a correctness fix (it resolves B-2026-06-08-1, where narrow arithmetic wrapped or truncated the wider operand) and implements design.md's 'traps ... at the declared width'. The semantics are right. The lowering is just unoptimized.

WHAT IS EMITTED, from src/codegen/expr_ops.rs `compile_narrow_int_binop`: for every narrow-int ARITHMETIC op (`+ - * / %`) codegen zero/sign-extends both operands to i64, computes at i64, range-checks the result against the declared width's `[lo, hi]` with two `icmp`s plus an `or`, and conditionally branches to a trap block. Bitwise/shift ops correctly skip the check. There is no attempt to prove the check unnecessary.

MEASURED COST (arm64 M5 Pro, matched pairs 7896db16 vs a12a1a69, both orders, --warmup 5 --runs 30, sinks verified, runtime archives byte-identical across the pair so this is codegen-only):
  kata #9  palindrome (16x i32)        77.0 -> 86.5 ms   1.123x SLOWER
  kata #8  atoi (11x i32, 5x u8)       54.2 -> 57.4 ms   1.059x SLOWER
  kata #11 container (1x i32)         191.6 -> 191.6 ms  FLAT -- negative control

WHAT WOULD FIX IT: range/value analysis to elide the check where the result provably fits the declared width -- a loop counter bounded by a constant, an accumulator over a bounded element type, an operand pair whose ranges cannot overflow the width. THIS REPO ALREADY DOES THIS SHAPE OF ELISION ELSEWHERE: B-2026-06-16-1 folds the binary-search midpoint bounds check via `assume(lo <= mid < hi)`, so the machinery and the precedent both exist. A cheaper partial win, if full range analysis is too big: the two `icmp`s + `or` can often collapse to a single unsigned compare of `(result - lo)` against `(hi - lo)`, which is the standard bounds-check idiom and halves the compare cost without any analysis at all.

NOT MEASURED, and it is the first thing to check before optimizing: whether the trap block's terminator lets LLVM delete the branch on its own in some shapes but not others -- that would explain why #8 (which has MORE narrow-int tokens than #9) costs half as much. Density does not predict magnitude here; loop hotness and whatever LLVM already manages to fold do.

CROSS-ARCH: the lowering is not arch-conditional, so this should cost on x86 too and is very likely NOT an arm64-only issue -- see the testable prediction in B-2026-08-05-34. Unlike B-2026-08-05-5, there is no evidence of an architecture split here.

MEASURED ON x86_64 (2026-08-06) — AND THE ROW'S PREMISE DOES NOT SURVIVE IT.
Both cheap fixes it proposes are ALREADY DONE, and the kata it names first is
the one where the expensive fix pays LEAST. Partial fix landed at ac79f284; the
row stays OPEN because that fix does nothing at -O2, which is what this row is
about.

FIRST: THE CROSS-ARCH QUESTION IN THIS ROW'S TRACKER IS ANSWERED. It asks that
this "be measured on x86 first to confirm it is not arm64-specific".
B-2026-08-05-34's x86 leg did exactly that on the 7896db16 vs a12a1a69 pair:
#9 1.191x and #8 1.141x MORE INSTRUCTIONS, #11 identical to the unit, wall
clock 1.096x / 1.172x / 1.000x. It reproduces on x86. Nothing here is
arch-specific and the row is unblocked.

CHEAP FIX 1 — THE SINGLE BIASED COMPARE — IS ALREADY EMITTED, BY LLVM. This row
suggests collapsing the two `icmp`s plus `or` into one unsigned compare of
`(result - lo)` against `(hi - lo)`. That is what -O2 already produces. The
emitted x86 for a checked narrow add is:

    movslq %ecx,%rcx                    ; widen to i64
    lea    (%rax,%rcx,1),%rsi           ; the add
    add    $0xffffffff80000000,%rsi     ; result - lo
    cmp    %r14,%rsi                    ; vs (hi - lo), r14 = 0xffffffff00000000
    jb     <trap>                       ; UNSIGNED branch

InstCombine folds the range-check idiom on its own, so re-spelling it in
codegen wins nothing above -O0.

CHEAP FIX 2 — ELIDING PROVABLY-IN-RANGE CHECKS — WORKS, AND IS ALSO ALREADY
DONE AT -O2. Implemented at ac79f284 for the subset that needs no analysis pass
to be sound: `%` for every divisor (a remainder's magnitude never exceeds its
dividend, which already fits the width) and `/` for a constant divisor that is
not -1 (`INT_MIN / -1` is the sole overflowing division; a runtime divisor
keeps its check). That covers FOUR of kata #9's SIX hot narrow ops — `x % 10`,
`x / 10`, the `x % 10 == 0` guard, and `reversed / 10`. Instruction slope:

    #9  -O0   7,146,329 -> 5,951,421   0.833x   16.7% fewer
    #9  -O2   1,210,924 -> 1,210,924   1.000x   NO CHANGE
    #11 (negative control) identical to the unit at both levels

The elision demonstrably FIRES — 16.7% at -O0 proves it — and -O2 is unmoved,
because LLVM had already deleted every one of those checks itself.

THE CEILING, which is the number that reorders this row. Measured with a
temporary lever eliding ALL narrow checks (unsound, measurement only; every
sink verified identical to the checked build), giving the maximum any range
analysis could ever win at -O2:

    kata            checked      unchecked    ceiling
    #9  palindrome  1,210,924    1,178,191     2.7% fewer
    #8  atoi        3,215,000    2,430,000    24.4% fewer
    #11 container   6,220,013    6,220,013     0.0%  (control)

#9 IS THIS ROW'S HEADLINE KATA — it is named first, it carries the largest
arm64 figure (1.123x), and it is the one the a12a1a69 bisect was run on. Its
ceiling is 2.7%. Range analysis, however good, cannot win more than that
there.

DECOMPOSITION, against the pre-a12a1a69 baseline B-2026-08-05-34 measured
(#9 1,057,007 and #8 2,707,500 per 20k iterations):

  * #9's regression is 153,917 instructions. Removing every check recovers
    32,733 of it. So the RANGE CHECK IS ONLY 21% OF THE COST AND THE WIDENING
    IS 79% — the sext to i64 and computing at i64, which no range analysis
    touches.
  * #8's regression is 507,500, and removing every check recovers 785,000 —
    MORE than the whole regression. The unchecked build lands at 2,430,000,
    which is 10% BELOW where #8 was before a12a1a69. For #8 the widening is a
    net WIN and the checks are the entire cost and then some.

So the two katas need DIFFERENT fixes and this row currently conflates them:
#8-shaped code wants range analysis (24.4% available, and it would end up
faster than before the commit); #9-shaped code wants a cheaper WIDENING
strategy (2.7% available from analysis, 79% of its cost elsewhere).

THIS ROW'S OWN "NOT MEASURED" QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER IS THE
OPPOSITE OF ITS GUESS. It asks whether the trap block's terminator lets LLVM
delete the branch in some shapes but not others, "that would explain why #8
costs half as much". LLVM deletes MORE of #9's checks than #8's — that is
precisely what the 2.7%-vs-24.4% ceiling says. #9 costs more (on arm64)
DESPITE having fewer surviving checks, because its cost is not checking. The
row also notes "density does not predict magnitude"; the reason is now
concrete, and on x86 the #8/#9 ordering inverts entirely (1.172x vs 1.096x
wall), which no density account can explain.

WHAT IS LEFT, restated:
  (1) A range/value analysis, worth up to 24.4% on #8-shaped code and 2.7% on
      #9-shaped code. Still worth building — but sized by the first number,
      not the second.
  (2) The WIDENING, which is 79% of #9's cost and has no row of its own. Every
      narrow op sign/zero-extends to i64, computes there, and the consumer
      coerces back. Whether a narrow op whose operands and result all live at
      the declared width could compute at that width — with the trap on the
      native `llvm.{s,u}{add,sub,mul}.with.overflow.iN` intrinsics, which this
      codebase already uses for the i64 path — is the open question, and it is
      a different change from (1).

REPRODUCE the ceiling: make `narrow_binop_result_provably_fits` return `true`
unconditionally, rebuild `karac`, rebuild the probes, verify the sinks match,
and take the instruction slope between two iteration counts under
`valgrind --tool=callgrind`. Do NOT ship such a lever — unlike the
`KARAC_MAP_TAG` A/B lever B-2026-08-05-5 added, both of whose settings are
correct, this one disables overflow traps and is unsound by construction.

── ITEM (2), THE WIDENING, IS MEASURED AND REFUTED (2026-08-06, x86_64) ──

DO NOT BUILD IT. It was implemented, measured as a matched pair, and REVERTED.
The widening is not overhead — it is what ENABLES the elision that makes the
current lowering fast. The hypothesis in "WHAT IS LEFT" item (2) is wrong at
-O2, and the mechanism is visible in the disassembly.

WHAT WAS BUILT: `+ - *` whose operands are ALREADY at the declared width
compute there on the native `llvm.{s,u}{add,sub,mul}.with.overflow.iN`,
skipping the sext/range-check/truncate entirely — exactly what item (2)
proposes, and exactly how `compile_unaryop` has always negated. Guarded on
both operands already being `iN` (never truncating a carrier, which would turn
a trap into a wrap). Verified in IR: a narrow `*` became one
`llvm.smul.with.overflow.i32` and nothing else.

MATCHED PAIR, one compiler build, an A/B env lever, both settings correct.
The OFF leg reproduces this row's earlier 1,210,924 to the instruction, so the
rig is the same one the ceiling numbers came from:

    kata #9 palindrome    widened 1,210,924    native 1,369,223   13.1% WORSE

WHY — the two builds compiling `reversed * 10i32 + x % 10i32`:

  widened:  lea  -0xccccccd(%r11),%r10     ; ONE biased range check
            cmp  $0xffffffffe6666667,%r10
            jb   <trap>
            ...
            lea  (%rdx,%r11,2),%r11        ; reversed*10 + digit
                                           ; no imul, NO overflow check

  native:   imul $0xa,%r9d,%r9d            ; a real checked multiply
            jo   <trap>                    ; a branch LLVM CANNOT delete

In the widened form the arithmetic happens in a domain where `i32 op i32`
provably cannot overflow, so LLVM uses plain unchecked arithmetic, strength-
reduces `*10` into LEAs, and folds the following add into the same LEA — one
range check on the final result subsumes every intermediate check. The native
form hands LLVM opaque checked intrinsics it can neither strength-reduce nor
fold, and whose branches are real. Widening buys unchecked, optimizable
arithmetic; that is worth more than the sext it costs.

THIS ALSO EXPLAINS THE 2.7% CEILING recorded above, which previously had no
mechanism attached. LLVM was not merely "already deleting the checks" — the
widened form is what makes them deletable in the first place.

THE RESULT IS SHAPE-DEPENDENT, so no blanket switch is right in EITHER
direction. A probe whose narrow result is written back to a `Vec[i32]` (so the
range check must be materialized and cannot be hoisted out of the loop) goes
the other way — widened 660,000 vs native 580,000, 12.1% BETTER native. The
split is whether the narrow value is consumed in-register (widening wins) or
materialized at its declared width (native wins). Exploiting that needs the
consumer's shape at the op site, which codegen does not have, and a heuristic
guessing it would regress this row's own headline kata. NOT SHIPPED.

CONFIDENCE: the #9 regression is solid — reproducible matched pair, the OFF
leg independently reproduces the earlier baseline, and the mechanism is legible
in the disassembly. The store-heavy counter-example is weaker: a small probe
whose two builds differ in ways beyond the narrow arithmetic. It is recorded as
a direction, not a number to plan against. A third probe (a u8 atoi shape) was
DISCARDED as broken, not reported as a result — its slope of ~1,500 per 20,000
iterations means the loop was hoisted, so it measured nothing.

WHAT IS LEFT AFTER THIS: only item (1), the range/value analysis — up to 24.4%
on #8-shaped code, 2.7% on #9-shaped code. Item (2) is closed. The
narrow-negation blocker noted below is also closed (fixed at 736616d),
so item (1) is unblocked, but its own ceiling is unchanged by that.

CARRIER NOTE, which is why the fast path above had to be guarded. A narrow
value does not always arrive at an op as a native `iN` — it can be carried in
an i64 (the call site in assoc_call.rs says so: "an i64-canonical local and an
i8 buffer element of the same type compute together"). That is why the native
path was gated on BOTH operands already being exactly `bits` wide instead of
truncating them: truncating a carrier would silently WRAP a value the widened
path traps on, turning a trap into a wrong answer.

The same carrier split reconciles two apparently contradictory observations
about narrow negation, which B-2026-08-06-7 closed independently. Probing `-v`
where `v` is a NATIVE `iN` local showed codegen already trapping correctly
(`llvm.ssub.with.overflow.i32(i32 0, i32 %v)`, confirmed in IR and on JIT and
AOT); that row's fix was nonetheless real, because its fixture seeds the
operand from `env.args().len()`, producing an i64-CARRIED narrow value that
took the i64 path and did not trap. Both observations are correct; they probe
different carriers. Anything reasoning about narrow-int codegen should state
which carrier it measured.

BASELINE RE-VERIFIED after that row's `emit_narrow_range_check` extraction:
kata #9 still measures 1,210,924 to the instruction, so the matched pair above
describes current main, not a superseded lowering.

── ITEM (1), THE RANGE ANALYSIS, IS MEASURED AND ALSO REFUTED (2026-08-06) ──

BOTH of this row's proposed fixes are now answered, and neither is worth
building. Item (2) was refuted above; item (1) fails for two independent
reasons that between them leave almost nothing on the table.

BOTH CEILINGS FIRST RE-VERIFIED against the real katas, with the unsound
elide-everything lever, sinks identical to the checked builds:

    kata #8 atoi        3,215,000 -> 2,430,000    24.4%   (matches this row)
    kata #9 palindrome  1,210,924 -> 1,178,191     2.7%   (matches this row)

The earlier #8 number was reproduced from `kara-katas` .../8-string-to-integer
-atoi/bench/atoi.kara with only `k_iters` changed. (A hand-written atoi-shaped
probe was tried first and DISCARDED: its inner loop was hoisted, giving a
meaningless ~1,500-instruction slope. The kata reads its inputs through
`ref String`, which is what defeats the hoist. Do not hand-roll a probe for
this row — parameterize the kata.)

REASON 1 — WHERE INTERVAL REASONING SUFFICES, LLVM HAS ALREADY DONE IT. A
probe built to be trivially interval-provable (`acc` and `i` both bounded by
small constants, `acc = (acc + i * 3i32 + 1i32) % 1000i32` inside `i < 1000i32`)
measures checked 2,101,800 vs fully-elided 2,101,600 — a gap of 200
instructions in 2.1 million, 0.01%. There is no headroom for a karac-side
interval analysis on that class; the checks are already gone.

REASON 2 — WHERE THE COST ACTUALLY IS, INTERVAL REASONING CANNOT REACH IT.
Essentially all of #8's 24.4% is ONE line, `result = result * 10i32 + digit`,
confirmed by per-instruction callgrind attribution. Checked, its hot loop
carries `cmp $0xf3333333` + `jle`, a `movslq` to widen, 64-bit `lea`s, and a
`movslq`/`cmp` sext-roundtrip fit test; elided, all of that disappears and the
`lea`s drop to 32-bit.

That check is unprovable by interval analysis, and the margin is exactly 2.
The kata's guard is

    if result > max_div or (result == max_div and digit > 7i32) { return ... }

with `max_div = int_max / 10 = 214748364` (the `cmp $0xccccccc` in the
disassembly) and `digit` in 0..9 from the preceding `b < '0' or b > '9'` break.
Dropping the correlation, as an interval domain must:

    result <= 214748364, digit <= 9  ->  214748364*10 + 9 = 2,147,483,649
                                         i32::MAX          = 2,147,483,647
                                         EXCEEDS BY 2 — cannot prove

Keeping the correlated case split proves it, with both cases tight:

    result <  max_div:  214748363*10 + 9 = 2,147,483,639   fits
    result == max_div:  214748364*10 + 7 = 2,147,483,647   fits, exactly MAX

So the one op that costs is precisely the one whose safety depends on a
DISJUNCTIVE, CORRELATED predicate — the relational fact "if result is at the
bound then digit is small". That is a relational/predicate domain, not the
interval domain this row scoped, and it is a much larger build than "range
analysis" suggests.

RECOMMENDATION: do not build item (1) as specified. The reachable win is ~0.01%
on interval-provable code and 0% of #8's 24.4% without relational reasoning.
Anyone who still wants that 24.4% should FIRST check whether LLVM would even
act on the result: the guard is already in the IR as a branch and LLVM's own
correlated-value-propagation does not use it, so a karac-side proof would have
to be handed over as an `llvm.assume` and shown to survive — establish that on
a spike before building the analysis, not after.

WHERE THIS LEAVES THE ROW. The 1.19x/1.14x narrow-int regression it documents is
real and reproducible. What has been established is that it is NOT cheaply
recoverable: the checks are not the cost where they are elidable, the widening
is load-bearing rather than wasteful (item 2), and the residue sits behind

The row's question was whether a12a1a69's correctness fix left recoverable
performance on the table. Measured answer: no, not as scoped by this row. The
three options weighed:

(1) FUND THE RELATIONAL ANALYSIS — declined on expected value. The build is
large (path-sensitive, correlated facts across a branch — not an interval
domain); the payoff is confined to atoi-shaped guarded accumulators (24.4% of
one kata family, 2.7% of the other); and the delivery mechanism is unproven —
LLVM already holds the guard as a branch in the IR and its own CVP does not
exploit it, which is direct evidence an `llvm.assume` handoff may be ignored
too. Anyone reviving this MUST run the assume-spike recorded above FIRST.

(2) LEAVE OPEN WITH THE DO-NOT-BUILD NOTE — declined as a zombie row. Open
rows drive session work selection (this row alone drew three rounds of
investigation, and the open list produced two sibling-session collisions the
same day). An open medium row whose content is "do not build either fix" costs
future attention and can deliver nothing. All prose survives closure in the
jsonl, greppable by id; B-2026-08-05-34's tracker already cross-references it.

(3) CLOSE — taken, and `invalid` is the honest status: the COST is real (the
1.19x/1.14x reproduces), but the row's CLAIM — that this is an unoptimized
lowering with elidable checks — is refuted. The strongest single fact: the
native-width checked form this row implicitly treats as the optimized target is
the STANDARD checked lowering (it is what `rustc -C overflow-checks=on` emits,
at the type's own width), and karac's widened form measured 13.1% FASTER than
that form on kata #9 (both arms emitted by the same compiler via the A/B lever;
the mechanism — LLVM cannot strength-reduce or fold opaque `with.overflow`
chains, but can prove `i32 op i32` fits i64 and drop to unchecked arithmetic
plus one biased check — is compiler-independent). The residual delta against
the pre-a12a1a69 baseline is the price of the spec'd trap-at-declared-width
semantics (design.md § Integer overflow), which BENCHMARKS.md's equal-safety
framing already accounts for.

  * The store-shape residue: narrow results materialized to memory at their
    declared width measured 12.1% BETTER native (weak confidence — small

title: a `mut ref` AGGREGATE parameter's whole-value REASSIGNMENT stored past its slot — `x = mk()` on a `mut ref String` wrote 24 bytes into the 8-byte alloca holding the borrow POINTER, so the caller's value never changed and adjacent stack storage was clobbered; struct and Vec pointees the same, scalars alone were routed correctly
detail:
SHAPE, and note the argument is a BARE IDENTIFIER — this is not the place-argument class B-2026-08-05-37 fixed:

    fn app(x: mut ref String) { x = x + "c"; }
    fn main() { let mut s: String = "ab"; app(mut s); println(s.len()); }
    AOT 2, interp 3.

Same for `Vec`:

    fn rep(v: mut ref Vec[i64]) { v = [9]; }
    fn main() { let mut v: Vec[i64] = [1, 2]; rep(mut v); println(v.len()); }
    AOT 2, interp 1.

WHAT SEPARATES IT FROM THE WORKING CASES, measured on the same container:
  * `x.push_str("c")` — IN-PLACE mutation of the pointee — is correct on both backends, for an identifier AND for a field argument.
  * `x = 8` on a `mut ref i64` is correct on both.
So it is specifically REASSIGNING the pointee of a heap-carrying (`{ptr,len,cap}`) borrow that AOT drops. The callee most likely writes the new header into a local slot rather than through the borrow pointer, so the caller's header keeps the old buffer.

SEVERITY medium rather than high because the interpreter is right, so `karac run` and the self-host oracle disagree with `karac build` — a divergence this repo's tooling can see — rather than both agreeing on a wrong answer (which is what made B-2026-08-05-37 survive).

NOT MEASURED HERE: whether the old buffer leaks. A reassignment that never lands may also never free what it replaced; the checker for that is the ASAN suite, not this probe.

PROVENANCE: found sweeping the residuals of B-2026-08-05-37, which fixed the PLACE-argument class. This one is orthogonal to the place question — it reproduces with the simplest possible argument.

RESOLVED. THE SCOPE WAS WIDER THAN FILED, in two directions.

1. NOT HEAP-SPECIFIC. This row said 'heap parameter'. Measured, a `mut ref` STRUCT reassignment (`set(x: mut ref Q) { x = Q { v: 9 }; }`) loses its write the same way. The class is any AGGREGATE pointee; only scalars were routed correctly.

2. NOT MERELY A LOST WRITE — IT IS AN OUT-OF-BOUNDS STORE. The `mut ref` param's alloca holds the borrow POINTER, 8 bytes. The generic assign path emitted `build_store(slot.ptr, val)` with `val` a 24-byte `{ptr,len,cap}`, so the store ran past the slot into adjacent stack storage. The row's repro merely printed the stale length; `x = mk()` (a call-result RHS) ABORTED — the E2E test is stash-proven red with `left: ""`, no output at all. Severity is left at medium only because the interpreter is correct, so the divergence is visible to `karac run` and the self-host oracle; the corruption itself would justify high.

WHY IT SURVIVED, and it is written down at the fix site: the note there said an aggregate `mut ref` param 'mutates through methods / field stores that already deref via `get_data_ptr`'. That is TRUE of `x.push_str("c")` and `x.f = v` — both correct on both backends, then and now — and false of a whole-value REASSIGNMENT. The scalar arm was written for `a = a + b` on a `mut ref` lvalue and scoped to scalars with an explicit rationale; nobody checked whether the rationale covered the aggregate reassignment it excluded.

FIX 559a8cc (src/codegen/stmts.rs). The aggregate arm stores through `get_data_ptr(name)` — the caller's storage address — and reclaims the displaced pointee FIRST, which is the same obligation the local-variable reassign arms discharge against their own slot; only the address differs. Reclamation covers the two classes measured broken: a `{ptr,len,cap}` pointee frees its buffer cap-guarded via `emit_free_vec_buffer_if_owned`, and a plain non-generic user struct runs `emit_struct_drop_synthesis` (MEMORY ONLY, matching the caller-retained-roundtrip arm's choice — the NLL channel fires user Drop bodies at the OWNER's site and running the wrapper here would double them). A self-assign (`x = x`) skips both, and a moved source binding in the callee's frame is suppressed exactly as the struct-var reassign arm does, since the value now belongs to the caller.

DOCUMENTED RESIDUAL, deliberately not guessed at: a `shared` handle, `Map`, `Tensor` or enum pointee is stored correctly (those slots hold a single `ptr`, so the store is correctly sized and lands) but NOT reclaimed — the old value may leak. Each needs its own release protocol (rc_dec, the queued per-entry map drop, the tensor block free, the enum payload walk), and inventing one from the outside is how leak-class bugs get made. Filed as a residual here rather than left silent.

THE F-STRING ARM, found by running the memory fixture rather than by reading: `x = f"…"` builds its bytes in a STAGING accumulator whose own `FreeVecBuffer` is armed, and after the store the caller's storage points at that same buffer — leaving both armed aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`. Zeroing the acc's cap is the same disarm the local reassign arm's tail already applies, for the same reason. Every other RHS shape (self-concat, moved local binding, call result, struct literal with heap fields) was valgrind-clean without it, so the arm is specific rather than a blanket.

TESTS, three, each gating a different half:
  * `e2e_mut_ref_aggregate_param_reassignment_writes_through` (tests/codegen.rs) — five RHS classes, STASH-PROVEN RED against the unfixed compiler with `left: ""`.
  * `test_mut_ref_aggregate_param_reassignment_replaces_pointee` (tests/interpreter.rs) — the ORACLE. It passes before and after, which is its job: it pins the reference answer the codegen twin is measured against.
  * `asan_mut_ref_aggregate_param_reassignment_no_leak` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) — the ONLY gate on the reclamation half. MUTATION-CHECKED: with the reclamation disabled the program still prints the right answer and the codegen twin still passes, while valgrind reports 200 definitely-lost blocks per shape (13,780 bytes) and LeakSanitizer fails this fixture. Non-vacuous per B-2026-08-04-17 — opaque `env.args().len()` seed, every payload's content built from it at runtime, byte-level `contains` reads, 200 iterations, floored at 400.

The expected total is DERIVED rather than read off a run: per iteration 1+1+1+(i+3)+1+(i+1) = 2i+8, and sum over i in 0..=199 = 39800 + 1600 = 41400.

title: a `Slice[T]` / `mut Slice[T]` parameter fed from a PLACE (`f(g.a)`, `f(g.q.a)`, `f(t.0)`, `f(vv[0])`) did not COMPILE — the Vec's 3-word `{ptr,len,cap}` reached the 2-word `{ptr,i64}` slot and LLVM module verification hard-failed; only a bare identifier, a range index, a literal and a fresh rvalue were understood
detail:
SHAPE, minimal:

    struct P { a: Vec[i64] }
    fn setz(s: mut Slice[i64]) { s[0] = 9; }
    fn main() { let mut g = P { a: [1, 2] }; setz(mut g.a); println(g.a[0]); }

    error: codegen failed: Module verification failed: "Call parameter type does not match
    function signature!  %a = extractvalue { { ptr, i64, i64 } } %g1, 0
    { ptr, i64 }  call void @setz({ ptr, i64, i64 } %a)"

The interpreter runs the same program correctly. So this is a build-blocking codegen gap on a shape the language accepts, not a wrong answer.

SCOPE, measured with a clean probe (see the CORRECTION below for why that qualifier matters). Four place spellings, each refused for BOTH by-value `Slice[T]` and `mut Slice[T]`:
  struct field           `f(g.a)`
  nested struct field    `f(g.q.a)`
  tuple element          `f(t.0)`
  Vec element            `f(vv[0])`
A bare identifier argument was fine in every slot shape.

READ-ONLY `ref Slice[T]` WAS NEVER BROKEN, and that asymmetry is the interesting part. Its argument takes the borrow path in `call_dispatch.rs` and never reaches `coerce_to_slice` at all — the field arm passes a POINTER to the argument's Vec header, which is correct because `{ptr,len,cap}` starts with `{ptr,len}`, so the callee reads the right two words. That is also why the naive fix regresses it: a value-producing place arm winning on a ref slot pushes a `{ptr,i64}` VALUE into a `ptr` slot — the identical verification failure, one slot-shape over. Measured as a regression while building the fix, hence the explicit guard.

── CORRECTION TO THIS ROW AS FILED, and to the tool that produced it ──

This row originally said the argument 'writes into a copy under AOT — the caller's Vec is unchanged, while the interpreter mutates it', and quoted `AOT=1 (unchanged), interp=9`. THAT WAS WRONG. The program does not build; there is no AOT run to observe. The quoted AOT value came from a STALE BINARY: the probe shell function used `karac build … && out=$(./p)`, so when the build failed the `&&` short-circuited and the variable kept the PREVIOUS case's output. Every 'AOT=' number that row reported for a non-building program was the value of whatever ran before it.

The same defect briefly produced a phantom FIX, too: a later run of the same helper reported this shape as passing at HEAD, which would have closed the row as 'already fixed by someone else'. It was the control case's 9, held over. Bisecting three candidate commits to find a fix that did not exist is what surfaced the tool bug.

WHAT THE HELPER NOW DOES, and the rule worth keeping: `rm -f` the binary before building, then test `[ -x ./binary ]` rather than the build's exit status, so a failed build is reported AS a failed build and can never be silently attributed to a stale artifact. A probe that can report a result for a program that did not compile is not a measuring instrument.

CROSS-CHECKED AFTERWARDS: B-2026-08-05-39's headline numbers were re-measured with the fixed helper at the pre-fix commit and all held (AOT=2/interp=3, AOT=2/interp=1, AOT=empty/interp=5); B-2026-08-05-37's matrix is independently corroborated by its stash-proven E2E test. Only this row was affected.

The place arm rebuilds the `{ptr,len}` header from the place's storage — the same code as the Identifier `Vec` arm, with only the header's ADDRESS differing, factored into a shared helper so the two cannot drift. Positive evidence on both halves: the place's storage must be verified to BE a Vec header (from the containing aggregate's LLVM type) AND `field_chain_place_ptr` must be able to address it, so a shape either half does not model falls through unchanged rather than being guessed at. A `shared` / `par` struct receiver is refused explicitly — its binding slot holds a HANDLE, not the aggregate — the same guard the `mut ref` place arm from B-2026-08-05-37 carries.

NOT RELATED, though it turned up in the same probe: `g.q.a.len()` still bails with 'chained field receivers (`a.b.c…`) are deferred to v1.x'. Confirmed pre-existing and slice-independent — the same bail fires for a plain `.len()` with no slice in sight. A chained-field SLICE ARGUMENT (`f(g.q.a)`) works after this fix.

Four place spellings x by-value and by-ref slots, each MUTATED through a `mut Slice` before it is read: a header built over a COPY would compile and read fine while silently dropping every write, so the mutation is what proves the header points at the caller's real buffer. title: a `shared struct` field reached through a `mut ref` ARGUMENT bypasses the immutable-field write gate that rejects the assignment spelling, and the write is lost under AOT — `n.val = 5` is refused, `bump(mut n.val)` is accepted and does nothing
detail:
TWO DEFECTS STACKED, both on the same spelling.

1. GATE BYPASS. For an IMMUTABLE field of a `shared struct`:

     shared struct N { val: i64 }
     fn bump(x: mut ref i64) { x = x + 1; }
     fn f(n: ref N) -> i64 { bump(mut n.val); return n.val; }

   checks clean. The SAME write spelled as an assignment is correctly refused:
   `n.val = 5` gives error[typecheck] "shared struct field 'N.val' is not declared mut". So the rule exists and is enforced — just not through the `mut ref` ARGUMENT spelling.

2. LOST WRITE, and a divergence since B-2026-08-05-37. For a DECLARED-`mut` shared field the program is legitimate, and AOT still discards the write while the interpreter now performs it:

     shared struct N { mut val: i64 }
     ... bump(mut g.val); println(g.val);   -> AOT 7, interp 8

   Before B-2026-08-05-37 both printed 7. That commit fixed the plain-struct place class on both backends and, on the interpreter, routed shared places through `write_shared_struct_field` (which correctly refuses the immutable case and performs the `mut` one). Its CODEGEN arm refuses a `shared` / `par` place EXPLICITLY, because a shared binding's slot holds a HANDLE rather than the aggregate — GEPing it as the struct would write past the 8-byte slot into neighbouring stack storage. So the divergence is a deliberate fail-closed choice there, not an oversight: the shared spelling needs a pointer derived from the RC payload, plus the mutability gate, and that is this row.

NOT A MEMORY-SAFETY ISSUE as measured: the write went to a stack temporary, so no shared state was mutated and no `par` branch could race through it. That is what kept this at medium — and it is also why it survived, since the symptom is a missing effect rather than a crash.

NOT `frozen`-SPECIFIC, though that is where it was found: the identical program with the parameter declared owned `N`, `ref N`, or `frozen N` behaves the same in all three modes, so this predates the freeze work (B-2026-08-01-33) entirely. That row's escape checker is correct for what it sees — `n.val` lowers to a scalar read and is admitted as one.

FIX, both halves, as the row specified.

TYPECHECK HALF (src/typechecker/fields.rs). The `SharedFieldNotMut` gate keyed on `is_lhs` alone; it now also fires when the field access sits in a `mut ref` ARGUMENT context. The discriminator is the EXISTING `borrow_context`, set by `borrow_context_for_param`, which yields `Some("mut ref")` only for `Type::MutRef` — so a read-only `ref T` borrow and a `mut Slice[T]` argument are untouched. That scoping is the point: widening to every borrow would make an immutable shared field unreadable through any `ref` callee, and the row asks for parity with the ASSIGNMENT spelling, not for a broader rule than the assignment has. Nested chains behave exactly as the assignment already did — `bump(mut o.inner.v)` with an immutable intermediate `Outer.inner` is refused on `Outer.inner`, which is verbatim what `o.inner.v = 9` does today; whether that pre-existing nested behaviour is right is a separate question this row does not reopen.

CODEGEN HALF (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs). The explicit `shared` / `par` bail in `mut_ref_place_arg_ptr` is replaced by `shared_mut_ref_place_arg_ptr`, which loads the handle and GEPs through the RC payload via `shared_gep_layout` — the same funnel every other shared field site routes through, which is what keeps the headed / headerless / weak-headed layouts from ever mixing on one object. `par` needs no separate arm (identical layout; only the count ops differ, and none are emitted here — a borrow is not an ownership transfer), and a plain `mut` field on a `par struct` is unreachable anyway, since `ParFieldNotConcurrent` requires `Atomic[T]` / `Mutex[T]`.

The bail was safe and wrong, which is the useful part of the story: it fell back to the rvalue path, so the write landed on a shallow COPY and was silently discarded. A fail-closed refusal in a resolver whose caller treats `None` as "use the old path" is not fail-closed at all.

DELIBERATELY NARROW, because this family's history is over-broad widenings that had to be reverted. The receiver must be a PURE FIELD CHAIN (identifier or `self` root, `FieldAccess` hops) because both call sites may already have compiled the argument, so re-evaluating an arbitrary receiver would duplicate its side effects; an `Index` hop is excluded on the same rule. A shared ENUM is excluded (no named fields). A `weak` field and a niche `Option[shared]` field are excluded because neither slot holds the value its source type names — one is a non-owning back-edge that reads as an upgrade, the other a bare pointer standing in for a four-word Option — so handing a callee a raw pointer to either would let it write a value of the wrong shape. All exclusions fall back to the pre-fix rvalue path, i.e. no worse than before.

WHAT WAS AND WAS NOT A WITNESS, measured against the unfixed compiler rather than assumed. Four receiver shapes printed 7 and now print 8: a bare shared local, a shared `ref` PARAMETER, `self` inside a shared method, and a nested shared chain (`o.inner.v`). A STRING field was ALREADY CORRECT — an aggregate `mut ref` reassignment reaches the caller's storage through B-2026-08-05-39's path, not through the argument pointer — so it is carried as a control, not a witness, and the test comment says so. It is kept because the fix newly routes it through the place pointer, and a heap payload must keep reclaiming exactly once on that path: free it twice and the RC box's field dangles, free it never and it leaks per iteration. Neither failure was possible on the copy path, so that guarantee is new and gets its own ASAN evidence rather than an inherited assumption.

TESTS. `e2e_mut_ref_place_argument_shared_receiver_writes_back` (tests/codegen.rs) — five arms, PROVEN RED against the unfixed compiler via a temporary bail-restoring hatch (`a:7 b:7 c:7 d:7` vs the expected 8s). `test_mut_ref_place_argument_shared_receiver_writes_back` (tests/interpreter.rs) pins the reference leg, which was already right, so it cannot silently drift to match a future codegen regression. `asan_shared_field_mut_ref_arg_string_no_leak` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) covers the reclaim leg — 1008 allocations measured, floored at 100 per B-2026-08-04-17. Four typechecker tests pin the gate in both directions: the immutable field refused through a `mut ref` argument, the declared-`mut` field still accepted, a read-only `ref` argument NOT gated, and a plain struct NOT gated.

title: a generic wrapper's bare `T` field bound to a MAP leaks its whole handle tree: `fn sink(b: Box[Map[i64, String]])` loses 25,830 B / 40 blocks on a DEFAULT -O2 build, because the mono struct drop's bare-`T` reclassification recognises String/Vec/VecDeque heads only -- the concrete twin `Gmap[T] { m: Map[i64, T] }` is clean, since its DECLARED field name is `Map`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while closing B-2026-08-05-33 predicate (a), as a probe one
variable away from the fixture that row fixed. It is the intersection of that
row's predicates (a) generic-erased field and (b) Map-bearing field, and it
survives the fixes to BOTH.

REPRO, default -O2 `karac build`, under valgrind:

    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    fn sink2(b: Box[Map[i64, String]]) -> i64 { b.v.len() }
    fn main() {
        let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 40 {
            let mut m: Map[i64, String] = Map.new();
            m.insert(i, f"mapv-{i}-padded-out-to-force-a-real-heap-buffer");
            let b = Box { v: m };
            acc = acc + sink2(b);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    -> prints 40 (correct), 25,830 bytes in 40 blocks definitely lost
       (2,880 direct + 22,950 indirect over 120 blocks). Identical at -O0, so
       this is NOT an optimizer-masking artifact.

MECHANISM, established rather than inferred. B-2026-08-05-33(a) made the
by-value param register its scope-exit drop at the param's DECLARED
instantiation, so `__karac_drop_struct_Box$Map_i64_String` IS now synthesized
for this shape. It frees nothing. `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl`'s
name-based classifier reads the declared field `v: T`, matches no arm, and
leaves it `FieldDrop::None`; the subst-driven rescue loop below it then
promotes a bare generic-param field ONLY when the resolved type is a
String/`str` or a `Vec`/`VecDeque` head. A `Map` head falls through and stays
`None`. So the field is classified no-heap at exactly the point where the
subst has already told the compiler it is a Map.

THE ONE-VARIABLE CONTROL that isolates it: `struct Gmap[T] { m: Map[i64, T] }`
passed as `Gmap[String]` is CLEAN. Same generic struct, same Map, same by-value
param -- the difference is that its DECLARED field type is spelled `Map[i64,
T]`, so the name-based classifier sees the head `Map` without needing the subst
at all. Only a field whose declared type is the bare parameter misses.

FIX DIRECTION (deliberately not taken in the row that found it): add the
Map/Set arm to that same reclassification loop --

    Some("Map") | Some("HashMap") | Some("Set") | Some("HashSet")
      | Some("SortedMap") | Some("SortedSet")  ->  FieldDrop::MapOrSet

CAUTION, and it is why this is its own row rather than one more line in
B-2026-08-05-33. That loop is NOT param-specific: it runs for every struct drop
synthesized under a real subst, so the arm changes drop behaviour inside every
MONOMORPH body too, not just for by-value params. This family's history is
three reverted over-broad ownership widenings, and B-2026-08-05-33 records the
method note that the -O2 suite stayed fully green across one that introduced a
double free -- only the -O0 sweep saw it, and only by diffing the failure SET.
So the arm needs both gates in full, plus the specific move-suppression
question below.

THE SPECIFIC QUESTION TO ANSWER FIRST: a Map field freed by a struct drop has no
per-field move-out neutralizer. `zero_struct_field_move_cap` zeroes a Vec/String
cap, an Option tag, a Result payload area -- and for Map/Set does nothing;
`zero_struct_move_caps_mono`'s own comment states Map/Set handles "are NOT
zeroed by this helper today ... they need a `null`-marker convention through
`karac_map_free`". A CONCRETE Map-bearing struct survives that gap because a
whole-struct move retracts the source's entire StructDrop rather than
neutralizing one field (measured: `let g = h; sink(g)` on `struct MapH { m:
Map[i64, String] }` is clean at both opt levels). Whether a bare-`T` Map field
moved out INDIVIDUALLY has the same protection is the thing to establish before
adding the arm -- if it does not, the arm trades this leak for a double free.

NOT A REGRESSION from B-2026-08-05-33: measured against the pre-fix compiler at
8cb7440, where it loses the identical 2,880 B direct + 22,950 B indirect over the same 40 + 120 blocks.

PRECONDITION ANSWERED (2026-08-06), and the answer was NO — filed as B-2026-08-06-6 and FIXED. This row asked, correctly, whether a bare-`T` Map field moved out individually has the same protection a whole-struct move gets. The cheapest decisive experiment turned out to be on the CONCRETE spelling, which already classifies `MapOrSet`: `fn take(h: MapH) -> Map[i64, String] { return h.m; }` SEGFAULTED on a use-after-free. So the per-field neutralizer had no Map arm at all, and the hazard this row predicted was already live for concrete structs. That is now fixed.

THIS ROW STAYS OPEN ANYWAY, and here is the measured reason, so the next reader does not re-derive it. With the neutralizer in place I added the arm this row prescribes. Result:

  FIXED — every READ shape, in full: by-value param (`sink(b)`), plain local
          (`let b = Box { v: m }; b.v.len()` — so this is NOT param-specific,
          which widens the row), and a MID field of a multi-field wrapper.
  BROKE — `fn take2(b: Box[Map[i64, String]]) -> Map[i64, String] { return b.v; }`
          became a SIGSEGV. It is clean today only because nothing frees the field.

WHY THAT SHAPE AND NOT THE STRING ONE. The field-RETURN path (`runtime.rs`, the `te_owns_heap_below_buffer` block) does not neutralize the source — it DEEP-CLONES, so the caller owns an independent buffer and the owner's drop is free to run. Its `single_field_heap_wrapper` gate admits only String / Vec / VecDeque heads, so a Map head falls back to cloning through the bare declared `T`, which is a shallow handle copy, and the returned alias is freed twice.

EXTENDING THAT GATE DOES NOT WORK: there is no `karac_map_clone` in the runtime and no Map arm in `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`, so a Map cannot be deep-cloned at that site today. Closing this row therefore needs ONE OF — (a) a runtime map clone, or (b) that return path switching from clone-the-value to null-the-source, which is what every other move site does. Both are by-value-generic-param machinery, adjacent to B-2026-08-06-2.

The arm was written, measured, and REVERTED rather than landed behind a partial gate; the reason is recorded at the site in `synth_drop.rs` so the next attempt starts from the measurement instead of the idea.

FIXED 2026-08-06, and the row's own CAUTION was right on the substance and wrong
about the remedy. It said the arm 'trades this leak for a double free' unless
the move-suppression question was settled first. It does — measured, 1880
valgrind errors on `let c = b;`. But the settlement is not a runtime map clone
and not a change to the field-RETURN path; both of those were dead ends recorded
here earlier on 2026-08-06 and BOTH ARE NOW SUPERSEDED. The actual defect is
that three sites disagree about what a bare-`T` field IS:

  (1) `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl`'s rescue loop — resolves the bare param
      through the struct subst, but promoted only String/Vec/VecDeque heads.
      THE LEAK.
  (2) `zero_struct_field_move_cap` — classifies by the DECLARED field name and
      resolved it through `subst_monomorph_type_params`, i.e. the ACTIVE
      FUNCTION's monomorph subst. A generic wrapper taken at CONCRETE args sits
      in a CONCRETE function, which has no active subst, so the field stayed
      literally `T`, every name arm missed, and a moved-out field left the
      source handle live.
  (3) `zero_struct_move_caps_mono` — the same erased-name problem; its
      bare-param rescue covered only the Vec/String heads, so a whole-struct
      move left one live too.

(1) alone is the double free the row predicted. All three together are the fix:
both neutralizers now resolve a bare param through the SOURCE BINDING's recorded
instantiation (`enum_inst_var_types`) — the same binding the drop is synthesized
against via `track_struct_var_inst`. The invariant is one sentence: whatever the
free list frees, the neutralize list must be able to disarm.

WHY THE EARLIER DEAD END WAS A DEAD END, since it cost a session. The note above
blamed the field-RETURN deep-clone path in runtime.rs and concluded a
`karac_map_clone` was needed. That path never fires for the failing shape: it is
gated on `self.ref_params.contains_key(recv)` (or a for-loop element binding),
and `fn take(b: Box[Map[i64, String]])` is a BY-VALUE param, which is not a ref
param. Traced with a debug print at the site rather than reasoned about — the
neutralizer DID run, and reported `fname=T`, which is the whole bug in one line.
A shallow-clone hypothesis that happens to predict the right symptom is not a
diagnosis; instrumenting the site took ten minutes and would have saved the
detour.

MEASURED over 18 probe programs at -O2 AND -O0, each cross-checked against the
interpreter. TEN leaking shapes fixed (all 25,830 B / 40 blocks, or 20,710 for
the Set): read via by-value param, read via a plain LOCAL, read as the MID field
of a multi-field wrapper, the field RETURNED out of a by-value param, moved to a
local, passed to a consuming callee, a WHOLE-struct move, a `ref`-param read, a
`Set` instantiation, and a struct-pattern destructure. The plain-local and
destructure shapes mean this row is NOT param-specific as filed — it is wider.

TWO PRE-EXISTING -O0 DOUBLE FREES FIXED AS A SIDE EFFECT, and they are the
useful corroboration precisely because they have nothing to do with Map: a
bare-`T` field bound to a user struct with a String field (`Box[Inner]`)

CONTROLS clean before and after: String, `Vec[String]`, `Option[String]` and
