    karac check         -> All checks passed.
    karac run --interp  -> 6            (correct)
    karac build         -> error: codegen failed: codegen: cannot resolve
                           field 'f' on this receiver

ISOLATION -- one condition apart:

    let x = w.take(); println(x.f);     check ok  interp 6  AOT 6
    println(w.take().f);                check ok  interp 6  AOT FAIL

So the receiver is a NAMED binding with a perfectly good instantiation record;
it is the CHAIN that loses the type. Consistent with the same parser defect
B-2026-08-06-12 and B-2026-08-05-28 both trace to -- a `MethodCall` carries its
RECEIVER's span, so a chain collapses several nodes onto one span key and only
one survives -- but the consumer here is the FIELD ACCESS on the call's result,
not the receiver's layout, so B-2026-08-06-12's field-initializer recovery does
not reach it.

NOT a miscompile: it is a loud build failure with a one-line workaround (bind
the intermediate). Medium for that reason, and because it is a run-vs-build
divergence, which is the class the Mend loop is least able to route around.

Related note carried over from B-2026-08-06-12, not re-measured here: the same
chained shape with the method returning `Box[T]` failed with the same
"cannot resolve field" message.

── FIXED — AND THE ROW'S SUSPECTED MECHANISM WAS WRONG ────────────────

The row attributed this to the span collision B-2026-08-06-12 and
B-2026-08-05-28 trace to ("a MethodCall carries its RECEIVER's span, so a chain
collapses several nodes onto one span key"). That is not what fails here, and
the difference matters because it changes where the fix goes.

INSTRUMENTED, not reasoned about. `fn_return_type_names` was dumped at the
failing site: it holds 21 entries, ALL stdlib (`Command.arg`, `LogEvent.info`,
...). There is no `Box.take` key and no mangled monomorph key either — the
lookup MISSES ENTIRELY rather than returning a colliding wrong answer.

WHY: the declare loop (src/codegen.rs) deliberately skips the registration for a
generic return — "a generic return (`-> T`, where `T` is one of the fn's own
params) has no static name — skip it". That is correct for that map's contract
(it maps to a CONCRETE name). Nothing then records the erased `-> T` anywhere a
consumer could substitute it.

THE NON-GENERIC TWIN CONFIRMS IT, and is now a test control: `impl P { fn
take(self) -> Wide }` registers `P.take -> Wide`, and `p.take().f` has always
built. Same chain, same span shape, no collision — only the generic return
differs. So the span collision cannot be the cause.

THE FIX takes the erased return from the method AST the SAME declare arm already
keeps in `generic_fns`, and substitutes the receiver's instantiation — the exact
mechanism the `FieldAccess` arm above it already uses for a bare-`T` FIELD
(`e.inner` where `e: Wrap[Pair]`). No new compiler state.

It resolves a full `TypeExpr`, not a bare name, and that is load-bearing: the
row's own related note (`wrap(self) -> Box[T]`, chained as `w.wrap().v.f`)
needs the intermediate's generic ARGS to keep resolving, and a name-only answer
leaves `.v`'s bare `T` unresolvable. That shape is fixed too and is in the test.

ORDERING MATTERS: the new arm sits BEFORE `enum_inst_type_from_span` in
`enum_inst_type_of_expr`. The span fallback WOULD hit the collision the row
describes — asked for `w.take()`'s instantiation it finds `w`'s record and
answers `Box[Wide]` for an expression whose type is `Wide`. Resolving the call
first makes the chain's own type win. So the collision is real; it just was not
what produced this failure.

GATE: the fix is gated on the declared return naming one of the STRUCT's generic
params, not the method's — `fn map[U](self) -> U` is not determined by the
receiver's instantiation and must keep falling through — and on the substituted
head naming a type codegen knows.

ONE ADJACENT SHAPE REMAINS AND IS A DIFFERENT DEFECT, filed as B-2026-08-06-22:
a DOUBLY-nested chain `outer.take().take().f` at `Box[Box[Wide]]` still fails.
Instrumentation shows type resolution now SUCCEEDS there — `type_name_of_expr`
answers `"Wide"` and `field_index_for` answers `Some(5)` — and the blocker is
that the chained call's value is not a `StructValue` (it arrives as a pointer),
which `compile_field_access`'s tail has no arm for. Nothing to do with type
recovery. The fully-bound form of the same program builds and runs.

title: two instantiations of ONE generic struct reached through a MIX of literal and named receivers collide on the unmangled `@Type.method` symbol, whose signature is whichever instantiation is emitted first -- LLVM verifier error, while either receiver form alone builds
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-06-12. PRE-EXISTING: reproduces identically with and
without that row's fix (verified by building the same program against both
compilers), so it is neither caused nor fixed by it.

SHAPE, minimal and complete:

    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    impl[T] Box[T] { fn take(self) -> T { self.v } }
    fn main() {
        let n: i64 = env.args().len();
        println(Box { v: n + 41 }.take());              // literal receiver, i64
        let b = Box { v: "named-receiver-string".repeat(n) };
        println(b.take().len());                        // named receiver, String
    }

    karac check         -> All checks passed.
    karac run --interp  -> 21           (correct)
    karac build         -> Module verification failed: "Call parameter type
                           does not match function signature!"

THE EMITTED IR NAMES THE PROBLEM:

    %call7      = call i64 @Box.take({ i64 } %__urecv_tmp_2)
    %usermethod = call i64 @Box.take({ { ptr, i64, i64 } } %b182)
    define i64 @Box.take({ i64 } %0)

Two call sites, two different receiver aggregates, ONE unmangled callee. The
i64 instantiation is emitted first and fixes `@Box.take`'s signature at
`{ i64 }`; the String one reuses the same symbol.

WHY IT NEEDS THE MIX. Both receiver forms mangle correctly on their own -- two
NAMED receivers at different instantiations emit `Box.take$i64` and
`Box.take$struct` and run correctly (measured), and either form alone builds.
The unmangled `@Box.take` is a fallback slot reached when an instantiation
cannot be resolved, and the collision needs two different instantiations to land
in it. Here the i64 literal is the one that falls back: B-2026-08-06-12's
field-initializer recovery declines it, because `infer_arg_elem_te` yields an
empty type name for the arithmetic initializer `n + 41` and that recovery is
fail-closed on a nameless argument.

That suggests two independent fix directions, and the second is the real one:
  1. widen the initializer type inference so a scalar-arithmetic field pins its
     param -- narrows the population that reaches the fallback slot, but does
     not close it;
  2. make the unresolved fallback emission NOT share one symbol across
     instantiations -- the slot itself is the defect. Any expression whose type
     the recovery cannot name will keep reaching it.

Loud build failure, not a miscompile. Medium.

FIXED, and by neither of the two directions this row proposed -- the defect
turned out to be one step earlier than both.

The unmangled `@Box.take` was never DISPATCHED to by the monomorphizer. It was
claimed by the DIRECT method-dispatch arm, which runs first and takes any
function it can find by the unmangled `Type.method` name:

    if let Some(fn_val) = self.module.get_function(&qualified) { ... }

So the i64 literal receiver emitted the fallback slot, and the String named
receiver -- whose instantiation the monomorphizer resolves perfectly well -- never
reached the monomorphizer at all. It was handed the i64 body by name. That is
why the row's own note that "either receiver form alone builds" is exactly
right, and why the mix is required: one call has to CREATE the slot before the
other can be misrouted into it.

The fix is a one-line filter on that arm: a method the declaration pass
registered in `generic_fns` is never dispatched through its unmangled symbol.
Falling through sends it to the monomorphizer, which mangles per instantiation.
A non-generic method is untouched -- `generic_fns` carries a `Type.method` key
for generic ones alone. Emitted IR for the row's own program, after:

    %call  = call i64 @Box.take({ i64 } %__urecv_tmp_0)
    %call5 = call { ptr, i64, i64 } @"Box.take$struct"({ { ptr, i64, i64 } } %b4)
    define i64 @Box.take({ i64 } %0)
    define { ptr, i64, i64 } @"Box.take$struct"({ { ptr, i64, i64 } } %0)

Two symbols, each matching its call sites.

ON THE ROW'S PROPOSED DIRECTION (2), "make the unresolved fallback emission not
share one symbol across instantiations": not done, and stated plainly rather
than quietly declared equivalent. The slot still exists and is still shared
among instantiations the monomorphizer cannot resolve. What changed is that
resolvable instantiations can no longer be pulled INTO it, which is what the
reproducer was.

Whether a genuine two-unresolved-instantiations collision survives is UNPROVEN
in both directions. I could not build one: every non-i64 unresolved receiver
tried dies earlier, at the literal's own lowering (see B-2026-08-06-23), and
i64 cannot collide with itself. That is an argument from failed attempts on a
handful of shapes, not a proof, so the slot is worth removing on its own merits
if it resurfaces -- the reasoning in direction (2) stands.

The test carries BOTH orders. The defect is order-sensitive by construction
(whichever instantiation is emitted first wins the slot), and measured pre-fix
both orders fail -- so a test written in one order only would have been half a
regression gate. It also covers a second method (`peek`) on the same struct, so
the fix is not specific to one symbol. Verified RED against the pre-fix
compiler.

Gates: fmt, clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm, full --features llvm
suite at 0 failures.

tracker: The `call_arg_flows_into_return` arm of the by-value arg loop in src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs, which SUPPRESSES the move-zeroing so the caller keeps its drop — correct for an inline payload, but the returned value owns the BOX as well, so both free it.
title: a boxed `Option`/`Result` binding passed by value to a PASSTHROUGH callee is freed TWICE at -O0: `fn id(o: Option[Option[i64]]) -> Option[Option[i64]] { o }` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`, while the identical program is clean at the default -O2
detail:
SHAPE, 10 iterations, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`:

    fn id(o: Option[Option[i64]]) -> Option[Option[i64]] { o }
    fn main() {
        let mut i: i64 = 0; let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        while i < 10 {
            let bound: Option[Option[i64]] = Option.Some(Option.Some(3));
            let back = id(bound);
            match back { Option.Some(Option.Some(x)) => { acc = acc + x; }, _ => {} }
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    -O0: free(): double free detected in tcache 2   (valgrind: Invalid free())
    -O2: prints 30, valgrind clean

The inner `Option[i64]` is 4 words against `Option`'s 3-word payload area, so
it is heap-BOXED and the let site queues a `BoxedEnumDrop`.

MECHANISM, from the surrounding code rather than from IR — NOT yet confirmed by
reading the emitted module, which is the first thing the next person should do.
The by-value arg loop suppresses its move-zeroing when
`call_arg_flows_into_return` holds, deliberately: on a passthrough the caller
keeps its own drop because the callee returns the same value. That is right for
an INLINE payload. For a BOXED one the returned binding (`back`) ALSO gets a
`BoxedEnumDrop` for the same box, so the box has two owners and both free it.

SOURCE NOTE: found as a CONTROL while probing B-2026-08-06-9 leg A, and
A/B-confirmed identical before and after that (reverted) change, so it is not
caused by it. That row's caution 2 predicted this shape would be "exposed" by a
future callee-side registration and said it "should be measured rather than
assumed benign". Measured: it is already broken TODAY, with no callee-side
registration anywhere in the tree. Filed separately because whoever takes leg A
would otherwise inherit it and read it as their own regression.

WHY -O2 HIDES IT: unconfirmed. Most likely LLVM inlines the identity callee and
folds the pair of frees; the -O0 leg of memory_sanitizer is a ratcheted gate, so
a fixture for this belongs there.

ORDERING: this should be fixed BEFORE B-2026-08-06-9 leg A. Leg A's only
surviving route is a callee-side box registration, and caution 2 says that route
is exposed on exactly this shape.

── FIXED fe7fea77 ──

MECHANISM CONFIRMED FROM THE EMITTED MODULE, which is what this row asked for
first. The row's reading of the surrounding code was right:

    %enumbox = call ptr @malloc(...)      ; one box per iteration
    call void @free(ptr %back_box_ptr)    ; result binding's drop
    call void @free(ptr %bound_box_ptr)   ; source binding's, never suppressed

WIDER THAN FILED, in two ways worth recording:

  * not `Option[Option[i64]]`-specific — the whole boxed-payload family.
    `Option[Wide]` and `Result[Wide, i64]` (a 6-word struct payload) both
    double-free on the same path.
  * NOT -O0-only. The row's "-O2 hides it" holds for its own shape, where the
    payload is scalar and LLVM folds the pair of frees. Give the payload heap
    (`Wide` carrying a `String`) and `Option[Wide]` aborts at the DEFAULT -O2
    too. So this was an ordinary `karac build` crash, not a debug-build
    curiosity, and the fixture is red on both legs rather than only under
    `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`.

THE FIX SKIPS THE RESULT BINDING'S REGISTRATION, leaving the source sole owner.

The opposite direction is the one the row's own mechanism paragraph suggests —
suppress the source's move-zeroing so the result owns the box — and it was
implemented first and is WRONG. When the result is DISCARDED (`id(bound);`
with no binding) the source is the only owner there is, and zeroing it turned a
clean program into a 320-byte leak. Narrowing a registration is the safe
direction here; widening a free is not. That discard case is now a control in
the fixture.

RESIDUAL, unchanged from before the fix and documented rather than hidden:
`call_arg_flows_into_return` is conservative-TRUE on a mixed-path callee, so a
callee that sometimes returns a different value leaves the source's box
unowned. Measured at 160 B over the 5 iterations that take the other branch —
where it used to be a double free.

Test: `asan_boxed_enum_passthrough_arg_single_owner`, floored per
B-2026-08-04-17 and verified RED against the pre-fix compiler at BOTH opt
levels.

TWO SHAPES SPLIT OUT rather than folded in, each A/B-confirmed against the
pre-fix compiler before attribution:
  * B-2026-08-06-26 — `Result[Wide+String]` through the same passthrough with a
    payload-BINDING arm. Improved by this fix (both levels -> -O0 only) but not
    closed.
  * B-2026-08-06-27 — an INLINE heap payload (`Option[String]` built at runtime) through a
    passthrough. Double-frees at both levels, IDENTICALLY before and after this
    change: pre-existing and independent.

METHOD NOTE. A retraction-forwarding mechanism was built for the `Result`
residual on an inferred cause (the arm's `clear_boxed_enum_inner_drop` is
name-keyed to the RESULT binding, which after this fix owns nothing). It
changed NO measurement and was reverted rather than landed — the same standard
B-2026-08-06-12's reverted attempt was held to.

title: a DOUBLY-nested generic chain `outer.take().take().f` at `Box[Box[Wide]]` cannot be built: type resolution SUCCEEDS (the field index resolves to Some(5)) but the chained call's value arrives as a POINTER, not a StructValue, so `compile_field_access`'s tail skips its arm and loud-fails with a message that misleadingly blames type recovery -- the fully-bound form of the same program builds and runs
tracker: src/codegen/expr_ops.rs::compile_field_access, the `if let BasicValueEnum::StructValue(sv) = obj_val` tail. Split out of B-2026-08-06-19 (fixed); NOT fixed by it — verified with that fix in place.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: isolated while fixing B-2026-08-06-19, as a probe beyond that
row's reported shape. That row's single-level chain (`w.take().f`) and its
`Box[T]`-returning variant (`w.wrap().v.f`) are both fixed; this doubly-nested
one is not, and fails for an unrelated reason.

SHAPE, minimal and complete:

    struct Wide { a: i64, b: i64, c: i64, d: i64, e: i64, f: i64 }
    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    impl[T] Box[T] { fn take(self) -> T { self.v } }
    fn main() {
        let n: i64 = env.args().len();
        let inner = Box { v: Wide { a: n, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4, e: 5, f: 6 } };
        let outer: Box[Box[Wide]] = Box { v: inner };
        println(outer.take().take().f);
    }

    karac run --interp  -> 6            (correct)
    karac build         -> error: codegen failed: codegen: cannot resolve
                           field 'f' on this receiver

THE FULLY-BOUND FORM BUILDS AND RUNS, so it is chain-specific:

    let m = outer.take(); let q = m.take(); println(q.f);   -> 6 on both

TYPE RESOLUTION IS NOT THE PROBLEM — this is the part worth carrying, because
the error MESSAGE says it is. Instrumented at the failing site with
B-2026-08-06-19's fix in place:

    field=f  val_is_struct=false  fidx=Some(5)  tno=Some("Wide")
             inst=Some(Path(["Wide"]))

`type_name_of_expr` answers `"Wide"`, `field_index_for` answers `Some(5)` (`f`
IS the 6th field of `Wide`), and the recovered instantiation is right. The
guard that fails is the one BEFORE it:

    let obj_val = self.compile_expr(object)?;
    if let BasicValueEnum::StructValue(sv) = obj_val { ... }

`obj_val` is a POINTER, not a struct value, so the arm is skipped and control
falls to the loud "cannot resolve field" tail — whose message blames type
recovery for what is actually a value-representation mismatch. Anyone
debugging this from the message alone will look in the wrong place. Worth
considering whether that tail should discriminate the two cases in its text.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: why the doubly-nested monomorph returns by pointer
where the single-level one returns a struct value. Plausibly an sret /
indirect-return decision keyed on the nested instantiation's size or on the
monomorph's declared LLVM signature, but that was not chased. That is the first
thing to determine — if the pointer return is CORRECT, the fix is a pointer arm
(load the struct, then GEP the field) in `compile_field_access`; if it is
incorrect, the fix is upstream in the monomorph's return ABI and the tail
should be left alone.

SEVERITY medium, matching its parent: a loud build failure, not a miscompile,
with the same one-line workaround (bind the intermediate).

── FIXED, and BOTH of this row's own diagnoses were wrong ────────────

THE ROW SAID: "the chained call's value arrives as a POINTER, not a
StructValue", with the follow-on question "why does the doubly-nested
monomorph return by pointer where the single-level one returns a struct
value ... plausibly an sret / indirect-return decision".

MEASURED: it does not arrive as a pointer. Instrumented at the failing site,
`obj_val` is an **i64**. And the monomorph emitted for the second `take` takes
a `{ i64 }` self, where the working build emits `{ { i64 x6 } }`. There is no
sret decision anywhere in it — the callee was instantiated at the WRONG TYPE,
and `i64` is simply codegen's erased-parameter default. Dumping the working
form's IR confirms the return ABI was never in question: both monomorphs return
by value (`Box.take$Box` -> `{ { i64 x6 } }`, `Box.take$Wide` -> `{ i64 x6 }`).

So the row's proposed fork — "if the pointer return is CORRECT, add a pointer
arm to compile_field_access; if not, fix the return ABI" — was a choice between
two wrong options. Neither was needed and `compile_field_access` is untouched.

ROOT CAUSE, a SPAN COLLISION one level up. A chained receiver is materialized
into a synth local by `try_compile_freshtemp_user_method`
(src/codegen/method_call.rs), which then re-enters with an Identifier — that is
why the fully-bound form always worked, and it is the same mechanism the chained
form uses. The synth local's INSTANTIATION was seeded from
`enum_inst_type_from_span(object)`. The parser gives a `MethodCall` its
RECEIVER's span, so for `outer.take()` that lookup finds `outer`'s own record
and answers `Box[Box[Wide]]` — the type being called ON, not the type the call
RETURNS. It passes the generic filter, so the local was seeded one level too
high and the next link selected its monomorph at the wrong instantiation.

Exactly the collision B-2026-08-06-19 fixed INSIDE `enum_inst_type_of_expr`
(resolve the call's own return instantiation first, fall back to the span) —
which is why the fix is to call THAT function here instead of the raw span
lookup. ONE LINE.

TWO SPECULATIVE FIXES WERE WRITTEN AND THEN DELETED, which is worth recording
because both looked reasonable. A `MethodCall` arm on `type_name_of_expr`, and
another on `inferred_receiver_type` (whose Identifier/SelfValue-only match is a
real allowlist of the kind this ledger keeps finding). Each was A/B'd by removal
after the span fix landed: the program builds and prints 6 without either, so
both were dead. Shipping them would have added two untested arms to predicates
whose failure mode is precisely looking more complete than they are.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT auto-par / AOT
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) — `6` everywhere, matching the fully-bound twin.

TEST: `e2e_doubly_nested_generic_chain_builds` (tests/codegen.rs), which runs
the chained and fully-bound spellings side by side so the bound one acts as the
in-program oracle. Stash-proven RED: without the fix it reports the original
"cannot resolve field 'f'". (The two spellings need SEPARATE values —
`take(self)` consumes, and the ownership gate in tests/common correctly rejected
the first draft that reused one.)

A DEEPER BUG WAS FOUND BY PROBING BEYOND THIS ROW'S SHAPE, filed as
B-2026-08-06-25 and NOT fixed here: the monomorph name mangles only the type
argument's HEAD, so `Box[Box[i64]]`, `Box[Box[String]]` and `Box[Box[Wide]]` all
collide on `Box.take$Box`. It needs TWO distinct nested instantiations in one
program, fails LLVM module verification, and is PRE-EXISTING — it reproduces
identically with this fix reverted, checked both ways. Three-level chains fail
for that reason, not this one.

fix: FIXED (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs: new `scalar_type_name_of_expr` + `is_scalar_type_name`, chained onto `infer_arg_elem_te`'s namer). Pins tests/codegen.rs `e2e_generic_receiver_literal_with_arithmetic_field_initializer`, stash-proven RED.
tracker: src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs::scalar_type_name_of_expr (new), consulted from `infer_arg_elem_te`, which `concrete_type_expr_of_expr` (types_lowering.rs) uses for B-2026-08-06-12's field-initializer recovery
title: a generic struct LITERAL in RECEIVER position whose field initializer type cannot be NAMED lowers at the ERASED `{i64}` layout: `Box { v: f * 2.0 }.take()` builds an `insertvalue { i64 } undef, double` and fails verification, while the interpreter is correct
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-06-20, as the residual its detail
predicts -- "any expression whose type the recovery cannot name will keep
reaching [the fallback slot]". It is a DISTINCT defect, not that row's tail:
this one fails while building the LITERAL, before any call is emitted, so it is
not a symbol collision and -20's fix neither causes nor addresses it. PRE-EXISTING
-- verified by building the same program against the pre--20 compiler and getting
a byte-identical error.

SHAPE, minimal and complete:

    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    impl[T] Box[T] { fn take(self) -> T { self.v } }
    fn main() {
        let n: i64 = env.args().len();
        let f: f64 = 1.5;
        println(Box { v: n + 41 }.take());
        println(Box { v: f * 2.0 }.take());
    }

    karac check         -> All checks passed.
    karac run --interp  -> 42 / 3        (correct)
    karac build         -> Module verification failed: "Invalid InsertValueInst
                           operands!  %field = insertvalue { i64 } undef,
                           double %fmul, 0"

WHY. B-2026-08-06-12 recovers a receiver-position literal's instantiation from
its FIELD INITIALIZERS, and is deliberately fail-closed: every recovered
argument must carry a non-empty type NAME, because a wrong instantiation
silently lowers a struct at another type's layout and is worse than none.
`infer_arg_elem_te` names an expression through `enum_name_of_expr` /
`type_name_of`, and a BINARY ARITHMETIC expression is named by neither -- it
yields the empty string. So `f * 2.0` declines the recovery, the literal falls
back to the erased base layout `{ i64 }`, and the `double` field store is
invalid.

`n + 41` survives only by accident: the erased layout's default IS i64, so the
wrong answer happens to be the right one. Every non-i64 arithmetic field is
broken -- f64 above, and the narrow widths for the same reason.

NOT A RECEIVER-ONLY PROBLEM IN PRINCIPLE, but it is in practice: the same
literal in a NON-receiver position builds and runs correctly
(`let b = Box { v: f * 2.0 }; println(b.v)` -- measured), because the let-site
seeds the instantiation record from the binding rather than the initializer.
It takes receiver position, where -12's recovery is the only source, to reach it.

FIX DIRECTION, which is B-2026-08-06-20's direction (1) and is worth doing on
its own account: teach `infer_arg_elem_te` to name a scalar-arithmetic
expression by recursing into its operands (a binary arithmetic op has its
operands' type). That pins `f * 2.0` to `f64` from `f`, and the recovery
proceeds. Deliberately NOT done as part of -20: `infer_arg_elem_te` feeds
container element inference and monomorph mangling across the whole backend, so
widening what it names is its own slice with its own suite run -- not a rider on
an unrelated one-line dispatch fix.

── FIXED — AND THE OPERATOR IS ALREADY LOWERED, WHICH SIMPLIFIES IT ──

The row's fix direction was "teach `infer_arg_elem_te` to name a scalar-
arithmetic expression by RECURSING INTO ITS OPERANDS (a binary arithmetic op
has its operands' type)". The recursion turns out to be unnecessary for the
reported shape, and the reason is worth recording because it is not visible
from the source.

BY THE TIME CODEGEN SEES IT, `f * 2.0` IS NOT AN `ExprKind::Binary`.
`rewrite_binary` (src/lowering.rs) has already turned it into

    Call { callee: Path(["f64", "mul"]), args: [f, 2.0] }

— dumped at the failing site rather than assumed. The operand type is
`segments[0]` of the callee path, outright. So the namer reads it off the
callee instead of walking operands: simpler, and exact rather than inferred.
It is the same `type_name` channel `compile_assoc_call` already dispatches its
own narrow-int lowering on.

THE OPERAND RECURSION IS STILL THERE, on the `Binary` arm, because
`compile_expr` retains one — a shape lowering does not rewrite still reaches
codegen unlowered. It is a fallback, not the main path.

UNARY IS A SEPARATE SPELLING and was missed by the first attempt: `rewrite_unary`
emits a ONE-argument `Type.neg(x)` / `Type.not(x)`, so an `args.len() == 2`
gate left `Box { v: -f }` still failing after every binary shape passed. Both
arities are handled now.

COMPARISONS ARE THE TRAP IN THIS FIX, and the fail-closed design is what makes
them matter: `a < b` lowers through the IDENTICAL `Type.op(lhs, rhs)` shape as
`a + b`, but yields `bool`, not the operand type. Naming it `i32` would have
been a silently wrong instantiation — precisely the failure mode B-2026-08-06-12
made the recovery fail-closed to avoid. Comparison and logical `not` return
`bool`; `neg` and bitwise `not` keep their width.

GATED on the callee's head being an actual scalar type name, so a genuine
2-segment call (`Module.func`, an enum-variant constructor) is never mistaken
for a lowered operator. Bare INTEGER literals are deliberately left unnamed:
their width is context-dependent and the erased fallback is already i64, so
naming one would swap a correct-by-accident result for a guess. Every miss
returns `None`, which declines the recovery exactly as before — nothing that
worked previously can regress.

VERIFIED on nine shapes, all three surfaces (interp / AOT / default auto-par)
agreeing: f64 arithmetic, the `n + 41` correct-by-accident control, narrow
signed (`i32`) and unsigned (`u8`), a comparison, a cast, a nested expression,
lowered unary, a `String` non-scalar control, and the non-receiver position the
row measured as already working.

title: EVERY `extern` call under `--interp` reports an "internal ... This is a compiler bug ... please report it" runtime error for an operation the tree-walk interpreter cannot support BY DESIGN -- the sibling `CStr.as_ptr()` path on the same boundary already refuses cleanly and names `karac build`, so the honest message already exists one call away
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-06-17, whose text claimed `--interp` worked for its
repro. It does not, and the failure is not specific to that row's shape.

REPRO, as plain as it gets:

    unsafe extern "C" { fn abs(n: i32) -> i32; }
    fn main() { println(unsafe { abs(-5i32) }); }

    karac run --interp -> runtime error: internal: name 'abs' resolved but has
                          no binding at run time. This is a compiler bug (the
                          resolver should have rejected or bound it) -- please
                          report it with the source.
                            at r3.kara:3:22
    karac run (JIT)    -> 5
    karac build        -> 5

The message is wrong on three counts. It says INTERNAL, for a limitation that
is a deliberate design property (the tree-walk interpreter has no FFI
boundary). It instructs the user to REPORT A COMPILER BUG for a program that is
not buggy. And it blames the RESOLVER ("the resolver should have rejected or
bound it"), which is a red herring -- the resolver is correct to bind a
declared foreign import; there is simply nothing for the interpreter to call.

THE HONEST MESSAGE ALREADY EXISTS one call away, on the same boundary, for the
same reason -- this is what `CStr.as_ptr()` says under `--interp`:

    CStr.as_ptr() is not supported under `karac run`: the tree-walk interpreter
    has no raw-pointer representation (pointers exist for FFI/host-fn
    boundaries, which interpreted mode cannot call). Compile with `karac build`
    instead.

So the fix is to give a foreign-function CALL the same treatment: a structured
"the tree-walk interpreter cannot call extern functions; compile with `karac
build`" refusal, at the call site with the callee named.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. It is the first thing anyone following the FFI
docs hits if they reach for `karac run` before `karac build`, and it tells them
their working program is a compiler bug. It also pollutes the bug channel with
reports that are not bugs. Every FFI program is affected, which is what makes
this medium rather than low despite being diagnostics-only.

SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-06-17's claim that `--interp`
worked; measured on a scalar extern (`abs`) to confirm it is not specific to
that row's `ref CStr` shape.

FIXED. A foreign import is now intercepted AT THE CALL, beside the
MMIO-intrinsic arm it mirrors in `eval_call`, and refused with the message this
row asked for:

    `abs(..)` is a foreign import (`extern`) and cannot be called under
    `karac run --interp`: the tree-walk interpreter has no FFI boundary -- no
    foreign library is loaded and no calling convention is crossed. Compile
    with `karac build` (or run without `--interp`, which uses the JIT) instead.

The old message came from bare identifier evaluation, which owns the generic
"resolved but has no binding" internal error and is the correct home for it --
that arm stays exactly as it was (B-2026-08-02-6 put it there for real resolver
holes). What changed is that a declared import no longer REACHES it.
`is_declared_extern_fn` walks the program's `Item::ExternFunction` and
`Item::ExternBlock` items; the standalone form is unreachable today (the parser
requires the `unsafe extern { .. }` block, with its own focused diagnostic) but
is matched anyway, since the AST variant exists.

TWO DECISIONS WORTH RECORDING, because both could reasonably have gone the
other way:

  * GATED on the name not being bound, exactly like the MMIO arm. A local
    closure shadowing an imported name is a real, if unwise, program and must
    still run -- otherwise the fix trades a bad diagnostic for a broken program.
    Pinned by its own test.
  * ARGUMENTS ARE NOT EVALUATED FIRST, where the sibling `CStr.from_ptr` does
    evaluate its one argument for effects. FFI arguments are usually pointer
    producers, so `strlen(msg.as_ptr())` would hit `as_ptr`'s own refusal and
    report THAT -- pointing at the argument when the thing that cannot work is
    the call. Refusing first names the construct the author wrote. The program
    is ending either way, so no side effect is owed.

VERIFIED on the row's own repro and on the shape from the FFI docs
(`strlen(c"hello".as_ptr())`): both refuse cleanly under `--interp` and both
still print 5 under `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build`.

The test pins the three properties that made the old message wrong -- the callee
is NAMED, `karac build` is offered, and the "compiler bug / report it" framing
is gone -- rather than the exact prose, so rewording stays cheap. Verified RED
against the pre-fix compiler with the exact old text.

Gates: fmt, clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm, full --features llvm
suite 102 suites / 13173 passed / 0 failed.

fix: FIXED (src/codegen/mono.rs: new `append_nested_instantiation_mangle` appends `$<param>_gi_<token>` when a type argument is ITSELF a generic instantiation of a USER struct/enum, deriving the concrete args from the RECEIVER's recorded instantiation). Pins tests/codegen.rs `e2e_two_nested_generic_instantiations_get_distinct_monos`, stash-proven RED.
tracker: src/codegen/mono.rs::append_nested_instantiation_mangle (new), called from compile_generic_call alongside the existing collection and handle mangle axes
title: the generic-impl MONOMORPH NAME mangles only the type argument's HEAD, so `Box[Box[Wide]]` and `Box[Box[Box[Wide]]]` (and `Box[Box[i64]]`, `Box[Box[String]]`) all collide on `Box.take$Box`: whichever instantiation is emitted first wins and every other call site is type-checked against it, failing LLVM module verification with `Call parameter type does not match function signature`. Needs TWO distinct nested instantiations in one program, which is why single-chain probes miss it
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-06-22, by probing BEYOND that row's
reported shape — three chain levels instead of two, and several differently
instantiated chains in one program. The row's own two-level single-chain case
is fixed and is NOT this bug; this one is PRE-EXISTING and reproduces
identically with that fix reverted (verified both ways).

SHAPE. Each of these builds and runs correctly ON ITS OWN:

    let c2: Box[Box[i64]]    = Box { v: Box { v: 41i64 } };  println(c2.take().take());  -> 41
    let s2: Box[Box[String]] = Box { v: Box { v: "hi" } };   println(s2.take().take());  -> hi

Put BOTH in one program and the build fails module verification. Add a
three-level chain and it fails too. The interpreter prints the right answers
throughout.

THE MANGLED NAMES ARE THE EVIDENCE, straight out of the verifier message:

    %call36 = call { { { i64,i64,i64,i64,i64,i64 } } } @"Box.take$Box"({ { i64 } } %c235)
    %call49 = call { { { i64,i64,i64,i64,i64,i64 } } } @"Box.take$Box"({ { { ptr,i64,i64 } } } %s248)

ONE symbol, `Box.take$Box`, is called with `{ { i64 } }` (Box[Box[i64]]),
`{ { {ptr,i64,i64} } }` (Box[Box[String]]) and `{ { { i64 x6 } } }`
(Box[Box[Wide]]). The suffix is built from the type argument's HEAD SEGMENT
only — `Box` — so every `Box[Box[...]]` mangles identically regardless of what
the inner box holds. The first one emitted defines the signature; the rest are
type errors against it.

WHY THE ERROR IS A VERIFIER FAILURE RATHER THAN A WRONG ANSWER: LLVM catches
the signature mismatch at module verification, so this is a loud build failure
today. That is luck, not design — the collision is a NAME problem, and a pair
of instantiations that happened to share an LLVM layout would link silently and
run the wrong body. No such pair has been exhibited, so this is filed as a
codegen-gap rather than a miscompile, but the shape is one layout coincidence
away from being a silent one.

SCOPE, measured rather than assumed:
  * `Box[Wide]` vs `Box[i64]` vs `Box[String]` — NO collision. Distinct heads
    (`Wide` / `i64` / `String`) give distinct suffixes, which is why the whole
    single-level generic surface works and why this went unnoticed.
  * `Box[Box[X]]` for ANY two distinct X — collision.
  * `Box[Box[Box[X]]]` vs `Box[Box[X]]` — collision (both mangle `$Box`).
  So the trigger is a type argument that is ITSELF a generic instantiation.

WHAT A FIX NEEDS: mangle the FULL instantiation, not the head — recursively,
so `Box[Box[Wide]]` and `Box[Box[Box[Wide]]]` differ. The obvious care points
are name length for deep nesting and keeping the mangling stable across
compilations (the ledger already has a nondeterministic-reverse-lookup class,
B-2026-07-20-9, so a hash-based suffix wants a deterministic input order).

NOT ATTEMPTED HERE, deliberately: B-2026-08-06-22 is a one-line span fix and
this is a mangling-scheme change with a much wider blast radius. Bundling them
would make both harder to review and to revert.

── FIXED — THE INSTANTIATION HAD TO COME FROM THE RECEIVER ────────────

The row's fix direction ("mangle the FULL instantiation, not the head —
recursively") is what landed, but the interesting part is WHERE the full
spelling had to come from, because the two obvious sources are both empty at
exactly the colliding calls.

INSTRUMENTED, not assumed. At the mangle site for `c2.take()` where
`c2: Box[Box[i64]]`:

    subst_names = {"T": "Box"}          <- the head-only name, the bug
    call_type_subs_mangle[call_span] = None
    subst_type_exprs = {}

So the typechecker's element-aware token table (which the builtin-collection
axis reads) has NO entry for these call spans, and the codegen-side TypeExpr
map is empty too. Neither could supply the nested spelling. A first attempt
that read `subst_type_exprs` compiled, ran, and changed nothing — the gate
never fired.

WHAT IS on record is the RECEIVER binding's own instantiation, via
`enum_inst_type_of_expr` — the channel B-2026-08-06-19 and -22 made reliable.
`c2` carries `Box[Box[i64]]` in full. An impl method's type params map
POSITIONALLY onto the receiver instantiation's generic args (`impl[T] Box[T]`
on `Box[Box[i64]]` binds `T = Box[i64]`), so the token is read from there.
Arg 0 is the receiver at this site, confirmed in the same dump.

RESULTING SYMBOLS, from `nm` on the four-chain fixture:

    Box.take$Box$T_gi_Box_i64        Box.take$Wide                 <- unchanged
    Box.take$Box$T_gi_Box_String     Box.take$i64                  <- unchanged
    Box.take$Box$T_gi_Box_Wide       Box.take$struct$T_ct_String   <- unchanged
    Box.take$Box$T_gi_Box_Box_i64

THE GATE COST ONE REGRESSION AND IS THE PART WORTH READING. The first gate was
"the bound argument is itself a generic instantiation", which sounds like
exactly the row's trigger. It also catches `T = Vec[i64]` — a BUILTIN
collection, already separated by `append_collection_type_param_mangle`'s
`$<param>_ct_<token>` axis. Suffixing it was redundant AND renamed a symbol
outside this bug: a `mut Slice[T]` mono at `T = Vec[i64]` went from
`kara.state.driver` to `kara.state.driver$T_gi_Vec_i64`, failing
`test_slice_8af_mut_slice_t_composite_element_type`. The gate now also requires
a USER struct/enum head — the class `mangle_mono_name` disambiguates BY NAME
and therefore the only class where the head-only collision exists. `Box[Vec[
i64]]` vs `Box[Vec[String]]` stays with the collection axis, which already
separates them.

That regression is why the "no existing symbol changes" claim is asserted by
the suite rather than by inspection: the looser gate LOOKED inert and was not.

THE ROW'S TWO CARE POINTS: determinism is satisfied by construction — the token
is a pure function of the TypeExpr (`mono_mangle_token_for_type_expr`, which
already recursed), with no hashing and no iteration-order input, so the
B-2026-07-20-9 nondeterminism class is not reintroduced. Symbol LENGTH is
bounded by source nesting depth and deliberately left unhashed: a readable
symbol is worth more than the bytes, and hashing would reintroduce the
determinism question.

STILL TRUE, and unchanged by this fix: the row notes that two instantiations
sharing an LLVM layout would link silently rather than fail verification. This
fix removes the NAME collision for user generic types, which is the reported
defect; it does not add a structural check, and no such layout-coincident pair
has been exhibited.

title: a boxed `Result` passed through a passthrough callee and matched with a payload-BINDING arm still double-frees at -O0: `Result[Wide, i64]` where `Wide` owns a `String`, with `Result.Ok(x) => x.s…` -- the `Option` twin and the non-binding `Result.Ok(_)` arm are both clean
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-06-21, which IMPROVED this shape (double free at both
opt levels -> -O0 only) without closing it.

SHAPE, 10 iterations, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`:

    struct Wide { a: i64, b: i64, c: i64, d: i64, e: i64, s: String }
    fn idres(r: Result[Wide, i64]) -> Result[Wide, i64] { r }
    fn main() {
        // ... let r: Result[Wide, i64] = Result.Ok(Wide { .., s: mk(n + i) });
        //     let rbk = idres(r);
        //     match rbk { Result.Ok(x) => { .. x.s .. } _ => {} }
    }

    -O0: Invalid free() (valgrind), no output
    -O2: prints correctly, clean

ISOLATION -- three probes, one condition apart each:

    Result, arm BINDS the payload  (`Result.Ok(x) => x.s…`)   -O0 FAILS
    Result, arm does NOT bind      (`Result.Ok(_) => …`)      clean
    Option twin, arm BINDS         (`Option.Some(x) => x.s…`) clean

So it needs all three of: the `Result` layout, a heap-owning payload, and an
arm that binds the payload out. The `Option` twin being clean is the useful
part -- whatever disarms the interior on the Option path is not firing here.

INFERRED CAUSE, MEASURED AND REFUTED -- do not re-run this experiment. The
obvious reading is that the consuming arm's `clear_boxed_enum_inner_drop` is
keyed by BINDING NAME, and after B-2026-08-06-21 the live registration sits on
the SOURCE binding (`r`) while the arm retracts against the RESULT (`rbk`), so
the source's inner struct drop runs over an interior the arm binding already
freed. A result->source alias was added so retractions forward to the real
owner. It changed NOTHING: the shape fails identically with and without it, so
the retraction is not (or not only) what is wrong. The alias was reverted.

Next attempt should start from the emitted module for this exact shape and
diff it against the passing `Option` twin, rather than from the retraction
machinery.

── FIXED ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FOUND BY THE DIFF THIS ROW PRESCRIBED, and the prescription was the right one:
`main` emits TWO `__karac_drop_struct_Wide` calls in the Result version and
exactly ONE in the passing `Option` twin. The extra call drops
`GEP rbk, 0, 1` — an INLINE payload view — while the correct one loads word 0
as a pointer and drops THROUGH the box.

MECHANISM. `track_inline_result_payload_cleanup` (src/codegen/runtime.rs)
already guards against exactly this, and its comment describes the failure
almost verbatim ("would read word 1 (the box POINTER) as the first word of the
payload struct"). But the guard consults `boxed_enum_payload_vars`, a set keyed
by BINDING NAME and populated only where a binding is SEEN being boxed
(`track_boxed_enum_var_with_inner_drop`). A binding introduced from a CALL
result — `let rbk = idres(r);`, the passthrough this row is about — is never in
it, so it fell through and got the inline action for a heap-BOXED payload. The
drop then ran `__karac_drop_struct_Wide` over `&slot.w0`, the word holding the
box pointer, read the struct's `String` field out of whatever followed it, and
called `free` on that.

So the retraction machinery this row already refuted was never involved, which
is consistent with that refutation rather than in tension with it.

FIX: gate on the payload TYPE, not on the name set —
`llvm_type_word_count(T) > area`, the same predicate `coerce_to_payload_words`
boxes on and `reconstruct_payload_value` deboxes on, exposed as
`result_payload_is_boxed` beside the existing `option_payload_is_boxed` (both
now share one `enum_payload_is_boxed` body, since Result and Option seed
DIFFERENT areas and asking the Option predicate about a Result payload would
compare against the wrong width). Boxed-ness is a property of the type, not of
how the binding was created, so this closes the class rather than the one
binding shape. The existing `result_payload_tes` helper is reused rather than
duplicated.

THE TWO SIDES ARE GATED INDEPENDENTLY, and that is load-bearing rather than
tidiness. A blanket "either side boxed -> skip the whole registration" passes
the three probes this row names and SILENTLY LEAKS the Err payload of a
`Result[Wide, String]` — boxed `Ok` beside an inline-heap `Err`. That case was
built specifically to pin it: prints 55 matching the interpreter, valgrind
clean, so the Err drop is still emitted and still correct.

VERIFIED, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` under valgrind, all four probes:
  Result, arm BINDS      (the headline shape)   Invalid free() -> clean
  Result, arm does NOT bind                     clean -> clean (control)
  Err side carries the heap payload             clean
  Result[Wide, String], boxed Ok + inline Err   clean, 55 == interp

TEST: `asan_boxed_result_payload_no_inline_cleanup` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs),
floored per B-2026-08-04-17 (opaque `env.args().len()` seed, runtime-built
payloads, `contains` byte reads).

ITS HOME IS THE -O0 LEG, stated explicitly because the fixture would otherwise
read as default-leg coverage it does not provide: at -O2 this program is clean
BEFORE AND AFTER, so the fixture cannot catch this bug on the default leg. It
is red only under `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` — stash-proven there as an ASAN
DEADLYSIGNAL/SEGV without the fix. That is exactly the vacuous-at--O2
population `scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh` (B-2026-08-04-17) exists to gate.

NOTED WHILE VERIFYING: the -O0 leg is now GREEN WITH AN EMPTY QUARANTINE LIST
(958 passed / 0 failed / 0 known failures). The four fixtures quarantined when
that leg landed were drained by B-2026-08-05-7 and B-2026-08-06-10. That
retires the blocker B-2026-08-04-17 recorded for making the leg REQUIRED; the
decision itself belongs to that row.

GATES: fmt clean, clippy clean, memory_sanitizer 958/0, codegen 2832/0,
interpreter 1467/0, typechecker 2154/0, cli 574/0, -O0 leg 958/0.

title: an INLINE heap `Option[String]` payload passed by value to a passthrough callee is freed TWICE at the DEFAULT -O2 as well as -O0, when the payload is built at RUNTIME: `fn id(o: Option[String]) -> Option[String] { o }` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-06-21. PRE-EXISTING and INDEPENDENT: A/B-confirmed
identical with and without that row's fix, which touches only the BOXED path.

SHAPE, 10 iterations:

    fn id(o: Option[String]) -> Option[String] { o }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> String {
        let mut s: String = String.new();
        s.push_str("payload-"); s.push_str(n.to_string());
        s.push_str("-padding-to-force-heap"); s
    }
    fn main() {
        // ... let s: Option[String] = Option.Some(mk(n + i));
        //     let sbk = id(s);
        //     match sbk { Option.Some(x) => { .. x.contains(..) .. } _ => {} }
    }

    -O0 and -O2 alike: free(): double free detected in tcache 2

WHY IT WAS MISSED, and the authoring lesson. B-2026-08-06-21's inline CONTROL
used a string LITERAL payload (`Option.Some("some-text")`) and measured clean,
which is what established "the caller-retains behaviour is correct for an
inline payload" for that row. A literal payload is rodata -- there is nothing
to free, so the control could not have failed however wrong the ownership was.
Swap in a runtime-built `String` and the same passthrough double-frees. This is
the B-2026-08-04-17 hazard in control form: a control whose payload cannot fail
proves nothing, and unlike a vacuous FIXTURE it is not caught by an allocation
floor because the control is not the thing being floored.

HIGH: it aborts an ordinary `karac build` with no ASAN and no
KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, on a shape (`Option[String]` moved through a helper) that
ordinary Kāra code writes constantly.

NOT DIAGNOSED. B-2026-08-06-21 establishes only that the INLINE path is a
different mechanism from the boxed one it fixed -- the fix is boxed-gated and
moves this shape not at all.

── FIXED edee55d9 ──

TWO owners had to go, and the SECOND was only visible with a payload-BINDING
arm — after removing the first, a non-binding `Some(_)` arm went clean while a
binding arm still aborted. That pair is what made the second a measurement
rather than a guess:

  1. the let-site inline registration for the RESULT binding. That site is
     gated on the RHS being any `Call`, so a PASSTHROUGH call slipped through
     even though it aliases an existing binding — exactly what the
     `rhs_is_fresh_inline_enum` arm beside it already excludes, for this same
     double-free reason.
  2. the consuming arm's disarm, which is keyed on the SCRUTINEE's name. With
     (1) skipped the result owns nothing, so the disarm found nothing and the
     source stayed armed against a payload the arm binding now owned.
     `passthrough_owner_alias` forwards result → source.

Direction matches B-2026-08-06-21 and for the same measured reason: narrow the
RESULT's registration, never zero the SOURCE. A discarded result leaves the
source as the only owner there is.

SCOPE CORRECTION to this row as filed: it names `Option[String]`, but
`Result[String, i64]` fails identically and needed its OWN disarm forwarding —
each type carries a separate suppressor. Only the pair shows the fix is not
Option-specific, so both are in the fixture.

WORTH RECORDING AGAINST B-2026-08-06-26: the ownership-alias idea was tried
FIRST on that row's boxed `Result` path, measured to change nothing, and
reverted unlanded. Here the same idea is confirmed by the binding-arm /
non-binding-arm pair. Same mechanism, opposite verdicts, decided by whether a
measurement moved — and -26's real cause (d1aa4477) turned out to be a boxed
payload also receiving the INLINE cleanup, which no amount of reasoning about
retraction forwarding would have reached.

The fixture keeps two must-stay-clean controls — a NON-passthrough consuming
call and a fresh TEMP argument — because this change removes owners, and the
failure mode of getting it wrong is disarming one that is the only one.

NOT CLOSED BY THIS, and pre-existing rather than introduced: a DISCARDED
passthrough result still double-frees. Verified identical before and after.
Filed as B-2026-08-06-28.

fix: FIXED (src/codegen/runtime.rs: new `discarded_temp_aliases_armed_source` declines to register a discarded temp's free when the call is a passthrough of an armed source, applied to the inline-Option, inline-Result and boxed-Option registrars; src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs: `call_passthrough_armed_any_source` widens B-2026-08-06-27's detector to the boxed armed set WITHOUT changing that row's let-site gate). Pins tests/memory_sanitizer.rs `asan_discarded_passthrough_result_does_not_free_source_payload`, stash-proven RED.
title: a DISCARDED passthrough call result double-frees its argument's payload at the DEFAULT -O2: `let d: Option[String] = Some(mk()); idopt(d);` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`, while binding the result (`let x = idopt(d);`) is clean
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-06-27, which fixed the BOUND-result form of the same
passthrough shape. Pre-existing and untouched by that fix — verified by
building the identical program against both compilers — because nothing in it
reaches a call whose result no `let` binds.

SHAPE, minimal and complete:

    fn idopt(o: Option[String]) -> Option[String] { o }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> String {
        let mut s: String = String.new();
        s.push_str("payload-");
        s.push_str(n.to_string());
        s.push_str("-padding-to-force-heap");
        s
    }
    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 10 {
            let d: Option[String] = Option.Some(mk(n + i));
            idopt(d);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println("done");
    }

    -O2 (default): free(): double free detected in tcache 2   (valgrind: Invalid free())
    -O0:           identical

So it is NOT an -O0 curiosity: it aborts an ordinary `karac build`, which is
why this is high despite the shape looking contrived. It is not contrived —
calling a function for its effect and ignoring a passthrough return is
ordinary code.

ISOLATION, one condition apart (measured at edee55d9, i.e. WITH -27's fix):

    let x = idopt(d); match x { … }     clean     (what -27 fixed)
    idopt(d);                           DOUBLE FREE
    let e = …; peek(e);                 clean     (non-passthrough consuming call)
    idopt(Option.Some(mk(n)));          clean     (fresh temp, no named source)

So it needs a NAMED source binding AND a passthrough callee AND a discarded
result. The payload must be genuinely heap: a string LITERAL payload is rodata
and cannot fail — the same flawed-control trap this family has now sprung
twice (see -27's note on B-2026-08-06-21's inline control).

NOT DIAGNOSED. The obvious candidate is that the discarded return VALUE gets a
cleanup of its own — a temporary that is neither a `let` binding nor
suppressed — while the source binding stays armed, giving two owners with no
`let` anywhere for -27's `passthrough_owner_alias` to key on. That is a
hypothesis from the surrounding code, NOT a measurement; the first thing to do
is read the emitted module and count `@free` calls against `@malloc`, which is
what settled -21 and -26.

CAUTION, inherited from -21 and -27: the fix direction on this family is to
NARROW a registration, never to zero the source. Zeroing the source was tried
on -21 and turned a clean program into a leak precisely in the discarded-result
case — which is this row's case.

── FIXED — THE ROW'S HYPOTHESIS WAS RIGHT, AND IT HAD THREE LEGS ──────

The row flagged its own mechanism as a hypothesis and named the way to settle
it: read the emitted module and count frees. Doing that confirmed it exactly.
In the loop body of `main`:

    %call9 = call @idopt(%d8)                      ; passthrough
    store  %call9, ptr %__owned_opt_tmp            ; the DISCARDED result
    ... gep %__owned_opt_tmp -> karac_free_buf     ; free #1  (the temp)
    ... gep %d              -> karac_free_buf      ; free #2  (the source)

Two frees of one buffer per iteration: the discarded return is materialized
into a temp with a cleanup of its own while the source binding stays armed.

THE FIX NARROWS, as the row's inherited caution requires — the discarded-temp
registrar declines when the value aliases an armed source, leaving the SOURCE
sole owner. Zeroing the source is what B-2026-08-06-21 tried and it leaked in
precisely this case. Leaving the source armed can neither leak (it still frees)
nor double-free (nothing else claims the payload).

THREE PAYLOAD SHAPES WERE BROKEN, not one, each measured against the unfixed
compiler rather than assumed by symmetry:
  * inline `Option[String]`   — the reported shape;
  * inline `Result[String, i64]` — same abort;
  * heap-BOXED `Option[Wide]` — same abort, and needing the detector widened to
    the boxed armed set. That widening is a SEPARATE entry point
    (`call_passthrough_armed_any_source`) rather than a change to
    B-2026-08-06-27's `call_passthrough_armed_inline_source`, because the
    latter is that row's `let`-site gate and widening it would change which
    bindings record a `passthrough_owner_alias` — a different decision on a
    different row.
  * `Option[shared T]` was ALREADY clean (rc handles are not buffer-owned) and
    is carried as a control, not a fourth fix.

NEGATIVE CONTROLS, which matter more than the positive ones here because the
fix is a suppression: a FRESH temp (`idopt(Some(mk(n)))`) has no named source
and must still be freed, and a non-passthrough consuming callee must keep
freeing normally. Both verified at 0 leaked bytes.

A SEPARATE, PRE-EXISTING SHAPE WAS FOUND AND IS FILED AS B-2026-08-06-29: the
BOUND-and-then-CONSUMED passthrough (`let x = idopt(d); peek(x);`) still
double-frees. That is the form B-2026-08-06-27 fixed, so it reads like a
regression and is NOT one — verified broken against the pre-fix compiler as
well. Its mechanism is different (a consumed alias, not a discarded temp), so
it is a residual of -27 rather than of this row.

INCIDENTAL: `examples/b26_ir.rs`, an unreferenced IR-dump debug harness left
behind by B-2026-08-06-26's fix (d1aa4477), broke
`cargo clippy --all --all-targets` without `--features llvm` (it calls the
feature-gated `karac::codegen`). Removed as debris.

fix: FIXED (src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs: new `moved_arg_owner_name` resolves a moved-arg name through `passthrough_owner_alias` before the consume-suppressors look it up, so the suppression lands on the binding that actually owns the payload). Pins tests/memory_sanitizer.rs `asan_bound_passthrough_result_consumed_by_callee_frees_once`, stash-proven RED with a real ASAN error.
title: a BOUND-then-CONSUMED passthrough result double-frees at the DEFAULT -O2: `let x = idopt(d); peek(x);` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` -- the form B-2026-08-06-27 fixed for a MATCHED result, still broken when the alias is passed to a consuming callee instead
tracker: src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs::moved_arg_owner_name (new), applied in suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move (the user-fn arg path) and the three _for_moved_arg suppressors
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-06-28, as one arm of that row's
isolation battery. It looks like a regression of B-2026-08-06-27 and is NOT
one: the identical program aborts against the pre-28 compiler too, measured
both ways.

SHAPE, minimal and complete — note the loop, which the -27 fixture did not have:

    fn idopt(o: Option[String]) -> Option[String] { o }
    fn peek(o: Option[String]) -> i64 {
        match o { Option.Some(s) => s.len(), Option.None => 0 }
    }
    fn mk(n: i64) -> String {
        let mut s: String = String.new();
        s.push_str("payload-"); s.push_str(n.to_string());
        s.push_str("-padding-to-force-heap");
        s
    }
    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 10 {
            let d2: Option[String] = Option.Some(mk(n + i));
            let x = idopt(d2);
            acc = acc + peek(x);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    karac run --interp -> correct
    karac build        -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2
                          (valgrind: 10 Invalid free, one per iteration)

WHY IT IS NOT -27's CASE. That row fixed `let x = idopt(d); match x { … }` —
the result is BOUND and then MATCHED. Its fix records
`passthrough_owner_alias[x] = d` so `x` registers no cleanup of its own and the
source stays sole owner. Here the alias is instead passed to a CONSUMING callee
(`peek(x)` takes `Option[String]` by value). The callee frees the payload, and
the source binding `d2` — still armed, correctly, under -27's model — frees it
again.

So the alias record exists and is right; what is missing is that passing an
ALIASED binding to a consuming callee must disarm the SOURCE it aliases, not
just the alias. That is the first thing to check.

CAUTION, inherited from -21, -27 and -28: the fix direction on this family is
to NARROW a registration, never to blanket-zero the source — zeroing turned a
clean program into a leak on -21. But note this case may genuinely need the
source's ownership to TRANSFER at the consuming call, which is a different
operation from either; whoever takes it should establish that first rather than
reaching for the family's usual move.

MEASURE FIRST, as -28 did: read the emitted module and count `karac_free_buf`
calls against the allocations. That settled -21, -26 and -28 and is faster than
reasoning about the registration tables.

── FIXED — THE ALIAS RECORD WAS RIGHT; THE CONSUME IGNORED IT ─────────

The row predicted the fix ("passing an ALIASED binding to a consuming callee
must disarm the SOURCE it aliases, not just the alias") and that is what
landed. Two things it did not know, both found by instrumenting rather than
reasoning:

FIRST, THE ALIAS MAP IS POPULATED AND CORRECT — dumped at the suppression site,
`passthrough_owner_alias = {"x": "d2"}`. Nothing was wrong with
B-2026-08-06-27's bookkeeping. The consume simply never consulted it.

SECOND, THE SUPPRESSOR THAT MATTERS IS NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE. The three
`suppress_*_for_moved_arg` helpers look like the consume path and are where the
first attempt went; they are called ONLY from Map/Vec method sites
(`v.push(o)`, `m.insert(k, o)`), and the debug print showed no
`Identifier("x")` line at all — the user-FUNCTION argument path runs through
`suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move` instead. Resolving the alias in
all four is what actually fixed it; resolving it in the three alone changed
nothing, which is worth knowing before touching this area again.

THIS IS A NARROWING, in the sense this family's rows use the word. The
suppression already existed for a DIRECTLY-armed argument (`peek(d)`, always
clean); it now lands on the binding that owns the payload rather than on an
unarmed alias. It fires only where a consume is already happening — it is not
the blanket source-zeroing that B-2026-08-06-21 measured into a leak.

ONE HOP, NOT A CHAIN, deliberately: the map records a binding's immediate
source. A chained re-passthrough would want a repeated resolve, but that shape
does not arm today, and an unbounded walk over a map that could contain a cycle
is not worth adding unmeasured. Recorded at the helper.

THREE PAYLOAD SHAPES were broken and are all fixed — inline `Option[String]`,
inline `Result[String, i64]`, heap-BOXED `Option[Wide]` — each measured, not
assumed by symmetry.

THE FAMILY'S THREE ARMS ARE NOW ALL CLOSED, and the test carries the other two
as regression controls since all three run through the same alias record:
bound-then-MATCHED (-27), DISCARDED (-28), bound-then-CONSUMED (this row).
Plus the two over-suppression controls — a directly-armed consumed binding and
a FRESH temp that must still be freed — because the fix is a suppression and
going too far shows up as a leak.

title: a SELF-RECURSIVE reduction was scored at ~15,000,000 units per iteration (64^3, the depth cap unrolling the same body and compounding the nested-loop multiplier), so it cleared every cost gate and its body was OUTLINED into a par_reduce worker at every recursion node — ~60% CPU for zero parallelism; filed as an unexplained 1.6x between two spellings of one `frozen` traversal
detail:
SHAPE. Two programs differing ONLY in how the recursive call names its
child, verified by diff:

    let k = n.kids[i]; s = s + sum(k);     <- stage 2.5 alias binding
    s = s + sum(n.kids[i]);                <- stage 2 inline projection

Both take `n: frozen Node`, both compute the identical answer, and the
projection spelling measured ~1.6x slower on both wall and CPU time.

RESOLVED — it is auto-par, not an optimizer interaction, and this row's own
central surprise was backwards.

THE VARIABLE WAS AUTO-PAR, WHICH THIS ROW DID NOT CONTROL FOR. The stage-2
3.7x table was taken with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0; this measurement said "AOT at the
default opt level", i.e. auto-par ON. With it off the two spellings are
identical (0.222s/0.809u vs 0.239s/0.795u). That one comparison, which costs
one rebuild, would have localised this at filing time.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY WAS. `CostEstimator` (src/par_cost.rs) inlines resolvable
free-fn callees to estimate a loop's per-iteration work, bounded by
INLINE_DEPTH_CAP = 3. The cap terminated the walk but never stopped it
unrolling the SAME body at every level, compounding
RUNTIME_NESTED_LOOP_MULTIPLIER (64) each time. `sum`'s own loop therefore
scored, measured with the KARAC_COST_DEBUG=1 lever already on that gate:

    per_iter_cost = 14,883,918   floor = 64

~64^3 x CALL_COST_UNITS — a figure describing the whole subtree rather than
one iteration, and large enough to clear every gate in par_cost
unconditionally. So a two-child loop was lowered to karac_par_reduce and its
body OUTLINED into __karac_reduce_worker_2, at each of the tree's 32,767
internal nodes. The runtime then DECLINED to fan out (the cost gate and
KARAC_PAR_MAX_FORK_DEPTH both hold), but the outlining was already paid: an
indirect call through a descriptor instead of an inlined loop, ~9.6 ns per
`sum` invocation over 13.1M invocations.

The alias spelling was never faster. Its loop body contains a `let`, which
the analyzer does not recognise as a reduction at all (`loop_reductions: []`
in `karac query concurrency`, versus a full parallel_fanout entry for the
projection), so it was simply never outlined. Two spellings, one of which
accidentally avoided a defect.

THE "MORE IR IS FASTER" SURPRISE IS INVERTED. This row recorded `sum`'s body
as LARGER for the faster spelling (81 IR lines vs 42, 9 bounds checks vs 3)
and concluded the difference must be an optimizer decision downstream of
codegen. The slower spelling's `sum` is SMALLER precisely because its loop
body was moved out into a worker fn. The missing 39 lines were the cost, not
the absence of one. An IR line count is not a cost when the lowering under
suspicion relocates code out of the frame being counted; comparing the
binaries' SYMBOLS (`nm | grep __karac_reduce_worker`) answered in one command
what the line count had made mysterious.

NOT NESTING, WHICH IS WHAT THE FREEZE SPIKE ASSUMED. That document's "one
honest caveat about auto-par" attributed the same ~60% (1.19s vs 0.75s) to
nesting a reduction inside an already-parallel region. Refuted: with a
SEQUENTIAL driver — one fan-out total, `sum`'s reduction running inline under
the fork-depth cap, nothing nested anywhere — the projection spelling still
cost 0.330s CPU against the alias's 0.206s. The cost is the outlining itself,
independent of whether a fan-out ever happens.

MEASURED. 2^16-node tree, 4 cores, x86_64, three runs each:

                          alias           projection
  auto-par OFF        0.222s/0.809u    0.239s/0.795u   <- identical
  auto-par ON  before 0.213s/0.807u    0.367s/1.282u   <- the 1.6x
  auto-par ON  after  0.219s/0.804u    0.217s/0.789u   <- closed

The original numbers reproduced exactly (this row: 0.219-0.222 / 0.80 and
0.331-0.364 / 1.26), which is what made auto-par identifiable as the variable.

FIX (a23262c). A cycle guard in CostEstimator: a callee already on the inline
stack resolves to CALL_COST_UNITS rather than being walked again — the same
"opaque callee" fallback the depth cap already used, applied one step earlier.
Seeded with the ENCLOSING function (`new_within`), without which the guard
misses the case that matters: estimating `sum`'s own body starts with an empty
stack, so the first `sum(...)` call is not yet a cycle and the guard only
fires one level down, too late to change the verdict.

The seed is the DECISION KEY (`fn` / `Type.method`), not `Function::name`.
For an impl method those differ — `function_by_decision_key` returns a method
whose `name` is the bare method name — so seeding `func.name` on the query
side and `current_fn_name` on the codegen side would have let the two
disagree whenever a method shares a name with a free fn it calls. That is the
B-2026-07-31-13 class and the reason par_cost exists as one shared module.

Re-measured: `sum`'s loop 14,883,918 -> 24 (declines,
DeclinedVariableKParamBound); the driver's loop 14,883,921 -> 3,598 (still
fans out, because inlining `sum` ONCE legitimately reveals a runtime-bounded
loop). That split is the whole point — the real parallel win is preserved
(3.3x wall on 4 cores) and only the self-recursive level is declined.

Pinned by test_ir_self_recursive_reduction_declines_but_its_caller_still_fans_out
(tests/par_codegen.rs), asserting BOTH directions; the second assertion is
what fails if the guard over-fires and kills reductions merely for calling a
recursive callee, which is the plausible way to get this wrong.
Mutation-checked: disabling the guard turns it red on the first assertion.

SCOPE, and why severity went low -> medium. Filed low as a curiosity ("nothing
is wrong, no answer is affected"). It was a real, silent ~60% CPU cost on the
DEFAULT build for any self-recursive reduction — not frozen-specific and not
specific to this shape; `frozen` only made such bodies reachable by the
analyzer, so it surfaced here first. Impl methods were never affected:
`fn_bodies` keys free functions only, so a recursive method's call was already
opaque.

fix: efc9b308 (fresh-temp half); 85334b0f (retracts the first named-binding attempt); 72840c86 (named half + the let-destructure mirror, both sites)
title: the STRUCT-payload sibling of B-2026-08-06-9 leg A: a boxed struct `Option` payload lost its owner across a by-value call, in both the FRESH-TEMP form (box-only drop, interior leaked) and the NAMED-BINDING form (slot zeroed as a move, nobody took over) — the latter needed a THIRD consumer of B-2026-08-06-10's mirror for the LET-DESTRUCTURE move shape
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-06-9 leg A rather than folded into it,
because the fix there is gated to NON-STRUCT payloads and that gate is
load-bearing -- admitting struct payloads to the same callee-side registration
double-frees three shipped fixtures (see that row). This is what the gate leaves
behind.

SHAPE, KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, 10 iterations:

    struct H { label: String, k: i64 }
    fn readkey(h: Option[H]) -> i64 {
        match h {
            Option.Some(x) => { if x.label.contains("row") { x.k } else { 0 - x.k } }
            Option.None => 0,
        }
    }
    fn main() {
        let n = env.args().len() as i64;
        let mut acc: i64 = 0; let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 10 {
            let hb: Option[H] = Option.Some(H { label: "bnd-" + (n + i).to_string(), k: n + i });
            acc = acc + readkey(hb) - n;
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    -> definitely lost 320 bytes in 10 objects at -O0 (one 32-byte box per call)
       and 51 bytes in 10 objects at -O2 (the label buffers).

`H` is 4 LLVM words against `Option`'s seeded 3-word area, so
`coerce_to_payload_words` boxes it. `readkey` reads only, so ownership infers
`ref` for its own body -- but the CALL still runs
`suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move`, which zeroes the source slot and
disarms the let site's `BoxedEnumDrop`. B-2026-08-06-10's move-out mirror is the
callee-side owner for this payload class, and it fires only on an arm that
actually MOVES; a read-only arm moves nothing, so nobody frees the box.

MEASURED IDENTICAL before and after B-2026-08-06-9 leg A's fix (320 B / 10 at
-O0 on both), which is what makes it a separate row rather than a regression
from it.

TWO SUB-SHAPES, and they differ:

  * FRESH TEMP (`readkey(Option.Some(H { .. }))`) -- the BOX is owned (the
    caller-side arm `is_owned_boxed_option_param` keeps struct payloads exactly
    for this), but the payload's INTERIOR still leaks: 51 B / 10 at both opt
    levels, the label buffers. That arm is box-ONLY by design.
  * NAMED BINDING (above) -- the box leaks too at -O0, on top of the interior.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST "WIDEN THE MIRROR". The mirror's contract is that it frees the
box when an arm moves the payload out; making it fire when the arm moves NOTHING
means the callee frees a box the caller may still reach, which is the exact
shape B-2026-08-05-7's escape guard exists to prevent. The likely correct move is
caller-side and mirrors leg A's passthrough half: do not zero the whole slot for
a boxed struct payload when the callee's inferred mode is `ref` -- but that
predicate is not available at the call site today, which is why this is filed
rather than attempted.

FIXED efc9b308. TWO holes, not one, and the split is the useful part.

  * NAMED binding — the arg site's whole-slot zero is a MOVE, and it only
    balances when another frame takes the box over. Leg A's callee-side
    registration excludes struct payloads, so nobody did. Fix: skip the zero for
    a binding whose box carries a user-struct interior
    (`boxed_struct_payload_vars`, populated by `track_boxed_enum_var` when it
    resolved a `__karac_drop_struct_<T>`).
  * FRESH TEMP — the caller-side arm DID register, but BOX-ONLY, so the
    interior leaked at both opt levels. Fix: hand it the payload struct's name
    so the box drop runs that struct's field cleanup first
    (`owned_boxed_option_param_struct`, which replaces the boolean predicate).

WHICH FRAME OWNS A BOXED STRUCT PAYLOAD TURNS ON THE ARGUMENT FORM, not on the
callee. That is the generalization worth keeping, and it is what the earlier
reading got wrong. A FieldAccess argument leaves the owning struct's field drop
in charge — `place_optres_field_whole_move_info` refuses a boxed payload for
exactly this reason, and `f(nd.hp)` was already clean because of it. A named
binding keeps its let-site drop. A fresh temp has neither. Three forms, three
owners; the callee's own type tells you nothing about which.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW AND TO B-2026-08-06-9's: B-2026-08-06-10's mirror does
NOT free the box. Both rows' prose said the struct case was excluded because the
mirror "already owns" it. What the mirror actually does is ZERO THE BOX'S OWN
WORDS when a callee arm moves the payload (or a field of it) out, so the
CALLER's drop skips what was moved -- see `record_deboxed_payload_box`, gated on
`pattern_binding_scrutinee_is_owned_param`. That is a neutralizer, not an owner,
and it is precisely what makes leaving the caller armed safe here. The
CONCLUSION on leg A's row is unchanged and re-measured: struct payloads have a
caller-side owner and non-struct ones do not, so the gate stays where it is; only
the stated reason was wrong.

MEASURED MATRIX, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` and `-O2`, 10 iterations each, all clean
after and each A/B'd against the pre-fix compiler:

    named + read-only callee      320 B / 10 at -O0 (+ interior)  -> clean
    named + field move-out        (mirror)                        -> clean
    named + whole move-out        (mirror)                        -> clean
    fresh temp + read-only         51 B / 10 at BOTH levels       -> clean
    fresh temp + field move-out                                   -> clean
    fresh temp + whole move-out                                   -> clean
    FieldAccess arg (`f(nd.hp)`)  clean before, clean after
    never passed (`match` in place) clean before, clean after

SIDE FIND, not a regression and not fixed here: leg A ALSO closed a shape this
row did not name -- a FieldAccess argument whose boxed payload is NON-struct
(`f(nd.hp)` over `Node { hp: Option[Option[i64]] }`) leaked 320 B / 10 at -O0
before leg A and is clean after. The residual in that family is an UNCONSUMED
struct field of that type, whose box the owning struct's drop still does not
free; that is B-2026-08-06-32's neighbourhood rather than this row's.

TEST: `asan_boxed_struct_option_payload_by_value_call_no_leak_no_double_free` --
nine arms across the three argument forms and three callee shapes (read-only,
field move-out, whole move-out), plus None sources and a never-passed binding as
the over-suppression controls. Stash-proven RED at BOTH opt levels: 4,302 B in
200 allocations at -O0 and 462 B in 80 at the default -O2, so unlike most of this
family it bites on the default leg too. Expected value COMPUTED (`6i + 4` per
iteration) and oracle-checked against --interp, karac run, AOT and auto-par.

GATES: memory_sanitizer 964 at both opt levels (-O0 leg matches the quarantine
list exactly), codegen 2833, par_codegen 238, full `cargo test --features llvm`
-- 0 failures; clippy `--all --all-targets` with and without `--features llvm`,
and fmt, clean.

REOPENED 2026-08-07, SCOPED TO THE NAMED-BINDING HALF. The close above claimed
both halves; the FULL `cargo test --features llvm` run after the push found
`selfhost_parser_matches_rust_parser_items` aborting with SIGSEGV, bisected to
the named-binding half alone. Retracted in 85334b0f; the fresh-temp half stays.

WHAT SHIPPED AND STAYS (fresh temp). `readk(Some(H { .. }))` had a caller-side
`BoxedEnumDrop` but a BOX-ONLY one, so the payload's interior leaked at BOTH opt
levels (51 B / 10). `owned_boxed_option_param_struct` -- which replaces the old
boolean `is_owned_boxed_option_param` -- now hands that arm the payload struct's
name, so `__karac_drop_struct_<T>` runs before the envelope is freed. Clean on
self-host, on memory_sanitizer at both opt levels, and on the move-out matrix.

WHAT IS REFUTED (named binding). Skipping the arg site's whole-slot zero for a
binding whose box carries a user-struct interior -- a `boxed_struct_payload_vars`
set with one consumer. The argument was that the caller is the only possible
owner (leg A's callee-side registration excludes struct payloads) and that a
callee arm which moves the payload out neutralizes through the box's own words,
B-2026-08-06-10's mirror. It held on EVERY hand-built shape and on the entire
memory_sanitizer suite at both opt levels -- named x {read-only, field move-out,
whole move-out}, the FieldAccess control, the never-passed control -- and it
SIGSEGV'd the self-host parser, which is the sharpest oracle here precisely
because it is a real program with real aggregate returns. Leaving a binding armed
is a WIDENED FREE, and the suites are the only thing that catches an unsound one:
the hand matrix was green on it.

STILL OPEN, therefore: `let a: Option[H] = Some(H { .. }); readk(a);` strands
320 B / 10 of box at -O0 plus the interior. A third attempt should start by
finding WHICH self-host shape breaks -- the bisect stopped at "the named half",
not at a reduction -- because the answer is the constraint the two safe forms
(FieldAccess, fresh temp) already satisfy and this one does not.

TEST as landed: `asan_boxed_struct_option_payload_freshtemp_arg_no_leak_no_double_free`,
narrowed to the fresh-temp arms plus the two move-out arms (which pin the
interior walk in the double-free direction), the FieldAccess and never-passed
controls, and None sources. Stash-proven RED at both opt levels, 231 B in 40
allocations. Expected value COMPUTED (`4i + 2` per iteration), oracle-checked
against --interp. The named-binding arms were removed from it, with a note in the
fixture saying why.

THE SELF-HOST SHAPE IS NOW REDUCED (2026-08-07), which is what the reopen asked
for. Re-applying the refuted named-binding change and bisecting the 109-entry
`selfhost_parser_items` corpus: 17 entries fail solo and EVERY ONE of them is a
