B-2026-08-02-25's displaced-payload bodies walk and after B-2026-08-07-4's eager
free, both of which read the OLD value through the slot.

CAUTION 2 (PROVENANCE) WAS WRONG, and measuring it is what saved a leak. It
argued that `b = c` MAKES `b` a moved-in binding, so B-2026-08-07-4's provenance
record had to be updated at the store or a later reassignment of `b` would
eagerly free a box its source's channels may already have released. But once the
SOURCE is disarmed here, `b` is the box's sole owner and the eager free is
correct — marking it would have stranded the box instead. The
`a8` arm (`b = c;` then `b = fresh;`) is that measurement, and it is clean
without the marking. The two rows' mechanisms compose rather than conflict.

THE NESTED ACTION NEEDED ITS OWN SUPPRESSOR, AT BOTH MOVE POSITIONS, and the
`let` half of that is a gap NO row had recorded — the row lists only the
assignment form and flags the nested variant as "not investigated". It breaks
identically, and so does `let b2 = b;` over a nested binding, because
B-2026-08-05-20 only ever knew direct boxes and B-2026-08-06-32 introduced the
nested action without exercising a binding-to-binding move at all.

The existing suppressor cannot serve it: it is gated on
`boxed_enum_payload_vars` (nested bindings are deliberately in their own set, so
the move rules that are right for a direct box do not reach them) and it zeroes
word 0 of the OUTER enum, which for a nested box is the INNER enum's tag rather
than the pointer — zeroing it would corrupt the tag and free nothing. The new
`suppress_nested_boxed_payload_move` reads the word index off the queued action
(`inner_tag_field + 1`) so it cannot drift from the arithmetic that produced it,
and leaves the tag alone so a payload-absent slot is unaffected.

THE OTHER "NOT INVESTIGATED" ITEM: a self-assign (`b = b`) is clean today and
STAYS clean — excluded explicitly, because zeroing there would disarm the only
owner of the value just stored. Its nested twin is covered too.

THE RUNTIME ZERO IS WHAT MAKES THE BRANCH CASE WORK. `if cond { b = c; }` must
disarm `c` on the taken path and leave it freeing its own box on the other; the
suppressor stores into the branch's own block, so both hold. A compile-time
retraction could not tell the paths apart — the same property B-2026-08-07-1
relied on for the return positions.

TEST: `asan_boxed_payload_binding_move_between_bindings_frees_once` — eleven
arms. Direct / nested-assign / nested-LET / struct-payload / heap-interior
moves, plus five over-suppression controls, which is the direction that matters
because this fix DISARMS a source: a self-assign, a branch move with both paths
live, a source REASSIGNED after being moved from (its action must still free the
new box), a destination reassigned after the move (which pairs with
B-2026-08-07-4's eager free), and a CHAIN where the middle binding is both a
disarmed source and a live destination.

Unlike this family's leak rows the pre-fix compiler ABORTS at BOTH opt levels
(`free(): double free detected in tcache 2`, `Invalid free()` under valgrind),
so the default suite run is a real gate here; what the -O0 leg adds is the
over-suppression half, since at -O2 only a handful of allocations survive
folding. Expected value COMPUTED (`11i + 1` per iteration over 30 = 4815) and
oracle-checked against --interp, `karac run`, AOT and KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0.

ALSO CORRECTS `track_nested_boxed_enum_var`'s doc, which claimed "no destination
takes a NESTED box over" as the reason nested bindings stay out of
`boxed_enum_payload_vars`. A binding-to-binding move does take it over; the
membership decision is still right (that set's other move rules would be wrong
for a nested box) but the justification was too strong, and this row is the
counterexample.

GATES: memory_sanitizer 971 pass at both opt levels (-O0 leg matches the
quarantine list exactly), codegen 2834, par_codegen 241, interpreter 1467,
typechecker 2154, ownership 408, cli 574 -- all 0 failures. All seven self-host
oracles pass. clippy `--all --all-targets` with and without `--features llvm`,
and fmt, clean.

fix: e7a5ebc — SETTLED BY MEASUREMENT 2026-08-07, no behaviour change: the shipped x86 default already was the faster arm. That commit carries the EVIDENCE, in src/codegen/mono.rs::map_tag_compare's doc comment.
title: SETTLED, lane A's DIRECTION confirmed: on x86_64 the map hash-tag compare PAYS for primitive keys, so B-2026-08-05-5's `!self.target_is_aarch64` condition is load-bearing and stays. Dropping the tag costs x86 +12.2% (min) / +13.2% (median) on kata:170 `Map[i64,i64]` with DISJOINT distributions, +5.4% on kata:128 `Set[i64]`, +2.8% on kata:146, and is neutral on kata:217 and kata:219 -- never faster beyond the A/A control, on a host whose A/A control was shown to be 0.2% BEFORE the A/B. Lane B's cachegrind FACTS reproduce exactly; its INFERENCE from them is refuted -- instruction count is not the deciding quantity. The Set site, previously unmeasured on x86, is measured here and agrees.
detail:
RESOLVED 2026-08-07 by measurement, not by code change: the shipped x86 default was already the faster arm, so `map_tag_compare` keeps `MapProbeKey::Primitive => !self.target_is_aarch64` and the fix is the EVIDENCE the row demanded ("the row that says so should say WHY on evidence"), now written into that fn's doc comment.

HOST. x86_64, Intel Xeon @2.80GHz, 4 cores, Linux 6.18.5 container, karac d4259fdf built --release --features llvm. `perf_event_open` returns ENOENT for every hardware counter here too (no virtualized PMU; `scripts/pmc_linux.c` built and run, and it diagnoses exactly that) -- so this is a wall-clock + cachegrind settlement, not a PMU one.

METHOD, carrying the row's own rules. `KARAC_MAP_TAG=1` vs `=0` on ONE karac (the flag, never a commit pair), `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, strictly interleaved A/B/A/B, one unrecorded warm-up rep per binary, minimum AND median of N, sinks asserted equal on every rep. The A/A CONTROL -- one binary against a byte-identical copy of itself, same harness -- was run FIRST at each workload length and is the precondition this row set:
  kata:170 3.9 s  A/A 0.2% by min, 0.02% by median, max/min spread 1.03x
  kata:128 3.6 s  A/A 1.5% by min, 0.8% by median
  kata:217 6.8 s  A/A 0.0% by min, 0.4% by median
i.e. THIS host is quiet at these lengths, unlike the one that filed the row (which saw interleaved maxima at 2.1x their own minima).

RESULT, as the cost of DROPPING the tag (positive = the tag pays), min/median over interleaved reps:
  kata:170 `Map[i64,i64]` keys() walk, 3.9 s, n=10   +12.2% / +13.2%
  kata:128 `Set[i64]` 20k keys, scaled to 3.6 s, n=10 +5.4% /  +5.4%
  kata:146 `Map[i64,i64]` LRU churn, 0.6 s, n=8       +2.8% /  +2.4%
  kata:217 `Set[i64]` 800-key windows, 6.8 s, n=8     +0.7% /  +1.4%  (neutral)
  kata:219 `Map[i64,i64]` window, 0.8 s, n=8          +0.4% /  -1.6%  (neutral)
kata:170's two distributions do not overlap: tag-on max 3971.0 ms < tag-off min 4330.8 ms across all 10 reps. kata:217 was measured TWICE because the first run caught a host disturbance (one rep at 17.6 s against a 6.85 s minimum); the clean re-run is what is quoted, and both runs put it inside +-1.4%. kata:128's shipped bench is only 159 ms on this host -- far inside the noise floor this row warns about -- so it was scaled from 150 to 3500 iterations (the same practice the arm64 lane used for kata:1); nothing else in it changed. kata:146 and kata:219 are sub-second and are reported as directional support only, not as the settlement.

VERIFIED the shipped default IS the tag-on arm on x86: `karac build` with no `KARAC_MAP_TAG` set produces a binary byte-identical (md5) to the `=1` build, and different from the `=0` build. So no code change was needed to get the faster behaviour -- only the justification.

WHICH LANE WAS RIGHT. Lane A's DIRECTION is confirmed (its 1.20x vs this 1.12x is a magnitude difference across hosts, not a sign difference). Lane B is refuted -- but precisely, because its FACTS are not in question: this host reproduces its cachegrind counts essentially exactly (I-refs tag-on 15,081,020,585 here vs 15,081,020,557 there; tag-off 13,106,242,364 vs 13,106,242,350 -- the ~28-instruction deltas are process-startup noise), including D1 misses 3,103/3,104 and LLd 2,359/2,360, which are the same both ways. What is refuted is the INFERENCE that a deterministic 13.1% instruction-count reduction must mean the tag cannot be paying. It can and does: tag-off executes 13.1% fewer instructions and 6.5% fewer D-refs and is still 12% SLOWER, wall-clock, on a host with a 0.2% A/A control. Lane B's supporting argument (2) -- that this would require an implausible ~31% x86 IPC collapse -- is answered by the measurement rather than by argument; the collapse is real and it is what the tag is buying back.

MECHANISM, which is the transferable part. The cachegrind D-ref split is the tell: tag-on does 1,972,299,254 reads + 403,242,805 writes, tag-off 2,221,925,217 reads + 42,805 writes. 1.2M queries x 168 keys = 201.6M key-probes, so tag-off performs +1.24 extra READS per probe (the kv load the tag would have skipped) while tag-on performs exactly 2.00 extra WRITES per probe -- a spill in the hot loop. So on x86 the tag wins by 12% DESPITE spilling twice per probe, because what it removes is a data-dependent load on the probe's critical path: the status byte alone decides whether to advance, so the loop is not waiting on the kv line. arm64's instruction count moves the OTHER way on the same code difference -- there tag-ON is 12.8% FEWER instructions (per B-2026-08-05-5's pmc.c counters) and it still LOSES, 18.5% more cycles, IPC 3.04 -> 2.24. So on both architectures kata:170's instruction count points AWAY from the winner, in opposite directions. arm64 loses because the serialized compare against a computed operand costs more there than the shortened chain is worth. The two architectures are reading the SAME code difference with opposite signs, which is exactly why the gate is (probe shape x target arch) and cannot collapse to key type alone.

FOLLOW-ON worth someone's time, NOT blocking anything: the 2.00-writes-per-probe spill in the tag-on primitive probe is pure overhead on the arm that already wins. Removing it would widen x86's margin and might flip arm64's sign -- if the tag's arm64 cost is partly that spill rather than the compare, a spill-free tag could pay on both. Filed as an observation here rather than a new row because it is speculative until someone looks at the emitted loop.

METHOD NOTE for whoever re-runs this: `karac build` writes to CWD and the two binaries must be built from the SAME karac; use the flag, never a commit pair (this row and its parent both say so, and both had a reading wrecked by ignoring it).

    alias/ResultOk:           got Clean expected Leak

    closure_capture/ResultOk: got Clean expected Leak
    closure_capture/ResultErr:got Clean expected Leak

All 11 x 3 other cells report Clean and 0 are skipped. So four leaks in the shared-type ownership matrix have been FIXED by some commit that did not update the ratchet, and the gate has been red since.

Each step is cheap: the test builds in the DEBUG profile (~4 s rebuild) and runs in ~14 s, so a bisect over the 2026-08-06 range is a few minutes.

THE ADJACENT COMMITS WORTH TRYING FIRST, both of which move exactly the `alias` / passthrough surface these four cells exercise: c00ea51a ("consuming a passthrough alias disarms the binding that owns it", B-2026-08-06-29) and 7f1f3ab1 ("a discarded passthrough result no longer frees its argument's payload", B-2026-08-06-28).

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY BOOKKEEPING: while it is red, this gate cannot fail for the reason it exists -- a genuine NEW leak in any of the 33 cells would land on top of an already-red test and be invisible in CI. A red ratchet is a disabled ratchet.

NOT AN UNRECORDED WIN — THE DETECTOR WAS INERT. Fixed 8452994b, and the row's
own diagnosis is the thing being corrected.

REPRODUCED EXACTLY, which is what settles it. Prefixing the test with
`LSAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0` prints this row's four lines VERBATIM:

    alias/ResultOk:            got Clean expected Leak
    alias/ResultErr:           got Clean expected Leak
    closure_capture/ResultOk:  got Clean expected Leak
    closure_capture/ResultErr: got Clean expected Leak

The cause is one line in `classify`'s run closure: it sets `ASAN_OPTIONS` and
leaves `LSAN_OPTIONS` INHERITED, and the latter takes PRECEDENCE for leak
detection. So the closure asks for `detect_leaks=1` and does not get it.

AND THE FOUR CELLS ARE NOT FIXED. On this container they report `Leak` at the
row's own SHAs -- checked at ca037cb0 and a23262c, the two the row names as red.
Nothing was fixed, the ratchet table is correct as written, and the bisect this
row prescribed would have found nothing. The "adjacent commits worth trying
first" lead (c00ea51a and the alias/passthrough surface) is void.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE MISREADING, and why the fix is hardening rather
than a one-line env tweak: every assertion in this test reads a NEGATIVE result
as good news, so an inert detector makes the entire grid look perfect. The
ratchet's own failure message then invites the reader to relax FLOWS.expected --
which would have permanently deleted four real leaks from the gate. A ratchet
that an environment variable can silently unwind is worse than no ratchet,
because it launders the loss as progress.

TWO CHANGES. (1) The run closure sets `LSAN_OPTIONS` explicitly alongside
`ASAN_OPTIONS`. (2) A DETECTOR CONTROL runs before every other assertion: a C

with "LEAK DETECTION IS INERT" and an explicit "do NOT relax FLOWS.expected"
instead of a frontier diff.

compiler progress can turn it green and quietly retire the guard. A Kara canary
was written first and is UNWRITABLE for this purpose: every `shared` shape that
leaks today is a bug someone will fix, which makes the control circular -- the
first attempt used a `shared struct` in a loop and came back Clean because the
compiler is correct there.

GENERAL LESSON, worth carrying to any other ratchet or sanitizer gate: this is
B-2026-08-04-17 one level up. That row's floor proves the PROGRAM allocated; this
one proves the DETECTOR looked. A suite whose green depends on a tool actually
running needs a positive control for the tool, not just for the subject.

title: `self` cannot be passed to a BORROW parameter from any receiver mode — `byref(self)` from `ref self` is `expected 'ref Inner', found 'Inner'`, and so is every other receiver/borrow-param combination
detail:
SHAPE. A method cannot hand its own receiver to a function taking a
borrow, whatever mode either side declares:

    fn byref(i: ref Inner) -> i64 { i.v }
    fn frz(i: frozen Inner) -> i64 { i.v }

    impl Inner { fn a(ref self)    -> i64 { byref(self) } }  // error
    impl Inner { fn b(frozen self) -> i64 { frz(self)   } }  // error
    impl Inner { fn c(ref self)    -> i64 { frz(self)   } }  // error
    impl Inner { fn d(self)        -> i64 { byref(self) } }  // error

All four report the same thing:

    error[typecheck]: expected 'ref Inner', found 'Inner'

The typechecker types `self` as `T` regardless of the receiver mode, while a
`ref T` parameter's declared type is `ref T`. So there is no receiver mode
from which a borrow parameter is reachable.

NOT A `frozen` DEFECT, and that is why it is filed on its own. It was found
while building `frozen self` (B-2026-08-01-33 stage 2.7), where the shape is
`frz(self)` — but the `ref self` -> `ref T` case is the same error and
predates all of the freeze work. `frozen T` lowers to `ref T` at parse time,
so it inherits the gap rather than causing it.

WHAT IS UNAFFECTED. Method-to-method composition works: a `frozen self`
method may call another `frozen self` method on `self` or on any place off
it, which is the path the OO traversal actually takes. Only the
receiver-to-FREE-FUNCTION-borrow-slot direction is blocked.

THE MESSAGE IS ALSO CONFUSING IN THE MIRRORED CASE. Returning `self` from a
`ref self` method whose return type is the bare type prints "expected
'Inner', found 'Inner'" — the two sides render identically because the
borrow-ness is not shown. Whatever the fix to the rule, the renderer should
distinguish them.

NOT INVESTIGATED: whether the right fix is to type `self` by its receiver
mode, to coerce at the call site, or to leave the rule and improve the
message. Each is a different-sized change and the choice is a design call.

SEVERITY low: it blocks one composition direction, has an easy workaround
(make the callee a method, or take the parameter by value), and nothing
miscompiles.

── FIXED (2026-08-07) ──

NOT A BORROW-RULE GAP, and the row's whole diagnosis is the thing that needed
correcting. It reads: "The typechecker types `self` as `T` regardless of the
receiver mode, while a `ref T` parameter's declared type is `ref T`. So there is
no receiver mode from which a borrow parameter is reachable." Nothing about
borrows is involved.

THE ROW'S REDUCTION DOES NOT REPRODUCE AS WRITTEN. With `struct Inner` every one
of its four cases PASSES today, in every receiver/parameter combination. The
reduction only fails when `Inner` is a `shared struct` — which it must have been,
since the row's own `frozen Inner` parameter requires one (`frozen` on a
non-shared type is now an ownership error). The shared-ness was the load-bearing
detail and it went unrecorded.

ROOT CAUSE. `lower_type_expr` maps the bare name of a `shared struct S` to
`Type::Shared(S)` — deliberately distinct from `Type::Named { name: "S" }` so
consumers can match shared-ness off the type without consulting the item table
(see `Type::Shared`'s doc). The impl's `self_type` then ran the lowered type
through a `match` whose fallback rebuilds it as `Type::Named { name, args: [] }`.
That fallback exists to ERASE GENERIC ARGS, so `impl Foo[T]`'s `self` is `Foo`
rather than `Foo[T]` — but it also swallowed the shared form, and `self` ended up
typed as a DIFFERENT type from every annotation naming the same struct.

The two RENDER identically (`Type::Shared(n)` displays as `n`). That is the whole
explanation for the confusing message the row files as a separate renderer
concern: "expected 'Inner', found 'Inner'" is `Shared("Inner")` vs
`Named{"Inner"}`, not two identical types and not hidden borrow-ness. Where a
borrow was involved the same mismatch merely printed as "expected 'ref Inner',
found 'Inner'", which is what made it look like a borrow rule.

FIX: one match arm — `Type::Shared(_) => lowered.clone()` — preserving what the
lowering already computed. Safe precisely because the fallback's purpose is
arg erasure and a shared struct is non-generic at v1, so there are no args to
erase.

TWO CLAIMS OF "UNAFFECTED" WERE ALSO WRONG, both measured:
  * "Only the receiver-to-FREE-FUNCTION-borrow-slot direction is blocked." A
    BY-VALUE parameter (`fn byval(i: Inner)`, `byval(self)`) failed identically.
  * The mirrored RETURN case (`fn me(ref self) -> Inner { self }`) is the same
    root, not a separate renderer issue, and the same one-line fix closes it.

WHAT STAYS AN ERROR, correctly: `frozen self` passed to a plain `ref` slot now
reports "`frozen` receiver `self` is passed to a non-`frozen` slot" — the freeze
rule doing its job, no longer masked by the type confusion.

THE RENDERER QUESTION IS ANSWERED BY PROBING, not by leaving it open. With the
root fixed I could not construct a remaining `Shared`-vs-`Named` mismatch that
renders identically: trait-impl dispatch, a generic `id[T]`, a `Vec` element, a
shared field of a shared struct, and an associated-fn `-> Self` all type cleanly.
So no renderer change is warranted for this class today; if one resurfaces it
will be a fresh instance of the same swallow, not a rendering defect.

SHARED ENUMS WERE NEVER AFFECTED and the asymmetry is worth knowing: only shared
STRUCTS lower to `Type::Shared` (the interception in `lowering.rs` consults
`env.structs` only), so a `shared enum`'s `self` and its annotations are both
`Type::Named` and already agreed. Verified by probe.

TESTS: `test_shared_receiver_passes_to_free_function_in_every_mode`
(tests/typechecker.rs) — five receiver/parameter combinations, both return
shapes, and a NON-shared control that pins the reduction's missing detail so a
future change cannot "fix" the shared path by weakening the plain one.
Stash-proven RED.

Plus `e2e_shared_receiver_passed_to_free_function` (tests/codegen.rs), which is
FIRST coverage rather than a regression guard: these programs could not compile
before, so codegen had never lowered a shared receiver into a `ref`/by-value
free-function slot. Each callee scales by a distinct factor so a wrong argument
shows up as a wrong sum, seeded from `env.args().len()`; expected value COMPUTED
(2+3+5+5 = 15) and checked against --interp, `karac run` and AOT.

GATES: typechecker 2155, codegen 2835, memory_sanitizer 972, ownership 410,
interpreter 1467, cli 574, par_codegen 243 -- all 0 failures, plus all 100
non-llvm suites and all seven self-host oracles. clippy `--all --all-targets`
with and without `--features llvm`, and fmt, clean.

tracker: 36a7fa5a (2026-07-30, B-2026-07-30-9) — `__karac_write_console_line`; parent b84477dd is the fast side
title: kata:170 is 1.09x slower from CODE PLACEMENT ALONE: 36a7fa5a's println line-staging helper moves `main` and costs 9% on a program that calls println ONCE — identical instruction count AND identical binary size on both sides
detail:
THIS IS THE REST OF B-2026-08-05-5. That row's regression is now fully accounted for: the 7-bit tag compare (1.14x, fixed) times this (1.09x) is 1.24x against the 1.29x originally observed, the remainder being drift across the range. The two causes are unrelated and this one has nothing to do with maps, which is why the map-shaped search for it kept coming up empty.

BISECTED, 8 steps over 905 commits (58412d9f..d4259fdf), arm64 M5 Pro. Metric was CYCLES from `scripts/pmc.c`, median of 3, because the two endpoints differ by 8.3% in cycles and by 0.003% in INSTRUCTIONS — instruction-count bisection, which this repo's method notes otherwise prefer for determinism, is BLIND to this class and would have found nothing.

Every step was normalised so the search measured one thing: the tag compare patched OFF at the primitive map-get site (`KARAC_MAP_TAG` postdates the range, so early commits were patched directly) and the occupancy test held in the flag form. Without that normalisation the range contains two opposing effects — 58412d9f's own sign-bit penalty disappearing and this appearing — which net to -4% and bisect to nothing. Every binary sink-checked at 762965 before timing; a wrong sink exits the step rather than reporting a number.

  idx 1   58412d9f  3.584B cycles  GOOD
  idx 113 fac81a40  3.555B         GOOD
  idx 127 b84477dd  3.561B         GOOD   <- parent
  idx 128 36a7fa5a  3.958B         BAD    <- culprit
  idx 134 5441b44d  3.895B         BAD
  idx 141 1e95509f  3.905B         BAD
  idx 170 e53bf778  3.879B         BAD
  idx 226 f5bc78bf  3.919B         BAD
  idx 453 7b96b26f  3.892B         BAD
  idx 905 d4259fdf  3.880B         BAD

CONFIRMED ON WALL CLOCK, both orders, 30 runs, same two binaries: parent 781.5 / 780.7 ms vs culprit 849.9 / 849.3 ms => 1.09x, spreads under 1.5%.

THE COMMIT IS NOT WRONG. 36a7fa5a fixes a real defect (B-2026-07-30-9): `println` emitted two `write_console` calls, so concurrent tasks interleaved as payload-A, payload-B, newline-A, newline-B. It stages payload+newline into one buffer and issues a single write. kata:170 calls `println` EXACTLY ONCE, at the end, to print its sink.

WHAT IT IS NOT, checked rather than assumed:
  * NOT the 4 KiB alloca landing in the hot function. The staging buffer lives in the new `__karac_write_console_line` helper, not in the caller; `main`'s prologue is `sub sp, sp, #0x80` on BOTH sides, byte for byte.
  * NOT extra work. Instructions 12,968,920,902 (parent) vs 12,969,958,577 (culprit) — 0.008% apart, i.e. nothing.
  * NOT a bigger binary. Both are 285,592 bytes, EXACTLY equal.
  What does change is placement: `_main` sits at 0x7c8 in the parent and 0x860 in the culprit, a 152-byte shift from the helper being emitted ahead of it.

SO THE CARRIER IS CODE LAYOUT — the hot probe loop's alignment relative to fetch/branch-predictor structures. On Apple silicon a loop straddling a fetch boundary differently is worth this much. NOT PROVEN to the level of naming the exact structure: that needs either an LLVM alignment flag or a padding experiment, neither of which was run. What IS proven is that the cost survives no change in work, size, or frame layout.

IT IS STICKY, WHICH IS THE PART THAT MATTERS. This is not layout noise oscillating run to run — the step lands at idx 128 and the following 777 commits all sit on the slow plateau (3.88-3.92B cycles). kata:170 has been paying 9% for a week without anything in the map or its codegen changing.

WHY THIS ROW EXISTS SEPARATELY FROM A FIX. The obvious response — align hot loops (LLVM function/loop alignment, or `-align-all-nofallthru-blocks`) — is a compiler-wide change with its own size and speed tradeoffs across the whole corpus, and it is unmeasured. Filing it lets the map row close on its own evidence.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT, in order of cost: (1) force loop alignment in codegen behind an env lever and re-measure kata:170 and a handful of other benched katas — if the gap closes, the mechanism is named and a fix exists; (2) if it does, decide whether alignment is worth its binary-size cost corpus-wide, which is exactly the kind of question the seq-lane baseline (B-2026-08-05-34) exists to answer.

A WARNING FOR THE BENCH LANE, independent of any fix: kata:170's recorded number is sensitive at the ~9% level to code placement, and therefore to ANY commit that changes emitted code size ahead of `main` — including commits that touch nothing the kata uses. A future unexplained step on this kata should check placement before anything else.

── STEP (1) INSTRUMENT BUILT; MEASURED ON x86, WHERE ALIGNMENT IS NOT A FIX (2026-08-07) ──

ROW STAYS OPEN. The bisected 1.09x is arm64 and this session had no arm64
hardware, so the headline number is untouched. What is added is the lever the
row asks for and a measurement that changes what step (2) should expect.

THE LEVER: `KARAC_FN_ALIGN=<power-of-two bytes>` forces a minimum alignment on
every DEFINED function in the module (codegen.rs, just before `module.verify`,
so it covers user + stdlib + shim functions uniformly). Off unless set — no
default build changes. Verified behaviour-neutral by
`test_build_fn_align_lever_is_behaviour_neutral`, which matters because a lever
that silently altered results would make every measurement taken with it
worthless. Whoever has the M5 Pro can now run the row's step (1) directly.

MEASURED HERE (x86_64 Xeon @2.80GHz, 4 cores, virtualised; wall clock only —
no PMU (`perf_event_paranoid=2`, `perf` absent) and `scripts/pmc.c` is
macOS-only, so cycles were not available). kata:170 bench, sink-checked at
762965 on every binary, 4.3 s per run against the M5's 781 ms.

PLACEMENT SENSITIVITY IS REAL ON x86 TOO, which was not known — the row frames
it as an Apple-silicon fetch/predictor effect. Interleaved A/B, 20 pairs,
IDENTICAL work and IDENTICAL binary size (340,744 bytes for every alignment;
the padding is absorbed into existing gaps), only `main`'s address moving:

    base vs align-256   1.0203  then 1.0225 on repeat   (minima 1.023 / 1.025)
    base vs base        1.0009            (control)     (minima 1.002)

So ~2.2%, reproducible, and the same-binary control proves the harness has no
A/B bias. But that is ~4x SMALLER than the 9% the row measures on arm64. The
class is not Apple-specific; the severity looks like it is.

ALIGNMENT IS NOT A FIX — the finding that bears on step (2). The row hopes "if
the gap closes, the mechanism is named and a fix exists". On x86 it does not
close; every alignment tested is neutral-to-WORSE than the default layout:

    align   16    32     64     128    256
    vs base 0.998 1.001  1.012  1.009  1.020/1.023

Forcing alignment does not move the program to a better spot, it draws again
from the same lottery — and at 256 it draws reproducibly worse. Non-monotonic
in the middle (64 worse than 128), which is what an alignment-vs-fetch-structure
interaction looks like: what matters is where you land, not how aligned you
are. So the corpus-wide alignment question now has a data point AGAINST paying
its size cost, at least on this target.

METHOD WARNING, because it nearly produced a wrong answer here. Timing the
binaries in SEQUENTIAL blocks gave medians that clustered convincingly — 4247
and 4283 ms for align 16/32 against three near-identical 4363/4364 ms for
64/128/256 — which reads as a clean 2.8% step. Interleaving the same two
binaries dissolved it to 1.004. On a shared VM the block structure picks up
drift that looks exactly like a signal. Anyone re-measuring this row must
interleave and must run a same-binary control.

TWO CHEAPER PERTURBATIONS THAT DO NOT WORK, recorded so they are not retried:
  * REORDERING the source functions produces BYTE-IDENTICAL binaries (six
    permutations, same `main` address, same size) — codegen normalises
    emission order, so source order is not a placement lever.
  * A DEAD function inserted ahead of `main` is eliminated: identical size and
    identical `main` address, so padding via unused code is not one either.

WHAT IS STILL UNANSWERED, unchanged from the row: whether alignment closes the
gap ON ARM64. The x86 result argues it will not, but arm64 is where the 9%
lives and the two targets already differ 4x in magnitude, so it must be
measured rather than inferred. The lever is now in place for exactly that.
